The provider open (incises) and drains the contents of a pilonidal cyst.



Explanation
The lesion is cleaned and prepped, and then a small scalpel incision is made, and the provider expresses a small amount of pus.

A pilonidal cyst is a cyst or abscess near or at the bottom of the coccyx (tip of the spine) just above the buttock crease that contains hair and skin debris; pilonidal means nest of hair; also referred to as a pilonidal abscess or pilonidal sinus.


Terminology
Excision; resection: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part.

Incision and drainage (I&D): Surgical procedure in which cysts, abscesses, or other lesions containing infective material are incised (cut into) and the infective material drained; the procedure typically includes irrigation (washing out) of the affected part.

Pilonidal cyst: A cyst or abscess near or at the bottom of the coccyx (buttocks) that contains hair and skin debris; pilonidal means nest of hair; also referred to as a pilonidal abscess or pilonidal sinus.


Tips
If the procedure requires drain placement, more extensive packing, or subsequent wound closure, see 10081 for a complicated I&D of a pilonidal cyst.

See 11770 to 11772 for excision of a pilonidal cyst.

The provider opens (incises) and drains the contents of a pilonidal cyst  a nest of hair and debris that forms at the base of the spine; the procedure requires extra time and technique to perform. Explanation After appropriate preparation and anesthesia  with the patient lying in the prone (face down) position  the provider incises the area over a pilonidal cyst just above the central buttock crease. She opens the cyst and drains or scrapes out the contents. If the cyst is extremely enlarged  as it would likely be to require a complicated incision and drainage (I&D)  it may require a layered closure and drain. She irrigates the wound thoroughly and sutures the incision  in layers if necessary. She may pack the wound with gauze and allow it to heal by secondary intention or leave a tube inserted into the wound before closing  which will be attached to a pump to help drain any fluid that continues to form. The provider removes a foreign body such as a thorn  piece of wood  sliver of glass or fishook  from the lower layer of skin. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider uses appropriate instrumentation to remove the foreign body. As this is a simple incision  it is not complicated; therefore  this type of foreign body removal requires no dissection. The provider incises the skin around the foreign body to better expose it and then removes it with forceps. The provider closes the incision and cleans and dresses the wound. Terminology Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body  such as shards of metal  splinters of wound  slivers of glass  or a bone fragment. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue found just below the skin  or dermis  layers; there are three layers of skin known as epidermis  dermis  and hypodermis; subcutaneous tissue is the lowermost layer called hypodermis. Tips For a complicated I&D of a foreign body  report 10121. Be sure the documentation supports a complicated procedure. A complicated I&D may require more extended exploration  imaging guidance  and/or layered closure of the wound. Read Less

The provider makes an incision into the hematoma  seroma  or other collection of fluid and bluntly penetrates it to allow fluid evacuation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision into a hematoma  seroma  or other collection of fluids and bluntly penetrates it to allow the fluid to evacuate  with or without the necessity of packing. The provider closes the incision primarily  meaning at that session  or he leaves the incision to heal without closure. The provider may place pressure dressing over the skin. Terminology Hematoma: Swelling or mass of blood confined to an organ  tissue  or space; caused by a break in a blood vessel. Incision and drainage (I&D): Surgical procedure in which cysts  abscesses  or other lesions containing infective material are incised (cut into) and the infective material drained; the procedure typically includes irrigation (washing out) of the affected part. Seroma: A pocket of serous fluid  the watery component of blood  that sometimes develops in the body after surgery. Read Less

The provider inserts a needle into a fluid deposit area on the skin and aspirates fluid or pus to obtain a culture. Explanation The provider cleans and isolates the area on the skin and inserts a needle into the fluid deposit area. He then withdraws the fluid or pus through the needle aspiration device. The provider applies antibiotics and dressing. The provider may place a pressure dressing over the area. Terminology Abscess: Localized collection of pus of any size in any location  and as such represents an infection. Aspiration: Withdrawal of fluids or tissue from the body. Bulla: Localized fluid??illed lesions that are greater than 1 cm in diameter such as a large blister. Cyst: Cluster of cells which are grouped together to form a sac separated from nearby tissues. Hematoma: Swelling or mass of blood confined to an organ  tissue  or space; caused by a break in a blood vessel.

The provider uses surgical instruments to debride the dead tissue in skin for up to 10 percent of the body surface. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider cleans the area of infected skin. The provider then performs debridement by cutting away the dead tissue using surgical instruments like a scalpel or scissors. The provider performs debridement until he sees healthy bleeding on the skin edges. The provider then controls bleeding  applies an antibiotic  and dresses the wound. Use this code for debridement of up to 10 percent of the body surface. Terminology Debridement: Removal of dead  damaged  or infected tissue to facilitate natural healing of the remaining healthy tissue in an organ. Eczema: Common medical condition characterized by rough patchy skin with itching and inflammation. Tips Use +11001 as an add??n code for each additional 10 percent of the body surface. This code is for surgical debridement. For removal of devitalized tissue (nonselective debridement) from wound(s)  without anesthesia (e.g.  wet??o??oist dressings  enzymatic  abrasion  larval therapy)  ... per session  see 97602. Larval therapy refers to maggot therapy. This code also does not include dermabrasion; for dermabrasion services  see codes 15780 to 15787. Read Less

The provider uses surgical instruments to remove dead  infected tissue from bone as well as the epidermis  dermis  and subcutaneous tissue  muscle  and/or fascia if needed. She performs this service at the same session  as a separately reportable debridement procedure of an initial 20 cm2. This code represents up to 20 cm2 of additional area. Explanation At the same session that the provider performs a primary procedure for bone debridement of 20 cm2  the provider performs debridement for up to an additional 20 cm2. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider uses a scalpel  scissors  or other tools to remove large areas of necrotic affected tissue from bone as well as the epidermis  dermis  subcutaneous tissue  muscle and/or fascia as needed. Once she reaches healthy tissue  she closes the wound by primary closure or in layers or may leave the wound to heal by secondary intention. Terminology cm2: Abbreviation for square centimeter  a metric unit of measure of area; the 2 is usually superscripted; 1 cm equals approximately 0.39 inches  or just over a third of an inch  so a square centimeter would be 1 cm x 1 cm; alternative sq cm. Debridement: Removal of dead  damaged  or infected tissue to facilitate natural healing of the remaining healthy tissue. Dermis: Layer of skin between the epidermis and subcutaneous tissues. Epidermis: Thin outer layer of the skin. Fascia: A fibrous tissue sheet surrounding the body under the skin and enclosing muscles. Necrotic tissues: Dead cells or tissues in a body area that occur due to various external factors such as an injury  infection  or toxoid. Secondary intention healing: Healing process in which the wound is more open and prone to infection because it?? left to heal on its own. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue found just below the skin  or dermis  layers; there are three layers of skin known as epidermis  dermis  and hypodermis; subcutaneous tissue is the lowermost layer called hypodermis. Tips Because +11047 is an add??n code  payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code for debridement: 11044. Read Less

The provider removes a single benign hyperkeratotic lesion by using surgical instruments like a scalpel or curette. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider evaluates the size  depth  and location of the benign hyperkeratotic lesion. She uses a scalpel  curette  blade  or a spoon??haped surgical instrument to trim or pare down the lesion. The provider applies antiseptic to the site and  if necessary  removes the pressure points by fitting padding on the site. Terminology Benign: Condition or growth that is not cancerous in nature. Callus: Caused by skin pressure; mainly appears on soles of feet or hands as an area of toughened skin. Corn: Caused by skin friction; mainly appears on top or side of toes as a small thickened area with a dense central area. Curette: Surgical instrument used for scraping skin or tissues. Hyperkeratosis: Dead skin that builds up from repeated or prolonged pressure to the skin; examples are corns and calluses. Tips Use 11056 when the service involves 2 to 4 lesions. Use 11057 when the service involves more than 4 lesions. Note that 11055  11056  and 11057 should not be used to report the destruction of skin tags or cutaneous vascular proliferative lesions (see 17110 and 17111). Read Less

The provider removes more than 4 benign hyperkeratotic lesions by using surgical instruments like a scalpel or curette.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider evaluates the size, depth, and location of more than 4 benign hyperkeratotic lesions. She uses a scalpel, curette, blade, or a spoon�shaped surgical instrument to trim or pare down the lesion. The provider applies antiseptic to the site and, if necessary, removes the pressure points by fitting padding on the site.


Terminology
Benign: Condition or growth that is not cancerous in nature.

Callus: Caused by skin pressure; mainly appears on soles of feet or hands as an area of toughened skin.

Corn: Caused by skin friction; mainly appears on top or side of toes as a small thickened area with a dense central area.

Curette: Surgical instrument used for scraping skin or tissues.

Hyperkeratosis: Dead skin that builds up from repeated or prolonged pressure to the skin; examples are corns and calluses.


Tips

Note that 11055, 11056, and 11057 should not be used to report the destruction of skin tags or cutaneous vascular proliferative lesions (see 17110 and 17111).

The provider removes skin tags in any area of the body  up to and including 15 lesions. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider evaluates the location and size of the skin tags. She uses forceps  scissors  or a blade to remove the skin tags. She may remove smaller tags painlessly without applying anesthesia. She applies an antibiotic after removing skin tags. Use this code for removal of skin tag lesions  up to 15. Terminology Skin tag: Also known as acrochordon; small  cutaneous  benign projections; commonly seen on the neck  face  armpit  and groin. Tips Use +11201 when the services involve removal of one or more additional skin tags of any area. For excision of benign lesions other than skin tags  see 11400 to 11446. Read Less

The provider removes up to 10 additional skin tags in any area of the body  after removing an initial 15 lesions. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and having just undergone the removal of 15 lesions  the provider evaluates the location and size of up to 10 additional skin tags. She uses forceps  scissors  or a blade to remove the skin tags. She may remove smaller tags painlessly without applying anesthesia. She applies an antibiotic after removing skin tags. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Skin tag: Small  cutaneous  benign projections commonly seen on the neck  face  armpit  and groin; also known as an acrochordon. Tips Use this addon code for the removal of up to 10 additional skin tags after having removed 15 lesions in the same session reported as 11200 for removal of up to and including 15 lesions. For excision of benign lesions other than skin tags  see 11400 to 11446. Read Less

The provider removes one epidermal or dermal lesion of 0.5 cm diameter or less from the trunk  arms  or legs. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider evaluates the lesion on the trunk  arms  or legs. She then uses a scalpel blade to remove the lesion from its base by performing a horizontal slicing motion. She performs shaving typically to the middle dermis layer  without disturbing the subcutaneous tissue. The provider controls bleeding by cauterization  without any suturing. Use this code for a skin lesion of 0.5 cm diameter or less. Terminology Cauterization: Use of heat or chemicals to destroy abnormal cells or seal a wound. Dermis: Layer of skin between the epidermis and subcutaneous tissues. Epidermis: Thin outer layer of the skin. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue found just below the skin or dermis layer; there are three layers of skin known as epidermis  dermis  and hypodermis; subcutaneous tissue is the lowermost layer called hypodermis. Tips For the same procedure on a lesion with a diameter 0.6 to 1.0 cm  see 11301. For the same procedure on a lesion with a diameter of 1.1 to 2.0 cm  see 11302. For the same procedure on a lesion with a lesion diameter over 2.0 cm  see 11303. If a provider removes multiple lesions of the same or different diameters during the same session  apply modifier 59  Distinct procedural service  to the code(s) for the additional lesion(s). To differentiate between codes for shaving and excision  look at the removal's depth. Technically  any time a provider removes skin tissue  it is an excision. For coding purposes  however  excision is narrowly defined as involving full thickness  or through the dermis  removal of a lesion. Shaving  in contrast  involves sharp removal without a full thickness dermal excision. Read the documentation carefully  and pay more attention to the removal's depth than to the terminology your physician uses. When reporting shaving procedures  you must not consider the size of any margin the physician removes with the lesion. In fact  the physician may not document  or even take  a margin of tissue during a shave. This is a crucial difference from coding for excisions. Read Less

The provider shaves off a single epidermal or dermal lesion of 0.6 to 1.0 cm in diameter from the skin of the scalp, neck, hands, feet, or genitals.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the provider holds a blade horizontal to the skin of the scalp, neck, hands, feet, or genitals and moves it across a single lesion of 0.6 to 1.0 cm in diameter with a sawing motion. Shaving usually extends to the middle dermis without disturbing the subcutaneous tissue, followed by cautery to control bleeding, without any suturing. In some cases, the provider may remove the raised portion of a benign lesion and allow additional lesion tissue to persist in the dermis. He dresses the wound.


Terminology
Benign: Not cancerous, generally treatable or not needing treatment.

Cautery: The use of an energy source, such as electricity, laser light, heat, or plasma, or use of a chemical to burn away diseased tissue or to stop bleeding by coagulation, the formation of a blood clot. 

Dermis: Layer of skin that contains connective tissues, situated immediately below the epidermis, the outermost layer.

Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue.

Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin.


Tips
For the same procedure on a lesion with a diameter of 0.5 cm or less, see 11305

For the same procedure on a lesion with a diameter of 1.1 to 2.0 cm, see 11307.

For the same procedure on a lesion with a diameter over 2.0 cm, see 11308.

If a provider removes multiple lesions of the same or different diameters during the same session, apply modifier 59, Distinct procedural service, to the code(s) for the additional lesion(s).

To differentiate between codes for shaving and excision, look at the removal's depth. Technically, any time a provider removes skin tissue, it is an excision. For coding purposes, however, excision is narrowly defined as involving full thickness, or through the dermis, removal of a lesion. Shaving, in contrast, involves sharp removal without a full thickness dermal excision.

Read the documentation carefully, and pay more attention to the removal's depth than to the terminology your physician uses. When reporting shaving procedures, you must not consider the size of any margin the physician removes with the lesion. In fact, the physician may not document, or even take, a margin of tissue during a shave. This is a crucial difference from coding for excisions.

The provider excises a pilonidal cyst or sinus not requiring extensive dissection and without complication.

Sinus: Hollow passage.

Terminology

Tips
If repair of wound dehiscence occurs during the postoperative (or global surgical) period of a previous procedure, be sure to append modifier 78 to the appropriate repair code. This explains to the payer that the procedure is the result of a complication arising from an earlier procedure.

"Dehiscence" refers to a splitting open or bursting. As such, wound dehiscence usually describes the opening of a previously sutured area (for example, an incision following surgery, wound repair, etc.). If a wound becomes infected, it will more likely dehisce due to the natural inflammatory process. Wound dehiscence code 12020 (Treatment of superficial wound dehiscence; simple closure) describes repair when there is no sign of infection. In this case, the surgeon simply debrides and irrigates the wound and closes it in a single layer. If infection is evident, the surgeon may prefer to clean the wound and pack it with gauze strips, leaving the wound open to allow infection to drain. In this case, 12021 (... with packing) is the better choice. If the dehiscence has opened and requires closure in multiple layers, report 13160 (Secondary closure of surgical wound or dehiscence, extensive or complicated).

Note: Code 13160 can also describe secondary closure of surgical wounds (that is, the surgeon intentionally defers closure following surgery). Many payers define "primary" closure as the first or initial closure of a surgical wound, whether it occurs at the time of surgery or during the postoperative period, thereby limiting use of the secondary closure code.

The provider performs a rhitidectomy (facelift) by removing excess skin and fat to tighten up the skin and remove wrinkles from the face.



Explanation
The patient is given a general anesthesia. An incision is made along a wrinkle in the face (cheek, chin, or neck). The surgeon removes the excess skin and the underlying fat to straighten the skin folds. The underlying muscle and the tissue above it are tightened by lifting the top skin layer and by trimming and suturing the musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) which connects the facial muscles. The incisions are closed with sutures.

Glabella: The skin above the nose and between the eyebrows; also, flat bone between the eyebrows, used as a craniometric point.

Platysma: Flat and wide muscle encompassing the front of the neck, extending from the angle of the jaw to the collar bones.

Rhytidectomy: Plastic, or reconstructive, surgery to remove wrinkles by excising loose sagging skin and tissue; commonly known as a facelift.

Superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS): A sheet of muscle, fascia, and fat extending from the neck up to the forehead.

This is generally considered a cosmetic procedure. If determined to be medically necessary, be sure to obtain preauthorization from your payer.

The provider washes the first degree burn with plenty of cold water and wraps it in clean sterile gauze.



Explanation
The provider examines the first degree burn and washes it with cold water that may or may not contain a disinfectant solution. He then applies lotion or ointment locally and wraps the area in clean dry sterile gauze. First degree burns are painful, but do not blister, and heal within three to four days. After the pain resolves, the epidermal layer, the outer layer of skin, peels and sheds off.


Terminology
First degree burn: Burns involving only the outermost layer of skin, which is the epidermis.

Mohs surgery is a multistaged method of excising a malignant lesion layer by layer, along with histopathological assessment, to ensure negative malignancy of the margins.



Explanation
The provider applies a fixative paste (e.g., zinc chloride), removes a layered skin lesion, and maps the lesion (an individual cross�section of malignant tissue). The physician then marks the excised site with ink. Then, the provider freezes the lesion and examines it for malignancy. If malignancy is found, a fresh layer is excised and examined. Excision is continued until the pathology results show negative results for malignancy. The site is then closed with sutures or a graft.

The provider uses cryotherapy to treat acne  typically after the acne fails to respond to topical or systemic medications. Explanation The provider washes and cleans the area of skin to be treated. He then uses cryotherapy  which involves the application of carbon dioxide slush or liquid nitrogen  over the acne with a cotton tipped swab for a few seconds. This results in freezing of the area containing acne and therefore reduces the blood supply to that area. This treatment leads to scabbing  which desquamates and peels off the acne. Terminology Cryotherapy: Use of low temperature to treat lesions. Desquamate: Shedding off in the form of flakes. Scabbing: Crust formed during healing of a wound.

The provider uses chemical agents to peel off the acne. Explanation The provider washes and cleans the area of skin to be treated. He then applies a chemical agent such as alpha hydroxy acids or salicylic acid over the acne with a swab  typically for less than a minute. This causes the tissue to die off and fall from the surface of the skin. Terminology Exfoliation: Removal of old dead skin cells.

The provider uses short wave diathermy current to destroy and remove unwanted hair and prevent further hair growth. Explanation The provider inserts a needle into the hair follicle at the angle in which the hair is growing. He then passes a specific intensity of current through the epilator to the needle via an electrical cable. He holds the instrument in place for 20 to 30 seconds to destroy the hair follicle as well as the papilla. After this  the provider may remove the hair with forceps. He removes the rest of the hairs in the area in a similar fashion. Terminology Electrolysis epilation: Permanent method of removing unwanted hair from the body. Epilator: Electrical device to remove unwanted hairs. Hair follicle: Part of skin that produces hairs by packing old cells together. Papilla: Bulge over the skin at the root of the hair. Short wave diathermy: Passing electric current through the body to generate deep heat in body tissues. Tips Report 17380 for each 30 minutes of a session. Read Less

The provider performs a mastotomy (incision into the breast) and explores and/or drains a deep abscess in the breast. Explanation A deep abscess in the breast is generally identified and located through ultrasound. With the patient appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia  the provider makes a small incision in the skin above the abscess. She introduces a catheter to explore and drain the abscess. She may collect specimens of the drainage fluid for further diagnostic studies. She repeatedly irrigates and flushes the abscess cavity with sterile saline solution until the abscess is completely free from purulent material. She closes the wound with sutures. She may leave the catheter in place for a couple of days to facilitate saline instillation and drainage until no drainage occurs. Following which she may close the remaining opening with sutures or adhesive strips. An abscess in the breast is caused by the collection of pus due to an untreated bacterial infection and is most common during lactation. Mastitis or inflammation of the breast due to the accumulation of milk in the mammary ducts is another cause of abscess formation. Antibiotics in the initial stage can prevent infection and abscess formation. Once formed  the abscess may need surgical intervention such as incision and drainage for removal of the pus. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled??ff sac or pocket  the result of infection. Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits or treats bacterial infections. Mammary ducts: Ducts (tubes) that carry milk from the mammary glands to the nipples during lactation or secretion of milk; also known as Lactiferous duct  galactophorous ducts (milk ducts). The provider injects a contrast agent into the breast of a patient for the purpose of performing a mammary ductogram or galactogram to image the mammary (milk) ducts of the breast.



Explanation
The patient is made to sit or lie in a supine position. The provider identifies the duct responsible for the abnormal discharge by squeezing out fluid through the nipple with manual pressure. He inserts a small catheter into the milk duct and injects a small dose of contrast. He may use dilators for ease of catheter insertion. Mammographic images are taken following the contrast injection. Report this code only for the injection.

A ductogram or galactogram is an imaging procedure for visualization of the mammary ducts (the milk ducts of the breast). The procedure uses contrast�enhanced mammography to diagnose disorders of the milk ducts necessitated by conditions such as clear or bloody discharge from the nipples. The contrast is injected into the milk duct through a small catheter and a mammogram is done. The galactogram can be helpful in diagnosing tumors and cysts in the breast.

Contrast: A chemical, such as barium or iodine, or a radioactive substance used in radiologic imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral, intravenously, and as an enema; also known as contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, contrast dye, or tracer.

Mammogram: An imaging procedure of the breast used to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases, including cancer.

In this procedure  the provider removes a small amount of tissue from a breast lesion to identify any abnormality present. The provider uses an open incisional approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision for direct visualization of the area. She removes only a portion of the tissue using a scalpel. After the sample collection  the provider closes the wound and sends the sample to pathology for further analysis. Terminology Breast biopsy: A procedure to remove small sample from the breast to diagnose any abnormality  such as cancer  present in the breast. Incisional biopsy: A biopsy in which the provider takes a small sample of the affected tissues via an open incision for the purpose of diagnosis. Tips Incisional biopsy is different from excisional biopsy. In incisional biopsy  the provider removes only a small lump that she sends to pathology for further analysis; excisional biopsy involves removal of the entire lump. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider uses a cryoprobe to destroy a fibroadenoma  which is a solid  noncancerous breast tumor. He performs the procedure using ultrasound guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a cryoprobe through a small breast incision. He moves the cryoprobe to the fibroadenoma using ultrasonic guidance. The cryoprobe that the provider uses contains liquid nitrogen  which forms ice balls to destroy the fibroadenoma cells by freezing them. The immune system then absorbs these dead tissues over a period of several months. Terminology Cryoablation: A technique that destroys damaged or abnormal tissues using extreme cold. Fibroadenoma of breast: Solid  noncancerous breast tumors; usually painless; they do not increase the risk of breast cancer. Tips Do not report 19105 with code 76942 for ultrasonic guidance because 19105's description includes ultrasound guidance. Read Less

The provider explores the nipple through an incision and may or may not excise (remove) a single lactiferous (milk) duct or a papilloma (benign tumor) lactiferous duct. Explanation The provider explores the nipple through an incision made at the areolar border. During the procedure  she may excise a single abnormal lactiferous or papilloma lactiferous duct that is the source of abnormal discharge  if it needs further pathological evaluation. The provider closes the incision with sutures and pressure bandages. Pathologic nipple discharge can be an indication of carcinoma of the breast. Excision of a lactiferous duct or a papilloma lactiferous duct (a benign tumor in the lactiferous duct) may be indicated for further pathological studies. Terminology Areola: An area of darker pigmentation around the nipple; also  an area of darker color surrounding a pustule or blister  usually indicating inflammation. Lactiferous duct: Ducts (tubes) that carry milk from the mammary glands to the nipples during lactation or secretion of milk; also known as mammary ducts  galactophorous ducts (milk ducts). The provider excises (removes) a fistula (a tubular connection) between a lactiferous (milk) duct and the skin.



Explanation
With the patient appropriate prepped and under general anesthesia, the provider locates the fistula tract. She incises the skin around the fistula and elevates it. She excises the fistula along with ductal tissue. After cauterizing the bleeding points, she irrigates the wound with saline and closes it with layered sutures. She applies antibiotics to the wound and places a dressing over it. A drainage catheter may be left in place for one or two days.

A lactiferous duct fistula is an abnormal passage created between a diseased lactiferous duct and the skin in the periareolar region. Such a fistula is generally the result of periductal mastitis or a spontaneously draining abscess of the breast. It can be treated conservatively with antibiotics. But complete excision of the diseased lactiferous duct and the fistula followed by antibiotic treatment for prevention of recurrence is the most definitive treatment option.


Terminology
Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled�off sac or pocket, the result of infection.

Cauterization: Use of heat or chemicals to destroy abnormal cells or seal bleeding vessels or a wound.

Fistula: An artificial passage or tunnel created between two organs or body cavities. Fistulas can form on their own in certain disease conditions; or they can be created surgically to facilitate flow of body fluids.

Lactiferous duct: Ducts or tubes that carry milk from the mammary glands to the nipples during lactation or secretion of milk. They are also known as mammary ducts, galactophorous ducts, or milk ducts.

Mastitis: Inflammation of breast tissue characterized by redness, warmth, and pain, which may be an indication or or associated with infection.

Periareolar: Surrounding the areola of the breast, the circular, pigmented area around the nipple of the breast.


Tips
For nipple exploration with or without excision of a lactiferous duct (without fistula), see 19110.

The provider excises one or more suspicious breast lesions in a man or woman using an open approach. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and under local or general anesthesia  the provider excises aberrant breast tissue such as a cyst  tumor  or fibroadenoma. She makes an incision on the skin above the lesion to access the abnormal tissue. She takes the incision down to deep tissues and dissects fascia and muscle away from their attachment to the diseased tissue. She then excises the tissue and carefully removes it out of the breast. She controls bleeding with electrocautery and closes the wound in layers. She may excise additional lesions if necessary. The provider may leave a drainage catheter for some time to enhance healing. This procedure can be performed on either a male or a female. The amount of tissue removed depends mainly upon the risk the tumor presents to the patient. Pathological evaluation of biopsied tissue is done to decide the nature of the tumor (benign or malignant). A malignant tumor may need a more extensive excision that includes parts of the surrounding tissue. Terminology Aberrant: Unusual or abnormal. Areola: An area of darker pigmentation around the nipple; also  an area of darker color surrounding a pustule or blister  usually indicating inflammation. Benign: Not malignant  generally treatable or not needing treatment. Cyst: An abnormal closed saclike structure containing gas  fluid  or semisolid material  that has its own membranous lining delineating it from the surrounding tissue. Fibroadenoma of breast: Solid  noncancerous breast tumors; usually painless; they do not increase the risk of breast cancer. Malignant: Cancerous  capable of spreading and causing death if untreated. Open procedure: A surgical procedure requiring a large incision that allows the provider to directly visualize the target anatomy. Tips This procedure is reported for the excision of one or more lesions at the same session. If a lesion is removed from both breasts  you may apply modifier 50 for the bilateral procedure. If two different procedures are performed  one the left breast and the other on the right breast  you will want to identify which breast each procedure was performed on by adding the LT and RT modifiers to the appropriate procedure codes. Modifier 59 for a distinct procedural service may also be required in the case of different procedures on different breasts. Check with the payer to avoid denials and resubmissions. If the provider excises a solitary lactiferous duct or a papilloma lactiferous duct during nipple exploration  see 19110. For excision of a lactiferous duct fistula (tract between the duct and the skin)  see 19112. Additional Info A breast cyst is a sac of fluid formed in the breast. It can be felt by touch as a soft  rounded mass sometimes accompanied by pain. A fibroadenoma of the breast is a benign tumor of the breast that can be palpated externally as a movable  round mass of firm tissue. Radiological examinations such as mammograms or ultrasounds can confirm the type and location of such growths. Unless there is pain  discomfort  or risk of malignancy  the tumors or cysts of the breast are left untreated. Otherwise  treatment may vary from drainage to surgical excision or ablation depending upon the type and size of the aberrant tissue and the risk it poses. Read Less

The provider excises a single lesion previously identified by a preoperative radiological marker through an open incision. Explanation Using the preoperatively placed radiological marker as the guide  the provider accesses the aberrant tissue or lesion through an open incision over the breast at the site indicated by the marker. She carries the incision down to the depth of the marker. She excises the lesion and its surrounding tissue and cauterizes the vessels to prevent bleeding. She removes the marker. She closes the wound with layered sutures. A drainage catheter may be left in place postoperatively for a couple of days. Terminology Aberrant: Unusual or abnormal. Cauterization: Use of heat or chemicals to destroy abnormal cells or seal bleeding vessels or a wound. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue  particularly an area that is well??efined. Tips For each additional lesion excised during the same procedure  report add??n code 19126 in addition to 19125. This procedure does not include the placement of the localization device. For placement of localization devices in the breast  see 19281 through 19288. Additional Info Deeper breast lesions that are not palpable need radiological assistance to mark and excise them. Radiological marker placement is one method in which a needle/wire is inserted with the help of radiological guidance (e.g. ultrasound  mammography  MRI  stereotactic imaging) and put into position at the exact location of the tumor. The process commonly uses a 21??auge Kopans localization needle. The needle is advanced under sonographic guidance and a hook??ire is inserted  advanced  and placed at the site of the tumor. In some cases  a smaller 14??auge needle is used to place a localizing clip at the site of the tumor under sonographic guidance. The clip is normally contained in a collagen plug. This is used as guidance for the excision of the tumor. Read Less

The provider excises an additional lesion previously identified by a preoperative radiological marker through an open incision after excising an initial lesion from the same breast. Explanation Using the preoperatively placed radiological marker as the guide  the provider accesses additional aberrant tissue or lesion through an open incision over the breast at the site indicated by the marker. She carries the incision down to the depth of the marker. She excises the lesion and its surrounding tissue and cauterizes the vessels to prevent bleeding. She removes the marker. In this add on procedure  the provider uses magnetic resonance image guidance to place an additional device for breast localization  such as a clip  metallic pellet  wire/needle  or radioactive seeds. The provider places the localization device at the same session that he places another device at an initial lesion. Explanation After placement of the first localization device at the same session  the provider preps and anesthetizes the patient for placement of the additional device. He then takes magnetic resonance images to view the exact location of the lesion in the breast. He then places the additional localization device at the target tissue using a needle or other minimally invasive introducer instrument. The provider uses magnetic resonance imaging guidance after the placement of the device to ensure its correct placement. He closes the site with a bandage. The goal of the procedure is to locate the site of lesion prior to breast biopsy. Terminology Breast localization device: Small devices used to mark the location of a breast abnormality to make it easier for the provider to find the target during biopsy. Magnetic resonance imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging  or MRI  uses magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose  manage  and treat diseases. Tips Because +19288 is an add??n code  payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code: 19287. See 19081 to 19086 when the provider performs breast biopsy along with placing the localization devices. Breast localization device placement codes 19281 to +19288 vary based on the type of guidance the provider uses. Read Less

The provider prepares a tumor cavity for placement of a device that is used to deliver intraoperative radiation therapy (IORT) during the same session as a partial mastectomy. Explanation After appropriate preparation and anesthesia and after performing a partial mastectomy  the provider prepares the site from which the tumor was removed for the placement of an applicator to deliver intraoperative radiation therapy (IORT). He enlarges the cavity if necessary and controls any bleeding. He then places a small (usually 1.5 to 5 cm in diameter) applicator in the surgical bed from where the tumor was removed. Low energy radiation is then delivered through the applicator. The applicator may be removed or left in place for additional postoperative targeted radiotherapy. The provider then completes the partial mastectomy. IORT is indicated for early stage breast cancer and avoids damage to healthy tissue caused by external radiation therapy administered to a wider area. Report this code for preparation of the tumor bed and placement of the applicator along with the primary procedure code for the partial mastectomy. Terminology Mastectomy: A surgical procedure to remove all or a part of breast; may be unilateral or bilateral. Radiation therapy: Application of high??requency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors; also known as radiotherapy. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider  places a single or multichanneled expandable balloon catheter for radiotherapy treatment at the treatment site after partial mastectomy. He uses image guidance for the correct placement of the catheter. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision over the site of treatment in the breast. He then  using image guidance if needed  inserts an expandable balloon tip catheter at the site of the previously removed tumor. He fills the balloon with saline to check for proper positioning for future radiation treatment by afterloading technique. He stitches the catheter in place if needed. The provider performs the catheter placement procedure on a date separate from the date of partial mastectomy. Terminology Catheter: A flexible thin tube that is put into the body  allowing injection or removal of substances. Partial mastectomy: Surgery to remove a part of breast tissue along with some healthy tissue surrounding it. Radiation oncology: Radiation oncology  also called radiotherapy  applies high??requency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. Tips Report this code only for the placement of catheters. Report this code when the provider places the balloon tip catheter on a date separate from the date of partial mastectomy. Report +19297 if the provider places a balloon tip catheter at the same session as partial mastectomy. Read Less

The provider excises the patient's breast to treat excessive enlargement of the male breast (gynecomastia).



Explanation
This surgery is done only on male patients, so this code should never be reported for a female patient.

In this procedure, the physician surgically removes one or both breasts or part of the breast because of excessive growth of the male mammary glands. First, the patient is taken to the operating room and positioned supine. The operative site is washed out with some cleanser solutions and is sterilized. After administration of general anesthesia, an infraareolar incision is made at the rims of the areola. The physician then cuts around the nipple and areola to remove growth skin. Excessive skin, fat and breast tissue is then removed from the pectoralis muscle fascia in a specific pattern. To remove excess fat, a vacuum procedure may be used. Once excessive skin is removed, bleeding is restrained with an electrocautery and incision is closed with fine stitches. The physician may place a drainage tube through a separate pierce incision to drain any fluid substance. These drains may need to stay in place for several days. Lastly, the physician binds the wound with a dressing or a surgical bandage.


Terminology
Gynecomastia: Enlargement of the male breast, due to an imbalance of sex hormones.

The provider removes a lesion  including surrounding margins  or a significant portion (a segment or quadrant) of the breast without removing the entire breast or lymph nodes. Explanation The provider incises the skin of the breast over a suspicious lump and excises the lump or a significant portion of the breast along with the margins. Any additional lesions in the area are checked and also removed. When all cancerous or suspicious tissues are eradicated  he places a drain  closes the surgical wound  and applies a dressing. A partial mastectomy applies to a segmental mastectomy  quadrantectomy  lumpectomy  or tylectomy. In segmental mastectomy and quadrantectomy  the surgeon removes more breast tissue than with a lumpectomy or tylectomy. Lumpectomy and tylectomy involve the removal of a tumor along with surrounding margins. A partial mastectomy is performed to eradicate suspicious or cancerous lesions in the breast through an open and excisional process. Terminology Quadrantectomy: Surgical excision of a quarter of the breast by mastectomy; also known as a partial mastectomy. Lumpectomy: Removal of an entire lesion of the breast and a margin of tissue around it  also called a tylectomy. Segmentectomy: Surgery to remove part of an organ or gland. Tylectomy: Excision of a tumor and surrounding margin but without removal of the lymph nodes  also called a lumpectomy. Tips Get higher payment: If your surgeon removes a lesion plus a significant portion of the surrounding tissue  you may report a partial mastectomy code instead of lesion excision code. For this  documentation must show the adequacy of the margins removed. This will increase revenue for the provider. To report the same procedure but with the excision of axillary lymph nodes  see 19302. Beware "staged" exception: Following some partial mastectomies (19301)  the surgeon may return during the postoperative period to see if there has been any lymph node involvement and  if so  may choose to remove the nodes at that time. In such a case  you would report the lymphadenectomy as a staged procedure using 38745 with modifier 58  Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician during the postoperative period. Read Less

The provider removes a lesion  including surrounding margins  or a significant portion (a segment or quadrant) of the breast and removes axillary lymph nodes. Explanation The provider incises the skin of the breast over a suspicious lump and excises the lump or a significant portion of the breast along with the margins. Any additional lesions in the area are checked and also removed. The provider also dissects into the axillary region and removes suspicious lymph nodes. When all cancerous or suspicious tissues are eradicated  he places a drain  closes the surgical wound  and applies a dressing. A partial mastectomy applies to a segmental mastectomy  quadrantectomy  lumpectomy  or tylectomy. In segmental mastectomy and quadrantectomy  the surgeon removes more breast tissue than with a lumpectomy or tylectomy. Lumpectomy and tylectomy involve the removal of a tumor along with surrounding margins. Suspicious lymph nodes are removed and sent to pathology to determine whether cancer has spread and to stage cancer. A partial mastectomy is performed to eradicate suspicious or cancerous lesions in the breast through an open and excisional process. Terminology Quadrantectomy: Surgical excision of a quarter of the breast by mastectomy; also known as a partial mastectomy. Lumpectomy: Removal of an entire lesion of the breast and a margin of tissue around it  also called a tylectomy. Segmentectomy: Surgery to remove part of an organ or gland. Tylectomy: Excision of a tumor and surrounding margin but without removal of the lymph nodes  also called a lumpectomy. Tips Get higher payment: If your surgeon removes a lesion plus a significant portion of the surrounding tissue  you may report a partial mastectomy code instead of a lesion excision code. For this  your documentation must show the adequacy of the margins removed. This will increase revenue for the provider. To report the same procedure but without excision of axillary lymph nodes  see 19301. Read Less

Breast reduction is the removal of excess breast tissue which results from top scarring  calcification  or architectural distortion. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision around the areolar region  removes excess skin in an innervated T scar pattern  and removes parenchymal tissues. Then the nipple is reoriented into the proper position. If necessary  drains are inserted and then the site is closed. Terminology Calcification: Hardening caused by deposits of calcium within the tissues. Parenchymal tissue: The tissue that forms the working elements of an organ as opposed to the structural elements.

This procedure is for the removal of a previously placed breast implant. Explanation The physician opens an old surgical scar and removes a previously placed implant and then closes the incision. Terminology Breast implant: A silicone outer shell filled with saline or silicone gel implanted under the breast tissue or under the chest muscle to increase breast size (breast augmentation) or to replace breast tissue after mastectomy (breast reconstruction).

Breast implant material is removed if there is an implant rupture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the physician makes an incision over the breast and removes the implant material as well as contents such as saline and silicone gel. Terminology Breast implant: A silicone outer shell filled with saline or silicone gel implanted under the breast tissue or under the chest muscle to increase breast size (breast augmentation) or to replace breast tissue after mastectomy (breast reconstruction).

The physician immediately inserts a breast implant following a mastectomy (breast excision). Explanation On the same day a patient undergoes a mastectomy procedure  the provider creates a pocket (space in the tissue) and inserts a breast implant for that same patient. Following insertion  the provider closes the pocket over the implant and completes the procedure. Terminology Breast implant: A silicone outer shell filled with saline or silicone gel implanted under the breast tissue or under the chest muscle to increase breast size (breast augmentation) or to replace breast tissue after mastectomy (breast reconstruction). Mastectomy: A surgical procedure to remove all or a part of breast; may be unilateral or bilateral. Reconstruction: Revising a structure to approximate its normal anatomy or restoring it to its appropriate function. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one breast. Follow payer reporting guidelines for a bilateral service. For insertion or replacement of breast implant on separate day from mastectomy  see 19342. Many health insurance policies cover reconstructive surgery following mastectomy  although coverage may vary. Check with the payer to determine their requirements for reimbursement. Read Less

Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision over the previous incision site from a prior mastectomy. He creates a pocket (space in the tissues) and rearranges the tissues and skin. He places an implant in the pocket. Alternatively  he may remove an existing implant and replace it with a new implant. He closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Breast implant: A silicone outer shell filled with saline or silicone gel implanted under the breast tissue or under the chest muscle to increase breast size (breast augmentation) or to replace breast tissue after mastectomy (breast reconstruction). Mastectomy: A surgical procedure to remove all or a part of breast; may be unilateral or bilateral. Reconstruction: Revising a structure to approximate its normal anatomy or restoring it to its appropriate function. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one breast. Explanation
In the case that the physician performs nipple sharing, a composite graft is harvested from the opposite nipple by performing a wedge excision harvest. The harvested nipple is then transferred to the recipient site after de�epithelializing the vascular bed.

The areola is reconstructed with tattooing or a full�thickness technique. Both the donor and recipient sites are closed with a layered closure.

In this procedure  the provider corrects inverted nipples by releasing the ducts and fibers holding the nipples. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes small periareolar incisions to release the fibers and the ducts  allowing the nipples to come out. After the release of the milk ducts  the provider sutures the nipples to support and position them correctly. Terminology Inverted nipples: A condition  present in both men and women  in which the nipples are retracted into the breast; sometimes  if stimulated  the nipples protrude outward; however  inverted nipples make breast feeding difficult. Periareolar incision: Cut made by the provider into the breast skin immediately below the lower half of the areola of the nipple. The provider artificially creates the contour of a breast with a flap of tissue and muscle harvested from behind the shoulder and sutured at the site of the breast to restore cosmetic appearance following a modified or radical mastectomy  or to repair a defect. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a horizontal or vertical skin incision in the upper back  releasing the underlying fat and skin. He deepens the incision  exposing the latissimus dorsi muscle and elevates the muscle??kin flap  preserving the attachment of the flap to the main artery. He rotates the flap and tunnels it from the upper back to the front of the chest wall. He places the flap at the breast site  suturing the flap in place to create a breast. After achieving hemostasis  the provider places drains and applies a sterile dressing. He then closes the upper back with sutures. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end??o??ide and side??o??ide. Breast reconstruction: Artificial recreation of the breast contour following surgical removal. Deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) flap: A flap that a provider creates by harvesting blood vessels in the lower abdomen along with the skin and fat in their vicinity. Flap: A portion of tissue  usually including skin  fat  and muscle  with a viable blood supply that a provider takes from a donor site in the body and transplants to a recipient site elsewhere in the body. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Latissimus dorsi muscle: A broad  flat muscle in the upper back; extending from the spine and tapering to attach just below the shoulder and behind the armpit; useful in twisting actions of the shoulder. Latissimus dorsi flap: A provider lifts and sutures a small part of the latissimus dorsi muscle to another location in the body. Mastectomy: Partial or complete surgical removal of a breast to remove a malignancy or treat other conditions. Microvascular anastomosis: The surgical connection (joining) of very small blood vessels using an operating microscope. Pedicle flap: A flap consisting of the full??hickness of the skin  subcutaneous tissue  fascia  and/or muscle that remains attached to its original location by tissue through which it receives its blood supply; it is taken from a healthy area near a defect and rotated to cover the defect. Prosthesis: An artificial substitute for a missing body part. Tensor fascia lata (TFL) flap: A flap that a provider creates by harvesting tissue and muscle from the outer side of the thigh region. Transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous flap (TRAM flap): A tissue flap harvested from the transverse rectus abdominis muscle  in the lower abdomen  and extending from the rib cage to the pelvic bone below. Transverse upper gracilis (TUG) flap: A flap that a provider creates by harvesting tissue and part of the gracilis muscle \  which he takes from the inner part of the upper thigh close to the groin. Tips CPT? provides various options for coding breast reconstruction with flaps in the code family 19361??9369. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider surgically releases a capsule  or the scar tissue  that forms within the breast tissue around a previous implant. The provider performs this procedure to relieve pain from the contraction of the scar tissue or to address malpositioning of the breast implant. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises the mastectomy or implant scar on the skin of the breast to locate the implant. He incises the breast tissue and releases the scar tissue from around the implant. The service may include removing part of the capsule of scar tissue and/or repositioning the implant. After achieving hemostasis  he closes the operative site in layers. Terminology Breast capsulorrhaphy: Repair of malposition of breast implant and improving in results of breast revision surgery. Capsulotomy: Surgical release of the scar tissue that forms around a previously implanted prosthesis within the breast tissue. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ  graft  or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider surgically releases a capsule  or scar tissue  that forms within the breast tissue around a previous implant. He also removes all intracapsular contents such as tissues and fibrous scar. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises the mastectomy or implant scar on the skin of the breast to locate a previously placed breast implant. He excises the entire capsule of scar tissue surrounding the breast implant and removes the tissue as well as the breast implant. He then closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Breast implant: A silicone outer shell filled with saline or silicone gel implanted under the breast tissue or under the chest muscle to increase breast size (breast augmentation) or to replace breast tissue after mastectomy (breast reconstruction).

Breast revision is performed to improve unacceptable cosmetic appearance or other complication. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider removes excess amounts of tissues  skin  and fats to reshape the breast to look like the contralateral (other) breast. If necessary  the provider performs significant revision of the breast??mplant capsule (scar tissue) along with soft tissue excision. Drains are then placed and the incision site is closed.

Use this code to report a procedure on the breast for which there is no specific code available. Explanation The provider performs a procedure on the breast that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT? codes available. Consult the provider  if possible  to ensure that proper documentation has been done before billing for an unlisted procedure. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. Include one or more similar codes and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis  and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider aspirates the excess fluid from within the nasal cavity  which may be due to an abscess or hematoma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a small incision within the nasal mucosa over the abscess or hematoma. He then gently suctions and flushes the fluid filled pocket with sterile saline. After he achieves hemostasis  he may secure a drain and then he closes the operative site in layers. Terminology Abscess: A localized collection of pus that collects in a cavity  usually in response to infection. Hematoma: A localized swelling containing blood  accumulated due to a break in the wall of a nearby blood vessel.

In this procedure, the provider aspirates excess pus or blood from within the nasal septum due to an abscess or hematoma. A nasal hematoma results from the reaccumulation of blood or previous necrosis.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision within the nasal septum over the abscess or hematoma. He then gently suctions and flushes the fluid filled pocket with sterile saline. After achieving hemostasis, he may secure a drain, which he will remove usually within 48 hours. He may also pack the nasal cavity with gauze to compress the site and help with drainage. Finally, he may close the operative site in layers or leave it open to heal on its own. 


Terminology
Abscess: A localized collection of pus that collects in a cavity, usually in response to infection.

Hematoma: A localized swelling containing blood, accumulated due to a break in the wall of a nearby blood vessel.

Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow.

Nasal septum: The dividing wall that runs down the middle of the nose and separates the nasal cavities.

Necrosis: The process of death of cells and tissue.

The provider removes a tissue sample from within the nasal cavity for investigation. Explanation After the patient has been appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts nasal forceps and removes a tissue sample from a suspicious or diseased intranasal area. He sends that sample  along with a sample of the patient?? healthy intranasal tissue  to the pathologist for further evaluation and comparison study. He may apply a suture if necessary or leave the site open to heal on its own. Terminology Biopsy: An investigation by taking out a very small portion of the body part of interest. Forceps: A two bladed instrument a provider uses to compress or grasp. Intranasal: Within the nasal cavity.

In this procedure the provider removes a nasal polyp or polyps from within the nasal cavity. The provider performs this procedure to remove the obstruction that the polyp is causing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider identifies the location of a polyp or polyps. He uses biting forceps or a scalpel to remove the nasal polyps. He subsequently controls the minimal bleeding that may occur. He then applies an antibiotic and leaves the excision site open to heal. For larger polyps that leave a larger defect  he may suture the defect closed. Finally  the provider may pack the nasal cavity  leaving the packing in place for 24 hours. Terminology Forceps: A two bladed instrument a provider uses to compress or grasp. Nasal polyp: A noncancerous soft and painless growth of tissue within the nasal passages.

In this procedure  the provider excises or destroys a lesion in the nose through an internal approach  in which the provider places the surgical instruments into the nose to perform the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider uses one of several internal techniques for the destruction or excision of a lesion in the nose. She may use a laser  cryotherapy  a chemical  or other methods. She destroys the lesion and then applies an antibiotic at the site. When the procedure is complete  she leaves the wound open to heal. Terminology Cryotherapy: A technique in which a provider freezes a lesion to destroy it. Chemical method: A technique in which a provider uses a chemical to destroy a lesion. Intranasal: Within the nose. Laser therapy: A technique in which a provider uses a strong beam of light to destroy a lesion. Lesion: Any abnormality in a tissue. Tips Use 30118  Excision or destruction  eg laser  intranasal lesion; external approach  lateral rhinotomy  or an incision that runs from the inner edge of the eyebrow  along the length of the side of the nose  and may split the patient?? lip  when the provider performs the excision or destruction of an intranasal lesion through the external approach. The provider surgically excises or abrades the diseased skin tissue of the nose that results from rhinophyma  a skin condition usually affecting the tip of the nose in which skin is congested  swollen  and thickened  and the sebaceous glands are enlarged. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider excises the hypertrophic lesion in a tangential manner  preserving the sebaceous tissue to allow for spontaneous reepithelialization and complete healing. He may use techniques like the YAG laser in which he excises the lesion with minimal bleeding. Other surgical techniques that he may use are dermabrasion  cryotherapy  or electrocautery. He may perform a total eradication of the lesion  which involves procedures that are deeper  and can go down to the bone and nasal cartilage. For complex or very large lesions  he may also need to apply a skin graft  which is a separately reportable procedure. Read More

The provider removes a dermoid cyst from the subcutaneous tissue of the nose requiring only a simple removal. Explanation After appropriate preparation and administration of anesthesia  the provider makes a vertical incision over the cyst of the nose  elevates the skin and retracts the flaps laterally. He identifies the cyst and removes it. He then replaces the flaps and closes the incision with sutures. A dermoid cyst is a smooth rubbery saclike lesion  present at birth  that may contain skin  hair  fluid  and even teeth; dermoid cysts can occur on the face  ovaries  lower back  and even inside the skull. Tips For a complex excision of a dermoid cyst under bone or cartilage of the nose  see 30125.

The provider removes a dermoid cyst from under the bone or cartilage of the nose  which requires complex surgical techniques. Explanation After appropriate preparation and administration of anesthesia  the provider makes an intercartilaginous incision. He identifies the cystic tract under the nasal bone and makes a medial osteotomy in which both the tract and cyst are dissected free and removed. The incision is then closed with sutures. A dermoid cyst is a smooth rubbery saclike lesion  present at birth  that may contain skin  hair  fluid  and even teeth; dermoid cysts can occur on the face  ovaries  lower back  and even inside the skull. Tips For simple excision of a dermoid cyst from the subcutaneous tissue of the nose  see 30124.

Excision of the inferior turbinate is generally performed due to hypertrophy of the turbinate which causes airway obstruction. Explanation After administration of general anesthesia  the physician uses turbinate scissors to remove the entire turbinate along with the out??racture of the inferior turbinate. The out??racture involves the mucosa  tissue  and bones. To prevent adhesions  a silastic splint can be used. After the hemostasis is achieved  the incisions are closed. The use of an endoscope is not billed separately. Tips When an otolaryngologist performs the lesser procedure of 30130  they leave no mucosa or bone. The physician preserves nothing and leaves just the stump. Code 30130 should be reported when the otolaryngologist does not make an incision into the mucosa to resect the turbinate  but rather goes in and excises mucosa and bone at the same time. Sometimes the removal of the middle turbinate is required to gain access to the vault of the nose to repair a CSF leak from the sphenoid sinus. If that is the case  then report 30999 for the middle turbinate removal. Read Less

This CPT? code is for a submucous resection of the inferior turbinate (partial or complete by any method). Explanation Submucosal resection of the inferior turbinate is also called an inferior turbinoplasty. After administration of general anesthesia  the physician makes an incision into the anterior pole of the inferior turbinate and a submucosal dissection is performed. The inferior turbinates are elevated from the turbinate bone  allowing the surgeon to fracture the bone and reduce it while preserving the mucosa. The surgeon may also resect some of the lateral turbinate mucosa  to replace any remaining mucosa over the bare bone of the remaining turbinate.

Surgical removal of part of the nose is referred to as a partial rhinectomy. Removal of an entire external nose including the soft tissue is referred to as a total rhinectomy. Explanation After administration of anesthesia  the physician makes an incision from the lower lateral cartilage and up to the area of the upper lateral cartilage at the superior margin. The physician partially excises the nasal tip and its nearby tissues. Then the wound is closed with sutures or a graft. If the wound is closed with a graft  you should bill separately.

Surgical removal of part of the nose is referred to as a partial rhinectomy. Removal of an entire external nose including the soft tissue is referred to as a total rhinectomy. Explanation After administration of anesthesia  the physician makes an incision from the lateral edge of one naris to the other naris. The lateral wall is then sectioned and the septal and columella region is incised. Sharp cutting devices like cutting burrs are used to remove the affected cartilaginous margins and bones. Finally  the wound is closed with sutures or a graft. If the wound is closed with a graft  you should bill separately.

Therapeutic turbinate(s) injection (also known as an intraturbinal injection) is administered in the case of rhinorrhea  nasal obstruction  or sleep disturbance. Explanation After administration of topical decongestants  the physician injects an intraturbinal glucocorticoid therapeutic agent (e.g.  triamcinolone acetonide) submucosally along the anterior tip of the inferior turbinate to relieve the patient's problem.

To treat an infection of the ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses  the physician drains them in a Proetz??ype displacement therapy. Explanation The physician removes pus which is diluted with thin irrigating fluids  such as silver colloids or saline. A suction device is then used to help facilitate the drainage of pus.

In this procedure  the provider removes a foreign body from a patient?? nasal cavity. It is a simple procedure that the provider may perform in an office setting. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped  the provider administers a nasal decongestant into the patient?? nose to open the blocked nose. He locates the foreign body and then depending upon the shape and size of the foreign body; he removes it with a blunt hook  nasal forceps  or a suction apparatus. Foreign body: Any object that may be accidentally inserted into a cavity like the nose  and it does not belong there. Intranasal: Within the nose. In this complex procedure  the provider creates a full thickness incision in the nose to remove a foreign body from a patient?? nasal cavity. The foreign body for this procedure is deeper and implanted within the tissues due to trauma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider performs a lateral rhinotomy  which is an incision into the nose. The incision extends from the inner end of the eyebrow  moving down along the outer wall of the nose  over to the nasolabial fold  and passing along the nasal alar base to the philtrum  or groove of the upper lip. The provider then dissects the nasal soft tissue down to the level of bone  providing good nasal cavity access. He identifies the foreign body and dissects it from the underlying tissue using forceps. Finally  he closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Foreign body: Any object that may be accidentally inserted into a cavity  like the nose  and it does not belong there. Intranasal: Within the nose. Nasolabial folds: Two folds that run on each side of the nose to the corners of the mouth. Tips Use 30300  Removal foreign body  intranasal; office type procedure  when the provider performs a simple procedure to remove a foreign body from the nasal cavity in an office setting.
