A rhinoplasty is performed either through the open or closed approach. In an open approach  transfixion and infracartilaginous (rim) incisions are made. Closed approaches can be performed through a number of approaches such as an intercartilaginous incision  infracartilaginous incision  or transfixion incision. Explanation The skin of the nose is raised  and the necessary changes are made to the cartilage and soft tissue as desired. The nasal cartilaginous are then smoothed to straighten the nose and a graft may also be placed. A nasal tip plasty is also done and this is performed by working on the lower lateral cartilage and narrowing it in the region of the dome by removing an equal portion of lateral and medial crura leaving the cartilage at the domal area. A septoplasty is also performed to reposition the bony and cartilaginous septum. The physician also performs a repair of a cleft lip/palate (harelip) via a columellar lengthening??uch as basal Y?? technique  the forked flap technique  or a reverse columella??obule V?? plasty. Finally  the wound is closed with transmucosal sutures  adhesive tapes  and the splints. Terminology Cleft lip: A condition present from birth  in which there is a split in the upper lip on one or both sides; in a unilateral cleft lip there is improper fusion of the orbicularis oris muscle including its accessory muscle on one side  affecting one side of nose. Cleft palate: Congenital defect in which a cleft (gap) occurs in the palate at its midline  often occurring in conjunction with a cleft lip. Secondary repair: A repair performed after two weeks from the date of the injury; it may include tendon grafts or other more complex procedures. Read Less

A rhinoplasty is performed either through the open or closed approach. In an open approach, transfixion and infracartilaginous (rim) incisions are made. Closed approaches can be performed through a number of approaches such as an intercartilaginous incision, infracartilaginous incision, or transfixion incision.



Explanation
The skin of the nose is raised and the necessary changes are made to the cartilage and soft tissue as desired.  The physician performs lateral and transverse osteotomies if the nasal bones are infractured.  The nasal cartilaginous areas are then smoothed to straighten the nose and a graft may also be placed.  A nasal tip plasty is also done and this is performed by working on the lower lateral cartilage and narrowing it in the region of the dome by removing an equal portion of lateral and medial crura leaving the cartilage at the domal area.

A septoplasty is also performed to reposition the bony and cartilaginous septum.  The physician also performs a repair of a cleft lip/palate via a columellar lengthening, such as a basal Y�Y technique, the forked flap technique, or a reverse columella�lobule V�Y plasty.  Finally, the wound is closed with transmucosal sutures, adhesive tapes, and the splints.


Terminology
Cleft lip: A condition present from birth, in which there is a split in the upper lip on one or both sides; in a unilateral cleft lip there is improper fusion of the orbicularis oris muscle including its accessory muscle on one side, affecting one side of nose.

Cleft palate: Congenital defect in which a cleft (gap) occurs in the palate at its midline, often occurring in conjunction with a cleft lip.

Primary repair: Any repair of an acute injury completed within the first 24 hours after the injury; it involves direct surgical correction of the injury.

Secondary repair: A repair performed after two weeks from the date of the injury; it may include tendon grafts or other more complex procedures.

Nasal vestibular stenosis occurs due to congenital defects  trauma  or previous stenosis surgery leading to breathing problems. Explanation The physician incises the skin and the upper lateral cartilage of the nose. Then the physician performs an excision of the scar tissue and an osteotomy of the medial aspect of the nasal bone is performed. A composite graft is harvested from the auricle and fitted into the area of defect and then the incision is closed for healing. Several other surgical techniques can be used depending upon the condition. Techniques that are used are relocation and excision of reductant tissue (e.g.  nasal caudal deviation  enlarge columella  and projected lateral alar crus)  resection of scar tissue and replacement by a full thickness skin graft (e.g.  cartilaginous malformation)  replacement by local flaps  or by transplant of free cartilage  skin  or a graft (due to a shortage of skin/cartilage).

The provider repairs the collapse (narrowing) of a nasal valve by using one or more implants that rest beneath the skin or mucous membrane in the lateral wall of the nose. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider introduces an implant at the nasal valve area  a complex construct of several structures that is also known as the flow limiting segment. This implant is subcutaneous (beneath the skin) or submucosal (beneath the mucous membrane) in the lateral wall of the nose. This code applies to repair using one or more implants. The provider may perform the procedure to treat impaired nasal breathing  which may result from scar tissue  age??elated changes  and other causes. Terminology Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ  graft  or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part.

The provider applies radiofrequency energy to reshape the nasal valve in both nostrils. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a small hand??eld stylus (wand) into the patient?? nostril. The provider uses the stylus to deliver low??emperature radiofrequency energy to reshape the tissues of the nasal valve  the narrowest area within the nasal passages. The provider may apply the wand to multiple areas on the nasal mucosa  creating more room inside the nose to improve breathing. The provider performs the procedure on both nostrils and removes the wand. Terminology Mucosa: Another name for mucous membrane  the moisture??aden layer of endothelial cells that line the insides of body cavities and the insides of structures that open to the outside of the body  such as the nose  mouth  and rectum.

Septoplasty is most often performed for a deviated septum which can be either C??haped  S??haped  or a cartilaginous deviation. Explanation After administration of local anesthesia  the provider makes a Freer hemitransfixion incision or a Killian incision depending upon the area of septum affected. The cartilaginous and bony septum is then exposed  and the mucosal flap is elevated. A Tru??ut? is used to remove the irregular bones and cartilage. The flaps are then returned to their normal position. The incision is closed with sutures and the provider applies a splint.

In this procedure  the provider surgically repairs an intranasal choanal atresia  an acquired or congenital condition causing a blockage of the choana  an inverted funnel shaped passageway from the back of the nose to the upper throat that allows for breathing through the nose. The provider performs the repair through a transpalatine approach  or through an incision in the roof of the mouth. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a U??haped incision over the palate mucosa and continues down to the bony palate. She then uses an elevator to raise the mucosal flaps without entering the nasopharynx. She next uses a diamond burr to drill and remove the obstructive palatine bones posterior to the greater palatine foramina  the atretic plates  and the posterior vomer. Next  she punctures and enlarges the blocked choanal openings and places a silastic stent in each nostril to avoid further stenosis or blockage. Finally  she closes the mucosal incision in a single layer and keeps the stent in place for up to 8 weeks to ensure the patency of the newly created openings. Terminology Atretic plate: A plate at the end of the nasal septum that is continuous with the choanal opening  an opening between the nasal cavity and the nasopharynx. Burr: A surgical instrument used to drill the bone. Elevator: A surgical instrument that a provider uses to raise a depressed area or to separate adjoining parts. Greater palatine foramina: An opening at the back of the palate that gives passage to an artery and a nerve. Mucosa: Moist tissue that lines the surface of parts of the inside of the body. Palate: Roof of the mouth. Patency: Unobstructed or open. Posterior: Back or behind. Silastic: A rubber type material. Stent: A small rubber type tube that is used to treat a narrow passage. Vomer: A facial bone of the skull that forms the posterior end of the nasal septum. Tips Use 30540  Repair choanal atresia; intranasal  when the provider repairs a choanal atresia through an intranasal approach. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider removes nasal synechia  or adhesions that form in the nose due to the fusion  or connection  of scar tissue that interferes with the passage of air. This condition may occur as a result of trauma  or complication of nasal surgery and the nasal packing. He uses the intranasal approach  meaning he inserts the surgical instruments through the nose. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider uses an intranasal approach to destroy the nasal synechia. First  he uses a nasal decongestant to open the blocked nose. He then may use several techniques to lysis the scar tissue such as excision  cautery  or a laser. When the procedure is complete  he may place gauze packing and or splints to control the bleeding. Terminology Cautery: A surgical instrument that burns the lesion to destroy it. Laser therapy: A strong beam of light a provider uses to destroy the lesion. Lysis: Destruction or breakdown. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider surgically repairs an oromaxillary fistula  which is an abnormal connection between the mouth and the maxillary sinus  an air cavity in the body of the maxilla. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises the mucosa of the maxillary hard palate and creates a local flap. He then sutures this mucosal flap in layers to close the oromaxillary opening. He may also cover the fistula with a medical foil and then suture the flap over the foil. The provider instructs the patient to abstain from blowing their nose to limit sinus pressure to help promote healing and avoid reopening the fistula. Terminology Antrotomy: An incision through the wall of the antrum  or the pyramid shaped maxillary sinus. Fistula: Abnormal passageway between two structures  such as between two vessels or between an organ or the abdominal cavity and the skin. Hard palate: Roof of the mouth that separates the mouth and nasal cavity. Local flap: Skin taken from adjacent area and moved to fill the surgical defect. Maxilla: Upper jaw. Medical foil: Extremely thin aluminium sheet that provider uses for protective covering. Mucosa: Mucous membrane  or moist tissue that lines certain parts of the inside of the human body. Tips Use 30600  Repair fistula; oronasal  when a provider surgically repairs an oronasal fistula. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider surgically repairs an oronasal fistula  or an abnormal connection between the mouth and the nasal cavity through the maxillary hard palate. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision into the mucosa of the maxillary hard palate and creates a local flap. She then sutures this mucosal flap in layers to close the oronasal opening. Terminology Hard palate: Roof of the mouth that separates the mouth and nasal cavity. Local flap: Skin taken from adjacent area and moved to fill the surgical defect. Mucosa: Mucous membrane  or moist tissue that lines certain parts of the inside of the human body.

In this procedure  the provider removes damaged intranasal mucosal tissue and covers it with a graft. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a lateral rhinotomy incision  or an incision in the nose. The incision extends from the inner end of the eyebrow  moving down along the outer wall of the nose  over to the nasolabial fold  and passes along the nasal alar base to the philtrum  or groove of the upper lip. She now has access to the affected  fragile tissue covering the nasal septum and floor. She next removes the damaged mucosal tissue using a scalpel. She then obtains a separately reportable split thickness graft from the front of the thigh wall. She uses this graft to cover the defect that provider creates in the nose by removing the damaged tissue  and sutures the graft in place. Finally  she closes the nasal incision and places splints  and gauze into the nasal cavity to stop the bleeding. Terminology Dermatoplasty: Surgical repair of the skin. Dermis: The vascular inner layer of skin located below the epidermis and above the subcutaneous tissue. Epidermis: The outer nonvascular layer of skin above the dermis. Graft: A tissue transferred from one part of the body to other. Intranasal: Within the nose. Mucosa: Mucous membrane  or moist tissue that lines certain parts of the inside of the human body. Nasal septum: The dividing wall that runs down the middle of the nose and separates the nasal cavities. Split thickness graft: Graft involving only top two layers of skin; the dermis and epidermis. Tips Use 30630  Repair nasal septal perforations  when the provider repairs nasal septal holes. Read Less

The provider repairs nasal septal perforations. Explanation The provider may use an intranasal approach for a small perforation by making a hemitransfixion incision or use an external rhinoplasty approach for a larger perforation. The provider generally performs an intranasal bipedicle advancement flap by elevating it from the septum and rotating it back over the denuded perforated septal mucosa. In some cases  the provider may also perform a rotational flap. In the case of smaller perforations  grafts are generally not used  but larger perforations generally require harvesting of a graft  for example  conchal cartilage. Finally  the flaps and the incisions are closed for healing. Septal perforation generally occurs in the anterior cartilage and can be caused by trauma (such as nasal picking)  septal surgery (septoplasty or submucous resection of the septum)  septal abscess after a hematoma  granulomatous disease  or by any nasal drug abuse. In this procedure  the provider uses methods like bipolar cautery  reducing the tissue volume  radiofrequency  or somnoplasty to ablate the superficial area of the inferior turbinates. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider chooses from various possible ablation methods to shrink the superficial surface layer of the inferior turbinates. As an example  in bipolar cautery  the provider inserts a needle  approximately 2 mm deep  in the front of tip of the inferior turbinates. He then passes current through the needles to reduce the hypertrophy of the turbinates. The provider then removes the needles. Terminology Ablation: Surgical destruction of abnormal tissue or organ growth. Bipolar cautery: Passing electric current from active electrodes to passive electrodes; helps to seal bleeding vessels. Hypertrophy: Abnormal increase in the size of an organ because of enlargement of its component cells. Inferior turbinates: Tubular structures present inside the nose that humidify the air as it passes through the nasal passage. Somnoplasty: A surgical treatment to stop snoring. Tips Report 30801 if the provider performs superficial ablation of the inferior turbinates and 30802 if he performs submucosal ablation of the turbinates. Report unlisted procedure code 30999 for ablation of superior or middle turbinates. Coding guidelines require you to report an unlisted procedure code when there is not a precise code available for the procedure. Report 30130 if the provider excises the inferior turbinates. Report 30140 if the provider performs submucous resection of the inferior turbinates. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider uses methods like bipolar cautery  reducing the tissue volume  radiofrequency  or somnoplasty to perform ablation of the submucosal area of the inferior turbinates. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider chooses from various possible ablation methods to shrink the submucosal layer of the inferior turbinates. As an example  in bipolar cautery the provider inserts a needle  approximately 2 mm deep in the front of the tip of the inferior turbinates. He then passes current through the needles to reduce the hypertrophy of the turbinates. The provider then removes the needles. Terminology Ablation: Surgical destruction of abnormal tissue or organ growth. Bipolar cautery: Passing electric current from active electrodes to passive electrodes; helps to seal bleeding vessels. Hypertrophy: Abnormal increase in the size of an organ because of enlargement of its component cells. Inferior turbinates: Tubular structures present inside the nose that humidify the air as it passes through the nasal passage. Intramural: An organ situated within the wall or cavity. Submucosa: Layer of dense connective tissues that support the mucosa. Turbinates: Web of bones  vessels  and tissues within the nasal passageway that warms  humidifies  and filters the air. Tips Report 30802 if the provider performs submucosal ablation of the inferior turbinates and 30801 if she performs superficial ablation of the turbinates. Report unlisted procedure code 30999 for ablation of superior or middle turbinates. Report 30140 if the provider performs submucous resection of the inferior turbinates. Read Less

The provider uses a simple or limited approach to stop a nosebleed caused by a vessel in the front area of the nose. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized as needed  the provider uses a nasal speculum to locate the site of bleeding. She cleans and dries the site with a cotton tip applicator. She then applies continuous pressure  inserts pledgets soaked with an anesthetic??asoconstrictor solution into the nasal cavity  performs chemical cautery with a silver nitrate stick  administers nasal spray to anesthetize/shrink nasal mucosa  or uses another minor cautery or packing method to control the bleeding. The provider then again inspects the site to check for bleeding. The goal of the procedure is to control bleeding of the anterior nose. Terminology Chemical cautery: A chemical agent that destroys the abnormal tissues by burning or scarring. Nasal hemorrhage: Bleeding from the nose due to rupture of the small vessels overlying the nasal septum  which is the wall between the nostrils. Pledgets: A small lump of lint or absorbent cotton to protect a wound or an opening in the body. Vasoconstriction: Contraction of muscular walls of the vessels that leads to their narrowing. Vasoconstrictors: Drugs that cause vasoconstriction of the blood vessels. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Depending on payer preference  you may need to report the code once with modifier 50  twice with modifier 50 appended to the second code  or with RT/LT if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally. Check with the payer to determine their preference and avoid delays or rebilling. Report 30901 when the provider controls the bleeding through simple methods and 30903 when he controls bleeding through complex methods. Read Less

The provider uses a complex or extensive approach to stop a heavy nosebleed caused by a vessel in the front area of the nose. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized as needed  the provider places the patient in the proper position and uses a nasal speculum to locate the site of bleeding. She cleans and dries the site with a cotton tip applicator. She then uses extensive methods like packing with petroleum jelly or using nasal cautery to control bleeding. The provider sometimes may apply epinephrine and lidocaine HCl injections into the nasal cavity to control complex bleeds. Terminology Epinephrine: A hormone secreted by the adrenal medulla that raises the blood pressure and heart rate in response to stress  such as anger or fear. Lidocaine HCl: A topically local anesthetic that inhibits impulses from sensory nerves. Nasal hemorrhage: Bleeding from the nose due to rupture of the small vessels overlying the nasal septum. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Depending on payer preference  you may need to report the code once with modifier 50  twice with modifier 50 appended to the second code  or with RT/LT if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally. Check with the payer to determine their preference and avoid delays or rebilling. Report 30901 for control of bleeding through simple methods and 30903 for bleeding control through complex methods. In this procedure  the provider controls posterior nasal bleeding by any method. This code represents initial treatment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider chooses from various methods to stop bleeding caused by a vessel in the posterior part of the nose. He may insert a nasal balloon catheter and then inflate the balloon until there is pressure on the posterior nasal window. Pressure on the posterior nasal window controls bleeding. He then withdraws the balloon. The provider also may choose to pack the nose. Another option for bleeding that is difficult to control is to apply electrical coagulation. Use this code for initial treatment. Terminology Catheter: A flexible thin tube that is put into the body for various purposes  such as to inject or remove a substance. Electric coagulation: Clotting of blood or other tissues using high frequency currents. Nasal hemorrhage: Bleeding from the nose due to rupture of the small vessels  typically those overlying the nasal septum. Tips If the provider controls a subsequent posterior nasal hemorrhage  by any method  report 30906. Read Less

CPT� code 30906 is used when the patient makes a subsequent visit after the initial treatment.



Explanation
To control posterior nasal bleeding, the physician sedates the patient and administers anesthesia into the anterior nasal cavity and inserts a nasal balloon by guided by a catheter. The balloon is then inflated to apply pressure on the choana which controls the bleeding. The physician may also pack the nose and can perform electrical coagulation if needed.

In this procedure  the provider makes an incision in the side of the nasal cavity to advance into the ethmoid arteries. He then binds the arteries using clips or sutures. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision near the canthus and carries this incision down to the periosteum of the nose. The provider identifies the frontoethmoidal suture. Via this suture he approaches the ethmoid arteries that arise there and pass on to reach the nose. He then ligates the ethmoidal arteries using vascular clips or sutures. During the procedure the provider takes care to avoid any injury to the lacrimal sac and optic nerve. He closes the incision in layers. The goal of the procedure is to prevent bleeding from the nose. Terminology Canthus: Angle on each corner of the eye  where the upper and lower eyelids meet. Ethmoid artery: A branch of the ophthalmic artery that supplies the structures in and around the nasal capsule. Frontoethmoidal suture: A suture between the ethmoid bone and frontal bone; occupying the depression in the wall of the cranium that holds the frontal lobes of the brain. Lacrimal sac: Upper portion of the nasolacrimal duct that receives tears from the lacrimal ducts. Ligation: A surgical procedure of tying the body structures  such as blood vessels. In this procedure  the provider makes an incision in the upper gums to reach the internal maxillary artery and then ligates it using sutures or clips. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a Caldwell??uc incision in the upper gum under the posterior maxillary sinus and retracts the gum. She then raises the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus to gain access to the internal maxillary artery. She places vascular clips or sutures to ligate the arteries. The provider applies nasal packing to avoid bleeding and closes the incision in layers. The provider takes care to avoid any injury to the infraorbital nerve. The goal of the procedure is to prevent bleeding from the higher nasal cavity. Terminology Caldwell??uc incision: Incision in the front wall of the maxillary sinus through the upper gums. Infraorbital nerve: Continuation of the maxillary nerve into the socket of the eyes; it supplies the upper part of the cheek  the upper lip  and the lower eyelid. Internal maxillary artery: One of the branches of the maxillary artery  supplying the face. Maxillary sinus: A large sinus  or cavity  located on either side of the nose below the eye and above the teeth. Transantral: A type of incision that is performed across the antrum  i.e.  a cavity in bone or any other structure. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 or RT/LT  depending on payer preference  if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally. Use 30915 if the provider ligates internal ethmoid arteries. Use 37600 if the provider ligates the external carotid artery. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider fractures one or more inferior turbinates to correct the overgrowth of the inferior turbinates and release the nasal airway obstruction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider may make an incision in the mucosa of the inferior turbinates if needed. She then separates the mucous membrane from the underlying inferior turbinates. The provider uses forceps to remove the bony fragments and outfractures the inferior turbinates. The fracture repositions the turbinate to improve the patient?? breathing. The provider may use methods such as electrocautery or laser to control bleeding. The goal of the procedure is to treat hypertrophy of the inferior turbinates and release any obstruction in the nasal airway. Terminology Electrocautery: Passing electric current from active electrodes to passive electrodes; helps to seal bleeding vessels. Read More

In this procedure  the provider inserts a flexible cannula in the maxillary sinus through a cut in the antrum or through a natural opening to wash out the contents of the maxillary sinus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a cannula through the natural opening of the sinus or through a cut in the antrum beneath the inferior nasal turbinate in the nose. The provider then applies a constant pressure to introduce the cannula into the maxillary sinus. The provider irrigates  or washes out  the contents of the sinus with saline solution. He then withdraws the cannula and places cotton pledgets at the site to control excessive bleeding. The goal of the procedure is to treat acute or subacute maxillary sinusitis. Terminology Antrum: A cavity or a chamber in a bone or any anatomical structure. Cannula: A thin tube set in the body  typically either to insert an implant or to drain fluid. Inferior turbinates: Long  narrow structure present in the inner aspect of the nose that warms  humidifies  and filters the air. Lavage: Washing out of a body cavity  such as the stomach. Maxillary sinus: A large pyramid shaped sinus  or cavity in the body of maxilla  located on either side of the nose below the eye and above the teeth; also called antrum of Highmore. Sinusitis: Inflammation of sinuses  airspaces within the face connected to the nose. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally or use modifiers RT/LT  depending on payer preference. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider inserts a flexible cannula to wash out the contents of the sphenoid sinus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a cannula via the sphenoethmoidal break. The provider then applies a constant pressure to introduce the cannula in the sphenoid sinus. She irrigates  or washes out  the contents of the sinus with saline solution. The provider then withdraws the cannula and places cotton pledgets at the site to control excessive bleeding. The goal of the procedure is to treat acute or subacute sphenoid sinusitis. Terminology Cannula: A thin tube set in the body  typically either to insert an implant or to drain fluid. Sinusitis: Inflammation of sinuses  airspaces within the facial bones that open to the nose. Sphenoid sinus: Paired paranasal sinus in the body of sphenoid bone  deep in the skull  that communicates with the nasal cavity and drains mucus from the back of the nose via an opening called an ostium. Sphenoethmoidal recess: A small space in the nasal cavity  posterior to the superior concha and open into the sphenoid sinus of the skull. Superior concha: The upper of the two bony plates that form the boundary of superior meatus of the nose. Superior meatus: A short passage on each side of the nose between the superior and middle nasal concha. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally or use modifiers RT/LT  depending on payer preference. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider makes an intranasal incision. The provider then uses cutting forceps to perform a middle meatal sinusotomy. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an intranasal incision. The provider then creates an aperture  or opening  in the antrum by making the canal called the middle meatus larger. He uses cutting forceps to excise the inferior turbinates thereby further enlarging the aperture for better visualization of the maxillary sinus and to improve drainage. The provider may then irrigate  or wash out  the contents of the maxillary sinus. The provider then packs the nasal cavity to achieve hemostasis. The goal of the procedure is to allow sinus drainage to treat maxillary sinusitis or maxillary polyps. Terminology Antrum: A natural cavity in a bone or an organ. Antrostomy: A surgical break into the antrum  that refers to a cavity. Hemostasis: Stopping the flow of blood. Inferior turbinate: Long  narrow structure present in the inner aspect of the nose that warms  humidifies  and filters the air. Maxillary sinus: A large pyramid shaped sinus  or cavity  located on either side of the nose below the eye and above the teeth; also called antrum of Highmore. Middle meatus: A passage in the nasal cavity that lies below the middle nasal concha and extends along the superior border of the inferior concha. Sinusitis: Inflammation of sinuses  airspaces within the facial bones that open to the nose. Sinusotomy: A surgical incision into the sinus of the skull  mainly performed to treat an infection in the sinus. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally or use modifiers RT/LT  depending on payer preference. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider uses any approach for a surgery involving the pterygomaxillary fossa  a trench??ike structure roughly located between the upper jaw and orbit of the eye. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider begins the approach to the pterygomaxillary fossa. In a typical procedure  he makes an intraoral incision in the parapharyngeal space. The provider carries this incision across the maxilla exposing the anterior wall of the maxilla  which is the upper jaw. He then also creates an opening in the posterior wall of the maxilla  approaching the pterygomaxillary fossa. He then performs the required surgery  such as removing a lesion in the fossa and tying the vidian nerves and maxillary artery in the fossa. The provider then closes the incision in the mouth with sutures in a single layer. The goal of the procedure is to treat any tumor or abscess present in the parapharyngeal space. Terminology Ganglion: A structure that consists of nerve cell bodies. Parapharyngeal space: A pyramid shaped space in the head and neck; it contains the maxillary artery and ascending pharyngeal artery. Pterygomaxillary fossa: An erect fissure present in the skull that is formed by division of the maxilla  or upper jaw  from the pterygoid process of the sphenoid bone. Vidian nerve: A nerve that is present in the pterygoid canal and forms the pterygopalatine ganglion. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally or use modifiers RT/LT  depending on payer preference. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider makes an incision into the sphenoid sinus and may perform biopsy as part of the procedure.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins the approach to the sphenoid sinus, which may be through the mouth. The provider then approaches and dissects the septum, the wall that separates the nasal cavities, to expose the sphenoid sinus. Bleeding in polyps may lead to poor visibility. After creating the incision into the sphenoid sinus, she may take tissue samples for biopsy. She then restores the septum to its original position. The provider then closes the incision to prevent bleeding.


Terminology
Septum: Partition that separates two chambers.

Sinusotomy: Surgical incision into the sinus.

 


Tips
Use 31051 if the provider performs sphenoid sinusotomy along with the removal of a polyp.

This code represents a unilateral service, meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally or use modifiers RT/LT, depending on payer preference.

In this procedure  the provider incises the sphenoid sinus. She strips the mucosa or removes one or more polyps. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider begins the approach to the sphenoid sinus  typically by making an intraoral incision. The provider then severs the septal cartilage of the nose and advances to the sphenoid sinus. She removes the front wall of the sinus and drains off the diseased contents. The provider then removes any polyps from the sphenoid sinus or removes the mucosal lining. She restores septal cartilage to its original position and closes the mouth incision in a single layer. Terminology Mucosa: Moist tissue lining various parts of the body  such as the nose  mouth  and lungs. Polyp: An abnormal tissue growth that extends from the mucous membrane. Septum: A barrier separating two chambers or cavities. Sphenoid sinus: Paired paranasal sinuses in the sphenoid bone that is present at the base of the skull and communicate with the nasal cavities; not palpable during extraoral examination. Tips Use 31050 if the provider performs sphenoid sinusotomy without mucosal stripping or polyp removal. This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally or use modifiers RT/LT  depending on payer preference. Read Less

The provider performs trephination  meaning he punctures the skull  as part of a procedure to create an opening into the frontal sinus  Air spaces on each side of the forehead?? frontal bone lying above the eye?? orbits. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision roughly 1 cm under the inner side of the eyebrow. He then drills a small hole in the front wall of the frontal sinus. The provider then places a needle in the site and drains out pus  if present in the sinus. He then sends this material for pathological analysis. He sprays saline solution into the frontal sinus to clear off any purulent material present. The provider inserts one or more catheters into the orbit to improve drainage. During the procedure  the provider takes care to avoid injury to the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves. The goal of the procedure is to treat nonacute sinusitis. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube inserted through a narrow opening into a cavity  used for services such as injecting or removing fluids. Supraorbital nerve: A branch of frontal nerve  supplying the frontal sinus  upper eyelid  forehead  and scalp. Supratrochlear nerve: A branch of frontal nerve  supplying the central part of the forehead  inner side of the upper eyelid  and the root of the nose. Trephination: A procedure to perforate the skull. Tips Use 31276 if the provider performs Nasal/sinus endoscopy  surgical  with frontal sinus exploration  including removal of tissue from frontal sinus  when performed. This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally or use modifiers RT/LT  depending on payer preference. In this procedure  the provider makes an incision along the inner wall of the orbit of eye to reach the frontal sinus. The provider then removes the diseased tissue  such as a cyst or a benign neoplasm  from the frontal sinus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision along the median orbit that extends to the wall above the orbit of the eye. He then creates an opening into the ethmoid sinus to reach the frontal sinus. The provider then removes the diseased tissue from the frontal sinus using instruments such as curettes. He then closes the wound in layers. The goal of the procedure is to remove diseased tissues  such as a cyst called a mucocele or a benign neoplasm called an osteoma from the frontal sinus. Terminology Benign neoplasm: An abnormal mass of cells that lacks the ability to penetrate the neighboring tissues. Ethmoid sinus: Paired paranasal sinuses near the bridge of the nose. Frontal sinus: Air spaces on each side of the forehead's frontal bone  resting above the orbits. Lynch incision: Incision that runs midway between the medial canthus and extends to the inferior aspect of the eyebrow. Mucocele: A retention cyst of the lacrimal or the tear secreting glands  caused due to distension of a hollow organ or cavity with mucus. Orbit: Socket of the eye. Osteoma: A form of benign neoplasm in which a new bone grows over an already existing bone; affects mainly skull and facial bones. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally or use modifiers RT/LT  depending on payer preference. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider makes a coronal incision on the scalp and advances into the frontal sinus. He then packs the sinus with material to obliterate the sinus  making it nonfunctional. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision across the top of the scalp  usually above the ears  to reach the frontal sinus. She removes the diseased contents and all mucosa from the frontal sinus  ablating tissue to destroy it if needed. She then packs the sinus with material  such as abdominal fat taken from the patient  and plugs the passages to the nose. The provider then closes the incision in layers. Providers may perform obliterative procedures on patients with recurrent infections  cancer  or injuries affecting the sinus. Terminology Coronal incision: An incision made across the top of the scalp  above the ears up to the frontal sinus. Frontal bone: Single broad bone forming the forehead and upper part of each orbit. Frontal sinus: Air spaces on each side of the frontal bone  resting above the orbits. Mucosa: Moist tissue lining various parts of the body  such as the nose  mouth  and lungs. Tips Use code 31080 if the provider performs obliterative frontal sinusotomy  without osteoplastic flap through a brow incision. Use 31084 and 31085 if the provider performs obliterative frontal sinusotomy with an osteoplastic flap through brow and coronal incisions respectively. Use 31086 and 31087 if the provider performs nonobliterative frontal sinusotomy with an osteoplastic flap through brow and coronal incisions respectively. This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally or use modifiers RT/LT  depending on payer preference. In this procedure  the provider approaches three or more paranasal sinuses  incises them  and removes their diseased contents. The provider can use this technique to treat sinusitis of any sinus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider chooses an appropriate route such as intranasal  intraoral  or through an incision to advance to the diseased sinus. He uses forceps  curettes  and other appropriate instruments to remove diseased tissues from the sinus and sends samples to pathology for further analysis. He then closes the incision with a simple repair or repairs it in layers depending upon the route. He performs the service in three sinuses on the same side of the face. Terminology Intranasal route: Through the nose. Intraoral route: Through the mouth. Paranasal sinuses: Group of four paired air??illed spaces in the facial bones that surround and open to the nasal cavity: maxillary sinus  frontal sinus  ethmoid sinus  and sphenoid sinus. Sinusotomy: A surgical incision into the sinus of the skull mainly performed to treat an infection in the sinus. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side. Append modifier 50 or RT/LT  depending on payer preference  if the procedure is performed bilaterally. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider makes an intranasal incision to gain access into the anterior ethmoid sinus. The provider then removes all diseased contents from the anterior ethmoid sinus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an intranasal incision to gain access to the middle turbinate. He then partially resects the middle turbinate if needed to remove obstruction. The provider inserts a small noncutting instrument like a curette to break into the anterior cells of the ethmoid sinus. He then removes the diseased contents of the anterior ethmoid sinus and permits sinus drainage. He may pack the nasal area with gauze. Terminology Ethmoid sinus: Sinus present on either side of the ethmoid bone  between the nose and the eyes  that consist of ethmoid air cells. Middle turbinate: A web??ike structure present on each side of the nose between the inferior and superior turbinates that warms  humidifies  and filters the air. In this procedure  the provider uses an intranasal approach to access the anterior and posterior ethmoid sinuses. The provider then removes the diseased tissues and applies drains. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an intranasal incision. The provider then incises the mucosa and advances into the anterior cells of the ethmoid sinus. He removes the diseased tissues with the help of a curette. The provider dissects the posterior cells and removes diseased tissues from the posterior aspect also using curettes. He sends the tissues to pathology for further analyses. The provider then packs the nasal incision with gauze to prevent further bleeding. The goal of the procedure is to remove the diseased tissues present  typically in the form of a polyp. Terminology Ethmoidectomy: Removal or excision of cells in the ethmoid bone or ethmoid sinus. Ethmoid sinus: Pair of paranasal sinuses present on either side of the ethmoid bone  between the nose and the eyes  that consist of ethmoid air cells. Mucosa: A lining of mucus on the inner surface of the membranes that secretes mucus. Polyp: A small nonmalignant growth that projects from the surface of the mucous membrane of organs such as the nose  intestines  etc.; may cause obstruction. Append modifier 50 or RT/LT  depending on payer preference  if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally. In this procedure, the provider uses an approach other than through the nose to reach the ethmoid sinuses. He clears the diseased contents of the ethmoid sinus.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a curvilinear incision between the medial canthus and middle of the anterior nasal bone. The provider releases the tendon on the inner side of the inner corner of the eye and cuts the anterior ethmoid artery to enter into the ethmoid sinus. She removes the diseased tissues present in the sinus. The provider then places a drain in the sinus and repositions the medial canthal tendon. She closes the incision with sutures in layers. Providers may use this procedure to remove a polyp that recurs because of the failure of intranasal approach.


Terminology
Anterior nasal bone: Two small bones that form a bridge of bones in the front.

Canthus: The angle at the outer and inner corner of the eye where the upper and lower lids meet.

Ethmoidectomy: Removal or excision of cells in the ethmoid bone or ethmoid sinus.

Ethmoid sinus: Pair of paranasal sinuses present on either side of the ethmoid bone, between the nose and the eyes, that consist of ethmoid air cells.

Orbit: Bony cavity of the skull that contains the eye; provides passage for nerves and arteries.

Tendon: A flexible band of fibrous tissues that connect muscle to bone.


Tips
This code represents a unilateral service, meaning performed on one side of the nasal cavity. Append modifier 50 or RT/LT, depending on payer preference, if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally.

Use code 31201 if the provider performs total ethmoidectomy using an intranasal approach.

In this procedure  the provider inserts an endoscope into the nasal cavity to examine the structures of the nasal cavity on one or both sides. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a rigid or a flexible endoscope in the nasal cavity. She extends the scope along the floor of the nasal cavity into the nasopharynx. She examines the entire nasopharynx and then passes the scope between the middle and the inferior turbinates. The provider then repositions the head of the endoscope to an angle and advances it into the olfactory cleft to look for any polyps. She then carefully removes the scope. The procedure is easy to execute and does not require any incision. She may perform the endoscopy on one or both sides. Terminology Ethmoidal labyrinth: A mass of air cells that forms the lateral wall of the nasal septum. Nasal cavity: A large air??illed space on either side of the nasal septum  lying between the floor of the cranium and roof of the mouth; also called nasal fossa. Nasal endoscopy: Use of a medical device that has a thin rigid or a flexible tube for viewing the sinus and nasal passages. Nasopharynx: The upper part of the pharynx that bridges the nasal cavity to the soft palate. Olfactory cleft: A small chamber between the turbinate wall of the ethmoidal labyrinth and coincides with the nasal septum. Turbinates: A web of bones  vessels  and tissues within the nasal passageway that warms  humidifies  and filters the air. Tips The code definition designates this service as a separate procedure  so you should not report it separately when the provider performs it as a part of a larger  related service. Read Less

The provider perforates the canine fossa or inferior meatus to advance an endoscope into the maxillary sinus. She then opens the maxillary sinus to perform a diagnostic endoscopy. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider begins the insertion of a rigid or flexible endoscope into the nasal cavity. She makes a perforation into the inferior meatus of the nose or into the canine fossa through the gums and moves the endoscope up to evaluate the nasal structures and maxillary sinus. The provider withdraws the endoscope and closes the gum perforation  if made  with a single layer. Terminology Endoscope: A stiff (rigid) or flexible tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon  bladder  or stomach; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope. Maxillary sinus: A large sinus (cavity) located on either side of the nose below the eye and above the teeth. In this procedure  the provider inserts an endoscope into the nasal cavity. She examines the nasal contents. The provider then performs a nasal biopsy  polypectomy  or debridement. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts an endoscope into the nose and examines the entire nose. To perform polypectomy  the provider uses surgical instruments like nasal forceps  a snare  wire loops  or a scalpel to remove the polyp. She may instead perform a biopsy  using an instrument like biopsy forceps to take a small sample of tissue for diagnostic examination. The provider then withdraws the endoscope and places cotton pledgets at the site to avoid further bleeding. Terminology Debridement: Removal of dead  damaged  and contaminated tissues. The provider inserts an endoscope into the nose and performs radiofrequency ablation (destruction using heat from focused radio waves) of the posterior nasal nerve. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a rigid or flexible endoscope in the nasal cavity. The provider then maneuvers the scope to reach the posterior nasal nerve. The provider uses an instrument to perform radiofrequency ablation (destruction using heat from focused radio waves)  disrupting the posterior nasal nerve. The provider then withdraws the endoscope and may apply gauze to control bleeding. Terminology Nasal endoscopy: The use of a medical device that has a thin rigid or a flexible tube for viewing the sinuses and nasal passages. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA): Use of heat produced by focused radio waves (a type of electromagnetic wave) to destroy areas of abnormal  damaged  or diseased tissue. Read Less

The provider inserts an endoscope into the nose and performs cryoablation (destruction by freezing) of the posterior nasal nerve. The provider then maneuvers the scope to reach the posterior nasal nerve. The provider uses an instrument to perform cryoablation (destruction by freezing)  disrupting the posterior nasal nerve. In this procedure  the provider inserts an endoscope into the nasal cavity. The provider then uses bipolar cautery or other means to control bleeding. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a flexible nasal endoscope He examines the entire nasal cavity for possible areas of bleeding. The provider uses methods such as applying sticks of silver nitrate or using bipolar cautery to cauterize or burn the feeding vessels to control bleeding inside the nose. He then withdraws the endoscope and applies antibiotics to the site to prevent any further bleeding. The goal of the procedure is to prevent excessive nasal bleeding. Terminology Bipolar cautery: The provider passes high frequency electrical current from active to passive electrodes in tissues to control bleeding Nasal endoscopy: Use of a medical device that has a thin rigid or a flexible tube for viewing the sinus and nasal passages. Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) reduces or eliminates tearing or recurrent infections of the lacrimal system of the eye. The procedure involves the construction of a new pathway for tears to exit the eye. This is performed by way of an incision along the side of the nose that creates an opening in the nasal bone. Explanation After administration of anesthesia  the physician inserts an endoscope and dilators and/or a light probe is passed through the duct. Small silastic tubes (stents) may also be inserted into the two drainage points of the eye and passed through the opening in the nasal bone and into the nose  which are then tied and shortened.

Partial surgical anterior ethmoidectomy involves the removal of the uncinate process (infundibulotomy), opening of the bulla, and partial removal of the anterior ethmoid cells.



Explanation
After administration of anesthesia, a rigid or flexible endoscope is inserted into the nasal cavity.  The ethmoid bulla (air pocket surrounded by bone) is identified, opened, and resected with cutting forceps, providing a clear view of the nasal lamella and retrobulbar space.  The anterior cells are opened and removed.  Finally, the incision is closed and the scope is removed.


Terminology
Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body.

Endoscope: A stiff or flexible tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon, bladder, or stomach; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope.

Ethmoid sinus: One of the air filled cavities near the bridge of the nose.

Lamina (lamella) papyracea: A thin plate of bone between the ethmoid cavity and the orbital bone of the eye.

Retrobulbar: The area located behind the globe of the eye.

In this procedure  the provider inserts an endoscope into the frontal sinus to explore it for abnormalities. The provider may also remove bone  scar tissue  polyps  or other tissue from the frontal sinus. The provider then maneuvers the scope into the frontal sinus. He may use a scalpel attached to the endoscope to remove diseased tissues from the sinus. The provider then withdraws the endoscope and applies gauze at the site to control bleeding. Terminology Frontal sinus: Pair of paranasal sinuses on each side of the forehead?? frontal bone present above the eyes??orbits. Nasal endoscopy: Use of a medical device that has a thin rigid or a flexible tube for viewing the sinus and nasal passages. Tips This code represents a unilateral service  meaning performed on one side of the nasal cavity. The provider passes an endoscope through the nasal cavity of the patient to bring about dilation of the ostium  or opening  of the frontal sinus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider applies a topical nasal decongestant before beginning the dilation procedure. A typical method is balloon dilation. He places a flexible wire into the orifice that connects the sinus with the nasal cavity  within the frontal sinus. He inserts this wire through the nose. The provider also ropes a balloon catheter over the guidewire and places the guidewire into the frontal ostium. He confirms the position of the balloon and the flexible wire using an endoscope during the course of placement. He then dilates the sinus ostium by inflating the balloon. The provider deflates and removes the balloon at the end of the service. Terminology Balloon dilator: A catheter with an inflatable balloon that relieves a stricture or narrowing of a lumen or tube  such as the esophagus  by inflating the balloon to increase the diameter of the lumen and dilate the stricture. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed  blood withdrawn  or fluids instilled; also  a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. Endoscope: A stiff (rigid) or flexible tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon  bladder  or stomach; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope. Frontal sinus ostium: The frontal sinus is a sinus located in the frontal bone above the eyes in the forehead; an orifice in this sinus is the frontal sinus ostium  which allows drainage. Paranasal sinuses: Spaces filled with air within the bones of the face. Tips See 31297 for dilation of the sphenoid sinus ostium. See 31295 for dilation of the maxillary sinus ostium. When the provider performs this procedure bilaterally  report 31296 with modifier 50 for bilateral procedure or with modifiers LT for the left side and RT for right side appended  depending on payer preference. The provider administers oxygen to the patient through a catheter that it is inserted into the windpipe.



Explanation
In this procedure, to administer transtracheal oxygen (TTO), the patient is placed under anesthesia and in the supine position. The provider incises the trachea and inserts a transtracheal catheter, a flexible plastic tube, into the windpipe to administer oxygen. The catheter is connected to an oxygen source. The procedure treats patients with chronic respiratory problems. The procedure, which is now widely used, replaces an older method of inserting a needle, guide wire, and stent into the trachea, and then later inserting a catheter.

 


Terminology
transtracheal: across the trachea

A repair of the intrathoracic trachea  or windpipe  to treat patients who require open airway reconstruction. Explanation This procedure involves tracheoplasty  or repair of the intrathoracic trachea  to treat tracheal stenosis and other laryngotracheal disorders. While the patient is under anesthesia and in the supine position  the provider incises the thoracic trachea horizontally and then makes a vertical cut in the back of one segment of the trachea and in the front of the other segment. The provider joins the two segments and sutures them to create a wider tracheal airway. Terminology intrathoracic trachea: The part of the windpipe that is located in the posterior  or back  portion of the mediastinum. The esophagus separates it from the vertebrae. tracheal stenosis: abnormal narrowing of the windpipe laryngotracheal: pertaining to the larynx  or voice box  and the trachea  or windpipe

The provider reconstructs the carina after removing a tumor. Explanation Removing tumors of the carina and reconstructing the carina can be a challenging procedure. It is considered to be aggressive treatment for tumors. While the patient is under anesthesia and in the supine position  the provider incises the trachea and excises  or resects  the tumor of the carina. He reconstructs the carina through anastomosis  or joining  of the main bronchus to the lower trachea or of both bronchi to the lower trachea. Surgical approaches can vary depending on the type of resection the provider decides to perform. Terminology carina: A ridge of cartilage within the trachea that runs front to back between the two primary bronchi at the tracheal bifurcation  or the split into two parts.

Repair of an airway with a graft  or patch. Explanation While the patient is under anesthesia and in the supine position  the provider incises the area of the bronchus to reach the target area. He repairs the diseased or defective bronchus by placing a synthetic or cartilage graft on the bronchial defect to reestablish the airway so it is no longer obstructed. Terminology Bronchus (pl. bronchi): One of two main air passageways from the end of the trachea (windpipe) into the lungs; also known as the right and left bronchi.

The provider treats bronchial stensosis by dissecting the bronchus to treat the stenosis and then joining mucosal flaps to reestablish the airway. Explanation While the patient is under anesthesia and in the supine position  the provider incises the neck to mobilize the trachea  or windpipe  and the pharynx  or throat. The provider then examines the stenosis and excises the stenotic segment by dissecting and identifying both recurrent laryngeal nerves. The provider constructs tracheal and pharyngeal mucosal flaps and sutures them together  called anastomosis  then closes the muscles and skin. Terminology Mucosal flap: Flap created from mucosa  soft tissue that lines the inside of the trachea and pharynx. Stenosis: Narrowing in a tubular or hollow structure  such as an artery  valve  the colon  or ear canal.

The provider excises a narrowing of the cervicothoracic trachea and then joins tracheal segments to repair the defect and reestablish the airway. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a cervicothoracic incision down to the trachea  ensuring that he does not damage the underlying structures such as the thyroid gland  major neck vessels  or the recurrent laryngeal nerves. The provider opens the tracheal lumen  examines the area with the stenosis  and excises it. The provider releases the larynx and part of the tracheal segment from the hyoid bone and releases the tracheal segment from the mediastinum. The provider anastomoses  or joins the two parts of the trachea with sutures. Finally  the provider stops all bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Cardiothoracic trachea: Portion of the trachea that extends through the neck and chest region. Excision: Removal of tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. Hyoid bone: Horseshoe shaped bone situated in the front of the neck between the chin and thyroid cartilage. Mediastinum: The area of the chest located between the lungs. Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure; a stenosed valve becomes stiff affecting its ability to open and close properly. Thyroid gland: A gland in the neck that has two lobes connected by a narrow portion called the isthmus; secretes thyroid hormone  which is important to regulating metabolism  and the hormone calcitonin  which helps regulate calcium. Tracheal lumen: Channel within the trachea. Tips When the provider excises a narrowing of the cervical area of the trachea and then joins the tracheal segments to repair the defect and reestablish the airway  use 31780  Excision tracheal stenosis and anastomosis; cervical. In this procedure  the provider creates an open surgical incision into the pleural space/cavity of the chest and takes one or more biopsies of the pleura of the lung. Explanation The team brings the patient into the operation room and administers adequate anesthesia. The provider cuts into the chest from the front to the back  separating ribs to get access to the pleural space of the chest. The provider drains off excess fluid that might have accumulated because of pleural effusion. Then the provider removes one or more pieces from the pleura of the lung and sends them to the laboratory for investigation. Finally  he closes the wound. The provider may decide to leave some flexible tubes in the chest to drain out fluid  air  and blood. Terminology Pleural effusion: An abnormal collection of fluid between two layers of pleural membranes of the lungs. In cases of cardiac arrest  the provider creates an incision in the patient?? chest cavity to perform manual cardiac massage. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider creates a surgical opening or incision in the thoracic cavity to gain access to the organs  including the heart  lungs  esophagus  thoracic aorta  and anterior spine. The provider may use one of several approaches to perform the thoracotomy. The provider may perform a median sternotomy to reach the heart or other areas of the thoracic cavity. The provider makes an incision down through the middle of the chest and splits the sternum  or breastbone  down the middle by using special tools. Posterolateral thoracotomy and anterolateral thoracotomy are other possible approaches. The provider performs a posterolateral incision at the sternum and goes across to the side until she reaches the back. For an anterolateral incision  the provider makes an incision starting at the sternum and goes across to the side just under the armpit. She then widens the opening with rib spreaders. A clamshell thoracotomy gives almost complete exposure to the entire thoracic cavity. The provider usually starts as a standard left anterolateral thoracotomy  placed in the fifth intercostal space  just below the nipple. The provider then performs a right sided thoracotomy in the same interspace. She then splits the sternum and widens the opening with rib spreaders. Once the provider gains access to the heart  she performs internal cardiac massage by using two hands to squeeze the heart using rhythmic compressions. The compressions maintain blood circulation during a cardiac or pulmonary arrest. After performing the surgical procedure  the provider may place one or more chest drains with one end in the thoracic cavity and the other end exiting the body so the tube may be connected to a collection container. The chest tube re??xpands the lungs if necessary and allows for drainage of air  blood  or fluid. If the sternum requires repair  the provider uses wires to bring the halves together. The provider uses stitches and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Anterolateral thoracotomy: Surgical incision through the anterior  or front  chest wall to the side. Intercostal space: Space between two ribs. Posterolateral thoracotomy: Surgical incision through intercostal space on the back and toward the side. Rib spreaders: Surgical instrument to separate ribs during chest surgery. Sternotomy: Surgical procedure in which a vertical incision is made along the sternum to split it in two halves. Thoracic cavity: Body cavity above the diaphragm muscle surrounded by chest wall; contains the heart and lungs. Thoracotomy: Incision into the chest cavity. Read Less

She then dresses the wound with bulky gauze dressings to absorb the drainage. Use this code for drainage through an open procedure  not a percutaneous procedure. Terminology Abscess: Collection of pus surrounded by inflamed tissue. Cyst: Cluster of cells which are grouped together to form a sac separated from nearby tissues. Parietal membrane: Membrane lining walls of a body cavity. Percutaneous procedure: Minimally invasive procedure performed through skin. Pneumostoma: An opening in a lung. Pneumonostomy: Surgical procedure to create an artificial opening into the lung  often for the purpose of draining an abscess. Visceral membrane: Membrane covering internal body organs. Read Less

The provider performs surgical abrasion to remove trapped air in lungs in a patient with a repeat pneumothorax. Pleura: Serous membrane that lines the thorax and walls of the pulmonary cavity and envelops the lungs. Read More

The provider then closes the incision by sutures or staples, wiring the sternum back together in cases of sternotomy, and dresses the wound.

In this procedure  the provider performs closure of the chest wall after continuous drainage and irrigation of empyema  which is pus in the chest cavity. Explanation In a Clagett procedure  the provider removes a lower rib from the chest cavity and forms an open window to allow continuous drainage and irrigation of the cavity with antibiotic solution. The provider prepares a single donor lung for transplant into the patient. Explanation The provider receives the cold preserved lung allograft and places it on a sterile table  keeping the allograft in the preservation solution. He inspects the lung for suitability and begins the bench preparation by separating the upper and lower lobes. The provider examines the lung to determine the direction and completeness in the division of the lobes and to identify any abnormalities or injuries not noticed prior to procurement. The provider continues to inspect the lung  dissecting any residual soft tissue from the aorta and paying special attention to the pulmonary venous/atrial cuff  pulmonary artery  and bronchus. In this procedure  the provider removes one or more of the patient?? ribs or a section of a rib. Explanation Providers perform this procedure to treat rib fractures that could damage underlying tissues  to treat cancer or other disorders  or to use a section of a rib for a bone graft. While the patient is under anesthesia  the provider incises the skin and tissues that cover the rib that she wants to remove but does not cut through the pleural membrane. She cuts the section of rib and removes it from the chest cavity. She may also attach a bone graft or muscle flaps to repair the defect of the resection. The provider sutures the incised area closed. Terminology Pleural membrane: The membrane that covers the chest cavity. The outer layer is called the parietal pleura  and the inner layer is called the visceral pleura.

This procedure repairs the chest cavity  most typically performed to treat empyema. Explanation This procedure involves shortening ribs to treat scoliosis in order to reduce the size of a rib hump. Scoliosis causes abnormal curves of the spine. It also treats empyema  or pus in the chest cavity  and infections  such as tuberculosis. Max Schede  a German surgeon  invented the procedure  which involves removing dead tissue due to necrosis  or rotting away  of the bone. To treat empyema  the provider makes an incision in the chest to the ribs  peels away the parietal pleura  and resects the affected ribs. The provider inserts gauze to pack the area so that new tissue will form and sutures the incision closed. The provider removes the gauze in a few days. Terminology Parietal pleura: The outer layer of membrane that covers the chest cavity. The inner layer is called the visceral pleura.

In this procedure, the provider incises the chest cavity and releases the adherent lung from the surrounding chest wall tissues.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the side of the chest between two ribs. After exposing the ribs, the provider uses a spreader to spread the ribs to gain access into the chest cavity. With the help of a scalpel he releases the adhered surfaces of the outer layer of the pleura, known as parietal pleura, from the surrounding rib bones and other soft tissue structures in the chest cavity. After the procedure, the provider may fill the cavity with gauze and closes the incision.

In this procedure  the provider injects air inside the pleural cavity to partially collapse the lungs for treatment purposes  most commonly for tuberculosis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a needle attached to an air??illed syringe from the side of the chest into the space between two ribs. The tip of the needle then passes into the pleural cavity  and the provider injects air in the pleural cavity. In this procedure  the provider washes out the lung using saline water and the help of bronchoscopy. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts the scope through the nose or mouth and moves the scope down into the throat. She first places the patient on mechanical ventilation and the lung to be treated is isolated from the oxygen supply. She next advances the scope through the airways to the lung. She then  using the eyepiece  examines the mucus lining or covering of these airways and looks for any abnormality that may be present. She next introduces the saline water into the lung with the help of the bronchoscope to achieve complete degassing of the lung  and then she washes the lung. She then withdraws this fluid through suction and sends it to the lab for investigation. The provider most commonly performs this procedure to diagnose infection or lung cancer and to treat certain lung diseases. Terminology Bronchoscopy: A procedure in which the provider inserts a flexible or rigid tube  called a bronchoscope  through the nose or mouth to perform visual examination of the airways. Lavage: Washing out. Mechanical ventilation: Breathing support using an external machine. Tips Use one unit of this code for each lung if lavage is performed in both lungs. In total lung lavage  the provider uses general anesthesia  and it is a very complex procedure performed in an operating room. The provider most commonly performs total lung lavage for management of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis  a rare lung disease in which protein build up in the lungs clogs the air sacs. Read Less

The provider uses a needle inserted through the chest wall and into the pericardium to drain fluid from the pericardial space; imaging guidance is included in this code when performed. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider selects a site typically between the xiphoid process and the left sternocostal margin. The provider may create a small incision to reduce needle resistance and then advances a needle attached to a syringe or suction device into the pericardial space. The provider often uses fluoroscopic or ultrasound imaging guidance to ensure accuracy of the needle placement. The provider identifies the proper location and then aspirates fluid from the pericardial sac into the syringe  after which he withdraws the needle. Pericardiocentesis may be performed to relieve pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade as well as for diagnostic  palliative  or prophylactic purposes. Terminology Anomaly: An organ or body part that is not normal structurally or functionally  is out of place  or is absent; typically describes a congenital deformity. Aspiration: Removal of fluid  gas  or other material through a tube attached to a suction device  often for laboratory analysis or combined with irrigation  the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen  stomach  lungs  or joints; also  breathing in or sucking in food  fluid  or a foreign object into the airway. Cardiac tamponade: Accumulation of fluid within the pericardial sac so severe that it compresses the heart  preventing the ventricle from filling with blood and compromising heart function; it is a medical emergency and must be treated quickly. Fluoroscopy: A live X??ay where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Indwelling catheter or stent: A hollow tube left temporarily or permanently implanted in a body passage or organ  such as the bladder  to promote drainage  administer fluids or gases  provide access by surgical instruments  and other functions. Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Pericardial sac: A sac that contains the heart and the roots of the great vessels (the vessels that transport blood to and from the heart); also known as the pericardium. Pericardial space: A space between the layers of the sac surrounding the heart. Sternocostal margin: The area where the rib (costal) cartilages meet the sternum (breast bone); also referred to as sternochondral joints or costosternal joints. Ultrasound: The use of high??requency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Xiphoid: Bony process (protuberance) found at the lowest portion of the sternum (breastbone). Tips Imaging guidance  if performed  is included with this code. Do not report separately. For percutaneous pericardial drainage with insertion of an indwelling catheter  with or without fluoroscopy and/or ultrasound guidance  in a patient 6 years old and older without congenital cardiac anomaly  report 33017  and for the same procedure in a newborn through 5 years of age or in a patient of any age with congenital cardiac anomaly  report 33018. For percutaneous pericardial drainage with insertion of indwelling catheter under computed tomography (CT) imaging guidance  report 33019. Read Less

The provider uses a needle inserted through the chest wall to drain fluid from around the heart; he also inserts a catheter and leaves it indwelling for continued drainage. The provider removes a clot or foreign body from pericardial space. The provider creates an opening in the pericardium to facilitate drainage of pericardial fluids. The provider removes a tumor from the heart with the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass. She institutes cardiopulmonary bypass  often by cannulating blood vessels through this incision. The provider uses laser revascularization to restore blood flow to the heart using a thoracotomy for approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider approaches the heart via thoracotomy  opens the pericardium  and identifies the ischemic area. She then places a laser probe in contact with the epicardium and vaporizes the myocardium in its path. A small channel extends from the heart's surface to the ventricular cavity. The provider inserts one or more electrodes on the epicardial surface and pericardium as necessary through an open incision. The provider removes a previously placed pacemaker pulse generator from the patient and replaces it with a new one. The provider performs this procedure primarily for artificial regulation of heart beats by the device in patients with arrhythmia, which is irregular heart rhythm. He performs this procedure for a patient with a lead in a single chamber of the heart.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the skin of the subcutaneous pocket enclosing the existing generator. He then frees the existing generator from the fibrous adhesions surrounding it, and also separates the lead from the extensive fibrous adhesions in the pocket, taking care to protect the lead from any damage. He tests the existing lead for proper functionality.

If needed, he goes on to adapt the existing skin pocket to the dimensions of the new generator. He cleans the pocket by irrigating it with saline. He then places the new generator for the single lead system into the pocket and attaches it to the existing lead. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the skin pocket with sutures. He may alternatively use staples or tissue adhesive for the closure. The provider programs the device for functionality.


Terminology
Lead: Insulated wires that conduct electrical impulse from one end, attached to the pulse generator, to the other end positioned in the heart chamber.

Pacemaker: A device that continuously senses, monitors, and regulates the heart rate.

Pulse generator: A device that produces electrical signals that can make the heart beat.

Subcutaneous: Just underneath the skin.


Tips
You may report 33227 in circumstances when the provider removes a dual lead device, caps one lead and places it in the pocket, and attaches the other lead to the new device he inserts in place.

Code 33227 includes radiological supervision and interpretation related to the procedure as well.
