In this procedure, the provider repairs a wound to the heart without the need to place the patient on a cardiopulmonary bypass, or CPB, machine.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and taking emergency requirements into account, the provider performs a thoracotomy, or incision in the chest wall. Alternatively, she may access the heart through the sternum in a procedure known as a sternotomy. She then uses a rib spreader to allow access to the pericardium. She may create a window in the pericardial sac if she is unsure of an injury to the heart, and when a wound of the heart is known, she opens the pericardial sac.

She removes clotted blood and fluid, and she may use her finger, clamps, or a catheter to achieve hemostasis until she can close the wound. The provider thoroughly inspects the heart to identify and repair all wounds and may possibly suture over a small pad or synthetic graft material to anchor the stitches and close a wound. The provider then closes the incision and may insert chest or drainage tubes.


Terminology
Cardiopulmonary bypass, or CPB: Technique used during surgery that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs to maintain the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body; it allows the patient's blood to bypass the heart and lungs, and gives the provider a still operative field; a pump, oxygenator, cannula, and tubing together are often called a heart lung machine or pump; the use of CPB may be called on bypass or on the pump.

Catheter: A catheter is a tube that the provider inserts into a body cavity, duct, or vessel; catheters allow drainage, administration of fluids or gases, or access for surgical instruments; the process of inserting a catheter is called catheterization.

Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow.

Pericardial sac: The wall of protective tissue surrounding the heart; also known as the pericardium.

Thoracotomy: Surgical incision of the chest wall to expose organs such as the heart, lungs, esophagus or food pipe, or anterior spine, to diagnose a condition, disease or injury.


Tips

The provider performs a complex series of procedures to improve blood flow in and out of the heart and prevent further complications such as congestive heart failure and pulmonary hypertension. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the chest  typically a median sternotomy. He places the patient on cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). In the Norwood procedure  the provider performs an atrial septectomy  excising some of the atrial septum. He divides the ductus  the blood vessel that connects the left pulmonary artery to the descending aorta  and the main pulmonary trunk. He closes the pulmonary artery with a patch. He removes remaining ductal tissue under the aortic arch and makes an incision down the descending aorta. He uses a patch to enlarge the aorta and places a conduit between the superior vena cava and the pulmonary trunk  bypassing the atrium. The provider then examines the bands around the right and left pulmonary arteries. He carefully probes the main pulmonary artery through the tricuspid valve and ventricular outflow tract and also assesses the pulmonary artery branches. If the main pulmonary artery is badly stenosed  he enlarges the area with a bovine pericardial patch graft. If the narrowing is less significant  he excises the narrowed area and performs an end to end anastomosis (connection) of the pulmonary artery. The provider closes the incisions in the heart  takes the patient off CPB  checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the incision in the chest. The provider closes a sinus venosus defect directly or with a patch in a patient with or without anomalous pulmonary venous drainage. Explanation Most of the sinus venosus atrial septal defects (ASDs) can be closed with a simple autologous intracardiac pericardial patch. With the patient appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia  the provider makes an incision in the midline of the chest  dissecting down to the heart. She opens the atrium and typically starts a suture line between the orifice of the right superior pulmonary vein and the orifice of the superior vena cava. After completing the sutures in the superior location  she carries the suture line along the remaining orifice of the ASD. To prevent superior vena cava stenosis  she sometimes employs a "two??atch technique " in which she places a second pericardial patch on the superior vena cava. If the patient also has anomalous pulmonary venous drainage  where the pulmonary veins do not connect to the left atrium  she repairs that defect as well. Finally  after closing down the sinus venosus ASD and connecting the pulmonary veins to the left atrium  if necessary  she closes the atrium and eventually the skin incision to complete the surgery. Sinus venosus defects nearly always require closure with a patch because of their location at the junction between the superior vena cava and the right atrium. The goal of sinus venosus repair is to eliminate the intracardiac shunt without causing stenosis or obstruction of the pulmonary veins  right ventricle  or superior vena cava. Superior vena cava: A wide but short vein that returns blood to the heart from the upper part of the body. Based on the severity of the defect  sometimes the valve is replaced with a mechanical or tissue valve. Explanation A transitional atrioventricular canal defect is a combination of both the partial as well as complete atrioventricular canal defect. Also  the atrioventricular valves may only be partially separated into two valves. Under general anesthesia an incision is carried out through middle of the chest  and the heart is exposed. Cardiopulmonary bypass is started and the right atrium is emptied. A hole in the right atrium or in one of the ventricles is made. The hole in the ventricle is made in the area of the scar (if the ventricular septal defect is due to ischemia) or in the anterior part of the right ventricle (if the ventricular septal defect is congenital). In this procedure, the provider inserts a catheter through a vessel and threads the catheter into the right side of the heart under imaging guidance. The provider creates an opening between the atria, or upper chambers of the heart, to improve atrial flow in a patient with a cardiac birth defect.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision to access a vessel and introduce a catheter, for instance in the groin to access the femoral vein. Under imaging guidance, he advances the catheter over a guidewire into the heart. 

The provider creates an opening in the septum wall between the atria through any method, such as balloon atrial septostomy, Rashkind's (balloon) procedure, or blade atrial septostomy. These are minimally invasive procedures that help remove a restrictive congenital interatrial communication and improve oxygenation of the blood.

The provider withdraws the catheter and any other instruments and applies pressure to the wound to control bleeding.


Terminology
Atrium: One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle.

Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder.

Congenital interatrial communication: An opening in the interatrial septum, the wall that divides the atrial chambers in the heart, from a birth defect or surgically created to bypass an undeveloped heart chamber, another type of heart defect


Tips
This procedure includes percutaneous access, placing one or more access sheaths, advancing the delivery system using the catheter, and creating the opening between the atria. These procedures should not be separately reported.

In this procedure  the provider surgically repairs a cardiac defect present since birth  in which the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle. In this procedure  the provider makes an incision over a cluster of varicose veins and removes the entire cluster or a segment of the cluster. The provider performs penile vein ligation to prevent venous leakage or the return of venous blood to the body during erection to treat erectile dysfunction. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the inguinal area near the penis. He dissects down through tissues to expose the deep dorsal vein and its tributaries  excising and ligating (tying off) the vein and its tributaries. He may also ligate the cavernosal and crural veins. These veins drain the corpora cavernosa after ejaculation. After tying off the veins  he closes the incision in layers with sutures. This procedure is used to treat erectile dysfunction (ED) in males caused by penile vein leakage or corporal veno??cclusive dysfunction (CVOD)  a common cause of ED. Normally  during erection  these veins constrict to keep the blood in the corpora cavernosa until the individual ejaculates or is no longer sexually stimulated. When the veins fail to constrict or relax prematurely  blood flows out of the corpora cavernosa and the erection softens. Tying off the veins prevents the premature outflow of blood. Terminology Corpora cavernosa: Spongelike tissue in the penile shaft region which contains most of the blood that is in the penis during an erection; singular  corpus cavernosum. Ejaculation: The release of semen by a male during sexual excitement. Erectile dysfunction: The inability to achieve or maintain an erection of the penis. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider makes an incision into the abdominal cavity and repairs the damaged area of the spleen with sutures. He may also excise a portion of the spleen if that part of spleen is irreparable. He performs this procedure most often for trauma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises the abdomen just below the left ribs. He exposes the spleen and assesses the area of damage. After the procedure is complete  the provider irrigates the surgical site  controls all bleeding  and closes the surgical wound in layers. Terminology Hematoma: A localized collection of blood in the tissue outside the blood vessels. Laparoscope: An instrument with a camera attached to it  that a provider uses to perform exploration and surgeries in the abdominal cavity. Laparoscopy: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen  inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure  inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen  and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open  removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure  and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. In this procedure, the provider performs a complete excision of the spleen using a laparoscope.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in different locations of the abdomen. Through the incision near the navel he insufflates, or blows gas into the abdomen. This lifts the abdominal wall away from the organs and improves visualization. He makes additional small incisions and through those he inserts a laparoscopic camera and instruments to perform the procedure.

He accesses the spleen with the laparoscope and releases the spleen from the surrounding structures. He then ligates, or ties off, the arteries and veins of the spleen and dissects them. In addition, he incises all the ligaments supporting the spleen to completely free it. He then removes the spleen in its entirety from one of the incisions by inserting a surgical bag into one of the incisions and placing the spleen into the bag. The provider may morcellate, or cut the spleen into small strips or pieces within the bag, or he removes the spleen in its entirety. After the procedure is complete, the provider irrigates the surgical sites, obtains hemostasis, and closes the wounds with sutures.


Terminology
Hemostasis: Stoppage of bleeding from incisions and suture lines.

Laparoscope: An instrument with a camera attached to it, that a provider uses to perform exploration and surgeries in the abdominal cavity.

Laparoscopy: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen, inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure, inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open, removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures.

Ligation:  Using sutures or wire to close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure.

Morecellator: Surgical instrument used to divide and remove large masses of tissue during laparoscopic surgery.

Rupture: A tear in a structure due to injury.

Spleen: An abdominal organ which helps in blood cell production and immunity.

Splenectomy: Surgical excision of the spleen.


Tips
To report a splenectomy with an open approach, see codes 38100, Splenectomy; total, separate procedure or 38101, Splenectomy; partial, separate procedure.

The provider manages the search for a suitable donor and acquisition of hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) compatible with the recipient. Explanation The provider manages a team that reviews the records for potential donors and screens them for compatibility as donors for bone marrow or stem cells. Terminology Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood??orming cells found in the bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells.

The provider manages the process of preparing already frozen and stored hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) for transplantation. The provider thaws each donor?? cells without washing the cells to remove the cryoprotective solution. Explanation The process of thawing the HPCs requires precision in changing the temperature as it may destroy the cells if not done correctly. The provider assures that the temperature for thawing the solution is precisely at 37 degrees Celsius  as this is the optimal temperature to liquefy the cells without damaging the cells. The provider performs this procedure quite rapidly to prevent damage to the cells. Then he immediately infuses or processes the cells further without washing them. Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood??orming cells found in bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells. In this procedure  the provider manages the process of preparing already frozen and stored hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) for transplantation. The provider thaws each donor?? cells and washes it to remove the cryoprotective solution. He performs this service to remove the solution as well as to remove hemoglobin and debris to make the cells ready for transplantation. Explanation The process of thawing the frozen HPCs requires precision in changing the temperature as it may destroy the cells if not done correctly. The provider assures that the temperature for thawing the solution is precisely at 37 degrees Celsius  as this is the optimal temperature to liquefy the cells without damaging the cells. The provider performs this procedure quite rapidly to prevent damage to the cells. The provider additionally washes the cryoprotective solution off the cells. Depending upon the type of cells to wash  the provider may dilute the solution with saline  centrifuge the solution  and again add more saline then repeat the centrifuge cycle. Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood??orming cells found in the bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells. The provider prepares the hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) solution in such a way as to remove the greatest number of red blood cells to minimize transplant complications  especially when transplanting cryopreserved cells such as marrow. Explanation After the provider harvests  preserves  and thaws the hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs)  he prepares the solution for transplant using techniques to ensure there are the fewest possible red blood cells present. This process helps to minimize the risk of ABO incompatibility and avoids the agglutination process. The provider may perform centrifugation  apheresis  or he may use cell washers  most commonly buffered saline  to separate cells and plasma from the rest of the HPC solution. Terminology ABO incompatibility: An abnormal reaction between blood cells of incompatible blood groups; this results in the destruction of blood cells and the formation of clumps. Agglutination: Abnormal clumping of particles of any substances  most commonly in case of abnormal clumping of blood cells due to contact between incompatible blood groups. Apheresis: A procedure in which the blood of a donor or patient is passed through an apparatus that separates out one particular constituent and returns the remainder to the circulation. Centrifuge: Use of centrifugal force to separate solids suspended in a liquid medium. Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood??orming cells found in bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells. Tips Report this service only once per day. The provider takes one or more samples of bone marrow from the sternum or pelvic bone for diagnostic purposes only. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a trocar down to the bone or cuts a small opening into the bone  typically in the sternum of the chest or the iliac crest in the pelvic area  and collects a small amount of bone marrow for testing only. After scraping or excising out a bone marrow specimen in a small chunk  he transfers the sample to a container or slide for analysis. Finally  he removes the trocar or bone blade and covers the bone defect. He may place a single suture or use adhesive strips to close the skin incision. The procedure usually takes place in a minor procedure room or special suite for bone marrow procedures. Terminology Bone marrow: The spongy tissue inside the large bones; it is the place where new blood cells are produced. Iliac crest: Upper rounded portion of the pelvic bone. Pelvis: The hip bone  sacrum  the large triangular bone at the lower end of the spinal column  and coccyx or tailbone; often used to refer to the hip bones alone; may be used to refer to the pelvic cavity. Sternum: Breastbone  at the front of the rib cage. Trocar: A hollow pointed puncturing device  typically part of a cannula and trocar combination  usually in crisscross shape. Tips Code 38221 describes bone marrow sampling to obtain bone marrow for diagnostic purposes only. It does not involve obtaining a sufficient amount of bone marrow for transplant purposes  and a provider would not separately report this code if he performs this service at the same time as harvesting bone marrow for transplantation. If the provider performs a bone marrow aspiration for diagnostic purposes  see 38220  but if he performs a combined aspiration/biopsy  see 38222. Read Less

The provider takes a scraping or sample of bone marrow tissue  using biopsy and aspiration techniques  for diagnostic purposes. Bone marrow aspiration is typically performed prior to the biopsy when both are performed. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider performs an aspiration procedure to obtain a bone marrow sample. The provider inserts a specially designed needle with an attached syringe through the skin  generally in the sternum of the chest  and pushes the needle in a rotating manner into the bone marrow. After confirmation of the needle position  he aspirates (sucks out) liquid bone marrow tissue and transfers it to a container or slides for analysis. He removes the needle slowly and controls the bleeding with pressure at the needle insertion site. For the biopsy  the provider inserts a trocar through the skin  generally the iliac crest in the pelvic area  and into the bone marrow. After confirmation of the instrument?? position  he extracts a core of bone marrow tissue. He then transfers the sample to a container or slide for analysis. Finally  he removes the instrument slowly and controls the bleeding with pressure at the insertion site. The procedure usually takes place in a minor procedure room or special suite for bone marrow procedures. Terminology Bone marrow: The spongy tissue inside the large bones; it is the place where new blood cells are produced. Iliac crest: Upper rounded portion of the pelvic bone. Sternum: Breastbone  at the front of the rib cage. Trocar: A hollow  pointed puncturing device  typically part of a cannula and trocar combination  usually in crisscross shape. Tips This code combines 38220 (bone marrow aspiration) and 38221 (bone marrow biopsy)  so you would not report either of those codes in conjunction with this one. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider aspirates bone marrow tissue with the help of a needle  to place it back into the bone marrow cavity of the same patient  typically at a later date. Tips Report code 38230 if the provider harvests the donated tissue from someone other than the recipient. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider introduces into the blood stream of a recipient the hematopoietic progenitor cells  or HPCs  which he harvests from another donor. Explanation Hematopoietic known as blood forming progenitor cells (HPCs) is the name for the cell found in the bone marrow and also known as the parent cell from which other blood cells develop. The three main types of blood cells are red blood cell  white blood cell  and platelets. Progenitor cell transplant is a special treatment consisting of high doses of chemotherapy and then progenitor cell infusion. The goal is to provide complete suppression of the immune system so that the recipient's body does not reject these foreign cells from another person's body. After the provider collects hematopoietic progenitor cells from a donor?? bone marrow  he injects the cells into the recipient through an intravenous drip  under completely sterile conditions. Terminology Allogenic: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called allograft and homograft. Bone marrow: The spongy tissue inside the large bones; it is the place where new blood cells are produced. Chemotherapy: Use of chemical agents that the provider administers directly into circulation through a vein or artery to kill fast growing cells in the body  typically cancer. Hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs): Specialized blood??orming cells found in bone marrow that can develop itself into different types of blood cells. Intravenous: Within a vein. Platelets: One of three primary cell types in blood  which aids in clot formation to stop bleeding. Tips Report this code if HPC transplantation is done for a patient that is genetically different but from the same species. Read Less

In this procedure the provider incises or performs other procedures to improve lymph flow or drain any infection of a lymph node or the lymphatic channels.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider may incise the lymph node or structure of the lymphatic channel. The exact procedure varies as per the condition which requires treatment.  Opening of the lymph node channel may be done to remove a blockage or to drain an infection. The procedure might also involve dissection of entrapping tissue to allow lymphatic fluid to move through the area.

Another procedure might require an incision into the skin over the lymph nodes of the neck to remove a tumor, known as a lymphangioma. When the provider exposes the tumor, he dissects surrounding structures away from the tumor, and he removes the tumor. After completion of any procedure, the provider closes the wound in layers, and he may place drains and cover the wound with a sterile dressing or leave the wound open to drain.


Terminology
Lymph node: Collection of lymph tissue spread thorough out the body; or a knot or swelling at various spots along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system maintains fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system.

Lymphangiotomy: Incision of a lymph node.

Lymphatic channel: Network of lymph nodes and lymph vessels which is present in entire body.

In this procedure  the provider repairs the cervical thoracic duct using sutures or by tying it off. The provider accesses the duct through an incision in the neck to reach the thoracic duct. The most common reason for repair is a penetrating trauma to the chest. The provider carefully dissects the collar bone to reach the area of the proximal thoracic duct. The provider takes care not to damage the critical structures in this area including the trachea  or windpipe  proximal esophagus or food pipe  aorta  and other large arteries and veins. The provider identifies the area of concern and depending on the condition to be treated  uses sutures to repair the damage or to encircle the duct and tie it off. When the procedure is complete  he approximates the tissue in layers and the closes the neck incision. Thoracic duct: The main vessel passing upwards in front of the spine and draining into the vein near the base of the neck. Vein: Blood vessel that carries blood from the rest of the body to the heart for purification. Tips Separate codes exist for procedures on the thoracic duct via cervical  thoracic  and abdominal approaches. The approaches require different work so the provider must assign the code carefully after reviewing the approach in the documentation. All codes are for an open approach. There are no codes for an endoscopic approach  for example if a provider performs a mediastinoscopy to the thoracic duct and if the provider uses a scope to perform the procedure  report 38999  Unlisted procedure  hemic or lymphatic system. The provider performs an open excision or biopsy of the lymph nodes lying near the surface of the body using a scalpel. The provider commonly performs this procedure to identify and diagnose the cause of disease in the lymph nodes or surrounding tissues. In this procedure  the provider can excise any superficial node. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises the skin over the underlying affected lymph node. Typically  the procedure involves a lymph node near the surface of the skin so that a simple incision is adequate for exposure. The provider identifies the target lymph node or nodes and removes the node in whole or in part using a scalpel. He approximates the tissues in layers and closes the incision. If the provider performs this procedure for biopsy of a node or nodes  the provider takes more samples than in a needle biopsy and sends the specimens to the laboratory for testing. The sample is sent to the laboratory for indication of infection or disease. Terminology Biopsy: Examination of tissue a provider removes from a living body to discover the cause or severity of a disease. Lymph node: A knot or swelling at various spots along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system maintains fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Superficial lymph node: A lymph node that lies near the surface of the body. Tips Report code 38500 only once no matter how many nodes a provider biopsies in the same area. However  if the provider performs biopsies in other areas  report the code again with modifier 59  Distinct procedural service to indicate that a different area was tested. Biopsies on the contralateral  or opposite side may be coded with modifier 50  Bilateral procedure. Read Less

The provider performs an open excision or biopsy of the lymph nodes lying deep in the neck using a scalpel. The provider commonly performs this procedure to identify and diagnose the cause of disease in the lymph node or surrounding tissues. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider adjusts the neck of the patient to improve access to the target area. The provider uses a scalpel to incise the skin and dissect the tissue overlying the target node or nodes  taking care to preserve critical nerves and other structures in the area. The provider then excises the lymph node or nodes and approximates the tissues in layers. The provider may place a drain and suture it to the skin to drain blood or other fluids while the wound heals. Finally  he closes the incision with sutures. If  however  it shows the presence of disease  the provider may remove additional nodes as necessary. This process is known as a sentinel node biopsy. He excises the lymph node(s) and reapproximates the axillary tissues and skin in layers. He may leave a drain the deeper part of the wound and suture it to the skin to drain blood or other fluids while the wound heals. The provider excises lymph nodes from the retroperitoneal area  behind and outside the peritoneum and near the aorta or spleen to stage of cancer in these areas. Using the pathology results  he identifies the number and location of nodes with metastatic cancer and stages the cancer using this information. In cases of extensive metastatic cancer  the provider may sample lymph nodes in adjacent areas in order to identify the extent of the disease and plan treatment. The provider then approximates the tissues in layers and closes the abdominal wound. The provider incises either the thorax, or the sternum, or breastbone to reach the mediastinum. He inspects the mediastinum and removes a tumor. 



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider positions the patient for a median sternotomy incision, or in a left or right lateral position for thoracotomy, depending upon the location of the tumor. For a thoracotomy, the provider incises the ribs and uses a rib spreader as necessary to ease access to the target area. In a sternal approach, he incises the chest from the sternal notch to the xiphoid process and splits the sternal bone to access the space between the lungs.

He then carefully inspects the mediastinum for any signs of disease. He removes any benign or malignant tumors found. The provider ensures that he stops all bleeding. Once the procedure is complete, the provider reapproximates the tissue between the ribs in layers to close a thoracotomy approach, or he wires the sternum together and closes the soft tissue in layers over the bone for closure of a median sternotomy incision.


Terminology
Aorta: The main artery that comes out of the top of the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood to the body; consists of an ascending and descending aorta which serve the upper and lower parts of the body respectively.

Benign: Not malignant, generally treatable or not needing treatment.

Inferior vena cava: The major trunk of the venous circulatory system that brings blood back from the lower body circulation, the abdominal and pelvic organs, and the extremities.

Malignant: Cancerous, capable of spreading and causing death if untreated.

Mediastinal tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass of cells, can be benign or cancerous; found in the mediastinum.

Median sternotomy: A surgical procedure in which the provider makes a vertical inline incision along the sternum or the breastbone.

Mediastinum: Partition between two body cavities or two parts of an organ such as the mass of tissues and organs in the middle of the chest between the lungs.

Pulmonary artery: The major artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

Pulmonary vein: The primary vein that returns oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

Superior vena cava: The major trunk of the venous circulatory system that brings blood back to the heart from the upper body circulation, chest, arms, head, and neck.

Sternal notch: A large, visible dip present at the superior border of the sternum or breastbone.

Thoracotomy: Surgical incision of the chest.

Xiphoid process: The smallest and lowest division of the sternum or breastbone that is flexible early in life but becomes more or less rigid during adulthood.


Tips
Report code 39220 to describe excision of any benign or malignant tumor in the mediastinal space that a provider removes by open approach, except tumors of the heart and or great vessels such as the aorta, superior or inferior vena cava, caval trunk, pulmonary artery, or pulmonary vein. The provider should wait for the results of pathologic examination before coding so that diagnoses will be as accurate as possible unless previous biopsy has already found that the mass is malignant.

There is no code for excision of a mediastinal tumor via mediastinoscopy so report 39499, Unlisted procedure, mediastinum, to describe that service.

A cleft lip is a congenital defect that occurs when the lip doesn't fully fuse during development. The provider can treat a cleft lip once the baby is ten weeks old, weighs ten pounds, and is in good health to tolerate surgery. The provider may do several procedures to correct the cleft lip.

Report 40700, Plastic repair of cleft lip or nasal deformity; primary, partial or complete, unilateral and 40701, or 40702, Plastic repair of cleft lip or nasal deformity; primary bilateral, 1 of 2 stages, depending on whether the surgery is unilateral or bilateral and the provider performs the service in one or two stages.

The provider uses a pedicle flap from the bottom lip  known as an Abbe Estlander flap to repair a cleft lip and or nasal deformity. This procedure involves sectioning or dissecting a pedicle in the lower lip and inserting it in the upper lip. The provider performs this procedure to close the cleft lip or correct the nasal deformity  which also adds to the cosmetic appearance of the patient. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises either side of the margins of the cleft surface from the mouth to the nostril. He carries the incision through the full thickness of the mucosa  muscle  and skin. He corrects the vermilion border by turning the tissue downward to restore a normal shape. The provider then brings the muscles and skin together to close the cleft lip  maintaining muscle function. The provider next incises and creates a full thickness pedicle flap from skin on the lower lip  the location of which he determines by the presence of a sufficient blood supply. He rotates the flap on its pedicle to the desired location in the upper lip and sutures it in place. If a nasal deformity is present  the provider also repairs the affected tissue. He closes the prepared margins in layers from the intraoral mucosa through the muscle and finally closes the skin. Terminology Abbe Estlander operation: Transfer of a full thickness section of one lip to the other lip ensuring survival of the graft. Vermilion border: The external red area of the upper and lower lips that extends from where the surrounding facial skin connects on the exterior of the lip to the labial mucosa  or the inside lining of the lips. The provider removes all or part of the tongue, as well as part of the jaw bone and the tissue of the floor of the mouth using extraoral (outside the mouth) and intraoral (inside the mouth) incisions. This procedure does not include radical neck dissection. This procedure is most often used to treat cancer.



Explanation
The provider performs a glossectomy, where he removes all or part of the tongue, cauterizing tissue as needed to help control bleeding. He removes the tongue and sutures the wound closed. He also removes affected tissue from the mandible (jaw bone) and the tissue of the floor of the mouth using extraoral (outside the mouth) and intraoral (inside the mouth) incisions.

After removing the affected portions of the mandible, the provider places a metal plate or bone graft to reestablish continuity of the mandible. If needed, the metal plate is replaced with a bone graft during a later procedure. The provider closes the incisions with sutures, which might include skin or mucosal grafts. This procedure does not include radical neck dissection. This procedure is most often used to treat cancer.


Terminology

Hyoid bone: A small bone at the base of the lower jaw that is shaped like the letter U and serves to support the tongue to facilitate speech and swallowing; it is the only bone in the human body that does not connect to any other bone and is instead connected only through muscle tissue.

Lymph nodes: Small nodules at various points along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system returns fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system.

Radical resection (or dissection): Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed.

Resection: Surgical excision (removal) of tissues, organs, or other structures, in whole or in part.

Tracheostomy: A surgical procedure in which the provider makes an incision into the trachea or windpipe, through the neck, and inserts a tube to make an artificial opening to assist breathing; also tracheotomy.

During this procedure  the provider performs a major revision of a prior cleft palate repair (palatoplasty). Explanation During palatoplasty  the provider performs a major revision of a previous cleft palate repair. The defect  such as wound splitting  infection or scarring  determines which repair the surgeon performs. There are numerous techniques for cleft palate repair  depending on whether the repair is of the hard palate or soft palate  age of the patient  and whether the repair is performed at a single session or in stages. Techniques are still evolving as there is no one ideal technique. An improperly repaired cleft palate can lead to oral/nasal recommunication  developmental growth restrictions  or velopharyngeal incompetence. With the patient placed supine (face up) with the neck extended  appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia  the provider inserts an endotracheal (ET) tube through the mouth and places a mouth gag. He injects an epinephrine/saline solution into the area to be operated to constrict the vessels and help minimize bleeding. Depending on the technique employed  the provider corrects the abnormal position of the soft palate muscles  which may involve moving them retrograde (toward the back) and creates a muscle sling. If wound splitting has occurred  he may create flaps to cover the defect and any raw areas caused by the excision of scars or excision of infected tissues. He corrects any other defects caused by the previous palatoplasty and finally closes the remaining defect with tension??ree sutures. If the uvula is involved  he repairs it to a more normal contour and position. He irrigates the operative field and checks for bleeding after which he removes the ET tube and mouth gag. Terminology Cleft palate: Congenital defect in which a cleft (gap) occurs in the palate at its midline  often occurring in conjunction with a cleft lip. Endotracheal tube: A flexible tube inserted into the trachea via the nose or mouth to maintain an open airway. Palatoplasty: A surgical procedure to correct or reconstruct the palate  as in a person with cleft palate  and restore the palate's function. Velopharyngeal incompetence: Improper closure of the velopharyngeal sphincter (muscle of the soft palate)  resulting in difficulty in feeding and/or a voice resonance disorder. Tips For other palatoplasty procedures  see 42200 through 42225. For other repair procedures of the palate  see 42226 through 42235. Some of the techniques for palatoplasty that you may see in the documentation include von Langenbeck's bipedicle flap technique  Veau??ardill??ilner Pushback technique  Bardach's two??lap technique  Furlow Double opposing Z??lasty  two??tage palatal repair  hole??n??ne repair  raw area free palatoplasty  alveolar extension palatoplasty (AEP)  primary pharyngeal flap  intravelar veloplasty  vomer flap  and buccal myomucosal flap. Every surgeon  even if he uses a particular technique  may modify the procedure. Read Less

The provider repairs a cleft palate (palatoplasty) which includes secondary lengthening of the soft palate. Explanation Cleft palate is a congenital defect that occurs when the palate's median line doesn't fuse together properly during development. With a cleft palate  the main muscle of soft palate (the levator muscle) is abnormally attached to the posterior edge of the hard palate and to the cleft sides. There are numerous techniques for cleft palate repair (palatoplasty)  depending on whether the repair is of the hard palate or soft palate  the age of the patient  and whether the repair is performed at a single setting or in stages. Techniques are still evolving as there is no one ideal technique. An improperly repaired cleft palate can lead to oral/nasal recommunication  developmental growth restrictions  or velopharyngeal incompetence. With the patient placed supine (face up) with the neck extended  appropriately prepped  and under general anesthesia  the provider inserts an endotracheal (ET) tube through the mouth and places a mouth gag. He injects an epinephrine/saline solution into the area to be operated to constrict the vessels and help minimize bleeding. Depending on the technique employed  the provider corrects the abnormal position of the soft palate muscles  which may involve moving them retrograde (toward the back) and creates a muscle sling. He may create flaps to cover the cleft defect and any raw areas caused by the revision. The provider may use various techniques to lengthen the soft palate. For example  he may make a horizontal back??ut in the nasal lining at the junction of hard and soft palate and cover the raw area with a local flap like a vomer flap or buccal mucosal flap. Alternatively  he may create a double reverse Z??lasty for the oral and nasal surfaces of the soft palate with transposition of the triangles  which lengthens the soft palate. He finally closes the remaining defect(s) with tension??ree sutures. If the patient has a bifid (split) uvula  he repairs it to more normal contour and position. He irrigates the operative field and checks for bleeding after which he removes the ET tube and mouth gag. Terminology Buccal: Pertaining to the inside of the cheeks. Cleft palate: Congenital defect in which a cleft (gap) occurs in the palate at its midline  often occurring in conjunction with a cleft lip. Endotracheal tube: A flexible tube inserted into the trachea via the nose or mouth to maintain an open airway. Mucosa: Another name for mucous membrane  the moisture??aden layer of endothelial cells that line the insides of body cavities and the insides of structures that open to the outside of the body  such as the nose  mouth  and rectum. Palatoplasty: A surgical procedure to correct or reconstruct the palate  as in a person with cleft palate  and restore the palate's function. Vomer: A facial bone of the skull that forms the posterior end of the nasal septum. Tips For other palatoplasty procedures  see 42205 through 42225. For other repair procedures of the palate  see 42226 through 42235. Additional Info Some of the techniques for palatoplasty that you may see in the documentation include von Langenbeck's bipedicle flap technique  Veau??ardill??ilner Pushback technique  Bardach's two??lap technique  Furlow Double opposing Z??lasty  two??tage palatal repair  hole??n??ne repair  raw area free palatoplasty  alveolar extension palatoplasty (AEP)  primary pharyngeal flap  intralveolar veloplasty  vomer flap  and buccal myomucosal flap. Every surgeon  even if he uses a particular technique  may modify the procedure. Read Less

The provider lengthens the soft palate by creating island flaps in the mucosal tissue and suturing them in new positions. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes incisions at the junction of the hard and soft palate to resurface the oral defect. He harvests a palatal island flap made of nutrient vessels and rotates it 180 degrees to widen the palate without strangulation of the vascular pedicle which traverses a bony canal. The donor site is then allowed to heal by secondary intention. Terminology Flap: Tissue for grafting  typically removed from one place on the body and positioned in another; however  it may remain anchored and rotated from one side of an area to another. Hard palate: The anterior  or front  portion of the palate that forms the roof of the mouth and separates the oral and the nasal cavities. Mucosa: A moist lining of on the inner surface of many body structures  such as the mouth  nose  and lungs. Palate: The roof of the mouth that partially or completely separates the nasal cavity and the oral cavity; consists of the soft palate and hard palate. Soft palate: The back portion of the mouth composed mostly of muscular tissue; also called the velum. Tips If the provider uses a pharyngeal flap to lengthen the soft palate  see 42226. For cleft palate palatoplasty  see 42200 to 42225. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider repairs a nasolabial fistula  an abnormal connection between the nasal cavity and the space under the upper lip. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider repairs the fistula  an abnormal passage between the nasal region and the region under the upper lip. If the fistula is small in size  he excises tissue around the fistula and then sutures the wound in layers. For a larger fistula  the provider may excise the abnormal passage and then apply a flap created from nearby tissue over the site. He checks for any bleeding and closes the site with sutures in layers. Terminology Fistula: Abnormal passageway between the structures such as vessels  vessels and organs  or skin and organs or abdominal cavity. Flap: Tissue for grafting typically removed from one place on the body and positioned in another; however  it may remain anchored and rotated from one side of an area to another. Nasolabial region: The area between the nose and the lips. Tips A nasolabial fistula may occur in a patient born with a cleft palate. For plastic repair of cleft lip or nasal deformity  see codes such as 40700 to 40761. Read Less

The provider takes an impression for later building of a maxillary arch prosthesis  often used in patients with a cleft palate. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped  the provider takes an impression of the patient?? upper intraoral structure using a special material. The impressions allow for the creation of molds  which then allow for the creation of the palatal prosthesis. Taking care with the impression helps ensure the prosthesis will fit accurately in the patient?? mouth. The goal of the procedure is to create a prosthesis  such as one that restores the function of speech and feeding that the presence of the cleft palate affects. Terminology Cleft palate: Congenital defect in which a cleft  or gap  occurs in the palate at its midline  often occurring in conjunction with a cleft lip. Maxillary arch: The upper arch and the bone supporting it  called the maxilla  which forms the upper jaw. Palate: The roof of the mouth that partially or completely separates the nasal cavity and the oral cavity; consists of the soft palate and hard palate. Prosthesis: An artificial or manmade replacement for a body part. Tips For insertion of a prosthesis prepared by an outside lab  see 42281  Insertion of pin retained palatal prosthesis. If the provider performs the work to create a prosthesis to reshape the palate  use 21082  Impression and custom preparation; palatal augmentation prosthesis. If the provider performs the work to create a palatal lift prosthesis  use 21083  Impression and custom preparation; palatal lift prosthesis. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider places a pin retained device as a palate prosthesis to close an opening or defect present due to cleft palate. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped  the provider places a prosthesis held in place by multiple small pins. Providers may use the prosthesis in a patient with a cleft palate to cover the defect in the maxilla. The goal of the procedure is to restore the function of speech and feeding affected by the presence of cleft palate. Terminology Cleft palate: Congenital defect in which a cleft  or gap  occurs in the palate at its midline  often occurring in conjunction with a cleft lip. Maxilla: The upper jaw bone. Palate: The roof of the mouth that partially or completely separates the nasal cavity and the oral cavity; consists of the soft palate and hard palate. Prosthesis: An artificial or manmade replacement for a body part. Tips For creation of a maxillary impression for prosthesis  see 42280  Maxillary impression for palatal prosthesis. If the provider performs the work to create a prosthesis to reshape the palate  use 21082  Impression and custom preparation; palatal augmentation prosthesis. If the provider performs the work to create a palatal lift prosthesis  use 21083  Impression and custom preparation; palatal lift prosthesis. Read Less

Use this code to report a procedure on the palate or uvula for which there is no specific code available. In this procedure  the provider drains an infected abscess of the parotid salivary gland. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the mouth over the infected tissues in the parotid gland. She uses a surgical blade to dissect the abscess and drains off the pus. The provider flushes the area with saline solution and applies antibiotics at the site. She checks for any bleeding and closes the incision using simple repair. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket formed due to the accumulation of purulent material  pus  in the soft tissues. Parotid gland: One of a pair of saliva secreting glands present in front of and below the ear on each side; the largest of all the salivary glands. Tips For complex drainage  use 42305  Drainage of abscess  parotid; complex. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider performs a complex drainage of an abscess present in the parotid salivary gland. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the mouth in the infected region in the parotid gland. The provider uses a surgical blade to incise the abscess and drain off the pus. He flushes the site with saline solution and applies antibiotics. The provider checks for any bleeding and closes the incision in the parotid gland with sutures. The provider mainly performs this procedure in cases of a complex diagnosis  the need for extra time for satisfactory completion of the service  or a need to perform the procedure in the operating room. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket formed due to the accumulation of purulent material  pus  in the soft tissues. Parotid gland: One of a pair of saliva secreting glands present in front of and below the ear on each side; the largest of all the salivary glands. Tips For simple drainage  use 42300  Drainage of abscess  parotid; simple. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider makes an incision in the mouth to drain the abscess of the submaxillary or sublingual salivary gland. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the mouth into the abscess in the submaxillary  also called the submandibular  or the sublingual salivary gland. The provider drains off the pus from the abscess. She flushes the site with saline solution and applies antibiotics. The provider checks for any bleeding. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket formed due to the accumulation of purulent material  pus  in the soft tissues. Sublingual gland: Small salivary gland on each side of the mouth lying beneath the mucous membrane in the lower jaw. Submaxillary gland: Salivary gland inside of and near the lower edge of the mandible on each side; also called submandibular gland. Tips If the provider drains the submaxillary abscess using an external approach  use 42320  Drainage of abscess; submaxillary external. Read Less

The provider uses an external approach to drain pus from a submaxillary salivary gland. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider surgically creates a channel through an incision from outside of the mouth to allow adequate drainage of pus from the submaxillary salivary gland  which is located beneath the floor of the mouth. He then drains the pus and irrigates the site with sterile saline solution. He gives antibiotics after completing the procedure. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket formed due to the accumulation of purulent material  pus  in the soft tissue. Parotid gland: Salivary gland situated on each side of the face below and in front of the ear. Salivary glands: Glands that discharge a fluid secretion and especially saliva into the mouth cavity  include the parotid glands  the sublingual glands  and the submandibular glands. Read More

Sialolithotomy is the removal of a stone from the salivary gland. Explanation After administration of anesthesia  the provider makes an intraoral incision with an instrument like a blade or CO2 laser and identifies the stone  which is generally present near the duct papilla or near the gland hilum. The physician removes a large stone or multiple stones with a grasping device (such as Mosquito forceps). Topical antibiotics are then applied and the incision is generally left open for healing. In the case of a submandibular duct stone removal  the physician ties a loose suture which is proximally tied around the stone (to avoid displacement of the stone). A longitudinal incision is made and the duct is opened  and then a grasping device is used to remove the stone. Then the incision is closed. Terminology Intraoral: Inside the mouth. Sialolithotomy: Removal of a stone from the salivary gland. Tips For an uncomplicated intraoral submandibular/submaxillary  sublingual  or parotid sialolithotomy  see 42330  and for an extraoral or complicated intraoral parotid sialolithotomy  see 42340. If the provider uses an endoscope (for example  31575) at a different session to locate the stones  you may be able to report the endoscopy and office visit separately  if documentation and coding rules support doing so. Read Less

Sialolithotomy is the removal of a stone from the salivary gland. The parotid gland is one of the salivary glands that discharge a fluid secretion and especially saliva into the mouth cavity. Explanation In this procedure  the provider may use either an intraoral or an extraoral approach to remove a stone from a parotid gland. For an extraoral approach  the provider makes an incision with an instrument like a blade or CO2 laser over the facial lines. Further dissection is continued while the scar tissues surrounding the stone are separated. Then the stone is exposed and removed. The incision is closed in layers. For an intraoral approach  the physician makes an elliptical incision with an instrument like a blade or CO2 laser around the papilla of the parotid duct  also called the Stensen duct  the duct that takes saliva from the parotid gland to the mouth. Dissection is performed further  and the stone  along with some nearby duct layers  is removed. The incision is closed in layers. Terminology Extraoral: Outside the mouth. Intraoral: Inside the mouth. Sialolithotomy: Removal of a stone from the salivary gland. Tips For an uncomplicated intraoral submandibular/submaxillary  sublingual  or parotid sialolithotomy  see 42330  and for a complicated intraoral submandibular/submaxillary sialolithotomy  see 42335. If the provider uses an endoscope (for example  31575) at a different session to locate the stones  you may be able to report the endoscopy and office visit separately  if documentation and coding rules support doing so. Read Less

The provider takes tissue samples from the salivary gland by using a percutaneous needle. He sends the samples for pathological analysis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a large  hollow bore percutaneous needle into the salivary gland to obtain small tissue fragments for the purpose of a biopsy. He places the sample in formalin solution and sends it for pathological evaluation. Terminology Biopsy: Removal and examination of tissues and fluids from the body. Salivary glands: Glands that discharge a fluid secretion and especially saliva into the mouth cavity  include the parotid glands  the sublingual glands  and the submandibular glands. Tips Use an additional code when the provider uses imaging guidance to perform percutaneous needle biopsy. Use 42405 when the service involves biopsy of salivary gland by skin incision. Read Less

The provider takes tissue samples from the salivary gland through a skin incision over the salivary gland. He sends the samples for pathological analysis. ExplanationWhen the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a skin incision over the salivary gland to access the salivary gland. He obtains multiple, often 6 to 10, pieces of glandular tissue for diagnostic evaluation in a lab. He closes the incision through sutures. He places the sample in formalin solution and sends it for pathological evaluation. Terminology Biopsy: Removal and examination of tissues and fluids from the body. Salivary glands: Glands that discharge a fluid secretion and especially saliva into the mouth cavity, include the parotid glands, the sublingual glands, and the submandibular glands. Tips Use 42400 when the service involves biopsy of salivary gland by percutaneous needle.

The provider excises a ranula  a large mucous cyst  that is present in the tissues of the floor of the mouth below the tongue. Explanation The provider accesses the mucocele on the floor of the mouth under the tongue via a sharp incision with an instrument like a blade or scalpel. The mucocele (mucous cyst/ranula) is then removed by surgical instrument and the site is sutured. Tips For removal of a mucocele on the vestibular mucosa of the lip without repair  see 40810 (Excision of lesion of mucosa and submucosa  vestibule of mouth; without repair). The vestibule of the mouth (oral vestibule) is the anteriormost portion of the oral cavity  or the area between the teeth and the cheek or lips. Code 42408 would not be appropriate since the cyst was on the lip  not on the floor of the mouth; this code describes removal of a sublingual (beneath the tongue) salivary cyst. Note: Unlike skin lesion excision codes  oral lesion excision codes have the wound closure built in  so there is never any need to report a separate code for closure. You can choose from closure types  i.e.  "without repair " "simple repair " and "complex repair." Read Less

The provider performs marsupialization of a sublingual salivary cyst  incising it and leaving it partially open  like a pouch. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision on the floor of the mouth into the cavity of the sublingual salivary cyst. He then excises the overlying mucosa and opens the cyst widely. He drains the cyst  exposing the epithelium lining. He sutures the remaining edges of the cyst to the mucosa  creating a sort of pouch for the sublingual gland saliva to drain from. Sublingual gland: Smallest salivary gland on each side of the mouth lying under the floor of the mouth. Read Less

The provider removes a tumor from the lateral lobe of the parotid gland without nerve dissection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a curvilinear incision in front of the ear with a sharp instrument. He then extends the excision to the neck toward the mid jawbone. The provider dissects the skin further and may use a nerve stimulator to identify the trunk of the facial nerve. He identifies the lateral lobe of the gland or neoplastic growth in the parotid's lateral lobe and removes it  without nerve dissection. He closes the incision. Terminology Nerve dissection: Cutting of nerves. Parotid gland: Salivary gland situated on each side of the face below and in front of the ear. Tips Before selecting your final code  review 42410 to 42426 to be sure you??e chosen the correct code for excision of parotid tumor or parotid gland. Read Less

The provider removes the total parotid gland with a tumor and performs radical neck dissection on one side. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a curvilinear incision in front of the ear with a sharp instrument. He extends the excision to the neck and toward the mid jawbone. He dissects the nerve branches free along with the total gland  removing it. He also dissects the facial nerve. He performs a unilateral radical neck dissection  or RND  by further dissection of the area  identifying and removing the lymph nodes and other structures as needed. Terminology Parotid gland: Salivary gland situated on each side of the face below and in front of the ear. Radical neck dissection or RND: Surgical procedure which involves removal of a tumor from the neck with an additional margin of normal tissue  with the removal of the lymph nodes and possibly other structures from the neck. Tips Before selecting your final code  review 42410 to 42426 to be sure you??e chosen the correct code for excision of parotid tumor or parotid gland. Read Less

The provider surgically removes a submandibular gland. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision with a sharp instrument below the ramus  which is the back part of the lower jaw. He divides the platysma muscle and deep cervical fascia. He elevates the flaps and identifies the lower border of the submandibular gland. He dissects the gland free from the adjacent tissues and attachments. He may ligate and divide the facial artery and retract the mylohyoid muscle. He removes the gland. He closes the incision in layers with sutures. Terminology Facial artery: Artery that arises from the external carotid artery that supplies the neck and face. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers  protects  and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles  bones  nerves  and blood vessels. Ligate: Close  tie off  repair  or encircle a vessel or other structure with sutures or wire. Mandible: Lower jaw. Mylohyoid muscle: Flat triangular muscle on each side of the mouth. Platysma: A plate like muscle that originates from the fascia of the cervical region  the neck. Submandibular gland: Salivary gland inside of and near the lower edge of the mandible on each side; also called submaxillary gland. Read Less

The provider surgically removes the sublingual gland. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a sharp incision underneath the tongue. The incision is on the inside of the lower teeth and over the diseased sublingual gland. The provider elevates mucosal flaps  identifies the gland  and frees it from the nearby tissues. He then uses forceps to grasp and remove the gland. He closes the incision with stitches. Terminology Sublingual gland: Smallest salivary gland on each side of the mouth lying under the floor of the mouth.

The provider performs primary or simple repair of an infected or damaged salivary gland. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider passes a tube made of a material like polyethylene into the duct of the salivary gland in the mouth. He passes the tube through the duct. He leaves the tube in place  possibly secured with sutures. He removes the tube later  such as after 3 to 4 weeks  as healing takes place. This procedure involves primary or simple repair. Terminology Sialodochoplasty: Surgical repair of an infected or traumatized salivary duct. Tips Use 42505 when the service involves sialodochoplasty by complicated repair.

The provider performs secondary or complicated repair of an infected or damaged salivary gland. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider passes a tube made of a material like polyethylene into the duct of the salivary gland in the mouth. He passes the tube through the duct. Repair of the duct is further complicated by extensive salivary gland pathology. He leaves the tube in place  possibly secured with sutures. He removes the tube later  such as after three to four weeks  as healing takes place. This code represents secondary  delayed  or complicated repair. Terminology Sialodochoplasty: Surgical repair of an infected or traumatized salivary duct. Tips Use this code if the procedure takes a lot of time or the given diagnosis is complex or complicated. The operative report should indicate the complexity involved. Use 42500 when the service involves sialodochoplasty by simple repair. Read Less

A sialography  or radiosialography  is an imaging technique used to visualize the salivary gland ductal system. Explanation A sialography  or radiosialography  is an imaging technique used to visualize the salivary gland ductal system. The physician intends to perform radiographic imaging of the salivary gland duct (reported separately). He introduces a cannula into the ductal passage. A contrast material is then instilled through the cannula into the ductal system. The flow of contrast material through the salivary gland and duct facilitates diagnostic examination of the ductal system (by using additional radiographic monitor/device) to rule out underlying ductal pathology.

A salivary fistula may occur due to injury or infection. Explanation A salivary fistula may occur due to injury or infection. The physician removes and repairs the abnormal tube??ike passage (communicating with the salivary duct) by the process of anastomosis  where the passage is reconnected. The provider inserts a probe to dilate the salivary duct. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a small incision over the salivary duct and passes a slender  flexible surgical instrument such as a probe into the duct. He uses the probe  or a series of probes  to dilate the lumen of the duct  or enlarge its diameter  to overcome the narrowing or obstruction of the ductal system. Providers may use dilation in the treatment of adhesions. The provider may use another technique for dilating strictures by expanding the strictured region with grasping forceps used as a dilator. Terminology Lumen: The interior  open area of a vessel or organ; a tubular like cavity. Probe: An instrument placed to explore in a wound or the inside of a vessel  organ  or the body; to explore a wound or the inside of a vessel  organ  or the body with such an instrument.

The provider makes an intraoral incision to access a salivary duct so he can tie it off. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision within the mouth to access the salivary duct. He takes care to preserve the integrity of facial nerves. He then ligates  or ties  the duct to treat conditions such as excessive salivation or as a method of reducing a salivary gland's size before tumor removal. He then closes the incision with stitches. Terminology Intraoral: Inside the mouth. Ligation: Using sutures or wire to close  tie off  repair  or encircle a vessel or other structure.

The provider uses an incision to drain an abscess next to one of the tonsils. He then applies topical antibiotics over the surgical site with or without any packing or closure. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket formed due to the accumulation of purulent material  pus  in the soft tissue. Scalpel: Surgical knife. The provider makes an incision to drain a retropharyngeal abscess in the throat or a parapharyngeal abscess deep in the neck. He approaches the abscess through the mouth. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider uses an intraoral approach to make a horizontal incision into the target abscess with a surgical blade. He then may use additional tools to help open and drain the abscess in the back of the throat behind the posterior pharyngeal wall  also known as a retropharyngeal abscess  or the abscess in the space in the head and the neck also known as parapharyngeal. He then applies antibiotics with or without any packing or closure. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket formed due to the accumulation of purulent material  pus  in the soft tissue. Retropharyngeal abscess: An abscess  or collection of pus  in the tissues in the back of the throat. In this procedure the physician makes an incision to drain an abscess. In this particular case  a retropharyngeal parapharyngeal abscess is drained via an external approach. Explanation In this procedure the physician makes an incision to drain an abscess. In this particular case  a retropharyngeal or parapharyngeal abscess is drained via an external approach. After administration of anesthesia  the physician makes an incision in the neck at the anterior or posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle using a scalpel. The incision is extended to the abscess and a hemostat is used to break down the abscess. A drainage device/tube is then secured (with sutures) at the abscess site (to allow continuous drainage/flow of the infected pus). Antibiotics are then applied with or without any packing or closure. Terminology Retropharyngeal space: A space posterior to the pharynx lying between the prevertebral fascia and the buccopharyngeal fascia Read Less

The provider obtains a biopsy sample from the oropharynx  the part of the throat behind the mouth. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider ensures the patient will be able to breathe during the procedure such as by using an endotracheal tube. He excises a small amount of tissue  known as a sample  from the oropharynx  which is situated behind the oral cavity. He then sends the sample for diagnostic analysis. Epiglottis: Flap covering the trachea during swallowing of food to prevent food entering the lungs. Intraoral: Inside the mouth. Oropharynx: Part of the pharynx that is below the soft palate and above the epiglottis and is continuous with the mouth. Pharynx: Area of the throat where the nose passages connect to the trachea  or windpipe  and the esophagus  which is the tube to the stomach. Read Less

The provider obtains a biopsy sample from a visible lesion of the nasopharynx  the part of the throat behind the nose. The provider removes tissue for biopsy from a visible lesion in the nasopharynx. He may use a method such as snare technique. A brachial cleft cyst  or vestige  is a congenital cystic swelling arising from the lateral aspect of the neck. Explanation A branchial cleft cyst  or vestige  is a congenital cystic swelling arising from the lateral aspect of the neck. It is caused when the second branchial (pharyngeal) cleft fails to close during the embryonic development stage. The physician performs surgical resection of a congenital epithelial cyst of the neck using a sharp surgical blade. This incision is confined to the skin and subcutaneous tissues only. Although often benign  the cyst may become infected and require removal. The most specific code to describe the procedure is 42810. Although the surgical report notes that the surgeon "incised and drained" the cyst  the code you mention describes incision and drainage of skin lesions (10060  Incision and drainage of abscess [e.g.  carbuncle  suppurative hidradenitis  cutaneous or subcutaneous abscess  cyst  furuncle  or paronychia]; simple or single)  not a branchial cleft cyst. The provider removes the tonsils and adenoids in a patient younger than 12 years old. Explanation After administration of anesthesia  the patient is prepped and draped in a sterile fashion. A mouth gag is inserted  and then the tonsils are inspected and grasped with a curved clamp and retracted. A blade (e.g.  no. 12) is used to make a mucosal incision in the medial aspect of the tonsillar pillar. Then  the tonsillar capsules are isolated with sharp and blunt dissection. For an adenoidectomy  the provider uses an adenoid curette (such as a St. Claire Thompson curette) or biting forceps to remove the adenoid tissues  which are further confirmed with a laryngeal mirror. Bleeding is controlled with a snare or electrocautery. A tonsillectomy also can be performed using cryogenic (freezing)  laser  and electrocautery methods. Terminology Adenoids: Patches of lymphoid tissue right above the tonsils that trap germs and help fight infection. Cryoablation  cryosurgery  or cryotherapy: A technique that destroys damaged or abnormal tissues by freezing temperatures. Electrocautery: Control of bleeding or sealing of other tissues using high??requency electrical current; also called electric coagulation or electrocoagulation. Laser ablation or resection: Using heat produced by an adjustable focused light energy to destroy lesions or abnormal tissue. Tonsils: A pair of lymphoid masses located on each side of the throat. Tips The T&A codes don't distinguish between primary or secondary adenoidectomy. So  if the otolaryngologist performs both tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy for the first or second time  you should report only 42820 or a patient younger than 12 or 42821 or a patient 12 years of age or older. Insurers consider separately reporting the procedures using a tonsillectomy and an adenoidectomy code  such as 42825  Tonsillectomy  primary or secondary; younger than age 12 or 42835  Adenoidectomy  secondary; younger than age 12  unbundling. For primary or secondary tonsillectomy without adenoidectomy  see 42825 for a patient younger than 12 and 42826 for patients 12 years of age or older. For primary adenoidectomy without tonsillectomy  see 42830 for a patient younger than 12 and 42831 for patients 12 years of age or over. For secondary adenoidectomy without tonsillectomy  see 42835 for a patient younger than 12 and 42836 for patients 12 years of age or over. After removing a patient's tonsils and adenoids  the otolaryngologist may spray Vitagel??onto the wounds to promote blood clotting. The seal is integral to the procedure  just as any closing would be  so a Vitagel??tissue seal is included in the tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy (T&A) codes and should not be reported separately. For radical resection of tonsils  tonsillar pillars  and/or retromolar trigone  such as might be performed for cancer  see 42842 to 42845. A tonsillectomy can also be performed using cryosurgery (freezing)  laser  and electrocautery methods; be sure to know your payer's policy before filing a claim as such. Read Less

Explanation Using a flexible endoscope or laryngoscope to visualize the back of the mouth  the provider eradicates the lingual tonsils (lymphoid tissue at the posterior tongue region) using any method  such as a scalpel (surgical knife)  electrocautery  snare  CO2 laser  suction debrider  or bipolar plasma??ediated radiofrequency ablation (Coblation?) technique. During this procedure  the provider removes part of the pharyngeal wall  which can include removal of part of the thyroid ala  hyoid bone  and wall of the piriform fossa. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises the skin on the patient's neck and deepens the incision to explore the hyoid and sternomastoid muscles. The layer of cervical fibrous tissue is dissected free from the hyoid. A portion of the hyoid is then further divided to access the pharyngeal structure. He then removes a portion of the pharynx (i.e.  pharyngeal lesion)  which may include removing part of the thyroid ala  hyoid bone  and wall of the piriform fossa. The surgical wound is then flushed thoroughly and closed with interrupted sutures after achieving hemostasis. Terminology Hemostasis: Control of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Hyoid bone: A small bone at the base of the lower jaw that is shaped like the letter U and serves to support the tongue to facilitate speech and swallowing; it is the only bone in the human body that does not connect to any other bone and is instead connected only through muscle tissue. Pharyngeal wall: The posterior and lateral wall of the pharynx  which is behind the mouth; the superior aspect of the wall extends up to the soft palate. Pharynx: The throat; it connects the mouth  nose  larynx (voice box)  trachea (windpipe)  and esophagus (the muscular tube that connects the mouth to the stomach); the part of the pharynx above the soft palate and communicating with the auditory tube is called the nasopharynx  the part between the soft palate and the upper epiglottis is the oropharynx  and the part below that which opens into the larynx and esophagus is the hypopharynx or laryngopharynx. The provider makes an incision into the neck to reach the esophagus for removal of a foreign body.
