The provider then connects the remaining pieces to ensure an uninterrupted gastrointestinal tract. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the chest and locates the esophagus. He then opens the end of the esophagus and excises the affected portion. He also accesses and removes the lower part of the stomach. In the chest  he sutures the esophagus to the remaining part of the stomach and sutures the upper jejunum of the small intestine to that structure. If there was a previous jejunostomy for feeding  he removes and repairs the jejunum. The procedure may also include connecting part of the duodenum to the jejunum and closing the other end of the duodenum. The provider may check for anastomotic leaks with dye or air. He assures hemostasis. He then closes the incision in layers. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomosis include end to side and side to side. Esophagus: Muscular tube that carries substances from the pharynx  which is behind the mouth  down to the stomach. Esophagojejunostomy: Surgical formation of an artificial communication between the esophagus and the jejunum Gastrectomy: Surgical removal of all or part of the stomach. Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Jejunostomy: Surgical procedure to create an opening in the jejunum  the second part of the small intestine. Thoracotomy: Surgical incision of the chest. Tips If the provider uses an abdominal incision  use 43340  Esophagojejunostomy without total gastrectomy; abdominal approach. Read Less

He then incises the esophagus or prepares the end of the esophagus stump in preparation for connection to the fistula. He incises the external site chosen for the fistula. He then closes the thoracotomy incision in layers. Terminology Esophagostomy: Surgical creation of an artificial opening into the esophagus. Fistula: Abnormal passageway between structures such as vessels  vessels and organs  or skin and organs or abdominal cavity. Thoracotomy: Surgical incision of the chest. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes one or two incisions opening the chest  abdomen  or both. He examines the esophageal remnant and identifies the site of any obstruction or disease. He then removes the problem area  performs dilation  or otherwise repairs the esophagus. He moves the stomach into the chest and attaches it to the esophageal stump. The provider may also decide to widen the distal stomach  specifically the pylorus  to allow for easier passage of food. The provider ligates  or ties off  dilated  or widened  blood vessels in the esophagus to prevent rupture and bleeding. Explanation With the patient lying supine on the operating table and after the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the midline of the chest or abdomen to access the esophagus. He identifies the location of the varices and makes an incision to expose the blood vessels. He ties off the blood vessels with sutures and closes the esophagus in layers. The provider assures hemostasis and closes the midline incisions in layers. The provider closes a previously placed esophagostomy or fistula through a transthoracic or midline abdominal incision. Typically  the wound or injury for which the esophagostomy was placed has healed  and the patient no longer needs to be fed through a tube. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision between the 6th and 7th ribs or in the upper midline of the abdomen. He repairs the esophagus with layered sutures. The provider assures hemostasis closes the skin incision in layers. The provider passes dilators over a guide wire to widen a narrowed area of the esophagus and improve swallowing. Explanation With the patient lying supine on the procedure table and after the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider passes a thin stiff wire into the esophagus under fluoroscopic guidance. He then passes a series of dilators down the esophagus over the guide wire to dilate the stricture. At the end of the procedure  the provider removes the instruments. The provider makes an incision in the stomach through the abdomen and ties off a bleeding vessel. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision through the anterior abdominal wall and then one into the stomach. He identifies the area of bleeding and sutures the bleeding vessel. He irrigates  or washes out  the stomach and suctions out the irrigating fluid. He reexamines the area. If there is no more bleeding  the provider closes the incision in the stomach. If he thinks continued drainage is necessary  he places a tube in the stomach and closes the stomach incision around it; then he brings the tube out through the abdominal incision. The provider then checks once again for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the incision in the abdomen. Terminology Duodenum: First part of the small intestine. Gastrotomy: A surgically created opening in the stomach. Ulcer: A lesion  typically in the lining of an organ  such as a gastric or peptic ulcer in the stomach or duodenum; ulcers that need to be treated surgically include ulcers that bleed or that erode or perforate through the wall of an organ. The provider places an indwelling (permanent) intraluminal tube or stent through an area of stricture (narrowing) in the esophagus. Strictures typically result from cancerous overgrowth or scarring due to radiation therapy. He performs this procedure for palliative treatment of esophageal stricture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the abdomen. If the abdomen is already open as part of another procedure  he make a small high incision in the stomach. If he has not already dilated the stricture from above during an endoscopic procedure  he passes bougies and dilates from below through the gastrotomy. He then asks the anesthesia provider to attach the leader of an Atkinson tube to the bougie and draws the tube down until it is positioned inside the stricture. He cuts off excess tube and closes the gastrotomy. The provider then checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the incision in the abdomen. Terminology Atkinson tube: A tube that can be inserted and expanded inside the walls of the esophagus to dilate a stricture and left in place for an indefinite period of time. Bougie: A slender  flexible  solid or hollow tubular surgical instrument used for measuring the internal diameter of a structure  dilating strictures  or probing for foreign bodies; the devices generally come in packs of varying diameters and often with depth markings on the side. Celestin and Mousseau Barbin tubes: Tubes that can be inserted and expanded inside the walls of the esophagus to dilate a stricture and left in place for an indefinite period of time; these tubes have mostly been replaced by the Atkinson tube. Dilate: Expand or widen an opening  typically with an instrument that can be expanded in a vessel  valve  or other structure  or with a balloon on the tip of a catheter. Esophageal: Pertaining to the esophagus. Esophagus: The muscular tube that carries substances from the pharynx  which is behind the mouth  down to the stomach. Gastrotomy: A surgically created opening in the stomach. Intraluminal: Within the channel or hollow interior of a tube or tubular structure like a vessel. Palliative: Treating the symptoms but not curing the disease or condition. Radiation therapy  or radiotherapy: Another name for radiology oncology; radiation oncology applies high frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors  or abnormal growths of tissue or mass. Stricture: Narrowing; a stricture of the esophagus causes difficulty swallowing. Tips Esophageal stents or intraluminal tubes placed and left in the esophagus can be used to treat esophageal stricture  or narrowing  as palliative therapy for overgrowth of carcinoma in the esophagus  or in combination with brachytherapy  directed radiotherapy with radioactive seeds  but placement via gastrotomy is rare if not obsolete. Carefully check the details of the procedure to be sure you are choosing the correct code. Read Less

The provider incises or cuts into the hypertrophied (overdeveloped) pyloric muscle to correct pyloric stenosis  a narrowing of the part of the stomach that leads into the small intestine. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile vomiting in infants. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a small incision in the right side of the abdomen just below the rib cage. He uses gentle traction  first on the omentum  then the transverse colon  then the stomach  and then the antrum to expose the pylorus. He identifies a spot on the anterior pylorus without blood supply and makes a lengthwise incision in the pyloric tissue just down to but not through the mucosa. He spreads the cut muscle apart gently and then closes the outer covering of the muscle and fascia in layers. The provider then checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the incision in the abdomen. Terminology Antrum: Part of the pyloric channel at the base of the stomach. Fredet Ramstedt type operation  or pyloromyotomy: Cutting of pyloric muscle. Omentum: Part of the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that extends from the stomach to the adjacent organs. Pylorus: A circular band of muscular tissue at the base of the stomach; it acts like a sphincter controlling the passage of stomach contents into the duodenum. Traction: Pulling force. Transverse colon: The part of the large intestine that runs across the upper abdomen  between the ascending and descending segments of colon. Tips On palpation of the infant?? abdomen before surgery  the provider may describe feeling an olive  because the overdeveloped pyloric muscle feels just like an olive. Read Less

The provider performs an open biopsy and excises a portion or all of a suspicious lesion in the stomach to determine the origin and nature of the lesion  such as whether it is a malignant cancer or benign lesion. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the upper abdominal area. He spreads the incision open and holds it open with retractors so that the abdominal cavity can be directly examined. He makes an incision into the stomach and takes a portion of tissue from a suspicious area for biopsy. He checks the biopsy area for bleeding and  finding none  closes the incision in the stomach in layers. The provider then checks the suture line for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the incision in the abdomen. Terminology Benign: Not malignant  generally treatable or not needing treatment. Laparotomy: Surgical incision of the abdomen; providers frequently perform a laparotomy as an exploratory procedure to assist in determining a cause of abdominal pain or to take a biopsy of an abdominal tissue or tumors  abnormal growths or masses  in order to determine a stage of cancer. Malignant: Cancerous  capable of spreading and causing death if untreated. Open biopsy: Obtaining a tissue sample through an incision. Retractor: Surgical instrument used to retract  or hold back  wound edges or deeper tissues to give better visualization and access to the provider performing surgery. Read Less

The provider explores the stomach for an ulcer or tumor and excises the lesion if found. If untreated  ulcers or tumors may cause bleeding or obstruction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision is made in the upper abdomen. He retracts tissue and muscle layers and incises the stomach longitudinally. He explores the stomach for abnormalities. Once the ulcer or benign tumor is located  he cuts it away completely from the inner lining of the stomach. He sutures the incision in the stomach in layers. The provider then checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Benign: Not malignant  generally treatable or not needing treatment. Excision: Removal of tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. Local: Confined to a single or small area. Read More

The provider excises a cancerous tumor of the stomach to .prevent metastasis or reduce the bulk of the tumor in preparation for radiation or chemotherapy. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider opens the abdominal cavity through a midline incision. He retracts tissue and muscle layers. Then  he clamps the duodenum and transects it. He frees the stomach from surrounding tissues  locates the tumor  and excises it. After he removes the tumor with a sufficient margin of normal appearing tissue around it  the lesser curvature of the stomach is closed in layers. He may leave a tube in the abdomen for drainage. After hemostasis is accomplished and instruments are removed  the provider closes the incision in the abdomen in layers. Terminology Chemotherapy: The use of drugs to treat a disease. Duodenum: First part of the small intestine. Excision: Removal of tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. Gastrectomy: Partial or total excision of the stomach. Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Lesser curvature of the stomach: The inner inferior margin of the stomach  beginning where the esophagus enters the stomach and ending where the pylorus empties into the duodenum. Local: Confined to a single or small area. Malignant: Cancerous  capable of spreading and causing death if untreated. Radiation therapy: High frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors; also radiation oncology or radiotherapy. Retract: Hold back incisions or edges of a wound with instruments designed to do so without injuring tissue. Transect: To cut through. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass; can be benign or cancerous. Tips Other surgical procedures for malignant gastric tumors include partial or total gastrectomy; a partial gastrectomy is performed when the tumors are limited to one area. If part or all of the stomach is removed  use 43620 to 43622  Gastrectomy  total; etc. or 43631 to 43634  Gastrectomy  partial  distal; etc. Read Less

Code 43621 explains surgical removal of whole stomach and anastomosis of the distal divided of the small bowel to the stomach. Explanation The physician makes an upper left paramedian incision. He mobilizes the spleen with its hilar lymph nodes  splenic vessels  the tail  and the body of the pancreas from left to right. The operation is retroperitoneal. He resects the stomach with both lesser and greater omentum and lymph nodes around the celiac axis. In the process the left gastric artery  right gastric artery  and epiploic arteries are ligated. After excision of the whole stomach  the cut edge of pancreas is closed with sutures. The continuity of the alimentary canal is maintained with an anastomosis of the distal divided of the small bowel to the stomach. The proximal end is anastomosed to the small bowel below the anastomosis. Before closure a drain is inserted up to the pancreas and the other end is brought out through a separate stab incision at the sub costal region. Terminology Omentum double fold of peritoneum attached to stomach Retroperitoneal behind and outside the peritoneum Anastomosis??onnection between the two parts or organ. Read Less

The provider removes the lower part of the stomach and anastomoses the upper part of the small bowel to the part of the stomach that remains. Explanation The provider mobilizes the stomach and the first part of the duodenum by incising the peritoneum on the lateral aspect of the duodenum. He divides the duodenum between the clamps  just distal to the pylorus. The distal cut end of the duodenum is covered with gauze and kept aside for further anastomosis. The distal cut end of the stomach and the duodenum are brought together without any tension between them. The seromuscular stitch is applied on the posterior walls of the two viscera and the bowel ends lie apart. Stitches are tightened so that the seromuscular layers are in contact. The continuity of the alimentary canal is maintained with anastomosis of the distal divided part of the small bowel to the stomach. The proximal end is anastomosed to the small bowel below the anastomosis. Terminology Pylorus: A circular band of muscular tissue at the base of the stomach; it acts like a sphincter controlling the passage of the stomach contents into the duodenum; the first part of the small intestine. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end??o??ide and side??o??ide. The provider removes part of the distal (lower) stomach and creates an intestinal pouch. The provider transects the vagus nerve and removes the distal part of the stomach. Explanation In uncomplicated duodenal ulcer  vagotomy is often performed along with partial distal gastrectomy (removal of the lower part of the stomach). The provider makes an incision through an avascular area to reach the lesser sac. The dissection starts with the anterior vagus nerve in the lesser omentum  and all the gastric branches are ligated and divided one by one. For posterior selective vagotomy  the provider makes an incision through the peritoneum. His index finger is passed through the hole to reach gullet and thumb to reach lesser omentum  the two fingers meet behind esophagus where the posterior trunk lies. Tissues are dissected carefully  ligated and divided. The provider makes a right paramedian incision to explore the stomach. The transverse mesocolon is split vertically through an avascular area to enter the lesser sac. The posterior wall of the stomach is drawn out through the split of mesocolon and Allis tissue forceps are applied to the fold  pair of occlusion clamp is also applied so that bleeding or secretions do not disturb the anastomosis. A hand is passed along the undersurface of the transverse mesocolon  just below the tail of the pancreas  where the duodenojejunal flexure is found and the first loop of jejunum is situated here. It is picked up and placed by the side of the posterior wall of the stomach  should be such that the proximal part of jejunum should lie near lesser curvature and the distal part near greater curvature  thus an isoperistaltic anastomosis is formed. Terminology Antrum of stomach: The lower end of the stomach at the pylorus where it empties into the duodenum. Duodenum: The first part of the small intestine. Flexure: A curved or bent part of an organ or other structure  e.g.  hepatic flexure  sigmoid flexure  splenic flexure. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Lesser curvature of the stomach: One part of the stomach  the inner inferior margin of the stomach  beginning where the esophagus enters the stomach and ending where the pylorus empties into the duodenum. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Pylorus: A circular band of muscular tissue at the base of the stomach; it acts like a sphincter controlling the passage of the stomach contents into the duodenum; the first part of the small intestine. Vagotomy: Surgical division of the vagus nerve. Vagus nerve: One (number X) of the twelve nerves of the brain that emerge from the lower portion of the brain (cranial nerves); it is the longest cranial nerve and is involved in sensory and motor function of the respiratory and digestive system as well as the heart. Tips If the surgeon reports +43635 with 43631  but the notes do not mention directly or indirectly that a distal gastrectomy was performed; the coder should ask the surgeon to revise the note before the claim is submitted. Code +43635 is an add??n code; thus  it has already been reduced and is not subject to multiple procedure guidelines. This means it should not be further reduced in value when it is reported with partial distal gastrectomy and should be paid at 100 percent of the carrier's approved amounts. Read Less

The provider transects both trunks of the vagus nerve and repairs the pylorus to increase the caliber of the pyloric opening by stretching. Explanation The provider makes a midline or left paramedian incision. He carefully incises the peritoneum over the abdominal part of the esophagus transversely so that the inferior phrenic vessels are not damaged. He mobilizes the lowest 3 inches of the esophagus and retracts it downwards. The assistant pulls the stomach up to visualize the anterior trunk of the vagus nerve lying on the anterior surface of the esophagus and the posterior trunk away from the esophagus. The provider cuts 5 to 7 cm of both the trunks and ties the remaining ends with fine silk. He places a ligature to prevent bleeding from the ascending esophageal vessels  which run along with the nerve. Finally  he closes the incision with nonabsorbable sutures. Then  the provider again makes an incision through all the layers the pyloric canal midway between the greater and lesser curvatures starting from 3.5 cm proximal to the pylorus and extending up to 2.5 cm distal on the anterior wall of the duodenum. He aspirates all the contents of the duodenum and stomach and inspects the inner wall for the location of the defect to ensure that there is no stenosis distal to the incision. If the defect or ulcer is very close to the incision  he excises it along with incision. The upper and lower edges of the incision are pulled apart with the help of forceps so that the proximal and distal end of the incision approach each other and the defect becomes vertical  thus widening the pyloric canal. Finally  he closes the defect using sutures. Terminology Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Esophagus: The long tubular portion of the digestive tract that stretches between the throat and the stomach. Greater curvature of the stomach: The outer lateral margin of the stomach that forms the bulk of the stomach. Lesser curvature of the stomach: One part of the stomach  the inner inferior margin of the stomach  beginning where the esophagus enters the stomach and ending where the pylorus empties into the duodenum. Paramedian: Just to the side of the midline. Pyloroplasty: A surgical procedure to widen the opening in the lower part of the stomach so that stomach contents can empty into the small intestine. Pylorus: A circular band of muscular tissue at the base of the stomach; it acts like a sphincter controlling the passage of the stomach contents into the duodenum; the first part of the small intestine. Vagus nerve: One (cranial nerve X) of the twelve nerves of the brain that emerge from the lower portion of the brain (cranial nerves); it is the longest cranial nerve and is involved in sensory and motor function of the respiratory and digestive system as well as the heart. Tips Two codes in the stomach excision section describe vagotomies typically performed on infants with pyloric stenosis. Report 43640 for a vagotomy that requires pyloromyotomy but does not involve gastrectomy; use 43641 for a highly selective parietal cell vagotomy. Read Less

The provider performs a highly selective  parietal cell vagotomy and repairs the pylorus to increase its diameter; he may or may not create an opening in the stomach (gastrostomy). Explanation The provider incises the skin of the abdomen and extends it through the avascular area to reach the lesser sac. He dissects out the anterior vagus nerve in the lesser omentum and ligates and divides all the gastric branches one by one. For a posterior selective vagotomy  he incises the peritoneum at an angle. He uses blunt dissection to reach the posterior trunk. He carefully ligates and divides the tissues. Highly selective vagotomy differs from selective vagotomy in that it preserves the nerves of Latarjet which run along the lesser curvature and supply the antrum and pylorus. The nerves are preserved by passing forceps through the lesser curvature. The provider again makes an incision through all the layers of the pyloric canal midway between the greater and lesser curvatures  starting from 3.5 cm proximal to the pylorus and extending up to 2.5 cm distal on the anterior wall of the duodenum. He aspirates all the contents of the duodenum and stomach and inspects the inner wall for the location of the defect and to ensure that there is no stenosis distal to the incision. If the defect or ulcer is very close to incision  he excises it. He pulls apart the upper and lower edges of the incision with the help of forceps so that the proximal and distal end of incision approach each other and the defect becomes vertical  thus widening the pyloric canal. Finally  the provider closes the defect using sutures. Terminology Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Esophagus: The long tubular portion of the digestive tract that stretches between the throat and the stomach. Greater curvature of the stomach: The outer lateral margin of the stomach that forms the bulk of the stomach. Lesser curvature of the stomach: One part of the stomach  the inner inferior margin of the stomach  beginning where the esophagus enters the stomach and ending where the pylorus empties into the duodenum. Paramedian: Just to the side of the midline. Pyloroplasty: A surgical procedure to widen the opening in the lower part of the stomach so that stomach contents can empty into the small intestine. Pylorus: A circular band of muscular tissue at the base of the stomach; it acts like a sphincter controlling the passage of the stomach contents into the duodenum; the first part of the small intestine. Vagus nerve: One (cranial nerve X) of the twelve nerves of the brain that emerge from the lower portion of the brain (cranial nerves); it is the longest cranial nerve and is involved in sensory and motor function of the respiratory and digestive system as well as the heart. Tips Two codes in the stomach excision section describe vagotomies typically performed on infants with pyloric stenosis. Report 43640 for a vagotomy that requires pyloromyotomy but does not involve gastrectomy; use 43641 for a highly selective parietal cell vagotomy. This procedure may also be referred to as a proximal gastric vagotomy. Read Less

The provider places gastric stimulation electrodes laparoscopically on the antrum of the stomach when medical treatment stops helping a patient with gastroparesis  or paralysis of the stomach. Gastroparesis is often a complication of diabetes mellitus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  using laparoscopic techniques  the provider places the stimulator leads on the muscle at the base (antrum) of the stomach. He connects the other ends of the leads to a pulse generator which is placed in a surgically created space (pocket) below the skin of the abdomen. Typically  a representative of the manufacturer tests and programs the generator. The provider then deflates the abdomen  removes all instruments  and closes the laparoscopic incisions. Terminology Antrum: Part of the pyloric channel at the base of the stomach. Electrode: A device used to transmit electrical impulses. Gastric: Pertaining to the stomach. Gastric electrical stimulator  GES  or gastric pacemaker: A programmable device similar to a pacemaker for the heart except that the stimulating electrodes are placed on the muscle at the base of the stomach to cause the muscles to contract  restoring function to the pylorus. Implantation: Surgical placement inside the body of something that was not there before; it can refer to organs  tissue  devices  grafts  etc. Laparoscopy: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen  inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure  inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen  and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open  removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure  and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Neurostimulator: A device that uses electrical impulses to activate muscle contraction. Pulse generator: A programmable device that emits electrical pulses; also gastric electrical stimulator or gastric pacemaker. Tips This cutting edge treatment  gastric electrostimulation (GES) has two codes for laparoscopic technique; compare 43647  implantation or replacement  with 43648  Laparoscopy  surgical; revision or removal of gastric neurostimulator electrodes  antrum. Another duo covers the same procedures using an open approach  43881 for implantation or replacement of gastric neurostimulator electrodes on the antrum and 43882 for revision or removal of gastric neurostimulator electrodes from the antrum. A gastric neurostimulator is approved to treat gastroparesis due to diabetic or idiopathic causes in a patient unresponsive to drug therapy and experiencing severe nutritional deficits; it is not approved for weight loss. Use this code to report a new or unusual laparoscopic procedure on the stomach for which there is no specific code available. Explanation The provider performs a laparoscopic procedure on the stomach that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT? codes available. Consult the provider  if possible  to ensure that proper documentation has been done before billing for an unlisted procedure. He places devices called ports in the other incisions to keep them open and uses the other incisions to insert instruments. Tips CPT? guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. Include one or more similar codes and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also  include the operative notes and/or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case??y??ase basis  and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less

The provider inserts a tube into the duodenum. He administers a stimulant to cause the stomach to produce acid and obtains a specimen of duodenal secretions through the gastric tube. He sends the specimens to the laboratory for analysis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider passes a tube through either the mouth or the nose  through the esophagus and stomach  and into the duodenum under image guidance. He administers gastrin  a hormone produced in the stomach that stimulates acid production  intravenously. Through a syringe attached to the tube he aspirates  or suctions  the contents of the duodenum and sends it for analysis. The provider then removes the tube and checks for injury as he pulls the tube out. Terminology Afferent loop culture: A sample of secretions from the proximal loop of the duodenum and jejunum for bacterial analysis. Aspiration: Removal of fluid  gas  or other material through a tube attached to a suction device  often combined with irrigation  the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen or stomach. Bile: A substance produced in the liver  stored in the gallbladder  and secreted into the duodenum; important in the breakdown of fats  or lipids; crystals in a bile study may indicate the presence of cholelithiasis  or gallstones. Diagnostic: Refers to procedures performed for the purpose of determining the type of disease and its causes as opposed to therapeutic  which means for treatment purposes. Duodenal intubation: Insertion of a tube into the duodenum; the tube may be used for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. Duodenum: First part of the small intestine. Image guidance: Typically  fluoroscopic guidance  a live X??ay where the image appears on a monitor  to view body structures while performing procedures but also includes other types of imaging. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure?? point of attachment. Stimulant: A substance that actives or initiates a reaction. Read Less

The provider inserts a tube into the duodenum. He administers a stimulant to initiate the production of pancreatic juices and bile and obtains multiple specimens of duodenal secretions through the gastric tube. He sends the specimens to the laboratory for analysis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider passes an intubation tube through either the mouth or the nose  through the esophagus and stomach  and into the duodenum under image guidance. He suctions the fluid in the duodenum for baseline analysis  and then administers secretin intravenously to check the pancreatic secretion. He suctions out the fluid once again to check for undesired side effects of the secretin administration. If there are none  then he suctions out multiple samples of duodenal fluid and sends them to the laboratory for analysis. The provider then removes the tube and checks for injury as he pulls the tube out. Terminology Aspiration: Removal of fluid  gas  or other material through a tube attached to a suction device  often combined with irrigation  the instillation of fluid to wash out a cavity  such as the abdomen or stomach  or to clean a wound. Diagnostic: Refers to procedures performed for the purpose of determining the type of disease and its causes as opposed to therapeutic  which means for treatment purposes. Double lumen tube: A tube with two channels  typically a large one for suctioning fluid and a smaller one for instilling fluid. Duodenal intubation: Insertion of a tube into the duodenum; the tube may be used for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. Esophagus: The muscular tube that carries substances from the pharynx  which is behind the mouth  down to the stomach. Image guidance: Typically  fluoroscopic guidance  a live X??ay where the image appears on a monitor  to view body structures while performing procedures but also includes other types of imaging. Multiple fractional specimens: Dividing material obtained for laboratory testing into separate containers for testing of individual substances. Secretin: A hormone produced in the duodenum and upper jejunum that stimulates the secretion of pancreatic juice  an enzyme that aids in protein digestion. Single lumen tube: A tube with only one channel; fluid is instilled and suctioned out through the single channel. Stimulant: A substance that actives or initiates a reaction. Read Less

A nasogastric or orogastric tube inserted through the nose (naso?? or mouth (oro?? of the patient for enteric nutrition normally ends in the duodenum. The physician may take the help of radiological guidance for the placement of the tube. Enteric nutrition is done to patients who cannot take food in the normal way due to disease conditions or trauma. Explanation The physician uses fluoroscopic guidance for repositioning of a gastric feeding tube. The tube is inserted through the nose or mouth of the patient into the esophagus  stomach  and duodenum. It is positioned at the distal end of the duodenum. Fluoroscopic guidance is not included in the code 43761 and hence  should be reported separately when used.

The provider removes a previously placed gastrostomy tube and replaces it without imaging guidance or gastrostomy tract revision. The replacement may be routine or necessary to replace a dislodged or infected/clogged tube. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped  the provider frees up the existing gastrostomy tube from the skin and pulls it out. He inserts a new tube through the same path and secures it to the skin with sutures. The procedure requires no endoscopic or other imaging guidance and does not require revision of the gastrostomy tract. Terminology Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live  real??ime X??ay where the image appears on a television monitor)  ultrasound (high??requency sound waves)  or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. Gastrostomy tube (G tube): A tube inserted through a surgically created opening through the skin and into the stomach  typically through a small incision in the abdomen. Tips For the same procedure requiring revision of the gastrostomy  see 43763. Read Less

The provider creates a surgical connection between the stomach and the duodenum  typically after a portion of the stomach or duodenum has been excised; also known as a gastroduodenal anastomosis. Explanation The provider mobilizes the stomach and the first part of the duodenum by incising the peritoneum on the lateral aspect of duodenum. He divides the duodenum between the clamps  just distal to pylorus. The distal cut end of duodenum is covered with gauze and kept aside for further anastomosis. The distal cut end of stomach and the duodenum are brought together without any tension between them. A seromuscular stitch is applied on the posterior walls of the two organs and the bowel ends lie apart. Stitches are tightened so that seromuscular layers are in contact. The stomach and duodenum are joined using sutures  which is continued to join the anterior walls of the two structures  and thus anastomosis is completed. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end??o??ide and side??o??ide. Duodenum: The first part of the small intestine. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Pylorus: A circular band of muscular tissue at the base of the stomach; it acts like a sphincter controlling the passage of the stomach contents into the duodenum; the first part of the small intestine. Seromuscular suture: A suture that is placed through the inner lining (serous membrane) and the muscular layer of an organ or the colon. Read Less

The provider creates direct access to the lumen of the stomach for babies who need to be fed directly through the stomach. Explanation The physician makes two incisions; he puts a tube with a balloon or mushroom??haped bulb at one end and into the stomach through the larger incision. The other end is pulled through the second incision and the tube is secured. The stomach is stitched to the abdominal wall. The balloon helps to prevent the tube from falling out. Terminology Gastrostomy: Surgically created opening in the stomach for insertion of a feeding tube. Lumen: The interior  open area of a vessel or organ; a tubelike cavity  or the interior of a catheter or tube. Tips A Foley catheter  Malecot catheter  Bard? button  and Mic??ey? button are examples of tubes that may be used in a surgical gastrostomy.

The provider revises and or reconstructions a previously created anastomosis between the stomach and jejunum. He may also perform a partial gastrectomy. He performs these procedures to relieve obstruction  pain  or other symptoms caused by scarring and adhesions resulting from the previous procedure or progression of the disease for which the previous procedure was performed. In addition  he performs vagotomy to treat gastroesophageal reflux disease or gastric ulcer unresponsive to other treatment. Explanation With the patient supine on the operating table and after the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the upper midline of the abdomen and may extend the incision past the umbilicus to provide additional exposure. Once the abdomen is entered  he assures good visualization of the cavity and takes down any adhesions. He examines the site of the previous anastomosis  excises any scar tissue  and removes any staples or other materials used to create the previous anastomosis. He isolates and inspects the stomach and intestines. He may partially resect the stomach to treat disease or to improve the anastomosis to the jejunum. He constructs a new anastomosis between the stomach and the jejunum using staples or sutures. He identifies and isolates the vagus nerve and transects it with a scalpel or scissors. The provider checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Adhesions: Fibrous bands that form between tissues and organs  often as a result of injury during surgery; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Gastrectomy: Removal of part or all of the stomach. Gastric ulcer: An erosion in the mucous lining of  typically  the stomach caused by gastric acid. Gastroesophageal reflux disease: Backward flow or regurgitation of bile and stomach acid stomach into the esophagus causing heartburn  esophagitis  and erosion or ulcer of the esophageal tissues; this condition can lead to Barrett esophagus  precancerous changes in the esophageal tissues at the cellular level. Gastrojejunostomy  or gastrojejunal anastomosis: Surgical procedure that joins the stomach and jejunum  the second part of the small intestine. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Obstruction: Blockage. Supine: Lying in the face up position. Vagotomy: Resection  or cutting  of the vagus nerve. Read Less

The provider closes the gastrostomy  which was made for the patients who needed to be fed or have their upper gastrointestinal tract emptied directly through the stomach. Explanation After the induction of general anesthetic  the provider makes an incision around the gastrostomy site and carries it down through the skin and subcutaneous tissue with sharp dissection. He frees up the tract and the stomach and places stay sutures on either side of the tract. The tract is amputated. He then closes the intervening stomach with interrupted Lembert Nurolon? sutures. He closes the fascia and skin in layers and applies a dressing. Terminology Gastrostomy: Surgically created opening in the stomach for insertion of a feeding tube.

The provider removes the port component of a gastric restrictive band device. He performs this procedure because the port is defective or because of infection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision over the implanted port and enters the pocket. The port and pocket are inspected. The port is removed. The provider checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Adjustable gastric restrictive device: A band placed around the stomach to restrict the size of the stomach; it encloses a balloon which can be adjusted by adding or removing saline via a reservoir and port attached just below the skin of the abdomen  effectively reducing or enlarging the outlet to regulate the amount of food that can pass through. Gastric restrictive procedure: A surgical procedure that employs various techniques to reduce the size of the stomach for purposes of weight loss in morbidly obese patients. Morbidly obese: So overweight that it endangers health; although definitions vary  typical values for determining morbid obesity include a body mass index  a method for determining body fat  equal to or greater than 40 or being 100 pounds  or 45 kg  overweight. Port component of gastric restrictive band: An opening; in a gastric restrictive procedure  the port allows the provider to loosen or tighten the outlet between the stomach the intestine; to tighten the band  the provider instills saline into the port; to loosen the band  he withdraws saline from a reservoir that is connected via a tube to the band around the stomach. Reservoir: A created space for storage; it may be a replacement for an anatomical cavity like the stomach or an artificial container for storage of medicine. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Read Less

The provider frees up adhesions from the colon and other abdominal structures using a combination of techniques. Adhesions result from the previous surgical procedures  trauma  or pelvic inflammatory disease and cause pain and sometimes obstruction of the digestive tract. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a midline incision in the abdomen. Typically  he places retractors to keep the incision open and improve visibility of the internal abdominal structures. He examines the abdomen thoroughly. The provider then frees up  or lyses  the adhesions between sections of the intestines or between the intestines and other organs or the abdominal wall  typically using a combination of sharp and blunt dissection. The provider then checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Adhesiolysis: Separation of adhesions. Adhesions: Fibrous bands that form between tissues and organs  often as a result of injury during surgery; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Laparoscopic procedure: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen  inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure  inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen  and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open  removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure  and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Lysis: To free up organs or structures that are attached to other structures by adhesions. Obstruction: Blockage. Retractor: Surgical instrument used to retract  or hold back  wound edges or deeper tissues to give better visualization and access to the provider performing surgery. Sharp and blunt dissection: Sharp dissection separates tissue layers using a blade; blunt dissection separates tissue layers using the finger. Tips Intestinal adhesions most commonly occur after intestinal or abdominal surgical procedures but pelvic inflammatory disease can cause adhesions as well. Intestinal adhesions primarily cause abdominal pain but can cause intestinal obstruction. Open lysis of adhesions as described by 44005 includes division of an adhesive band  the specific adhesion causing the obstruction. Note that 44005 is designated a separate procedure. CMS and other payers bundle the exploratory laparotomy with the enterolysis. Therefore  you would not bill separately for the exploratory laparotomy. This means also that had the provider performed another procedure in the same anatomical area during the same session  for example  an appendectomy  you would code for the appendectomy  the major procedure  and would not bill separately for the enterolysis. The provider places a feeding tube into the jejunum and brings it out through an opening in the abdomen to provide the patient with nutritional support  typically to allow healing of the esophagus or stomach from disease or prior surgery. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a small incision in the abdomen. Using a needle catheter or direct placement  he places a feeding tube through a small incision in the jejunum. He brings the tube out and attaches it to a surgically created opening  or stoma  on the abdominal wall. The provider then checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Enteral alimentation: To feed by means of a tube in the small intestine. Esophagus: The muscular tube that carries substances from the pharynx  which is behind the mouth  down to the stomach. Jejunostomy: An surgically created opening into the jejunum to allow for feeding tube placement. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Needle catheter: A catheter through which a needle can be inserted; the needle may be used to make a small opening in a hollow structure  in this case  the jejunum. Tips CPT? guidelines explain that separate procedures are commonly carried out as an integral part of a larger service and as such do not warrant separate identification. In other words  you should only report a service designated as a separate procedure if it was the only service the provider provides in the same operative area or anatomic location. Code 44015 is an add??n code that must accompany an appropriate primary procedure code. Read Less

The provider explores the abdomen  jejunum  and ileum through an abdominal incision. He examines the small intestine  except for the duodenum  for diseased tissue  a lesion  or foreign body. Depending on what he finds  he excises the diseased tissue  takes a biopsy  or removes the foreign body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision into the abdomen through skin  fascia  and muscle layers. He inspects the abdomen and identifies the small intestine below the duodenum. He incises the intestine and excises diseased tissue  biopsies the target specimen  or removes the foreign body. He repairs the intestine  fascia  and muscle in layers. The provider then checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination. Duodenum: The first portion of the small intestine. Enterotomy: Surgically created opening in the small intestine. Excise: Surgically remove tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part; also resect. Fascia: The fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers  protects  and gives support to other structures. Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body; foreign bodies in the upper gastrointestinal  or GI  tract are typically swallowed; a swallowed object may travel to the lower GI tract or be inserted through the anus and rectum; traumatic injury can also introduce foreign bodies into the GI tract. Ileum: Third or last part of the small intestine; do not confuse with ilium  the upper part of the pelvic bone. Incise: Cut into a structure  typically with a surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Pathologic examination  or histopathologic examination: Laboratory analysis of tissue for abnormalities in structure or function. Small intestine  small bowel: The portion of the digestive tract directly below the stomach and before the large bowel or colon; it consists of the first and second portion of the duodenum  the jejunum  and the ileum. In this procedure  the provider makes an incision in the abdomen to identify the affected part of the small intestine other than the duodenum. He places a tube to allow for decompression  such as in a patient with an intestinal obstruction with a buildup of gas pressure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the abdomen  such as from the xiphoid to the pubis. He identifies the intestine and incises the small intestine  in an area other than the duodenum  to insert a tube for decompression. The tube  with one end in the intestine and one end pulled through the abdominal wall  releases pressure built up in the intestine. After completion of the procedure  the provider ensures control of bleeding and closes the abdominal incision appropriately. Terminology Duodenum: First part of the small intestine. Enterotomy: The surgical incision into an intestine. Xiphoid: Bony process found in the lowest portion of the sternum  which is the breastbone. Pubis: Area located in front of the pelvis where the pubic bones meet. Abdominal wall: Boundaries of the abdominal cavity. Tips Use 44020 if the provider performs enterotomy  small intestine  other than duodenum; for exploration  one or more biopsies  or foreign body removal. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider makes an incision in the affected part of the colon and examines it or performs biopsy or removal of a foreign body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the abdomen. She makes an incision in the target area and explores the colon. She obtains one or more samples for biopsy or removes intestinal foreign bodies. After completion of the closure of colon  the provider ensures control of bleeding and closes the abdominal incision appropriately. Terminology Colotomy: A surgical incision in the colon. Colon: The part of the large intestine extending from the cecum to the rectum.

In this procedure  the provider makes an incision in the affected part of the intestine for repair of twisted  telescoped  or herniated bowel  other than the rectum. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an abdominal incision. He explores the target area of the intestine  carefully dividing the adhesions and freeing the intestine from the abdominal organs and other viscera. He reduces the abnormal twisting of the intestine  the segment of the bowel sliding into an adjacent part of the intestine  or the internal hernia manually to prevent the defect?? reappearance. After releasing the obstructed segment of bowel  he divides any other additional adhesions. After completion of the procedure  the provider ensures control of bleeding and closes the incision with sutures in layers. Note that this code does not apply to services on the rectum. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands of scar tissue that form between internal organs and tissues  joining them together abnormally. Incision: A surgical cut into a body tissue or organ. Internal hernia: Protrusion of an internal organ  such as a loop of the intestine  into an opening located within the abdominal cavity. Intussusception: A medical condition in which a part of the intestine invaginates into another section of intestine. Laparotomy: Surgical incision of the abdomen. Rectum: The terminal portion of the large intestine  extending from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal. Viscera: The soft internal organs in the body cavity  especially those contained within the abdominal and thoracic cavities. Volvulus: Condition in which the bowel twists on itself  causing obstruction to the flow of material through the bowel. Tips Use 44055 if the provider performs correction of malrotation by lysis of duodenal bands or reduction of midgut volvulus. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider makes an incision to reach the affected part of the intestine other than the rectum. She alleviates and derotates the intestinal malrotation by reduction or by destruction of bands of tissue kinking the duodenum. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an abdominal incision. She explores the presence and degree of volvulus in the intestine. If midgut volvulus is present  she straightens the malrotated bowel manually without resection. If duodenal bands are present  she mobilizes the duodenum and dissects the adhesions coursed over it. The provider may use reduction  lysis  or both. After completion of the procedure  the provider irrigates the cavity and ensures control of bleeding. She closes the incision with sutures in layers. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands of scar tissue that form between internal organs and tissues  joining them together abnormally. Cecum: Pouch or large tubelike structure connected to the junction of the small and large intestines. Duodenal bands: Bands of tissue formed between the cecum and the intestinal wall creating a blockage in the duodenum; also called Ladd?? bands. Duodenum: First part of the small intestine. Ladd?? procedure: A surgical operation to alleviate intestinal malrotation by straightening the intestine  incising duodenal bands  moving the small intestine to the right  and the colon to the left; the provider may remove the appendix  if present. Lysis: Destruction or dissolution. Midgut volvulus: Twisting of the entire midgut; secondary to intestinal malrotation; more common in infants and children. Resection: Surgical removal of tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part; also called excision. Tips Use 44050 if the provider performs reduction of volvulus  intussusception  internal hernia  by laparotomy. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider performs biopsy of the small intestine using a capsule introduced through the mouth. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider places a capsule attached to a tube into the mouth of the patient. Under fluoroscopic guidance  the provider advances the tube with the capsule into the small intestine. As the capsule reaches the small intestine  the provider uses a syringe to trigger the capsule to remove a small piece of intestinal lumen. He maintains suction using the syringe as he withdraws the tubing and capsule to obtain the sample for biopsy. The provider may take more than one biopsy during the session. Terminology Lumen: The interior  open area of a vessel or organ; a tubularlike cavity. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X??ay where the X??ay image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Peroral: Administered or performed through the mouth. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider removes a single affected segment of the small intestine and connects the remaining intestinal ends. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the abdomen and identifies the target area of the intestine. He isolates the area of the small intestine and resects the segment  retaining as much blood supply as possible. He connects the remaining intestinal ends in an end to end  end to side  or side to side manner  depending on the location of the resection. After completion of the procedure  the provider ensures control of bleeding and closes the abdominal incision appropriately. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Enterectomy: Surgical removal of a segment of the intestine. Resect: To excise or cut out tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part; also called excise. Small intestine: The part of the intestine that runs between the stomach and the large intestine; the duodenum  jejunum  and ileum collectively. Tips Use +44121 for each additional small intestine resection and anastomosis performed in addition to 44120. Use 44125 if the provider performs enterectomy  resection of small intestine; with enterostomy. Use 44202 if the provider performs laparoscopy  surgical; enterectomy  resection of small intestine  single resection and anastomosis. Read Less

At the same session as initial small intestine resection and anastomosis  the provider resects one or more additional affected segments of the small intestine. She isolates the area of the small intestine and resects one or more additional segments  retaining as much blood supply as possible. She connects the remaining intestinal ends in an end to end  end to side  or side to side manner  depending on the location of the resection. After completion of the procedure  the provider ensures control of bleeding and closes the abdominal incision appropriately. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Enterectomy: Surgical removal of a segment of the intestine. Resect: To excise or cut out tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part; also called excise. Small intestine: The part of the intestine that runs between the stomach and the large intestine; the duodenum  jejunum  and ileum collectively. Tips Because +44121 is an add??n code  payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code: 44120. For laparoscopic enterectomy  see 44202 and +44203. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider makes an abdominal incision to resect a segment of small intestine. He sutures the remaining end of the small bowel  which is attached to the stomach  to the abdominal wall through an opening called a stoma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the abdomen and identifies the target area of the intestine. He isolates the area of the small intestine and resects the affected segment  retaining as much blood supply as possible. He closes the distal end of the small bowel and sutures the proximal end through a separate incision into the abdominal wall as a stoma. After completion of the procedure  the provider ensures control of bleeding and closes the abdominal incision used for enterectomy. Terminology Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure?? point of attachment. Enterectomy: Surgical removal of a segment of the intestine. Enterostomy: Surgical operation in which the small intestine is diverted to an artificial opening in the abdominal wall  called a stoma  or in another part of the intestine. There are multiple reasons that colon resection might be required including cancer  other diseases of the colon  necrosis from entrapped bowel  and trauma. The surgeon makes an abdominal incision and removes the entire colon and rectum. The rectal mucosa may be removed. The end of the small bowel is attached to the anus. The surgeon makes a long abdominal incision  usually from the xiphoid to the pubis. The colon and rectum are freed from their attachments and the blood vessels are ligated. A loop of the ileum is brought up to skin level and attached to create a temporary fistula to allow for healing. The surgeon assures hemostasis. The abdominal incision is closed in layers. The provider tests donor stool for bacteria  viruses  and syphilis and then prepares it for instillation. The provider examines and prepares previously harvested small intestine  which includes preparing the superior mesenteric artery and vein for anastomosis. Explanation The donor intestine arrives in the operating room in a preservative solution. The provider examines the graft and removes any extraneous tissue such as the duodenum and head of the pancreas. He carefully frees up the superior mesenteric artery and vein and prepares them for anastomosis. Terminology Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called allogeneic graft and homograft. Backbench: A sterile environment in the operating room but separate from the operating table where a provider prepares grafts before transplantation. Cadaver donor: A deceased person whose organs or tissue may be harvested for transplantation. Duodenum: First part of the small intestine. Graft: Skin  part of a vessel  bone  or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Harvest: Remove skin  a portion of a vessel  bone  or other tissue from a patient or donor  generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis  i.e.  to surgically connect two structures together. Living donor: A related or unrelated individual who donates organs or tissue for transplantation. Pancreas: An organ situated between the spleen and duodenum; it produces insulin and enzymes that aid in the digestion of protein. Superior mesenteric artery  or SMA: An artery that arises from the aorta  the main artery that comes off the left ventricle and supplies blood to the entire body; the SMA supplies blood to the small intestine. Superior mesenteric vein  or SMV: The SMV follows the same distribution as the superior mesenteric artery and merges with the splenic vein that carries blood from the spleen; the two veins form the hepatic portal vein  the main vein that carries blood from the liver. The provider removes a lesion on the peritoneum  or mesentery  the lining of the abdominal cavity to which the intestines attach. He removes the lesion for pathologic examination and or to prevent intestinal obstruction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the abdomen and exposes the mesentery. He identifies and excises the lesion. He repairs the mesentery with sutures or staples. The provider removes all instruments  checks for bleeding  and closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Et seq: Latin for and the following. Excise: Remove tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part; also resect. Intestine: The digestive  or alimentary  tract from the pylorus  the opening at the bottom of the stomach all the way to the anus. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Mesentery: Synonymous with peritoneum  the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that attaches various organs to the abdominal wall. Pathologic examination  or histopathologic examination: Laboratory analysis of tissue for abnormalities in structure or function. Resection: Surgical removal of tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part; also called excision. Read Less

The provider sutures a defect in the mesentery  the lining of the abdominal cavity to which the intestines attach. He performs the procedure to treat or prevent intestinal obstruction  or blockage. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the abdomen and exposes the mesentery. He identifies the defect and repairs it with sutures or staples. The provider checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Hernia  herniation: Bulging of an organ or tissue through a weakness or opening in membranes such as the peritoneum  the abdominal wall  or other structures. Intestine: The digestive  or alimentary  tract from the pylorus  the opening at the bottom of the stomach all the way to the anus. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures  dislocations  or hernias. Read Less

The provider incises an appendiceal abscess and drains the pus to relieve pain and prevent the spread of infection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision in the right lower abdomen and identifies the abscess pocket. He incises  or cuts into  the abscess pocket and drains the contents. Typically  he leaves a tube in place to drain any accumulation of purulent material during healing. The provider checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket that results from the accumulation of purulent material  or pus  in the soft tissue. Appendiceal: Pertaining to the appendix  a saclike structure between the small intestine and large intestine whose function is unknown. Catheter: A flexible tube inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed  blood withdrawn  or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids  allow passage of urine  or examine the urethra and bladder. Image guided: Use of fluoroscopy  a live X??ay where the X??ay image appears on a television monitor; ultrasound  high frequency sound waves to view tissues; or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Incision and drainage: A surgical procedure that involves cutting into and draining cysts  abscesses  or other lesions containing infective material; the procedure typically includes irrigation  or washing out  of the affected part. Infection: A disease condition caused by bacteria  viruses  or other microorganisms. Intestine: The digestive  or alimentary  tract from the pylorus  the opening at the bottom of the stomach all the way to the anus. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Purulent material: Pus. Read Less

The provider removes an inflamed appendix  a saclike structure situated in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen at the junction of the large and small intestines. He performs the procedure to relieve pain and to prevent infection or rupture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision over the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. He enters the abdomen and identifies the appendix. He suctions out any pus and washes the area with saline solution. He then removes the appendix. The provider closes the cut edges of the intestines  checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Appendectomy: Surgical removal of the appendix due to inflammation  the response of tissues to injury which includes pain  heat  redness  and swelling. Incidental appendectomy: Removal of the appendix at the time of a major primary procedure on the abdomen or pelvis; this includes removal of a noninflamed or healthy appendix as a precautionary measure. Intestine: The digestive  or alimentary  tract from the pylorus  the opening at the bottom of the stomach all the way to the anus. Read Less

Use 44979 to report new or unusual procedures on the appendix that do not have an assigned code. Explanation The provider performs a procedure on the appendix that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT? codes available. Terminology Appendix: A saclike structure situated in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen at the junction of the large and small intestines; its function is unknown. Intestine: The digestive  or alimentary  tract from the pylorus  the opening at the bottom of the stomach all the way to the anus. Laparoscopy: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen  inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure  inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen  and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open  removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure  and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Tips CPT? guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code  submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined  active code. Include one or more similar codes  and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis  and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less

The provider incises an abscess  a collection of pus in a walled off sac or pocket  below the mucosal surface of the rectum and drains it. He performs the procedure to prevent infection and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider identifies the submucosal rectal abscess. He makes a small transanal incision through the rectal lining into the abscess cavity. He leaves the incision open to drain the abscess. He does not close the incision so that the damaged tissues can heal from the inside toward the skin over a period of time. He sends a portion of the drainage material to the laboratory for analysis to determine the type of infecting bacteria. After a short recovery period  he releases the patient. Terminology Bacteria: Single celled microorganisms  i.e.  visible only with a microscope  some of which cause infection. Infection: A disease condition caused by bacteria  viruses  or other microorganisms. Intestine: The digestive  or alimentary  tract from the pylorus  the opening at the bottom of the stomach all the way to the anus. Rectum: The terminal portion of the large intestine  extending from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal. Submucosal: Below the mucosa or mucous membrane  the interior lining of organs and the intestines. Transanal: Through the anus  the distal opening of the large intestine. Read Less

The provider incises an abscess in the supralevator  pelvirectal  or retrorectal area and drains it. He performs the procedure to prevent infection and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider performs digital rectal examination  palpation  or anoscopy to identify the area of abscess. The provider chooses among various techniques for reaching the abscess  depending on its location. Once he reaches the abscess  the provider incises and drains it. If the abscess is extensive or involves the abdominal or pelvic cavity  he irrigates the area with saline or antibiotic solution. Typically  he leaves the evacuated area open or places a tube from the area and out through the skin for continued drainage. After a short recovery period  he releases the patient. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled off sac or pocket as a result of infection. Anoscopy: Using a lighted tubular instrument inserted into the anus to examine the anus and lower portion of the rectum; also called proctoscopy if the examination goes deeper into the rectum. Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Anus: The distal opening of the large intestine. Digital rectal examination: Using the fingers inserted through the anus to examine the rectum for swellings or fluctuations. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure?? point of attachment. Intestine: The digestive  or alimentary  tract from the pylorus  the opening at the bottom of the stomach all the way to the anus. Pelvirectal: Pertaining to the pelvic cavity or pelvic structures and the rectum. Retrorectal: Behind the rectum. Rectum: The terminal portion of the large intestine  extending from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal Supralevator: Located above the levator ani  an important group of muscles that lift and support the floor of the pelvis. The provider uses an anal approach to take a biopsy of the anorectal wall. He sends the tissue to the laboratory for pathologic examination. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider first performs a digital rectal examination. He inserts an anoscope  a type of endoscope for examining the anus and rectum. He inserts scissors or biopsy forceps through the scope and removes a small amount of tissue from the anorectal wall for diagnostic analysis. If necessary  he closes the biopsy site with sutures. He check the biopsy area for bleeding; seeing none  he removes the scope and instruments. He sends the specimen to the laboratory for pathologic examination. He releases the patient after a brief recovery period. Terminology Anorectal: Pertaining to the anus  or the distal opening of the intestine  and the rectum. Anus: The distal opening of the large intestine. Diagnostic: Refers to procedures performed for the purpose of determining the type of disease and its causes as opposed to therapeutic  which means for treatment purposes. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure?? point of attachment. Megacolon: A condition in which there is abnormal widening of a segment of the colon. Rectum: The terminal portion of the large intestine  extending from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal. Read Less

Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider dilates the anus and holds it open with retractors. He incises the mucosa on the posterior wall of the anal canal. He excises a section of muscle and closes the edges of the incision  leaving a small area open for drainage. He sends the specimen to the laboratory for pathologic examination. He checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and sends the patient to recovery. Terminology Anorectal myomectomy: The removal of a myoma  or tumor of the muscle  from the anal or rectal region. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure?? point of attachment. Rectum: The terminal portion of the large intestine  extending from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal.
