The provider removes the rectum and joins the colon to the anus using both an abdominal and perineal approach. He typically performs the procedure to treat rectal cancer. The procedure leaves the patient with an uninterrupted digestive tract so that the patient can pass stool normally. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped  draped  and anesthetized  the provider incises the abdomen. He then dissects the distal colon and rectum to the level of the sphincter muscles. He divides the colon and removes the rectum at the level of the sphincter muscles. He incises the perineum. The provider pulls the distal colon through the sphincter complex and then joins it to the anus  suturing the structures together. He closes the perineal incision and closes the fascia and subcutaneous tissue in the abdomen in layers. He checks for bleeding  removes any instruments  and finally closes the abdominal skin incision. Terminology Abdominoperineal: A surgical procedure that requires two approaches  one through the abdomen and a second through the perineum which requires excising the anal sphincter. Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Coloanal: Pertaining to the colon  or large bowel  and the anus  the distal opening of the large intestine..Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure?? point of attachment. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers  protects  and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles  bones  nerves  and blood vessels. Intestine: The digestive  or alimentary  tract from the pylorus  the opening at the bottom of the stomach all the way to the anus; the lower portion or large intestine starts at the distal  or lowermost  part of the small intestines and includes the cecum  the ascending  transverse  and descending colon  the rectum  and the anal canal. Perineum: Area between the anus and scrotum in males and between the anus and vagina in females. Proctectomy: Partial or total removal of the rectum; the most common surgery performed to treat rectal cancer. Rectum: The lower part of the large intestine where the body stores stool. Reservoir: A created space for storage; it may be a replacement for an anatomical cavity like the stomach or an artificial container for storage of medicine. Sphincter complex: Muscle fibers surrounding the opening of the anus. Sphincter muscles of the anus: Muscles located within and outside of the anal canal  contracting to close the anus  and expanding to open the anus  typically during a bowel movement. Subcutaneous: Below the skin. Tips Code 45112 represents a coloanal anastomosis without a reservoir. When the provider performs a coloanal anastomosis with a surgically created internal reservoir  report code 45119  Proctectomy  combined abdominoperineal pull through procedure  e.g.  coloanal anastomosis  with creation of colonic reservoir  e.g.  J pouch  with diverting enterostomy when performed. The procedure described by 45119 increases the amount of intraoperative work that the provider performs. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider surgically removes or bypasses a diseased portion of the rectum and connects the colon and anus. He performs this procedure using both an abdominal and perineal approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an abdominal incision. He next locates the rectum and lower portion of the colon and divides the colon just above the diseased rectal segment. He then removes the diseased rectal segment and pulls the lower portion of the colon closer to the anus with sutures using a perineal approach. Alternatively  he may pull the lower portion of the colon close to the anus with sutures bypassing the rectum. Once the procedure is complete  the provider stops all bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. The Swenson  Soave  and Duhamel procedures vary slightly from each other but achieve equivalent results. The Swenson procedure leaves a small portion of the diseased rectum. The Soave procedure leaves the outer wall of the colon unaltered. The Duhamel procedure uses a surgical stapler to connect the good and bad bowel. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures  anatomical or surgically created  such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Anus: External opening of the rectum where gastrointestinal tract ends. Colon: Tube like portion of digestive tract that extends from the stomach to the anus. Congenital megacolon: A birth disorder in which there is dilation or overgrowth of a portion of the colon due to paralysis of the colon. Proctectomy: Surgical removal of the rectum. Perineal approach: Through the perineum  or the area in front of the anus. Rectum: End part of the large intestine that connects to the anus. Tips When the provider surgically removes the rectum along with removal of part or the entire colon  use code 45121  Proctectomy  complete for congenital megacolon  abdominal and perineal approach; with subtotal or total colectomy  with multiple biopsies. He also performs multiple biopsies of the diseased colon tissue during this procedure and approaches this procedure using both an abdominal and perineal approach. When the provider surgically removes a portion of the rectum through a perineal approach without connecting the remaining colon with the anus  use code 45123  Proctectomy  partial  without anastomosis  perineal approach. In this procedure  the provider surgically divides  or incises a stricture  or narrowing of the rectum  or the end part of the large intestine that connects with the anus. This procedure is done to treat narrowing due to such conditions as a tumor or scarring. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a longitudinal incision in the scar tissue in one or more places surrounding the stricture  or narrowed area  of the rectum. He may also dilate the narrowed area of the anal canal. Additionally  he may incise the internal anal sphincter  or the layers of circular muscle tissue lining the inner surface of the anal canal. Terminology Anus: External opening of the rectum where gastrointestinal tract ends. Anal canal: The terminal portion of the digestive tube from the rectum to the anus. Anal sphincter: The anal sphincter consists of the internal anal sphincter and the external anal sphincter; the internal anal sphincter is formed from smooth muscle of the anal canal; the external anal sphincter  which is larger and of importance in fecal continence  is made up of striated muscle. Scar: Fibrous tissue that replaces the normal skin after injury. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider makes an incision in the rectum to excise a tumor. He may perform this procedure using a transsacral approach through the sacrum  or a transcoccygeal approach through the coccyx. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision at the junction of the sacrum and coccyx. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue and removes the coccyx. He then mobilizes the rectum  which he exposes when he removes the coccyx  and localizes the tumor site. Next  he incises the rectum to remove the tumor of the rectum. Finally  he stops all bleeding and sutures the rectum. Then he closes the wound by suturing the layers of soft tissue together. Terminology Anus: External opening of the rectum where gastrointestinal tract ends. Proctotomy: Surgical incision into the rectum. Rectum: The end part of the large intestine that connects with the anus. Sacrum: Triangular shaped bone at the base of the spine  just above the tailbone  or coccyx. The patient is placed in the lithotomy or prone (face??own) position  appropriately prepared  and given general anesthesia. Local anesthesia may also be used. The provider inserts a gel lubricant into the anus and then inserts the proctoscope fitted with a Doppler probe and light source through the anus and up to the lower rectum. Once the artery has been identified  he turns off the Doppler and ligates the artery with a Z stitch of 2?? absorbable sutures on a 5/8??n. needle at the site of the best Doppler signal. He marks the rectal mucosa with cauterization at the site of the best Doppler signal. He sutures the prolapsing mucosa with a continuous running suture in a proximal to distal direction  with the sutures about 0.5 cm apart to avoid making the sutures too tight. The provider performs a surgical procedure using a section of an intestine to replace all  or part  of the duct that passes urine from the kidney to the bladder. The procedure is indicated for conditions such as  recurring stones  ureteral cancer  and extensive ureteral injury. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider inserts a nephrostomy tube if one is not already present. The provider makes a paramedian  or midline incision depending on if one ureter is affected  or both. The provider frees the beginning of the large intestine from the surrounding tissue  and divides the lateral attachments of the ascending colon. The provider also frees the ascending colon  peritoneum from the bladder  and the lateral aspect of the bladder. The provider then carefully determines the intestinal length needed to replace the ureter  and she selects an appropriate segment of the intestine. She divides the bowel close to the connective tissue  and removes the needed section. She then reconnects the divided intestine  and restores continuity. The provider then flushes the excised bowel segment with saline solution until the discharge runs clear. She then dissects the portion of the ureter being replaced. The provider passes the intestinal segment into the space  rotates the segment to place the distal end near the bladder  and the proximal end close to the renal pelvis or the ureter. The provider joins the proximal end of the intestinal segment to the ureter  or renal pelvis while joining the distal end either to the bladder  or to the top spread open end of the lower ureter  depending if it is a partial or a complete ureteral replacement. The provider then closes the defect in the colonic connective tissue. At the end of the procedure  the provider may place a ureter stent  and a urethral catheter. The provider performs a surgical procedure to remove a constricting device  such as a thread  wire  or constricting band placed on the ureter during a previous surgery to control the flow of urine due to urinary incontinence. Cystostomy  cystotomy with drainage. Explanation After the application of general anesthesia  a small incision is made over the lower abdominal skin  to access the bladder. All the muscles  fat layer  and fascia are cut to reach to the bladder. A very small incision (cystotomy) is made in the bladder. A catheter is passed into the bladder which acts as a drainage tube. Successful passage of the catheter tube can be confirmed under fluoroscopy (report separately). This catheter tube is again directed to the lower abdominal skin from the bladder and ultimately placed outside the skin  thus creating an opening (cystostomy) between the bladder and the abdominal skin on body exterior. The catheter is fixed either by balloon inflation or by sutures. Terminology A suprapubic cystostomy (also known as a vesicostomy) is a surgically created connection between the urinary bladder and the skin which is used to drain urine from the bladder in individuals with obstruction of normal urinary flow. In this procedure  the provider incises the urinary bladder to remove a calculus  or stone  from the bladder. He performs this procedure without resection of the bladder neck. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises the skin of the abdomen overlying the urinary bladder. He then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue  or just under the skin and the muscles. He then identifies the bladder and checks it by inserting a syringe and draining out the urine. He then makes an incision in the urinary bladder wall according to the size of stone. He spares the neck of the bladder as a vesical neck resection is not part of this procedure. Next  he removes the stone with the help of forceps or a grasping device. He examines the bladder for any other defects. He then sutures the bladder incision and places a catheter to drain the urine. This prevents urine leakage from the surgical site which can lead to an abscess formation. Finally  he stops all bleeding  inserts a drain  and closes the abdominal wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. He removes the drainage tube and catheter after five days. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled off sac or pocket  caused by infection. Calculus: A buildup of minerals forming a stone. Cystolithotomy: A surgical procedure to remove a stone from the bladder. Cystotomy: A surgical process to make an incision into the bladder. Urinary bladder: A hollow organ in the pelvic cavity that collects urine. Vesical neck: Neck of the bladder. Tips Use 51060  Transvesical ureterolithotomy  when the provider makes an incision into the urinary bladder to remove a stone along with a bladder neck resection. Read Less

Bladder aspiration is performed to collect urine sample or provide temporary relief from acute urinary retention. Needle aspiration is performed percutaneously. The process is fast  simple  and easy to perform. Explanation Needle aspiration is performed percutaneously. The process is fast  simple  and easy to perform. Ultrasonography is done to locate the bladder. After the application of local anesthesia  the physician identifies the urinary bladder region. The physician uses a 22??auge needle with a typical 10 or 20 mL syringe attached to it. The physician inserts the needle over the skin of the lower abdomen until urine appears within the syringe. If insertion is unsuccessful  the physician does not withdraw the needle completely  but rather pulls it back in the subcutaneous tissue and re??nserts it in another direction. After the urine is obtained  the physician removes the needle carefully and gentle pressure is applied to the insertion site. Then physician places sterile dressing on the site. Usually a small amount of urine is collected  but if necessary the physician may aspirate more urine to provide temporary relief from acute urinary retention. The physician may send the urine sample to the lab for urinalysis or culture. The provider makes an incision into the urinary bladder and excises one or more bladder diverticula  which are congenital or acquired herniations in the bladder wall caused by a protrusion or bulging of the lining of the bladder. This prevents urine leakage from the surgical site  which can lead to an abscess formation. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket formed due to the accumulation of purulent material  pus  in the soft tissue  caused by infection. Tips The descriptor for this code indicates that the procedure is a separate procedure and should not be reported when performed along with a related procedure (e.g.  same anatomic area or through the same incision  orifice  or surgical approach). If the provider performs this procedure with an unrelated procedure  append modifier 59  Distinct procedural service to the code. Be sure the documentation supports the procedure as a separate procedure and not part of some other related procedure. Do not append modifier 59 when a more specific modifier  such as XE (same date  separate encounter)  XP (different practitioner)  XS (separate organ or structure)  or XU (service does not overlap with the usual components of the main service). Documentation must support the use of the modifier. Do not confuse modifier 59 with modifier 51 for multiple procedures (e.g.  same procedure on different anatomic sites  related procedures on the same anatomic site  or the same procedure multiple times on the same anatomic site). Use 51999  Unlisted laparoscopy procedure  bladder  when the provider performs a laparoscopic bladder diverticulectomy. Read Less

In this procedure  the provider performs a surgical bloc resection of the pelvic structures  which may include the uterus  cervix  and vagina in a female patient  or prostate in a male  along with the bladder  lower ureters  lymph nodes  urethra  colon and or rectum. He performs this procedure in patients suffering from bladder  prostatic  or a urethral malignancy. He first clamps the blood vessels and removes the bladder  urethra  lower ureters  lymph nodes  and ureters. He next may remove the reproductive organs  the prostate in men  and the uterus and ovaries in females if necessary  along with the rectum and colon depending upon the spread of the tumor. If the provider removes the rectum and bladder  he creates two openings  or stomas on the abdominal wall for collecting bowel through creation of a colostomy  and urine by transplantation of the ureters to the abdomen wall. Rectum: End part of the large intestine that connects in the anus. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass of cells  can be benign or cancerous. Urethra: A tube that drains urine out of the bladder and carries the urine to the outside of the body. Ureter: Tube that carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall  the side located above the rectum  than the anterior wall  the side located below the bladder. Vesical: Refers to the bladder. Read Less

Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is also known as micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG). This is a technique which is performed to detect reflux by watching a person's urethra and urinary bladder during his or her micturition. The test is performed in a hospital radiology department or in a health care provider's office by an X??ay technician. Explanation A urinary catheter is inserted through the urethra into the bladder and a radiopaque liquid (contrast or contrast agent) is injected. Under the guidance of a fluoroscope the physician observes the filling and voiding once the contrast enters the bladder and finally the reflux when the person voids. If the liquid flows from the bladder into the urethra during voiding  then it's normal. But abnormality is seen if the contrast moves into the ureters and the kidney and it may be diagnosed as vesicoureteral reflux. Finally  the catheter is removed. Terminology A voiding cystourethrogram is an X??ay examination of the bladder and urethra that is performed while the bladder is emptying. Tips 74430 (Cystography  minimum of 3 views  radiological supervision and interpretation) and 74455 (Urethrocystography  voiding  radiological supervision and interpretation) can be coded separately along with this code. Explanation A cystometrogram is a graphical recording of urinary bladder pressure with different volumes of urine in the bladder. For a complex cystometrogram  the provider generally uses a transurethral catheter to fill the bladder with water while at the same time obtaining rectal pressures using a manometer. In this technique  he fills the bladder with sterile water and records the bladder pressure to determine whether the patient has spontaneous contractions  also known as bladder spasms. He also usually performs a urethral pressure study during this procedure  where once the bladder fills up and he measures the bladder pressure  he withdraws the catheter from the bladder into the urethra. He then asks the patient to perform a task  such as to cough  and he records any urine leakage. Leakage of urine while coughing is a symptom of stress urinary incontinence. Terminology Calibrated electronic equipment: A device that a provider uses to test the accuracy of other equipment as per the required standards. Catheter: A flexible tube that a provider inserts into a vessel through which he can pass instruments  blood can be withdrawn  or fluids instilled; a provider can insert this flexible tube into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids  allow passage of urine  or examine the urethra and bladder. Manometer: A device that a provider uses to measure fluid pressure. Overactive bladder: A urological condition in which there is a sudden and uncontrollable urge to pass urine. Stress incontinence: Uncontrollable leakage of urine during activities that increases pressure on bladder like sneezing. Transurethral: Through the urethra. Urethra: A tube that drains urine out of the bladder and carries the urine to the outside of the body. Urethral closure pressure profile: A continuous measurement which represents the pressure in the urethra keeping the urethra closed over the baseline bladder pressure; the provider measures it by subtracting the bladder pressure from the urethral pressure. Urinary bladder: A hollow organ in the pelvic cavity that collects urine. The provider uses a cystoscope passed through the urethra to inspect the ejaculatory ducts (a pair of tubes through which semen moves out); he cuts out (excises) a part of the duct that is obstructed or incises (cuts into) the ducts to open a stricture (narrowing). Alternatively  he may simply incise the opening to enlarge it and treat a stricture (narrowing). Upon completion  the provider removes the instruments and scope and drains the bladder.

Explanation After the application of anesthesia  the physician inserts an endoscope (cystourethroscope) to view the bladder neck and urethra. The physician carefully cuts the tissues under the glans of the penis/urethra  which is also called as meatotomy or urethrotomy  in order to move the resectoscope through the urethra. Once this is done  a resectoscope is inserted to resect the scar tissues; a cautery can also be used to resect the tissues further. Once this is done the bleeding is controlled and the scope is removed. A drainage tube can be placed for removal of urine from the bladder during the postoperative period  and the patient is transferred into the recovery room.

Transurethral resection of the prostate is performed in cases of BPH (benign prostate hyperplasia) which commonly occurs in middle??ged and elderly men. Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) combined with mechanical morcellation represents the latest refinement of holmium:YAG surgical treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Explanation Laser coagulation / vaporization / enucleation is performed under general anesthesia. During the procedure the physician inserts a cystoscope into the urethra to view the surgical field. If necessary  irrigation is performed for proper visualization of the area. Under its visualization  a resectoscope is inserted through the urethra and passed on to the prostate. A laser??mitting fiberoptic probe device is inserted  and the target tissue is then fired with the laser. The heat energy conducted through the probe coagulates the target tissue  reducing the size of the prostate. The prostate or the target big prostate adenoma gets cut into smaller pieces (morcellation) that can easily be removed from the body. For this purpose  a commercially available Morcellator instrument is used. In order to attain maximum efficacy  a side??o??ide sweep technique is used in a clockwise and counterclockwise movement creating an open cavity. Also  during this procedure the physician can perform a vasectomy  meatotomy  and internal urethrotomy. Once the procedure is finished a catheter is inserted and the patient is transferred to the recovery room. The provider drains an abscess in the urethra. The abscess may be due to an infection or injury to the urethra. The provider performs the procedure to treat infection and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a small longitudinal incision in the urethra and extends it to the level of the fascia and muscle to identify the periurethral abscess. The provider further uses a sharp surgical knife to make a stab incision in the abscess and aspirates the fluid. Finally  he controls any bleeding and closes the incision in layers using absorbable sutures. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled off sac or pocket  the result of infection. Aspiration: Removal of fluid  gas  or other material through a tube attached to a suction device  often combined with irrigation  the instillation of fluid to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen or stomach or to clean a wound; also withdrawal of material  often with a needle; can also refer to breathing in fluid or food material. Carbuncle: Severe abscess in the skin. Cutaneous: Pertaining to the skin. Cyst: Sac usually containing fluid; the term cyst can refer to an abnormal growth or to any saclike structure  such as the urinary bladder or gallbladder. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers  protects  and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles  bones  nerves  and blood vessels. Furuncle: A boil  a lesion around a hair follicle due to infection. Paronychia: Nail infection that bacteria or a fungus causes. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Suppurative hidradenitis: Skin disease usually affecting the sweat glands  characterized by abscess and cysts. Tips If the abscess is not deep or the lesion is superficial  use code 10060  Incision and drainage of abscess  e.g.  carbuncle  suppurative hidradenitis  cutaneous or subcutaneous abscess  cyst  furuncle  or paronychia; simple or single. The provider drains an abscess or cyst of the Skene's glands. Explanation After the administration of local anesthesia and sterilization of the vulva  the provider explores the cysts in the posterolateral wall of the vagina. A direct connection to the urethra may be identified using a urethroscope. The provider makes a sharp incision over the abscess or cyst and drains the material from the Skene's cysts  also called periurethral cysts. She may insert a Foley catheter into the urethra to identify the cyst location throughout the dissection. She controls bleeding and closes the defect with absorbable sutures. The Skene's glands are periurethral (or paraurethral) glands on the anterior (front) wall of the vagina that lead to mucus glands around the lower end of the female urethra. These glands are located in the floor of the terminal end of the urethra and open external to the meatus. They secrete fluids during sexual activity. Tips See 53270 for excision of the Skene's glands. Read Less

The provider creates an opening in a diverticulum by making a surgical incision. He performs the procedure to improve urination and relieve pain in both male and female patients. Explanation When the female patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a longitudinal small incision in the anterior vaginal wall to access the urethra. He extends the incision to the level of the fascia and muscle. He then identifies the urethral diverticulum and marsupializes it  i.e.  he raises the edges of the diverticulum and sutures them together to create a pouch. This sac eventually separates from the urethra and the defect heals by granulation. The provider closes the urethral incision over a catheter that he places in the urethra to allow for better healing. He will remove the catheter at a later date. Finally  the provider controls any bleeding and closes the incision in the vagina in layers using absorbable sutures. In the case of a male patient  the provider preps and anesthetizes the patient and proceeds to perform a urethroscopy. He inserts a catheter through the urethra and ties off  or sutures  the neck of the diverticulum to close it. He performs copious irrigation. The provider typically leaves the catheter in to be removed at a later date. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed  blood withdrawn  or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids  allow passage of urine  or examine the urethra and bladder. Marsupialization: Surgical creation of a pouch or sac by oversewing a cyst which has been evacuated of its contents or the neck of a diverticulum; it causes the lining of the pouch to eventually separate from the membrane and the defect fills in by granulation. Urethra: Duct or tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body; in males  it is also responsible for carrying semen. Tips Open marsupialization can only be applied to mid and distal urethral diverticula. The CPT? code 53240 is applicable to both males and females. Read Less

As there are many clinical scenarios that represent a foreign body involving the external genitalia  consider 55899  Unlisted procedure  male genital system in these clinical situations. You may need to submit a detailed operative report and a cover explanatory letter to your payer to achieve reimbursement. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider partially removes the penis. The provider performs this procedure in the case of serious  injury or disease of the penis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider excises only the distal part of the penis due to a severe injury or disease. The provider makes an incision in the penile shaft and carefully divides the underlying structures, excising the abnormal or injured tissues. He leaves enough of the shaft or urethra to allow the passage of urine for voiding purposes.  The provider then closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Amputation: Removal of a body extremity because of trauma or surgery; the surgical removal helps to control pain or a disease process in the affected limb. Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure�s point of attachment. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass of cells, can be benign or cancerous. Urethra: The duct through which urine passes out of the body from the bladder. Tips Performing a second penile procedure during the global period of a surgical diagnostic procedure may require the use of modifier 58, Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician or other qualified health care professional during the postoperative period. For instance, the provider performs a deep biopsy of a tumor of the penile shaft. He reports 54105, Biopsy of penis; deep structures, which has a 10�day global period, for that initial procedure. On day three following the surgery, the biopsy reveals cancer of the penis, which requires a partial amputation. Bill 54120, for the amputation, which the provider performs the next day. Because partial amputation occurs within the global period of the initial surgery, append modifier 58, Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician or other qualified health care professional during the postoperative period, to 54120. The provider will be paid the full fee and start a new 90�day global period.

The provider performs a circumcision  a surgical procedure that removes the foreskin of the penis  using a clamp or other device and regional anesthesia consisting of a dorsal penile or ring block. Explanation The patient is placed on his back. His arms and legs may be strapped down to prevent any unwanted movement during the procedure. The skin of the perineum and thighs are prepared with Betadine liquid (an antiseptic) and the area is draped in a sterile fashion. Examples of devices the provider may use include the Gomco? clamp  Mogen clamp  or PlastiBell?. After injecting a regional anesthetic into the top of the penis or in a ring around the penis and with the patient appropriately prepped  the provider makes a dorsal slit and separates the foreskin from the glans penis. As an example of the procedure  the bell portion of the clamp is then placed over the glans  and the foreskin is pulled over the bell through the plate and yoke of the clamp. The nut of the clamp is tightened onto the bell so that it holds the foreskin in place. The Gomco? clamp compresses the foreskin between the metal clamp and bell  allowing it to be cut and removed with minimal bleeding. After the foreskin is excised  the clamp and bell are removed. Patients may undergo the procedure because of potential preventive benefits  such as reducing the risk of urinary tract infection in the first year of life and reducing the risk of acquiring or transmitting sexually transmitted infections. Terminology Corona of the glans penis: The protruding rounded border of the glans  which resembles a crown. Dorsal slit: An incision along the length of the foreskin on the top of the penis from the tip of the glans to the corona. Foreskin: Skin covering the end of the penis; this skin is a retractable skin. Frenulum of the penis: A small fold of membrane that attaches to the undersurface of the penis connecting the glans to the shaft and limiting the movement of the glans. Glans penis: Tissue present at the head of the penis; this tissue has erectile properties. Regional anesthesia: Medications administered by local injection used to block sensation in a specific part of the body during and after surgery; spinal and epidural anesthesia are two main types of regional anesthesia. Tips If the provider doesn't administer dorsal penile or ring anesthetic block  report this code with modifier 52 to indicate reduced services. For circumcision using surgical excision other than a clamp  other devices  or dorsal slit  report 54160 for a neonate 28 days old or less and 54161 for a patient older than 28 days. The procedure described by 54150 is likely to be performed using a Gomco? clamp  Mogen clamp  or PlastiBell?  but other devices have been developed  such as Zhenxi rings  Tara Klamp  SmartKlamp  Shang Ring?  and PrePex?. In this procedure  the provider incises the frenulum of the penis. The provider performs this primarily to release the tissue restricting the movement of the glans penis. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider examines the glans penis and the urinary meatus to ensure that the meatus is of proper diameter. He incises the undersurface of the penis lengthwise. He also inspects the frenulum to find whether it is pulling on the glans. When he finds pulling  he incises the frenulum. After ensuring that there is no bleeding  he closes the wound and places a loose??itting bandage around the penis so as not to obstruct passage of urine. Terminology Frenulum: A small fold of membrane that attaches to the undersurface of the penis connecting the glans to the shaft and limiting the movement of the glans. Glans: The conical  end projection of the penis. Meatus: External opening of the urine outflow channel known as the urethra. Tips Do not report 54164 for frenuloplasty. Instead  use a repair code such as 12001??2007. If documentation indicates both circumcision and frenulotomy  you should report only the circumcision code  choosing from 54150??4161  54162  and 54163. Read Less

The provider injects a medication into the external area of the penis. He performs this procedure to treat a disease known as Peyronie disease in which there occurs an abnormal curvature of the erect penis. Explanation The provider commonly performs this procedure to treat Peyronie disease in which a patient may experience severe penile curves and pain during erection  or a lump within the shaft of the penis including shortening of the penis due to fibrous tissue growth inside the penis. The provider injects medication such as verapamil  interferon  or collagenase into the external area of the penis directly into the fibrous tissue that causes the condition. The medication lessens the deformity and the patient?? pain. Terminology Collagenase: A chemical substance that helps to destroy certain bacteria. Interferon: A protein  which the cells release usually when a virus enters the body  to inhibit virus replication. Peyronie disease: A medical condition in which a plaque or a hard lump forms on the superior or inferior side of the penis; sometimes results in severe curvature of the penis and pain during erection  and or shortening of the penis; cause is commonly uncertain. Verapamil: A synthetic substance which the provider commonly uses to treat irregular heart rhythms and to dilate the blood vessels in conditions such as hypertension. Read Less

The provider injects a medication into the external area of the penis. He also incises the external skin of the penis and exposes the plaque for injection. The provider performs this procedure to treat a disease known as Peyronie disease in which there occurs an abnormal curvature of the erect penis. Explanation The provider commonly performs this procedure to treat Peyronie disease in which a patient may experience severe penile curves and pain during erection  or a lump within the shaft of the penis including shortening of the penis due to fibrous tissue growth inside the penis. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  before injecting the medication  the provider makes a small incision in the dorsal penile skin to expose the plaque  or abnormal fibrous tissues. Next  he injects medication such as verapamil  interferon  or collagenase  directly into the plaque of the penis using a needle syringe. The medication lessens the deformity and the patient?? pain. Terminology Collagenase: A chemical substance that helps to destroy certain bacteria. Interferon: A protein which the cells release usually when a virus enters the body  to inhibit virus replication. Penile plaque: An accumulation of an abnormal fibrous tissue in the penis. Peyronie disease: A medical condition in which a plaque or a hard lump forms on the superior or inferior side of the penis; sometimes results in severe curvature of the penis and pain during erection  and or shortening of the penis; cause is commonly uncertain. Verapamil: A synthetic substance which the provider commonly uses to treat irregular heart rhythms and to dilate the blood vessels in conditions such as hypertension. Read Less

The provider irrigates the corpora cavernosa to treat priapism  a condition causing a persistent erect penis. Explanation The provider commonly performs this procedure to treat priapism  a painful condition where the penis remains erect and does not return to its flaccid state. Most of the blood remains present in the sponge like tissue of the corpora cavernosa in the penile shaft for a long period of time  sustaining the abnormal erection. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider draws out blood from the corpora cavernosa by inserting a large bore needle. He then irrigates the area with a saline liquid. The provider repeats this procedure as necessary to resolve the abnormal erection. Terminology Corpora cavernosa: Characteristic sponge like tissue in the penile shaft region which contains most of the blood that is in the penis during an erection. Irrigation: A flushing or washout procedure. Read Less

The provider injects contrast material into the corpora cavernosa to check the extent of venous leakage. Explanation In this procedure  the provider first withdraws some blood from the corpora cavernosa. The provider then injects contrast material under fluoroscopic guidance into the corpora cavernosa for X??ay examination. The provider checks venous leakage  which is the common cause for erectile dysfunction. Venous leakage is usually seen quickly via the deep dorsal vein or via the crural veins. He also checks the X??ay images to see the integrity and course of blood flow in the penis. Terminology Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body  which providers administer to patients through various routes  including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material  contrast medium  contrast media  contrast agent  or contrast dye. Corpora cavernosa: Sponge like tissue in the penile shaft region which contains most of the blood that is in the penis during an erection. Crural vein: Blood vessel that drains blood from the leg and thigh. Deep dorsal vein: Blood vessel that lies deep in the penis and drains blood out of the penis. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X??ay where the X??ay image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Venous leakage: A condition in which the veins in the penis cannot prevent blood from leaving the penis during an erection; this is called venous leakage which leads to erectile dysfunction. X??ay: X??ays  or radiographs  involve using radiation to diagnose  manage  and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips Erectile dysfunction may no longer be payable for 54230. Many diagnostic tests for erectile dysfunction were payable in the recent past  but may no longer be payable. These include 93980  Duplex scan of arterial inflow and venous outflow of penile vessels; complete study; 93981  Duplex scan of arterial inflow and venous outflow of penile vessels; follow up or limited study; 54250  Nocturnal penile tumescence and or rigidity test; 54231  Dynamic cavernosometry  including intracavernosal injection of vasoactive drugs eg  papaverine  phentolamine; 54230  Injection procedure for corpora cavernosography; 74445  Corpora cavernosography  radiological supervision and interpretation; 36247  Selective catheter placement  arterial system; initial third order or more selective abdominal  pelvic  or lower extremity artery branch  within a vascular family; and 95926  Short latency somatosensory evoked potential study  stimulation of any or all peripheral nerves or skin sites  recording from the central nervous system; in lower limbs. The above tests may still be payable under certain circumstances  such as if the patient has a lifetime history of erectile dysfunction  a history of perineal trauma  or no response to injection therapy. However  you will need supporting documentation of such histories to report. Read Less

The provider injects pharmacologic agents such as papaverine  phentolamine  or prostaglandin E1 into the corpora cavernosa of the penis. He performs this procedure to treat patients with erectile dysfunction. Explanation In this procedure  the provider first withdraws some blood from the corpora cavernosa. The provider then injects a drug such as papaverine  phentolamine  or prostaglandin E1 into the corpora cavernosa within the shaft of the penis. This gives immediate results and erection is regained in majority of the patients. Terminology Corpora cavernosa: Sponge like tissue in the penile shaft region  which contains most of the blood that is in the penis during an erection. Papaverine: A drug that a provider commonly uses to relieve muscle tightness. Phentolamine: A drug that helps to dilate blood vessels  especially in patients with hypertension. Prostaglandin E1: A drug that helps the blood vessels to dilate in patients with erectile dysfunction. Titrate: To determine the concentration of a dissolved substance in terms of the smallest amount of compound of known concentration needed to bring about a given effect in a reaction. Venous leakage: A condition in which the veins in the penis cannot prevent blood from leaving the penis during an erection  which leads to erectile dysfunction. Tips The provider usually performs injection of the corpora cavernosa to produce an erection as represented by 54235. When done by the patient at home  it is not billable. In the office  report 54235 only once to assess the patient's reaction to the drugs or to titrate the proper dosage. Check payer policy regarding separate payment for the drugs involved in the procedure. Read Less

The provider performs a plethysmography of the patient?? penis. A plethysmograph is a device which consists of a flexible band with mercury in it that the provider fits around the penis of the patient and hence records any changes in the penis circumference during erection. This service helps determine penile blood flow and assess erectile dysfunction. Explanation The provider fits a plethysmograph band around the patient?? penis. He then connects the band to a device with a video screen and data recorder. When the penis erects at any stage  the machine records any changes in the penis circumference in response to audio or video stimuli. Terminology Erectile dysfunction: Condition resulting from a male?? inability to have or maintain an erection of his penis. Plethysmography: A noninvasive procedure for measuring the amount of blood flow present in an organ or artery or other part of the body; it may also involve the measurement and recording of changes in the size of a body part as modified by the circulation of blood in that part. Tips Medicare does not view certain tests as medically necessary in cases of erectile dysfunction. These include 54240  along with: 93922  Limited bilateral noninvasive physiologic studies of upper or lower extremity arteries  eg  for lower extremity: ankle or brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial or dorsalis pedis arteries plus bidirectional  Doppler waveform recording and analysis at one to two levels  or ankle or brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial or dorsalis pedis arteries plus volume plethysmography at one to two levels  or ankle or brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial or dorsalis pedis arteries with  transcutaneous oxygen tension measurement at one to two levels 93923  Complete bilateral noninvasive physiologic studies of upper or lower extremity arteries  three or more levels eg  for lower extremity: ankle or brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial or dorsalis pedis arteries plus segmental blood pressure measurements with bidirectional Doppler waveform recording and analysis  at three or more levels  or ankle or brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial or dorsalis pedis arteries plus segmental volume plethysmography at three or more levels  or ankle or brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial or dorsalis pedis arteries plus segmental transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements at three or more levels  or single level study with provocative functional maneuvers eg  measurements with postural provocative tests  or measurements with reactive hyperemia   93975  Duplex scan of arterial inflow and venous outflow of abdominal  pelvic  scrotal contents and or retroperitoneal organs; complete study  93976  Duplex scan of arterial inflow and venous outflow of abdominal  pelvic  scrotal contents and or retroperitoneal organs; limited study and 93978  Duplex scan of aorta  inferior vena cava  iliac vasculature  or bypass grafts; complete study. The provider performs the third stage of a surgical procedure to correct hypospadias. He releases the temporary sutures put in place previously  and releases the penis from the scrotum  such as in the third stage of cecil repair. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises and detaches the temporary sutures between the penis and scrotum. These sutures were previously put in place during the second stage of the repair of hypospadias. He may place a Foley catheter in the bladder for the diversion of urine. Finally  he closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Cecil repair: A three staged repair of a urethral narrowing  in which the provider excises the narrowed segment  constructs a new urethral segment  and separates the new segment from the scrotum. Foley catheter: A catheter with an inflatable balloon tip for retention in the bladder; it is a flexible tube that the provider commonly passes through the urethra into the bladder. Hypospadias: A medical condition present from birth in some males in which the opening of the urethra is under the penis rather than at the tip of the penis. Scrotum: A pouch of skin containing the male sex glands. Urethra: The duct through which urine passes out of the body from the bladder. Urethroplasty: The surgical repair of an injury or defect of the urethra. Read Less

The provider performs a single stage surgical procedure to correct hypospadias at the base of the penis  along with an extensive dissection to correct an abnormal curvature of the penis known as chordee. He also repairs the urethra with a skin graft tube or island flap as part of this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision at the base of the penis near the scrotum and around the meatus. He prepares a wide rectangular flap from preputial skin and sutures it together to form a tube to use it as a part of the urethra. Then he secures the resultant tube flap in place between the urethral opening underneath the shaft of the penis near the scrotum and the meatal opening he creates at the tip of the penis. At the end of the procedure  he may also perform a circumcision to ensure smooth movement of the glans through the prepuce. The provider closes the incision with sutures. Read More

The provider inserts a semirigid noninflatable synthetic material into the penis of the patient. This procedure is done to treat erectile dysfunction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes a transverse incision on the pubic area above the penis. He partially removes the corpora cavernosa  or the spongy tissues of the penis  and inserts the prosthesis into the penis. The provider takes special care to preserve important nerves and blood vessels. This implant consists of two semirigid rods  such as silicone rods  which the provider inserts into the erectile compartments in the penis. He makes an opening into each of these two long tubes of spongy tissue inside the penis and inserts one rod into each tube. After completion of the insertion of the prosthesis  the provider closes the tissues and incisions by suturing. Alternatively  the provider may access the erectile tissue through an incision below the scrotum or at the base of the penis  and then performs a similar procedure to insert the implant. Terminology Corpora cavernosa: The sponge like horizontal tissue in the penis  along the penile shaft which holds most of the blood that is present during an erection. Penile prosthesis: An implant inserted into the penis to treat erectile dysfunction; there are rigid  semirigid  and inflatable implants that simulate a normal erection. Tips See 54401 to report insertion of an inflatable  self??ontained penile prosthesis and 54405 for insertion of a multicomponent  inflatable penile prosthesis including pump placement  cylinders  and reservoir. In a scenario where the provider has to terminate the procedure while inserting a noninflatable  semirigid penile prosthesis for erectile dysfunction  because of a urethral tear  the coding depends in part on how much of the insertion procedure the provider was actually able to perform and what type of urethral repair done. For the corporal dilation and rod insertion portion of the procedure  you should report 54400. Append modifier 52  Reduced services  which indicates a reduced service because of the early termination of the procedure due to the urethral injury. Depending on the type of repair  also report either 53410  Urethroplasty  one stage reconstruction of male anterior urethra or 53505  Urethrorrhaphy  suture of urethral wound or injury; penile. Append modifier 51  Multiple procedures for non??edicare carriers to indicate that the provider performs more than one procedure. Medicare will append modifier 51  Multiple procedures on its own. Although the urethral repair results from a complication at the time of surgery  because the provider spends significant time and effort for its repair  this also becomes a billable service at the time of the reduced primary procedure. For other procedures to treat erectile dysfunction  see 54231 for intracavernosal injection and L7900 for a vacuum erection device. Additional Info Nonsurgical treatments for erectile dysfunction include Viagra? or similar drug  which is not payable by original Medicare part A and B but may be covered by part D or an advantage plan or private insurer. The labelling indicates no more than one tablet a day  so private payers decide how many tablets are allowed  as many as six to ten tablets a month. For men  treatment for erectile dysfunction includes treating the underlying organic cause such as diabetes mellitus. Read Less

The provider creates a passage of blood between the corpora cavernosa and corpora spongiosum to allow blood to move freely between these two areas and relieve pain due to priapism. The provider may create the shunt unilaterally or bilaterally. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider creates a shunt to correct priapism  an erection of the penis for an unusual long length of time. The provider routes blood from the fatty tissue or corpora cavernosa of the penis to another area of erectile tissue called the corpus spongiosum of the penis. He makes an incision at the base of the penis. He then dissects through the thick fibrous tissues from the corpus cavernosum to the corpus spongiosum  and then sutures the defect due to the dissection to create a shunt or passage between the swollen corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum at the glans penis. This will allow blood flow to move freely between these two areas and relieve the erection  and the pain due to having an erection for an extended period of time. He may repeat this procedure on the same structures on the opposite side as necessary. Terminology Bilateral: On two sides; opposite of unilateral. Corpora cavernosa: The sponge like horizontal tissue in the penis  along the penile shaft which holds most of the blood that is present during an erection. Corpus Spongiosum:The circular mass of spongy tissues surrounding the male urethra within the penis  which carries maximum blood during erection. Glans penis: Tissue present at the head of the penis; this tissue has erectile properties. Priapism: A painful medical condition in which the erect penis of the patient does not return to its flaccid state within a few hours  even if there is no external stimulation. Shunt: A surgical anastomosis or connection. Unilateral: On a single side; opposite of bilateral  on two sides. Read Less

The provider repairs a tear or tears in the corpora cavernosa  spongelike tissue in the penile shaft region which contains most of the blood in the penis during an erection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider typically begins by degloving the penis (removing the outer skin to reveal the corpora). To help localize a tear  or later to check that the repair is tight  he may inject saline or indigo carmine  a blue dye. He removes any blood clots and controls bleeding with clamps  pressure  or sutures. He removes any damaged tissue that cannot be repaired. He then sutures the identified tears in the corpora  replaces the penile skin  and wraps the penis with a bandage.

The provider manipulates and stretches the foreskin of the penis of a patient to breakdown adhesions. He performs this procedure to treat phimosis by lysing adhesions between the uncircumcised foreskin in an uncircumcised male and the head of the penis or by removing adhesions between the remaining foreskin and glans penis in a circumcised male. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider manually pulls back the foreskin over the head and back along the shaft of the penis to gently break up adhesions. In an uncircumcised male  the provider may stretch the foreskin by inserting a clamp or a ring between the foreskin and glans penis and then spread the clamp open to gently break the foreskin away safely. Terminology Circumcision: The act of cutting off the foreskin of the penis. Foreskin: The roll of skin present at the tip of the penis; it has retraction properties. Glans penis: Tissue present at the head of the penis; this tissue has erectile properties. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Lysis: Breakdown. Phimosis:A condition where the foreskin of the penis is not retracted from the head or glans of the penis due to a possible stricture or narrowing of the foreskin; a painful condition which causes difficulty with urination. Prepuce: Foreskin. Preputial adhesions: Condition in which the foreskin adheres to the glans penis. Tips In a scenario where a patient comes to the provider?? office complaining of phimosis and the provider reduces the adherent foreskin of the penis  in addition to the appropriate office visit code with modifier 25  you can report code 54450 for the reduction of the adherent foreskin. If a pediatric provider performs lysis of penile adhesions post circumcision in the office  check if the lysis involves instrumentation and general anesthesia. If the provider can easily  manually break down the post circumcision adhesions  usually filmy lesions  without using an instrument to cut the adhesions  consider the work part of the office visit code. If the provider performs lysis of adhesions post??ircumcision with an instrument under sterile conditions  use 54162. The procedure requires pain relief  such as a local anesthetic  as well as general anesthesia to surgically release the skin bridge that forms on the circumcision incision line. Because tissues bleed more freely at older ages and the provider must manage postoperative pain  the lysis requires more skill than an earlier post??ircumcision service. An alternative to 54162 is 54450. Use this code if the foreskin is still partially adhered to the penis and creates problems  which usually occurs in children older than seven or adults. Read Less

The provider removes a tissue sample one or both testicles using a needle. After biopsy  the tissue sample is examined under a microscope. Explanation The skin over the testicle is cleaned and local anesthetic is administered as needed to numb that area. A needle is inserted to obtain a small piece of the testicle tissue. If biopsy is performed to evaluate the absence of living sperm in semen then sample is placed in Bouin's fluid  which is a preserving solution  and sent to laboratory to check infertility. This is a separate procedure and would be billed separately. Terminology Testicles  or testes (sing. testis): Oval??haped glands that hang in the scrotum beneath the base of the penis and produce sperm (necessary for reproduction) and male hormones  such as testosterone. Bouin's fluid: A fixing and preserving solution which is a mixture of picric acid  formaldehyde and glacial acetic acid. Needle biopsy: The withdrawal of a tissue sample through the use of a needle without requiring an incision. Open biopsy: Obtaining a tissue sample through an incision. Tips The descriptor for this code indicates that the procedure can be performed separately but should not be reported when performed along with a related procedure (e.g.  same anatomic area or through the same incision  orifice  or surgical approach). If the provider performs this procedure with an unrelated procedure  append modifier 59  Distinct procedural service to the code. If the provider performed this procedure on both testes  append modifier 50. If the provider performed this procedure through an open incision  report 54505. Read Less

The provider removes a tissue sample one or both testicles through an open incision in the scrotum. After biopsy, the tissue sample is examined under a microscope.Explanation A testicular biopsy is a procedure in which a tissue sample is obtained from one or both testicles. The skin over the testes is cleaned with an antiseptic liquid. Under the local anesthesia, the physician makes a small cut through the skin and takes a small piece of the testicular tissue. After the biopsy, he sends the tissue sample to the laboratory for further examination. This is a separate procedure and would be billed separately.Terminology Testicles, or testes (sing. testis): Oval�shaped glands that hang in the scrotum beneath the base of the penis and produce sperm (necessary for reproduction) and male hormones, such as testosterone. Needle biopsy: The withdrawal of a tissue sample through the use of a needle without requiring an incision. Open biopsy: Obtaining a tissue sample through an incision. Tips The descriptor for this code indicates that the procedure can be performed separately but should not be reported when performed along with a related procedure (e.g., same anatomic area or through the same incision, orifice, or surgical approach). If the provider performs this procedure with an unrelated procedure, append modifier 59, Distinct procedural service to the code. The provider excises the lesion of the testis  which is not related to the parenchyma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an inguinal incision in the scrotum to remove a benign lesion such as a fibroma  or an adenomatoid tumor. The provider incises the tunica vaginalis and inspects the testis and epididymis. He then identifies and excises the lesion. The provider may send the sample to the laboratory for evaluation. He replaces the testis in the scrotal sac and then closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Adenomatoid tumor: Benign growth that generally presents in the genital tract  in regions such as the testis. Benign: Not malignant  generally treatable or not needing treatment. Epididymis: A highly tubular duct behind the testis  along which the sperms pass. Fibroma: A benign tumor of connective tissue. Inguinal: Means of the groin which is the area between the abdomen and the upper thigh on either side of the body. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Paratesticular: Next to the testicles. Parenchyma: The functional tissue of an organ in contrast to the supporting tissue. Scrotum: The sac that contains the testes  or testicles  a pair of reproductive organs in males that produce sperm. Testis: An organ which produces the male reproductive cells. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass of cells  can be benign or cancerous. Tunica vaginalis: Membrane covering of a testis  one of a pair of reproductive organs in males. Tips In a scenario where a provider performs a scrotal exploration via an inguinal incision for a paratesticular mass  which he follows by an excision of a mass. Report 54512 for the excision of the paratesticular mass. The exploration is inclusive of this code and would not be a separately billable service. Read Less

The provider surgically removes one or more testicles with or without insertion of a testicular prosthesis. He uses a scrotal or inguinal approach for this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider incises the side of the testicle he is to remove. He extends the incision down through the fat layer until he encounters the external oblique fascia. The provider incises it along its fibers and identifies and isolates the spermatic cord. The provider preserves the ilioinguinal nerve which runs anterior to the spermatic cord. Then he pulls the testicle through the scrotal incision and removes the testis. He clamps off the spermatic cord in two places and cuts between the clamps. He may insert an artificial testis into the scrotum if there are no contraindications and then close the incision. Alternatively  the provider incises the groin to access the testicle for removal  and follows a similar technique as above. Terminology Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body or a structure. External oblique fascia: A flat and wide part of the external abdominal oblique muscle. Ilioinguinal nerve: A nerve that arises from the first lumbar nerve and supplies the skin of the upper medial thigh. Inguinal: Means of the groin which is the area between the abdomen and the upper thigh on either side of the body. Orchiectomy: Surgical removal of one or more testicles. Orchiopexy: Surgical operation to bring an undescended testicle into the scrotum. Prosthesis: An artificial replacement of a body part; it may be rigid or semi rigid. Scrotum: The sac that contains the testes  or testicles  a pair of reproductive organs in males that produce sperm. Spermatic Cord: A cord like structure in males surrounding tissues that run from the abdomen down to each testicle. In this procedure, the provider performs a puncture aspiration of a hydrocele, which is a collection of fluid that results from a defect or irritation in the tunica vaginalis of the scrotum and may arise in the spermatic cord as well. The provider may also inject a medication as part of this procedure.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider cleanses the skin over the hydrocele by applying an antiseptic on the scrotal skin over the hydrocele. The provider punctures the skin and advances the needle into the sac for fluid collection. He aspirates, or withdraws, all the fluid content inside the hydrocele and afterwards, with the needle still in the sac, he may inject the sac with a sclerosing medication to prevent recurrence of the hydrocele.


Terminology
Aspirate: To draw out.

Hernia, herniation: Bulging of an organ or tissue through a weakness or opening in membranes or other structures.

Hydrocele: A collection of fluid around the scrotum, often affecting newborn infants.

Hydrocelectomy: Surgical removal of a fluid collection in the scrotum.

Sclerosing solution: Chemicals that inflame tissue lining, and makes the tissue harder.

Scrotum: The sac that contains the testes, or testicles, a pair of reproductive organs in males that produce sperm.

Spermatic cord: A group of structures that pass, cordlike, through the inguinal canal and include blood and lymph vessels, nerves, and the vas deferens, the tube through which spermatozoa, male sex cells, pass.

Testis: The pair of reproductive organs in males responsible for the production and storage of sperm and the male hormone testosterone; also known as testicles.

Tunica vaginalis: Membrane covering of a testis, one of a pair of reproductive organs in males. 


Tips
If the provider removes a hydrocele on one side, report 55040, Excision of hydrocele; unilateral. A hydrocele commonly occurs with a hernia. In pediatrics, the two are so similar that the procedures are bundled. However, this is not true for an adult with a hernia and a hydrocele. If the provider performs only the hydrocelectomy and not the hernia repair, report 55040 with modifier LT or RT to indicate the left side or the right side.

Sometimes the urology provider assists a surgery provider in the hernia repair and hydrocelectomy. According to CPT� rule, a provider who assists a surgery provider is a payable service with adult hernia repairs, but not with hydrocelectomy. If the urology provider assists in both, and the patient is an adult, only report 49505, Repair initial inguinal hernia, age 5 years or older; reducible. Append modifier 80, Assistant Surgeon to 49505. In children under the age of five, report 49500, Repair initial inguinal hernia, age 6 months to younger than 5 years, with or without hydrocelectomy; reducible, and append modifier 80, Assistant Surgeon.

Sometimes the urology provider, particularly in the case of a pediatric patient, performs the hernia repair and the hydrocelectomy at the same time. Select the hernia code carefully: these codes are age specific and refer to the type of hernia, and some refer to hydroceles. In children over five years of age, it is advised to use excision codes in addition to hernia repair codes.

The provider biopsies the prostate gland with a special biopsy needle or during surgery for pathological examination. Report this code regardless of the approach, for example, transrectal, perineal, or transurethral. Explanation A prostate biopsy is a procedure in which small samples are removed from the prostate gland with a special biopsy needle or during surgery, to be tested for the presence of cancer or other abnormal cell growth. A prostate biopsy can be performed by several different methods: Transrectal approach: The skin over the surgical site is cleaned with an antiseptic liquid. The provider inserts a needle through the wall of the rectum and into the prostate to obtain tissue samples. These tissue samples are then sent to pathology for further examination. Transurethral approach: The provider inserts a cystoscope through the opening at the end of the penis and into the urethra. He then inserts instruments through the cystoscope and obtains tissue samples. These tissue samples are then sent to pathology for further examination. Perineal approach: The perineum is cleansed with an antiseptic. The provider inserts an ultrasound probe into the rectum to guide needle placement. He inserts a special biopsy needle through the perineum and into the prostate where he activates the needle and withdraws tissue, which he sends to pathology for further examination. Terminology Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Needle biopsy: The withdrawal of a tissue sample through the use of a specially designed needle without the need for an incision. Perineum: The surface area between the scrotum and anus in men, bounded by the thighs, and the external genitalia and skin between the genitalia and anus in women. Prostate: A small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder; it secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Transrectal: Through the rectum, the terminal portion of the large intestine, extending from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal. Urethra: Canal that conveys urine out of the body from the bladder. Tips Providers can perform prostate biopsies with or without the presence of a radiologist and in both facility and nonfacility settings. In addition, doctors almost always perform needle biopsies of the prostate (codes 55700 and 55706) under ultrasonic guidance for needle placement (code 76942) and frequently do them in addition to transrectal echography (code 76872). If a surgeon performs a prostate biopsy with ultrasonic guidance and a transrectal echography and there is a radiologist in the room supervising the radiology procedures and documenting an interpretation and report of the findings, the surgeon may only report code 55700. That is because the surgeon performs only the biopsy and does not supervise and interpret the ultrasonic guidance and transrectal echography (codes 76942 and 76872). The hospital is responsible for reporting both the technical and professional components of the radiology services for the radiologist who was present. If the physician performs a prostate biopsy with ultrasonic guidance and a transrectal echography in the hospital setting and there is no radiologist present during the surgical session, the doctor not only documents taking the biopsy but documents two radiology reports, one for the ultrasonic guidance and another for the transrectal echography. Code the surgeon's services as codes 55700, 76942–26 (Professional component), and code 76872–26. The use of modifier 26 is to indicate that a physician only read and interpreted a test without actually owning the equipment. When a urologist performs both the surgical procedure and a radiology service in his office without the presence of a radiologist, you can report both the surgical code(s) and the radiology code(s) without ap­pending any modifiers. Reporting both the technical and professional components is considered reporting the "global" code. The urologist can report the full radiology service because he owns the equipment and supervises and interprets the services. So, if the urologist alone performs a prostate biopsy with ultrasonic guidance and a transrectal echography, report codes 55700, 76942, and 76872. Read Less

A simple vulvectomy represents a surgical procedure to remove all or part of the vulva for benign or premalignant conditions of the vulva that are extensive or numerous and their removal cannot be accomplished by local excision of a discrete lesion. Explanation In a simple partial vulvectomy, the physician removes only affected portions of the vulva (such as labia minora, labia majora, clitoris, etc.) including the skin, mucous membrane, and any superficial fat and connective tissue. As this is a vaginal approach surgery, the patient is usually placed in the dorsal lithotomy position. A Foley catheter is placed. After the patient is administered a general anesthetic, the area to be excised is marked, and the physician makes an oval–shaped incision around the diseased portion of the vulva and removes any fatty and/or connective tissue along with the affected skin. Once removal is successfully accomplished, the physician securely ties the pudendal vessels and controls the bleeding with electrocautery. The physician may place packing in the vagina. At the end, the defect is closed with synthetic absorbable sutures. The physician may use a skin graft to replace the removed skin if the area is large and cannot be closed with sutures alone. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Partial vulvectomy: The physician removed less than 80% of the vulva (for example, all or part of the left labia). Simple vulvectomy: Removal of skin and subcutaneous tissues that are located immediately below the skin and include superficial fat, fascia, and connective tissue. Tips The harvesting of a graft is always coded in addition, by type of graft. Possible graft codes may include: split–thickness autograft (15120), epidermal autograft (15115), dermal autograft (15135), or tissue cultured epidermal autograft (15155). Sewing a graft in place without doing the work to obtain the graft is part of the surgical procedure. A skinning vulvectomy involves removal of only the surface skin. It is reported with code 56620 if the area removed was less than 80% of the vulva. Most skinning vulvectomies are closed with a split thickness graft. If the physician excises a discrete lesion with margins, the codes 11420–11426 may be more appropriate to report if it was benign or codes 11620–11626 if it was malignant. These codes only include simple closure so if the closure was intermediate codes from 12041–12047 can also be reported. Coders should use caution in reporting a simple partial vulvectomy for the removal of excess labial tissue (clinically referred to as labial hypertrophy) without the presence of a benign or premalignant condition. Most payers have a policy with regard to the removal of excess tissue and will reject a vulvectomy code with a diagnosis of hypertrophy of the vulva. More appropriate coding for this condition would be 15839, Excision, excessive skin and subcutaneous tissue (includes lipectomy); other area. Read Less
