The area can be removed all in one piece (en bloc), or the provider can remove one side and then the other in two separate incision areas. All of the vulvar structures (mons, clitoris, labia minor and labia majora) are removed including the skin, deep fascia and muscle down to the bone. Once removal is successfully accomplished, the physician securely ties the pudendal vessels and controls the bleeding with electrocautery. The physician may place packing in the vagina. At the end of the procedure, the defect may be closed with layered sutures or a skin graft. Terminology Complete radical vulvectomy: Vulvectomy where 80% or more of the vulva is removed. Dorsal lithotomy: the patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Inguinofemoral lymph nodes: Located in the groin; there are chains of 10 on each side, and they are considered superficial nodes; usually Cloquet’s node is also removed with the superficial nodes even though it is the first lymph one in the chain of deep inguinal nodes; cancer will spread throughout the body by the lymph nodes; the superficial inguinofemoral lymph nodes drain into the deep inguinal nodes, and these nodes drain into the pelvic nodes; the pelvic nodes drain into the para–aortic nodes; if there are no cancer cells found in the Cloquet’s node, the vulvar cancer has not spread outside of the surgical area. Lymphadenectomy: Also called lymph node dissection, a surgical procedure in which lymph glands are removed from the body and examined for the presence of cancerous cells. Radical vulvectomy: Removal of the vulva carried through all vulvar tissues down to the underlying deep fascia, muscle,and bone. Supine position: The patient is placed on her back with her legs extended straight out. Tips The harvesting of a graft is always coded in addition, by type of graft. Possible graft codes may include: split–thickness autograft (15120), epidermal autograft (15115), dermal autograft (15135), or tissue cultured epidermal autograft (15155). Sewing a graft in place without doing the work to obtain the graft is part of the surgical procedure. Read Less

A radical vulvectomy represents a surgical procedure to remove all or part of the vulva for malignant disease of various stages. The surgery includes bilateral removal of inguinofemoral lymph nodes. The provider may remove the clitoris depending on the extent of the disease. Since it is radical surgery, tissue adjacent to the malignancy will be removed as well. Explanation The radical complete vulvectomy with bilateral inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy includes removal of all vulvar tissue and structures and the lymph nodes in the groin on the right and left sides. The surgery may also include removing the deep fascia of the thigh next to the vulva, part of the lower abdominal area adjacent to the vulva, and/or and the perineal area below the vulva to ensure that adequate margins to non–cancerous tissue have been removed. For this surgery, the physician may remove the entire area in one piece (en bloc). A Foley catheter is placed. After the patient is administered a general anesthetic, the surgeon will place the patient is a modified dorsal lithotomy position. The surgeon then marks the area to be excised and the shape of the marking will look like the head of a rabbit – the ears representing the groin area or the lymph nodes. An incision will also be made around the outside of the urethra and the vaginal opening. An incision is made into the skin and through all of the subcutaneous layers to the deep fascia following the marked line. The lymph nodes are identified and isolated and then taken out from surrounding tissues. All of the vulvar structures (mons, clitoris, labia minor and labia majora) are removed including the skin, deep fascia, and muscle down to the bone. Once removal is successfully accomplished, the physician securely ties the pudendal vessels and controls the bleeding with electrocautery. The physician may place packing in the vagina. At the end of the procedure, the defect may be closed with layered sutures or a skin graft. The incision is closed and drains may be left in place in the groin area to remove excess fluid. Terminology Complete radical vulvectomy: Vulvectomy where 80% or more of the vulva is removed. Inguinofemoral lymph nodes: Located in the groin: there are chains of 10 of them on each side, and they are considered superficial nodes; usually Cloquet’s node is also removed with the superficial nodes even though it is the first lymph one in the chain of deep inguinal nodes; cancer will spread throughout the body by the lymph nodes; the superficial inguinofemoral lymph nodes drain into the deep inguinal nodes, and these nodes drain into the pelvic nodes; the pelvic nodes drain into the para–aortic nodes; if there are no cancer cells found in the Cloquet’s node, the vulvar cancer has not spread outside of the surgical area. Lymphadenectomy: Also called lymph node dissection, a surgical procedure in which lymph glands are removed from the body and examined for the presence of cancerous cells. Modified dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with legs extended but with the knees bent and the hips rotated slightly outward but supported by stirrups. Radical vulvectomy: Removal of the vulva carried through all vulvar tissues down to the underlying deep fascia, muscle, and bone. Tips The harvesting of a graft is always coded in addition, by type of graft. Possible graft codes may include: split–thickness autograft (15120), epidermal autograft (15115), dermal autograft (15135), or tissue cultured epidermal autograft (15155). Sewing a graft in place without doing the work to obtain the graft is part of the surgical procedure. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider performs plastic repair of the vaginal opening. Explanation The surgical technique will vary depending on the extent of the problem. The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers a general anesthetic. Typically, the provider removes scar tissue from around the vaginal opening to restore normal anatomy and enlarge or tighten the vaginal opening, as required. This is usually accomplished by placing sutures, but in some cases, it might require a tissue flap to correct an overly tight vaginal opening. Once the provider successfully repairs the areas of the defects, the physician closes the areas with stitches or sutures. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Introitus: The opening of the vagina. Tips The word plastic, when used with a surgical procedure, implies a cosmetic procedure and, therefore, insurance may not reimburse the procedure unless the patient has a documented clinical condition. Diagnosis coding with this procedure code needs to be as specific as possible. Read Less

During this procedure, the provider either constructs or repairs the patient's clitoris. In some instances, the clitoris is created for the patient, and sometimes the provider reconstructs the clitoris to change its appearance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider repairs part or all of the clitoris to surgically reconstruct it. After the procedure, he uses plastic surgery techniques including grafting, flaps or sutures to cover the defect. The provider then closes the incisions in the clitoris, controls any bleeding, removes all instruments, and finally closes the incision in the clitoris. Terminology Clitoroplasty: Surgical formation of clitoris. Clitoris: Small and delicate female sex organ that is present at the opening of the vagina. Flap: Tissues for grafting typically removed from one place on the body and positioned in another; however, it may remain anchored and rotated from one side of an area to another. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Intersex state: Congenital anomaly in which the genitals of the newborn are such that it is difficult to identify the infant’s gender. Plastic surgery: Surgery which the providers perform with skin grafts, shaping or tightening to repair or renew body parts. Vagina: A muscular passage that leads from the uterus to the vulva in females. Tips If the provider repairs the perineum, use 56810, Perineoplasty, repair of perineum, nonobstetrical. Read Less

The provider aspirates peritoneal fluid from the vaginal vault using a spinal needle in a procedure referred to as colpocentesis or culdocentesis. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and inserts a speculum to view the cervix, which he grasps with a toothed instrument called a tenaculum. This is done to expose the back of the vagina, clinically referred to as the posterior vaginal fornix. He cleans the area with an antiseptic solution and injects a local anesthetic into the vaginal mucosa. Once he properly exposes the area, the provider inserts a hollow needle attached with a syringe into the cul–de sac behind the posterior vaginal wall. He then aspirates a sample of fluid into the syringe and withdraws the needle. He sends the sample for pathologic analysis or culture. The clinical term that most providers use to describe this procedure is culdocentesis, but it was referred to as colpocentesis when this code was added to the code set prior to 1990. Culdocentesis is listed in the index and refers you to colpocentesis. Terminology Cul–de–sac: The extension of the peritoneal cavity between the rectum and back wall of the uterus; also known as the rectouterine pouch or the pouch of Douglas; also, may refer to any dead–end pouch. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient lies on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure. It has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when the speculum is in place. Tips Because 57020 is a separate procedure, it is bundled with any female genital surgery that involves the vagina, cervix, or uterus. It cannot be billed separately if the physician decides to perform a colpotomy to drain the cul–de–sac at the same session. Read Less

The provider evaluates a lesion on the vaginal mucosa and performs a biopsy. Explanation The provider places the patient in the lithotomy position. The provider cleans the biopsy site with an antiseptic solution and applies a local anesthetic. The provider then obtains a tissue sample of the vaginal mucosa using a special biopsy tool, called a punch biopsy, or by cutting a small sample with a thin, sharp surgical knife. The provider sends the tissue specimen to the laboratory for a diagnostic examination. Terminology Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups Punch biopsy: Biopsy that the provider performs using a tool with a circular blade. The provider rotates the blade through the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous fat, taking a core of tissue. Vaginal mucosa: The membrane lining the vagina. Tips Report 57100 if the biopsy of vaginal mucosa is simple, where the provider removes the biopsy specimen superficially that does not require sutures. Report 57105 if the biopsy of vaginal mucosa is extensive and requires sutures. Read Less

The provider evaluates a large lesion or cyst on the vaginal mucosa and performs a biopsy. Explanation The provider places the patient in the lithotomy position and cleans the biopsy site with an antiseptic solution. The provider injects a local anesthetic around the biopsy site. The provider then obtains a tissue sample from a large lesion or cyst on the vaginal mucosa using a special biopsy tool, called a punch biopsy, or by cutting a small sample with a thin, sharp surgical knife. Because of the extensive nature of the biopsy required, the provider closes the biopsy site with sutures. The provider sends the tissue specimen to the laboratory for a diagnostic examination. Terminology Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Punch biopsy: Biopsy that the provider performs using a tool with a circular blade. The provider rotates the blade through the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous fat, taking a core of tissue. Vaginal mucosa: The membrane lining the vagina. Tips Report 57105 if the biopsy of vaginal mucosa is extensive and requires sutures. Report 57100 if the biopsy of vaginal mucosa is simple, where the provider removes the biopsy specimen superficially that does not require sutures. Read Less

The provider removes either the upper one third or the lower two thirds of the vagina along with paravaginal tissue. Explanation In this procedure, the provider performs a radical vaginectomy, removing only part of the vaginal wall, but he also removes additional tissues alongside the area excised because cancer has spread beyond the surface of the vaginal wall. The provider places the patient in a lithotomy position, and administers a general anesthetic. The provider usually places sutures to mark the extent of the planned excision. Because the vagina has so many blood vessels, the provider will usually inject the area with an agent that helps with constriction of the blood vessels to minimize bleeding. If the surgery is performed via the vaginal approach, the provider makes an incision at the lower end of the area to be removed using a scalpel in a circular manner all around the vagina. At the upper edge of the area, the provider will dissect the vagina off the underlying structure with scissors to remove the diseased portion, including margins and adjacent tissues. The provider applies sutures as the work progresses to stop any bleeding. Once the provider successfully removes the diseased portion of vaginal wall, he closes the incision with sutures or packs the vagina with bleached cotton cloth. The provider may perform vaginal reconstruction at a later time. If the provider performs the procedure via the abdominal approach, the provider first identifies the vaginal vault with a gauze roll or sponge holder that is placed in the vagina to stretch the vault. The provider incises the area over the vaginal vault and dissects off the vagina. Special care is taken not to injure the ureters, since they are very close to the incision area. The provider then makes an incision into the area of the posterior cul–de–sac and separates the rectum from the vagina and the uterosacral ligament. Once the bladder, ureters, and the rectum are clear, the provider excises the diseased tissue as described by the vaginal approach procedure. Providers can remove additional structures and lymph nodes in the area next to the vagina at the time of a radical vaginectomy. The provider normally places drains when performing the abdominal approach procedure. Providers perform this surgery as a treatment for vaginal cancer, removing any adjacent tissue that may be diseased. Terminology Cul–de–sac: The extension of the peritoneal cavity between the rectum and back wall of the uterus; also known as the rectouterine pouch or the pouch of Douglas; also, any dead–end pouch. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Paravaginal or paracolpium: The tissues that run along the sides of the vaginal canal and under the vaginal wall. Radical resection (or dissection): Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor; describes any extensive surgery to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed. Uterosacral ligament: Ligament of the uterus, extending from the cervix to posterior pelvic wall. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus (womb) to the external genital opening (introitus); also known as the birth canal. Tips For a partial vaginectomy without excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57106. For an even more extensive partial vaginectomy procedure that includes bilateral total pelvic lymphadenectomy and para–aortic lymph node biopsy in addition to excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57109. For a complete vaginectomy procedure, see 57110, and for complete (radical) vaginectomy with excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57111. Read Less

In this procedure, the physician removes a flap of tissue that is dividing the vaginal canal. This is a vaginal approach surgery. Explanation The provider administers local or general anesthesia to the patient and places her in the dorsal lithotomy position. The provider preps and drapes the perineum. The provider uses an instrument called a vaginal retractor to retract the vaginal wall and to expose the septum. Once he properly exposes the septum, he makes a vertical incision through the middle of the longitudinal septum to divide it. He then separates the septum from the vaginal mucosa using forceps. The provider then removes the septum and sutures the vaginal mucosa in an interrupted fashion circumferentially. If the septum is transverse, the provider will make an incision along both walls of the vagina where the tissue is attached and remove it. The provider then packs the vagina with bleached cotton cloth. Terminology Circumferentially: In a circular manner. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus (womb) to the external genital opening (introitus); also known as the birth canal. Vaginal septum: A congenital partition within the vagina that separates it into two portions. A transverse vaginal septum completely or partially blocks the upper one third of the vaginal canal because the tissue is attached to the sides of the vaginal canal. A longitudinal septum consists of a wall of tissue running down the length of the vaginal canal, which partitions the space into two vaginal canals. Tips If the physician also performs a hymenectomy along with removal of the vaginal septum, you may not code 56700 separately. Some payers may not reimburse for the hymenectomy in addition because this is part of the surgical approach to the operative site. On the other hand, the Correct Coding Initiative does not bundle these codes, so from a purely coding perspective, you can report 56700 and 57130 together. Report 56700 first because the code has higher relative value units (RVUs). Read Less

In this procedure, the provider fits and inserts a pessary or similar device into the vagina to treat vaginal wall prolapse or other disorders. Explanation The provider performs a vaginal exam to determine the proper type and size of pessary; he may try multiple sizes until he finds the correct fit. The provider will also check for possible incontinence once the pessary is in place and will instruct the patient on how to insert, remove, and clean the pessary. The provider will ask the patient to walk with the pessary in place, and then the provider will reexamine the vagina to ensure the pessary is still correctly in place. Terminology Pessary: A small rubber, plastic, or silicone device of varying sizes and shapes that the provider inserts into the vagina to correct prolapse of the vaginal wall or uterus, provide support for the rectum or bladder, help with stress urinary incontinence, or to deliver medication. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane. It extends from the vestibule to area where the cervix buts up against the vaginal vault. It is longer on the posterior wall, side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, side located below the bladder. Tips For the supply of the pessary, report HCPCS codes A4561 for a rubber pessary or A4562 for the more common silicone pessary. You may only bill the code 57160 once per pessary. That is, when the patient returns for pessary cleaning and checking, report only an E/M code if the provider performs the necessary components of an E/M exam. You may report code 57160 each time the provider fits and places a new pessary for the same patient. Read Less

The bleeding is not a result of pregnancy or childbirth. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and places a speculum into the vaginal canal to inspect the area. The provider then inserts a hemostatic agent into the vagina to prevent excess blood loss; the agent acts to stop bleeding by augmenting the clotting of blood. Or the provider may place a gauze pack into the vagina, which exerts pressure on the sides of the vaginal walls to stop the bleeding. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure. It has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when they are in place. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane. It extends from the vestibule to area where the cervix buts up against the vaginal vault. It is longer on the posterior wall, side located above the rectum. than the anterior wall, side located below the bladder. In this procedure, the provider sutures a laceration of the vaginal wall that is not related to childbirth or pregnancy. Explanation The physician may use local, regional, or general anesthesia to block any pain and keep the patient sedated throughout the surgery. The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. The physician inserts a vaginal instrument to hold open the vagina during the procedure. The physician then makes an incision into the vagina to identify the open wound area or fascial defect. Once he identifies the underlying fascial defect, he closes the wound defect with sutures. The physician removes the vaginal instrument, may remove any excess amount of vaginal skin, if required, and finally closes the vaginal incision with sutures. Terminology Colporrhaphy: Surgical repair of a defect or laceration in the wall of the vagina. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Vagina: a canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane. It extends from the vestibule to area where the cervix buts up against the vaginal vault. It is longer on the posterior wall, side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, side located below the bladder. Read Less

The purpose of the surgery is to reduce the diameter of the urethra and or provide support for the urethra in front of the bladder neck. Explanation After inserting a catheter into the urethra, the provider opens up the vaginal mucosa and dissects the vaginal wall and continues until the bladder and end of the urethra that is closest bladder are separated from the vaginal mucosa. Once the provider identifies the urethrovesical angle, he places sutures in the wall of the urethra and at the junction of the bladder. He then performs the inversion and plication of the urethral tissue. The provider excises vaginal tissues to remove any extra tissue left. Finally, he closes the vaginal wall and places a Foley catheter. Terminology Foley catheter: Tube typically placed through the urethra and into the bladder. Plication: The process of folding and suturing of tissues. Stress incontinence: Leakage of urine when there is increase in pressure in the abdomen associated with any physical activity like laughing, coughing, straining, running, etc. Urethra: A tube that starts at the urethral opening of the bladder and ends at the urinary meatus, where urine leaves the urethra, in the vestibule, or entryway, of the vulva. Urine passes from the bladder through the urethra when urination takes place. Urethrovesical angle: The angle between the urethra and the posterior bladder wall. which is usually about 90 degrees. When a patient develops a cystocele, a prolapse of the bladder into the vaginal vault, or the vaginal canal at the vagina's internal end. This angle narrows and causes stress incontinence. Read Less

In this procedure, the physician repairs a urethrocele, when the urethra prolapses into the vagina. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia to the patient and places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position. Using a vaginal approach, the provider makes an incision in the anterior vaginal wall over the prolapsed area. The provider sutures the torn or loose tissue in the urethra to supply support by pushing the urethra back into its normal location. The provider then closes the vaginal wall and usually inserts a Foley catheter at the end of the procedure. Terminology Cystocele: Occurs when the pubocervical fascia, the wall between the bladder and vagina, tears during childbirth, which causes the bladder to herniate, or protrude, into the vagina. Urethroceles can occur with cystoceles. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Foley catheter: A tube that the provider places through the urethra and advances into the bladder. Urethra: A tube that starts at the urethral opening of the bladder and ends at the urinary meatus in the vestibule of the vulva. Urine passes from the bladder through the urethra when urination takes place. Tips An urethrocele almost always accompanies a cystocele. When this occurs, code 57230 would be bundled as part of code 57240 for the anterior colporrhaphy. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider repairs the vaginal wall where the rectum is pushing through to the vaginal canal. The provider also usually repairs and strengthens the perineum below the vaginal opening. Explanation After administering regional or general anesthesia, the surgeon inserts a speculum into the vagina to hold it open during the procedure. He then performs a rectal exam to check for the extent of the rectocele. He makes an incision in the posterior vaginal wall from the top of the vagina to the levator muscles. He plicates the fascia and brings the edges together and sutures them, making sure that some of the levator muscle is included in the repair. He removes excess vaginal wall tissue. When the provider performs perineorrhaphy, he also repairs the levator and perineal muscles. The provider then adds vaginal packing. Terminology Colporrhaphy: Surgical repair of a defect in the vaginal wall. Levator ani: A compound muscle in the pelvis that is formed by the pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus muscles.It helps to prevent pelvic prolapse and brings the anus back up after a bowel movement. Perineorrhaphy: Surgical suturing of the perineum. Plication: It is a process of folding and suturing tissues. Rectocele: A bulging of rectal tissue into the vagina through a tear in the rectovaginal fascia or septum. Rectovaginal fascia: Also called rectovaginal septum, the supportive layer of the posterior vaginal wall. Tips Code 45560 for the repair of a rectocele, which is listed in CPT®'s Digestive System Surgery section under Rectum, has only slightly higher relative value units, RVUs, than the posterior colporrhaphy code 57250. And while you might be tempted to use the higher paying code, beware: if your physician has described performing a posterior colporrhaphy, even if he does not use that exact terminology, you should report 57250. The provider repairs a paravaginal defect using an abdominal approach. Cystocele repair is included when performed. Explanation With the patient under general anesthesia and in the supine position, the physician opens the peritoneum above the bladder and behind the pubic bone, and then enters the space of Retzius. He extends this dissection to expose the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis on both sides. The physician places several sutures along the side of the vagina through the pubocervical fascia, and he brings them through the obturator internus muscle, which is just above the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis. He then ties all sutures in order to close the defect. He closes the fascia and sutures the skin wounds together. If there is also a cystocele, the physician incises the vaginal wall and repairs the area to tighten the layers of tissue that separate the organs. This provides better support to the bladder. The provider revises or removes a prosthetic vaginal graft that was previously placed. He removes it because it has eroded, or the tissue over the mesh has thinned and the mesh is now exposed. The provider uses a vaginal approach. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers anesthesia. He inserts a speculum into the vagina and inspects the location of the previously placed graft. He analyzes whether the graft can be revised by placing some additional sutures or whether it should be excised completely. Depending upon the severity and abnormality of the graft, the physician revises it by excising the tissue around the surface lines of the graft, or he may completely excise the graft. Finally, the physician closes the endopelvic fascia and the vaginal mucosa. He inserts a Foley catheter and packs the vagina with gauze. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: the patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Endopelvic fascia: Fascia that covers the muscles on the lateral walls of the pelvis, passes onto the superior surface of the pelvic diaphragm, and extends onto the urethral sphincter and up onto the base of various pelvic organs. Foley catheter: A tube that the provider places through the urethra and advances into the bladder. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure. It has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when they are in place. Tips If the surgeon chooses to replace the graft with a new graft held in place with sutures, this would be included as part of the revision. Sometimes, the provider performs this procedure in the office and uses scissors to remove excess vaginal graft material under a local anesthetic, rather than taking the patient to the operating room. The code 57295, according to the CMS database, should only be performed in the hospital setting, and it has very high relative value units, RVUs. To report simple removal of sling material in the office setting, report the unlisted code 53899 or 58999, and compare the work to a simple excision of a foreign body of the subcutaneous tissues, code 10120. In this procedure, the provider repairs a fistula that has formed between the urethra and the vagina. The provider uses a vaginal approach. Explanation The physician places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers anesthesia. The physician identifies the fistula and cuts the vaginal mucosa. Once he excises the vaginal mucosa, he excises the fistula tract and sutures the area closed. He then sutures a pad of fatty tissue between the urethra and vaginal wall to plump up the hole that was left in removing the fistula. He will leave a catheter in place for drainage to help the urethra heal after the fistula was removed. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Urethra: A tube that starts at the urethral opening of the bladder and ends at the urinary meatus in the vestibule of the vulva. Urine passes from the bladder through the urethra when urination takes place. Urethrovaginal fistula: An abnormal opening between the urethra and the vagina. Read Less

In this procedure, the physician uses calibrated instruments to gradually dilate the vagina that is closed due to adhesion formation or injury. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers anesthesia other than local. The physician then inserts a series of progressively larger vaginal dilators to open the vaginal canal. Before placing the dilators, the physician moistens the tip of the dilator with some jelly or baby oil and then inserts the dilators through the vaginal opening repeatedly and slowly in upwards and backwards directions. The physician is then able to increase the width and length of the tissue of the vaginal walls to stretch the vaginal canal. Once the dilation process is successfully accomplished, the physician withdraws the vaginal dilators.

In this procedure, the physician examined the female genital organs while the patient is under anesthesia other than local. Explanation The provider places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position and administers anesthesia other than local. The provider examines the external and internal genitalia. He inserts a speculum to examine the cervix and vagina. At this time, the provider may collect a Pap smear specimen from the cervix or vaginal canal, if indicated. Once he collects the specimen, he will perform a bimanual examination of the pelvis to identify any changes in organ size. For this, the physician places two fingers inside the vagina and presses the other hand gently on the exterior of the pelvis. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure. In this procedure, the provider repairs a paravaginal defect using a laparoscopic approach. The provider may also perform a cystocele repair as part of this procedure. Explanation First the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. He then preps and drapes the abdomen, and he administers a general anesthetic. The provider enters the abdominal cavity near the belly button by using a Veress needle or an open incision, and he places a laparoscope. The provider insufflates the abdomen with CO2, or carbon dioxide gas to create a pneumoperitoneum, and then he puts the patient into the Trendelenburg position. He then makes small incisions around the abdominal area to insert trocars to better view the operating site and add surgical tools. If he is performing robotic surgery, he docks the robot to the laparoscope at this time. The provider enters the peritoneum above the bladder and behind the pubic and then enters the space of Retzius. He extends this dissection to expose the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis on both sides. The provider then places several sutures along the side of the vagina through the pubocervical fascia, and he brings them through the obturator internus muscle, which is just above the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis. He then ties all sutures in order to close the defect. The provider removes the docked robot arm as necessary, the laparoscope and all the trocars. Then he closes the small incisions with sutures. If there is a cystocele, the provider incises the vaginal wall from below, and sutures the pubocervical tissue to add support to the bladder. Terminology Arcus tendineus fascia pelvis (ATFP): Also referred to as the white line, this is the attachment point for the pubocervical fascia to support the anterior walls of the vagina that have prolapsed; it is a thick band of the fascia over the obturator internus muscles running in an arching line from the pubis to the ischial spine. Cystocele: A medical condition that occurs when the tough fibrous wall between a woman's bladder and her vagina weakens, allowing the bladder to droop into the vagina. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Insufflates: To blow a medicated powder, gas, or vapor into a bodily cavity. Laparoscopy: An operation performed to view the abdominal and pelvic contents through small incisions with the aid of a camera; it can either be used to inspect and diagnose a condition or to perform surgery for a problem; a fiberoptic instrument inserted through an incision in the abdominal wall and used to examine visually the interior of the peritoneal cavity, trocars are also inserted to allow for the addition of surgical tools. Obturator internus muscle: Covers the pelvic surfaces of ischium, and ilium, and obturator membrane, and also attaches to the femur to allow the thigh to rotate outward. Paravaginal defect: A loss of support of the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis, which forms the lateral attachments of the vagina; without the support of the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis, the bladder and urethra prolapse, which may result in cystocele or urethrocystocele. Peritoneum: The lining of the abdominal and pelvic cavity Pneumoperitoneum: The presence of gas or air in the abdominal cavity; when laparoscopic procedures are performed, carbon dioxide is pumped into the abdominal cavity to expand the viewing space. Pubocervical fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the anterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the bladder; when this tissue is weak it can cause the bladder or urethra to prolapse into the vaginal canal. Robot assisted surgery: An operation that is started with the laparoscope, but a robot arm is docked with the laparoscope and the surgeon completes the operation while sitting at a console that is next to the operating table. Space of Retzius: A space in the pelvis where the bladder and its supporting ligaments are found. Trendelenburg position: The patient is laid flat on her back with her feet higher than her head; this position moves the bowel and upper organs away from the operative site when a laparoscopic procedure is performed. Trocar: A medical device that is made up of an obturator, which may be a metal or plastic, sharpened or nonbladed tip, a cannula, or hollow tube, and a seal; trocars are placed through the abdomen during laparoscopic surgery, and they function as a portal to place other instruments such as graspers, scissors, staplers, and a laser needed during the surgical procedure. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Veress needle: A spring loaded needle used during a laparoscopic procedure to create a pneumoperitoneum. Tips In order to report a paravaginal defect repair, the operative note must refer to the key terms of space of Retzius, and arcus tendineus fascia pelvis. Because this procedure includes repair of a cystocele, do not report 57423 with codes that include any kind of bladder or urethral repair such as a Marshall Marchetti Krantz procedure or a laparoscopic urethral suspension. CPT® codes 51840, 51841, 51990, 58152, and 58267. Also bundled would be any of the codes that include an anterior colporrhaphy which is done to repair a cystocele. Therefore, do not report CPT® 57240, Anterior colporrhaphy, repair of cystocele with or without repair of urethrocele, including cystourethroscopy, when performed; 57260, Combined anteroposterior colporrhaphy, including cystourethroscopy, when performed; or 57265, Combined anteroposterior colporrhaphy, including cystourethroscopy, when performed; with enterocele repair. Although code 57265 is not listed by CPT® as bundled nor is it a Correct Coding Initiative bundle, it does include a cystocele repair and many other code editing products will bundle this procedure. Report 57267, Insertion of mesh or other prosthesis for repair of pelvic floor defect, each site, anterior, posterior compartment, vaginal approach, for a mesh insertion with 57423 even though it is not a Correct Coding Initiative bundle. This is because CPT® specifically cites the codes to report with an add–on mesh, code 57423 is specifically not listed, and CMS does not normally create bundles for code combinations that CPT® defines. Finally, a diagnostic laparoscopy, 49320, Laparoscopy, abdomen, peritoneum, and omentum, diagnostic, with or without collection of specimens by brushing or washing, would always be bundled with any laparoscopic procedure as it constitutes the examination of the operative field, which is integral to every surgical procedure. When the provider performs robotic surgery, the provider can only report the code that describes the laparoscopic approach. This is because the robot is a surgical tool, not a separate surgical procedure. The code S2900, Surgical techniques requiring use of robotic surgical system, may be reported for informational purposes to let the payer know the procedure was done with a robot, but there is no additional reimbursement for this code. The provider revises or removes a previously placed vaginal graft using a laparoscope. The graft may require removal due to erosion, exposure, or inflammation. Explanation First, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. He then preps and drapes the abdomen and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the abdominal cavity near the belly button or uses a Veress needle to place a laparoscope. The provider insufflates the abdomen with CO2 (carbon dioxide) gas to create a pneumoperitoneum and places the patient into the Trendelenburg position. He then makes small incisions around the abdominal area to insert trocars to better view the operating site and insert surgical tools. If he is performing robotic surgery, he docks the robot to the laparoscope at this time. He then elevates the vaginal tissue by using his free hand or by placing an instrument into the vagina. He identifies the graft and opens the peritoneum above it. Next, he dissects the graft attachment from the vaginal wall in a circular fashion and removes the graft and attached tissue. He then incises the graft from where it attaches to the sacrum along with any sutures that remain and closes this area with sutures. The provider removes the laparoscope, all trocars, and the docked robot arm as necessary. He then closes the small incisions with sutures. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Insufflates: To blow a medicated powder, gas, or vapor into a bodily cavity. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Pneumoperitoneum: The presence of gas or air in the abdominal cavity; when laparoscopic procedures are performed, carbon dioxide is pumped into the abdominal cavity to expand the viewing space. Robot–assisted surgery: An operation that is started with the laparoscope, but a robot arm is docked with the laparoscope and the surgeon completes the operation while sitting at a console that is next to the operating table. Sacrum: The large heavy bone at the base of the spine made up of fused sacral vertebrae. Trendelenburg position: The patient is laid flat on her back (supine) with her feet higher than her head; this position moves the bowel and upper organs away from the operative site when a laparoscopic procedure is performed. Veress needle: A spring–loaded needle used during a laparoscopic procedure to create a pneumoperitoneum. The provider identifies the abnormal cervical tissue and then inserts a laser beam device for destruction of abnormal tissues or lesions found on the cervix. In the laser method, the abnormal tissue is heated by laser energy and evaporates. Once the provider completes the procedure, he withdraws the device. In this procedure, the physician excises the cervical stump remaining after a previous subtotal hysterectomy through a vaginal approach and also performs repair of enterocele. Explanation The provider places the patient in a lithotomy position and inserts a speculum into the vagina. The provider uses retractors to hold the labia out of the way. He injects the cervical stump with a local anesthetic mixed with a vasoconstrictor to minimize bleeding. He makes a circular incision around the stump, which he dissects away from the vaginal tissue using scissors. He places clamps on the cardinal ligaments and uterosacral ligaments to further detach the cervical stump, and if the round ligaments are attached to the stump, he transects them. He removes the cervical stump. The physician then performs repair of the enterocele overlying the vaginal mucosa. The physician dissects the perirectal fascia of the posterior vaginal mucosa to reveal the enterocele sac. Once the sac is clearly displayed, the physician cuts the sac and pushes the small intestine back into the abdomen and sutures it closed, or he may attach the upper portion of the vaginal vault to the uterosacral ligaments to close the enterocele. The physician then closes the sac with sutures. The physician finally closes the vaginal incision with sutures. Terminology Cardinal ligament: Uterine ligament which contains the uterine artery and uterine vein. Cervical stump: Remainder of the cervix after a supracervical hysterectomy. The cervix will be mainly a shell as during the hysterectomy, the inside of the cervix was cored out to prevent cancer within the endocervix or transformation zone. Enterocele: A bulging of the small intestines and peritoneum into the vaginal canal. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Perirectal fascia: Fascia in the area around the rectum. Supracervical, or subtotal, hysterectomy: A procedure to remove the uterus but leave the cervix intact. The cervix will be mainly a shell as during the hysterectomy: the inside of the cervix is cored out to prevent cancer within the endocervix or transformation zone. Uterosacral ligament: A ligament extending from the cervix to the posterior pelvic wall and stabilizes the uterus in the pelvic cavity. Tips This procedure is only performed at a later time following a supracervical hysterectomy when the patient also has an enterocele. Read Less

Once the dilation with scraping of tissue is complete, the provider withdraws the surgical vaginal instruments. He then adds various media to the semen, and the specimen is gently centrifuged, or spun, for several minutes. He performs this process usually only once but may repeat it. In this procedure, the provider introduces a catheter with saline or contrast material into the woman's uterus or the fallopian tubes at the same time as ultrasound or X–ray imaging. This procedure is done to examine the uterus and fallopian tubes for a blockage or abnormality. Catheterization and introduction of saline or contrast material for saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS) or hysterosalpingography Explanation The provider places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position and inserts a speculum into the patient’s vagina. For sonohysterography, or SIS, the provider inserts a flexible catheter through the cervix into the cavity of the uterus. The provider then instills saline into the uterus through the catheter and uses a separately reportable ultrasound to detect any abnormal growth inside the uterus. For hysterosalpingography, or HSG, the provider injects a dye into the uterus, which spreads to the fallopian tubes, so he can observe the tubes by X–ray examination and check for abnormalities or blockage. When the procedure is complete, the provider removes the catheter and speculum. Terminology Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove a fluid, or to keep a passage open. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Fallopian tubes: A set of two fine tubes that begin at the upper body of the uterus and lead to the ovaries; the ovaries lie very close to the fringed ends of the fallopian tubes; they are also known as the oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges, salpinx if singular. Hysterosalpingography: X–rays of the uterus and fallopian tubes. Sonohysterography: An ultrasound of the uterus. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure, it has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when they are in place. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips If the provider performs the ultrasound to view the inside of the uterus after saline injection, report 76831, Saline infusion sonohysterography, or SIS, including color flow Doppler, when performed. If he injects contrast material instead of saline, an X–ray is required to evaluate the uterus and fallopian tubes. In this procedure, the provider introduces a catheter through the cervix and into the fallopian tube to diagnose and clear blockages of the tube. The procedure may include the injection of contrast material and taking an X–ray in a procedure called a hysterosalpingogram done to evaluate the fallopian tubes and uterus for abnormalities or blockage. This service is done as a treatment for infertility. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and places a speculum into the patient’s vagina. In this procedure, the provider uses extreme cold to destroy the lining of the uterus. He uses ultrasound to guide the cryoprobe instrument to all the quadrants of the uterine cavity. The provider uses a tenaculum, a surgical clamp designed to hold or grasp tissue, to hold open the cervix. The provider then puts an ultrasound transducer above the uterus so he can see the cryoprobe as he is using it. He inserts the cryoprobe into the uterine cavity and injects sterile saline into the uterus. He then evaluates the area to ensure visualization of the probe and the ice–ball that forms during the procedure. The provider then engages the cryoprobe to freeze the section of the uterus on which he is working. In this procedure, the provider suspends the uterus, pleating and suturing the stretched ligaments that normally hold the uterus in place so that the uterus and cervix return to their normal positions. The stretched ligaments that he pleats could include the round ligaments or the sacrouterine ligaments. This service is done for uterine prolapse where a woman's uterus sags or slips from its normal position. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider then makes a low transverse abdominal incision and exposes the uterus and the round and sacrouterine ligaments. Or he makes an incision in the vagina. Once he exposes the ligaments, the provider utilizes different methods to shorten the ligaments, such as Gillian suspension, Olshausen operation, Baldy Webster procedure; all procedures where the provider plicates or sutures the ligaments to shorten them. In the Olshausen operation, the provider sutures the round ligaments to the abdominal fascia with nonabsorbable suture material. In a Gillian suspension, the provider takes out each round ligament in the peritoneum through an opening and brings each ligament below the anterior rectus sheath. Similarly, in the Baldy Webster procedure the provider passes the round ligaments through the anterior and posterior broad ligaments and sutures them to the posterior surface of the uterus. The provider may fold and tack the sacrouterine ligaments to shorten them. He then closes the abdomen with sutures. Terminology Anterior rectus sheath: portion of the rectus abdominis muscles, the two parallel vertically aligned muscles on each side of the anterior wall of the abdomen surrounded by layers of flat broad tendons. Broad ligaments: A large fold of peritoneum that is attached to each side of the uterus and extends to the walls of the pelvis; these ligaments encase the ovaries and fallopian tubes. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Transverse incision: An incision that runs across the body to provide access to the abdomen and pelvis. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. The provider removes the uterus using a laparoscope but leaves the cervix and the fallopian tubes and ovaries. The uterus is normal in size, which means it weighs 250 g or less. Explanation First, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. He then preps and drapes the abdomen and administers a general anesthetic. The provider enters the abdominal cavity near the belly button by using a Veress needle or an open incision and places a laparoscope. The provider insufflates the abdomen with CO2 gas to create a pneumoperitoneum and then puts the patient into the Trendelenburg position. He makes small incisions around the abdominal area to insert trocars to better view the operating site and insert surgical tools. If he is performing robotic surgery, he docks the robot to the laparoscope at this time. The provider opens the peritoneum over the bladder and dissects the bladder off the lower uterine segment. The provider then incises the attachments of the uterus, the round ligaments, and if there are any fibroids, he removes them or tags them for separate removal before removing the uterus. He identifies the uterine artery, clamps, and incises it. Because he is leaving the cervix in place, the provider does not incise the cardinal or uterosacral ligaments. He separates the fundus of the uterus from the cervix using a scalpel and treats any bleeding from the cervical stump. The provider now uses a morcellator to cut the uterus into small pieces, which he removes from the abdominal cavity though one or more of the trocar sites. After he removes the entire uterus, he deflates the abdominal cavity and removes all of the instruments and trocars. He closes the trocar site fascia and skin. Terminology Cardinal ligaments: A ligament found at the base of the broad ligament that contains the uterine arteries and veins, and attaches to the pelvic sidewall at the ischial spine; it holds the uterus in its normal position at the level of the cervix. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Carbon dioxide (CO2): A colorless and odorless gas produced as a result of respiration; it is naturally present in air and is absorbed by plants; in laparoscopic surgical procedures, CO2 is insufflated into the abdomen to distend it. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Fallopian tubes: A set of two fine tubes that begin at the upper body of the uterus and lead to the ovaries; the ovaries lie very close to the fringe like ends of the fallopian tubes; they are also referred to as the oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges, or salpinx if singular. Fascia: Sheet or band of muscle, fat, and fibrous tissue that lies under the skin. g: Abbreviation for gram, a metric unit of measure of mass or weight; in pharmacology, a gram is equal to 1000 mg; the previous abbreviation for grams (gm) is outdated. Insufflates: To blow a medicated powder, gas, or vapor into a bodily cavity. Laparoscopy: An operation a provider performs to view the abdominal and pelvic contents through small incisions with the aid of a camera; a provider uses it to inspect and diagnose a condition or to perform surgery for a problem; a fiberoptic instrument a provider inserts through an incision in the abdominal wall and uses to examine visually the interior of the peritoneal cavity; the provider also inserts trocars to allow for the addition of surgical tools. Morcellator: A surgical instrument used to divide and remove large masses of tissue during laparoscopic surgery. Ovaries: Female reproductive organ where eggs are produced. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Pneumoperitoneum: the presence of gas or air in the abdominal cavity. When laparoscopic procedures are performed, carbon dioxide is pumped into the abdominal cavity to expand the viewing space. Robot–assisted surgery: An operation that is started with the laparoscope, but a robot arm is docked with the laparoscope and the surgeon completes the operation while sitting at a console that is next to the operating table. Round ligaments: Bands of muscle and fiber that are attached to the top of the uterus on each side and travel through the inguinal canal to end at the labia majora. Surface fibroids: Tumors that appear on the outside of the uterus; also referred to as subserosal myomas. Trendelenburg position: The patient is laid flat on her back with her feet higher than her head; this position moves the bowel and upper organs away from the operative site when a laparoscopic procedure is performed. Trocar: A medical device that is made up of an obturator, which may be a metal or plastic, sharpened or nonbladed tip, a cannula, or hollow tube, and a seal; trocars are placed through the abdomen during laparoscopic surgery, and they function as a portal to place other instruments such as graspers, scissors, staplers, and a laser needed during the surgical procedure. Ureter: Duct by which urine passes from the kidney to the bladder. Uterine fundus: The top rounded portion of the uterus, above the openings of the fallopian tubes and is where an egg usually implants; a provider measures the fundus to determine the growth of the fetus. Uterosacral ligament: A band of fascia that inserts into the sacrum and then connects to the back wall of the uterus at the internal cervical os, or opening; this ligament supports the uterus, and holds it in place. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips The provider who does a supracervical hysterectomy may describe performing a reverse conization of the cervix. If this is found in the procedure note, it simply means he is removing as much of the endocervical tissue as possible before suturing. This part of the procedure is not coded separately. Removal of fibroids at the time of laparoscopic hysterectomy is not separately coded unless the fibroid is not attached to the uterus. Usually when large fibroids are present, the uterus will weigh more than 250 g, so instead of adding a modifier 22 for increased procedural service to code 58541, report 58543, Laparoscopy, surgical, supracervical hysterectomy, for uterus greater than 250 g, instead. The provider excises fibroid tumors of the uterus through a laparoscope. The provider removes a total of one to four tumors with a total weight of 250 g or less and may or may not also remove tumors on the surface of the uterus. The provider enters the abdominal cavity near the belly button using a Veress needle or an open incision and places a laparoscope. The provider insufflates the abdomen with CO2 gas to create a pneumoperitoneum and then puts the patient into the Trendelenburg position. He then makes small incisions around the abdominal area to insert trocars to better view the operating site and insert surgical tools. If he is performing robotic surgery, he docks the robot to the laparoscope at this time. The provider then carefully moves the small and large intestines out of the way and into the upper abdomen. He inspects the fibroids and decides which to remove first. He begins by removing any small surface myomas. Then, he injects a hemostatic drug into the muscle of the uterus to minimize blood loss. The provider uses a scalpel to incise the area over the first intramural myoma. After he finishes exposing the fibroid, he grasps it with myoma forceps and, using sharp and blunt dissection techniques, carefully dissects it free of the uterine muscle layer. He then coagulates the blood supply to the fibroid and repairs the area where the fibroid was located with sutures. Finally, he closes the uterine wall over this area. He then repeats this procedure for the remaining two or three fibroids. Before the provider can remove the fibroids from the abdominal cavity, he tags each with a suture so that he can easily identify them at the end of the procedure. The provider removes a total of one to four tumors that have a total weight of 250 g or less. Then, after the provider removes all the fibroids, he obtains hemostasis, retrieves each tagged fibroid and morcellates, or cuts, the fibroids into small strips or pieces using a knife or electrical device. He then removes each strip from the abdomen through the trocar sites. He completes the procedure by closing the uterine wall incisions, removing the trocars, and closing the skin incisions. In this procedure the provider laparoscopically removes the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, the parametrium, cardinal and uterosacral ligaments, and excises the pelvic lymph nodes on both sides of the body as well as removing some of the para–aortic nodes. Explanation First, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. Then, the provider preps and drapes the patient’s abdomen and administers a general anesthetic. The provider enters the abdominal cavity near the belly button using a Veress needle or an open incision and places a laparoscope. The provider insufflates the abdomen with CO2 gas to create a pneumoperitoneum and then puts the patient into the Trendelenburg position. He then makes small incisions around the abdominal area to insert trocars to better view the operating site and to insert surgical tools. If he is performing robotic surgery, he docks the robot to the laparoscope at this time. The provider then carefully moves the small and large intestines into the upper abdomen and incises the round ligaments. Next, he incises the peritoneum from the external iliac to the common iliac vessels and removes all of the lymph nodes along these vessels on both sides, including separate specimens of right and left external iliac nodes, obturator nodes, internal iliac nodes, and common iliac nodes. He then takes samples of the para–aortic nodes. The provider then divides the uterine arteries and clamps them after he frees up all of the structures that run along these vessels. The provider then opens up the parametrium he will remove and creates a bladder flap over the lower uterine segment and upper vagina. He frees up the ureters from the broad ligament and dissects the rectum off the posterior vaginal wall. He then divides the uterosacral ligaments and incises them. Next, he removes all of the parametrial tissue. In the next step, the provider divides the area around the vagina. He opens the vagina using a circular incision around the upper vagina and around the cervix. He then removes the uterus, cervix, parametria, and ovaries through the vagina. He closes the vagina with sutures, then irrigates the pelvis, and cauterizes the bleeding sites. The provider may at this time perform a cystoscopy to make sure the ureters were not compromised during this radical surgery. He releases the CO2 gas, removes the trocars, and closes all incision sites. The provider inserts a radiofrequency probe through the cervix to destroy one or more uterine fibroids under ultrasound guidance and monitoring. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a probe through the cervix, the entrance to the uterus. The probe contains a radiofrequency energy source and may have a built–in ultrasound device. The provider uses ultrasound guidance and monitoring for the procedure. The provider identifies one or more fibroids (solid benign tumors) in the uterine wall and inserts the radiofrequency device into them. This device is heated to the desired temperature, and the heat is applied to the center of the fibroid for a few minutes, which destroys the fibroid tissue. The provider may also use the device to cauterize the puncture site in the uterine wall. When the procedure is complete, the provider removes the probe.

After the provider delivers a baby via a cesarean incision and after she closes the uterine incision, the provider ties off or incises one or both of the fallopian tubes to prevent a future pregnancy. The provider reports this add–on code in addition to a primary procedure code. Explanation In this add–on procedure, the provider performs a cesarean delivery, and after she closes the uterus with sutures, she performs a sterilization procedure to prevent pregnancy. To begin, the provider grasps the fallopian tube with a clamp and passes a hemostat through the part of the fallopian tube that has a limited blood supply. She then places sutures through the opening she creates with the hemostat and ties the tube in two locations leaving the ends of the suture thread long. Next, she incises the section between the two sutures. The provider then usually removes a portion of the tube and sends it to the laboratory to confirm removal of a section of the tube. Next, she uses a hemostat to make a hole into the muscular layer of the uterus. She then takes the long thread ends of the suture in the tube closest to the hole and threads them into a needle. She passes the needle into the hole and exits the needle to the outside of the uterus. She repeats this again so there are two suture ends. Then she ties the two sutures together, buries the end of the fallopian tube into the hole, and sutures the uterine lining closed over the hole and tube. The provider then checks for bleeding and obtains hemostasis. Finally, she closes the abdominal incision that was made to begin the cesarean procedure. The provider creates a new opening at the end of the fallopian tube through a laparoscope so that eggs from the ovary can pass into the uterus. Explanation First, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. He then preps and drapes the abdomen and administers a general anesthetic. The provider places a uterine manipulator through the cervix so he can move the uterus around during the surgery. The provider enters the abdominal cavity near the belly button using a needle or an open incision and places a laparoscope. The provider insufflates the abdomen to create a pneumoperitoneum and then puts the patient into the Trendelenburg position. He then makes small incisions around the abdominal area to insert trocars to better view the operating site and insert surgical tools. If the provider is performing robotic surgery, he docks the robot to the laparoscope at this time. The provider isolates the distal, or far end, of the fallopian tube, which is completely closed. He makes a crosscut incision in an avascular area near the end of the tube with scissors, electrosurgery, or a laser, and creates multiple flaps. The provider folds the flaps back on themselves with a laser or sutures to create a new opening in the fallopian tube. He then performs chromotubation to be sure the end of the tube is open. He then irrigates and deflates the abdominal cavity and removes all instruments and trocars. He closes the trocar site fascia and skin and removes all instruments from the vagina. In this procedure, the provider removes all or part of a fallopian tube on one or both sides. The provider performs the procedure via an abdominal incision. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the lower abdomen just above the pubic bone. She then incises the peritoneum and explores the abdomen. The provider then makes another incision to expose the broad ligament. Once she exposes the broad ligament, the provider dissects the fallopian tube away from the ligament and removes the tube from the abdomen. She repeats this procedure for the other fallopian tube if performing a bilateral salpingectomy. The provider then controls the bleeding and obtains hemostasis. Finally, she closes the abdomen and places a Foley catheter to promote gravity drainage. Fallopian tubes: A set of two fine tubes that begin at the upper body of the uterus and lead to the ovaries; the ovaries lie very close to the fringe like ends of the fallopian tubes; they are also referred to as the oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges, or salpinx if singular.Foley catheter: Catheter with an inflatable balloon tip for retention in the bladder. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Salpingectomy: The surgical excision, or removal, of a fallopian tube. In this procedure, known as a tubotubal anastomosis, the provider sutures back together the portion of the fallopian tube that was previously transected during a sterilization procedure. This provider performs this procedure to reestablish the patient’s ability to become pregnant. The procedure is done via an abdominal incision. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the lower abdomen just above the pubic bone. He then incises the peritoneum and explores the abdomen. The provider inspects the abdominal cavity, uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. Once he completes his inspection, the provider elevates the uterus and the tubal segments with packing and lyses adhesions if present. The provider then frees the tubal segments, being careful not to disturb any existing blood supply. Using an operating microscope, he excises a portion of each end of the blocked fallopian tube to obtain an opening and sutures the two sections together. He then performs a chromotubation to ensure the fallopian tube is open. Finally, he removes the packing and closes the abdominal incision with sutures. In this procedure, the provider drains one or more ovarian cysts from one or both ovaries from a vaginal approach. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers a regional anesthetic. The provider makes a small incision into the vaginal canal and inserts a needle to drain fluid from the ovary, or she uses ultrasound guidance with a needle to drain the ovary. When she uses a needle, the provider inserts the needle into the ovary where a previous ultrasound identifies the fluid pocket or pockets. After the provider completely drains all the fluid, the provider removes the needle and places a suture at the site as necessary. When she uses ultrasound guidance, the provider places an ultrasound probe she attaches to an automatic and retractable needle puncture device into the patient’s vagina. She then uses the ultrasound image to detect density differences between the tissue and fluid inside the pelvic area. Using these images, the provider advances the needle through the vaginal wall and into the ovary to drain the fluid from the cyst. After the provider completely drains all of fluid, she withdraws the needle and removes the ultrasound probe. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Ovarian cysts: Fluid filled sacs or pockets within or on the surface of an ovary. Ovaries: Female reproductive organ where eggs are produced. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Tips Report this code no matter how many cysts the provider drains and whether one or both ovaries contain cysts. When the provider uses ultrasound guidance, report codes 58800 and 76942, Ultrasonic guidance for needle placement, e.g., biopsy, aspiration, injection, localization device, imaging supervision and interpretation. Usually ultrasound codes do not require a modifier. When using ultrasound guidance during a procedure, the provider must document the indication for doing it as well as what was visualized. Note that 58800 is a CPT® separate procedure. This means that it normally bundles with other procedures that involve the ovaries. Sometimes the payer will allow separate billing if you report a modifier 59, Distinct Procedural Service, but the criteria for using this modifier must be in evidence in the documentation. Read Less

The provider places the ovaries behind the uterus and sutures them in place via an abdominal incision. This procedure protects the ovaries before the patient receives pelvic radiation to treat cancer. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider makes an incision in the lower abdomen just above the symphysis pubis. She then incises the underlying tissue and peritoneum and examines the abdominal cavity. Once she completes her examination, the provider identifies the ovarian vessels and secures the vessels so that she will not interrupt the blood supply to the ovaries. The provider then moves the ovaries and places them just below the uterus. She then sutures them in place. Finally, the provider closes the abdominal incisions. Terminology Ovaries: Female reproductive organ where eggs are produced. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Symphysis pubis: The firm joint between the pubic bones in the front midline of the body; it is located anterior to the urinary bladder. Transposition: Removal from one place to another. Tips This procedure is usually done prior to a patient having radiation therapy of the pelvis to move the ovaries out of harm’s way. On occasion, the provider may perform this transposition to fix the ovaries into position after they have become twisted, known as torsion of the ovaries. The provider then sends the tissue sample to the laboratory for examination. The provider then withdraws the instruments and places a small stitch to close the vaginal wall as necessary. In this procedure, the provider removes an ovarian, tubal, or primary peritoneal malignancy by removing the fallopian tubes, ovaries, and omentum. He also performs a radical excision of intraabdominal or peritoneal tumors all through an abdominal incision. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the abdominal wall from the symphysis pubis to the rib cage and carries it down through the tissue until she enters the peritoneal cavity. The provider then takes cytologic washings and subdiaphragmatic scrapings. Next, she explores the abdomen and pelvis and assesses the extent of the malignancy. The provider then begins the procedure with the bilateral salpingo oophorectomy. She first dissects the pelvic sidewalls, ureters and sigmoid colon from the tumors located on the ovaries or fallopian tubes. She incises the infundibulopelvic ligaments and removes the ovaries. If the patient has masses on the pelvic peritoneum, the provider removes the peritoneum as part of the next step, the radical resection. In this part of the procedure, the provider attempts to remove all tumor nodules he finds in the abdomen and the pelvis that are larger than 1 cm. For the omentectomy, the provider makes another small incision in the abdomen, and she partially or completely removes the thin tissue lining the abdomen near the stomach. When the procedure is complete, she controls all bleeding, and she closes the abdomen in layers. In this procedure, the provider removes the uterus and cervix, the ovaries and fallopian tubes and then removes the omentum. He also performs a radical excision of intraabdominal or peritoneal tumors all through an abdominal incision. Explanation The provider places the patient the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the abdominal wall from the symphysis pubis to the rib cage and carries it down through the tissue until he enters the abdominal cavity. He then explores the abdomen. He collects samples of peritoneal fluid and sends them for cytologic examination. The provider then moves the abdominal contents out of the pelvis with a retractor. Next, he removes the uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, and the pelvic peritoneum. To accomplish this, the provider dissects the ureters off their peritoneal attachments along their entire course of attachment within the pelvis. If the patient has masses on the pelvic peritoneum, the provider removes the peritoneum as part of the next step, the radical resection. The provider attempts to remove all tumor nodules that he finds in the abdomen and the pelvis that are larger than 1 cm.
