The provider introduces a warm fluid into the uterus to increase the amount of amniotic fluid in case of oligohydramnios or anhydramnios (scanty or absent amniotic fluid) or to enhance the ability to see fetal anomalies. The provider performs this procedure via a transabdominal approach using ultrasound guidance. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position, preps the abdomen with an antiseptic solution, and drapes the abdomen. Using a transabdominal transducer over the lower abdomen for guidance, the provider identifies a pocket of amniotic fluid. He then uses color Doppler to identify an area that does not contain the umbilical cord to prevent any injury to it and to ensure he avoids all fetal and placental vascular structures during the amnioinfusion. He injects a local anesthetic into the area where he will place the needle. He inserts the tip of a spinal needle through the skin over the pocket and advances the needle into the amniotic sac. He then withdraws a small amount of fluid to verify proper needle placement. Once he verifies he is in the amniotic sac and no fetal vascular structures are in the way, he uses a syringe to infuse the minimum volume of warm fluid possible to provide the effect he desires. He may do this by slowly and manually pushing the fluid in or by using an infusion pump. He then monitors the amount of amniotic fluid and discontinues the infusion when the volume reaches a sufficient level. Next, he infuses a small amount of dilute indigo carmine, a blue dye, into the amniotic sac and withdraws the needle. The provider then uses ultrasound to assess the fetal heart rate and the puncture sites for bleeding. The provider performs a pelvic examination and places a tampon into the vaginal canal to detect any possible uterine rupture; he observes this through any leakage of the dye and staining of the tampon. He removes the tampon after thirty minutes. Terminology Amniotic fluid: The fluid within the amniotic sac that surrounds the fetus and helps to protect it from mechanical injury. Amniotic sac: A bag of fluid inside the uterus where the fetus develops and grows; it is sometimes called the membranes because the sac is made of two membranes called the amnion and the chorion. The provider performs this procedure for advanced stage twin–to–twin fetal transfusion syndrome to terminate the fetus that will not survive and ensure survival of the coexisting normal fetus. The provider performs this procedure via a transabdominal approach using ultrasound guidance. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position, preps the abdomen with an antiseptic solution, and drapes the abdomen. He places a transabdominal transducer over the lower abdomen. The provider then uses color flow Doppler to evaluate the mother’s abdominal wall and uterine vascular structures, the position of each fetus, the umbilical cord locations, the placental location, and the vascular structures to avoid as he approaches the umbilical cord of the abnormal fetus. Next, the provider may administer a regional or local anesthetic. He injects a local anesthetic into the area where he makes a small abdominal incision. The provider then makes a small skin incision at the puncture site, and under continuous ultrasound guidance, he introduces a cannula through the mother’s abdominal and uterine wall into the amniotic cavity. He places the cannula into a position that allows him access to the umbilical cord of the abnormal fetus. The provider then removes the introducer needle and uses dilators to expand the cannula so he can insert bipolar coagulation forceps. The provider may also infuse warm normal saline into the amniotic cavity if he needs more operating space. He then advances the coagulating forceps into the vicinity of the umbilical cord that he will close off. He grasps the umbilical cord with the forceps and verifies the fetal heart of the abnormal and normal fetus to confirm that he is holding the correct umbilical cord. He ensures the cord is separated from the fetal body, the uterine wall, the placental surface and the inter–twin membrane, and then ligates, occludes, or applies energy to compress the cord closed. The provider confirms the stoppage of the umbilical blood flow with color flow Doppler. He then repeats this procedure a short distance from the initial coagulation site, and again uses the color flow Doppler to confirm there is no blood flow. He then uses ultrasound to evaluate the cardiac activity in both fetuses to ensure that the abnormal fetus has no heartbeat but that the normal fetus does. The provider then removes the forceps and cannula from the uterus, inspects the uterine puncture site for bleeding using ultrasound, and closes the skin incision. The provider removes the fallopian tube or ovary, or both, to treat an ectopic pregnancy. There may be a large fetus imbedded around the ovary or in the fallopian tube or an ectopic pregnancy may have already ruptured the fallopian tube. In either circumstance, the provider determines that he must remove the fallopian tube or ovary or both. The provider performs this procedure abdominally or vaginally. Explanation In an abdominal approach, the provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the lower abdomen and explores the pelvic cavity for the location of the ectopic pregnancy and bleeding. He then aspirates any products of conception, blood clots, or free blood that may be present. Since the tube or ovary is damaged, the provider removes the ovary or fallopian tube, or both. To remove the fallopian tube, the provider incises a small wedge of uterine wall where the fallopian tube meets the body of the uterus and removes the damaged tube. He then sutures the entrance to the body of the uterus. If he is removing the ovary, the provider incises the infundibulopelvic ligaments, which releases the ovary. He then washes out the pelvic cavity with saline, checks for bleeding, and closes abdomen with sutures. In a vaginal approach, which is done very rarely since the advent of laparoscopy, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider places a weighted speculum on the posterior vaginal wall and grasps the posterior lip of the cervix with a tenaculum. Using the tenaculum to move the cervix out of the way, the provider makes a vertical incision in the posterior vaginal wall into the pouch of Douglas and then drains any blood or clots that may be present. The provider then extends the incision on both sides and places an abdominal pack to push the bowel out of the way. He then uses forceps to grasp the ovarian ligament so he can see the top part of the uterus where the fallopian tubes join the uterine body. He exposes the fallopian tube where the ectopic fetus is located, or was located if the tube has already ruptured. He then excises the fallopian tube or ovary or both in the same manner as the abdominal procedure. If the ectopic pregnancy has ruptured, he removes any of the products of conception. The provider then sutures the entrance to the body of the uterus, withdraws all instruments, and closes the incision in the vaginal wall. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, such as a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Ectopic pregnancy: Any gestation outside of the uterine cavity; these can occur in the interstitial portion of the tube, in the rudimentary horn of the uterus, the fallopian tube, the abdomen, the cervix or the ovary. Fallopian tubes: A set of two narrow tubes that begin at the upper body of the uterus and lead to the ovaries; the ovaries lie very close to the fringed ends of the fallopian tubes; they are also known as the oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges (sing. salpinx). Forceps: A two–bladed instrument used to compress or grasp. Infundibulopelvic ligaments: Also knows as the suspensory ligaments of the ovary, these ligaments hold the ovary to the pelvic wall and must be cut in order to remove the ovaries. Laparoscopy: An operation a provider performs to view the abdominal and pelvic contents through small incisions with the aid of a camera; a provider uses it to inspect and diagnose a condition, or to perform surgery for a problem; a fiberoptic instrument a provider inserts through an incision in the abdominal wall and uses to examine visually the interior of the peritoneal cavity; trocars are also inserted to allow for the addition of surgical tools. Ovaries: Female reproductive organ where eggs are produced. Pouch of Douglas: The extension of the peritoneal cavity between the rectum and back wall of the uterus in the female human body; also known as the rectouterine pouch or a cul–de–sac. Salpingectomy: The surgical removal of one or both fallopian tubes. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider sutures closed an incompetent cervix, meaning one that is prematurely dilating prior to a term delivery. The provider performs this procedure via a vaginal approach. Explanation The provider places the patient in the lithotomy position and administers a general or regional anesthetic. The provider then inserts a weighted speculum and cleanses the cervix. If he is to perform a McDonald cerclage, he grasps the anterior and posterior edges of the cervix with ring forceps and inserts a curved needle that is threaded with a thick nonabsorbable suture where the vaginal wall meets the cervix. He then passes the suture four to six times in a purse–string manner around the entire cervix, ensuring that the suture does not enter the endocervical canal. He then ties the two ends of the suture together and cuts them but leaves a long end so that he can remove it later. Once he controls all the bleeding, the provider removes the instruments. If he is to perform a Shirodkar cerclage, he inserts a Foley catheter and drains the bladder. The provider then pulls the cervix forward with ring forceps at the same time that he has a surgical assistant use a retractor to stretch the vaginal sidewalls. He then uses a scalpel or an electrocautery needle to make an incision in the area where the vaginal wall meets the cervix on both the front and back sides. Next, he dissects the rectum off the posterior cervix and the bladder off of the cervix. He then places suture or tape around the internal os and ties off the ends. If the patient will deliver by cesarean section, he buries the knot under the vaginal mucosa. Finally, he checks for bleeding and removes all instruments. Terminology Cerclage: Surgical procedure a provider performs through the vagina or abdomen where he uses sutures to close the cervix to prevent the premature delivery of a fetus; also called a cervical stitch. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Cesarean delivery: A surgical procedure to deliver an infant through an incision rather than vaginally; also known as a surgical birth or a cesarean section (C section). Electrocautery: An instrument using heat produced by a high frequency electrical current for destruction of tissue. Endocervical canal: A spindle–shaped canal extending from the uterus to the vagina; the neck of the uterus; also known as cervical canal, canal of the cervix, or the cavity of cervix. Foley catheter: Catheter with an inflatable balloon tip for retention in the bladder. Incompetent cervix: A defect in the strength of the internal os, or opening, of the cervix that permits premature dilation of the cervix. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. McDonald cerclage: Placement of a band of sutures at the upper part of the cervix; a provider uses places it between twelve and fourteen weeks gestation, and he removes the band of sutures at around the thirty seventh week of gestation. Retractor: An instrument for drawing aside the edges of a wound or for holding back structures adjacent to the operative field. Ring forceps: Scissor like instrument with loop handles on one end and open oval serrated, or smooth ringed, or looped jaws instead of a blade on the other end. Shirodkar cerclage: Placement of purse string sutures through the walls of the cervix so they're not exposed; this type of cerclage is more difficult to do than the McDonald, and sometimes involves a permanent stitch around the cervix, which he will not remove so a cesarean section is necessary to deliver the baby. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure; it has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted, and then opened when they are in place. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Tips Some providers use ultrasound guidance to judge the site of the suture relative to the internal cervical os, or opening, maternal bladder, and rectum. In this instance, report 76998, Ultrasonic guidance, intraoperative in addition to this code. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider repairs a uterus that develops a laceration or ruptures during pregnancy. The provider performs this procedure via an abdominal approach. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the abdomen to locate the uterus laceration or rupture. Once he identifies the site, the provider freshens up the edges of the defect until he reaches healthy viable tissue. He then closes the defect in layers using absorbable sutures. He controls bleeding with each level of sutures he places. Finally, the provider places a temporary drainage tube for evacuation of any bleeding, hematoma, or fluid material. He then closes the abdominal incision with absorbable sutures. Terminology Hematoma: A localized swelling containing accumulated blood, due to a break in the wall of a nearby blood vessel. Hysterorrhaphy: Suturing of an incised or ruptured uterus . Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. In this global service, the provider and nonphysician healthcare providers in the practice provide all of the antepartum care, admission to the hospital for delivery, labor management, including induction of labor, fetal monitoring, use of low forceps and episiotomy, vaginal delivery of the fetus and placenta, and inpatient and outpatient postpartum care. Typical global services begin at eight to ten weeks gestation, with a full term vaginal delivery at thirty–nine to forty weeks gestation, and routine outpatient postpartum care forsix weeks following delivery. Explanation Antepartum care: The care given to the mother at each antepartum visit varies with the requirements of the pregnancy, but there are some basic services a provider performs. The provider integrates these services into the antepartum care no matter when they occur, or which level of provider performs them such as an MD, NP, PA, CNM, RN. These services include: evaluation of the health status of both mother and fetus; estimation of the gestational age; identification of the patient at risk for complications; anticipation of problems before they occur and prevention of problems if possible; and education and communication with regard to all issues that relate to the pregnancy such as the pregnancy plan, counseling for antenatal testing, lactation and nutritional counseling. A provider will complete a comprehensive initial history and physical of the mother as well, with subsequent examinations at each visit thereafter that include both maternal and fetal markers to identify if the pregnancy is progressing normally. These markers include a urinalysis to measure protein and glucose, recording of the fetal heart rate, measurement of the uterine fundus, examination for maternal edema, or swelling, maternal blood pressure, position of the fetus, cervical status and ruling out labor. In some cases, the provider will collect a screening Pap smear specimen, and in that case, the collection is part of the antepartum visit. The frequency of visits is usually monthly up to 28 weeks gestation, then biweekly visits to 36 weeks gestation, and then weekly visits until delivery. Antenatal screening tests, care for conditions unrelated to pregnancy, injections, surgical procedures, and ultrasound examinations are generally not inclusive in normal antepartum care and the provider can report them separately based on payer policy. Complications of pregnancy in the antepartum period are rarely paid at the time of the complication, but a provider may bill them at the time of service for later appeal to avoid timely filing issues. Intrapartum Care: Management of labor usually begins when the patient informs the provider that she thinks she is in labor or presents to the hospital in apparent labor. If the patient calls the provider about labor, he advises the patient when to come to hospital, alerts hospital personnel of the patient’s arrival, and provides initial instructions for the patient's care. The provider then performs an initial history and physical examination at the time of admission to determine that labor has indeed begun. He then assesses the mother's and fetus’ condition, develops a treatment plan, and communicates with nursing staff, anesthesia, and pediatric staff as necessary. When his initial evaluation is complete, the provider periodically reevaluates the condition of his patient and her fetus throughout the course of labor and alters the treatment plan as necessary. The provider may induce or augment labor, but this is inclusive of labor management no matter if he performs this service using, IV drugs, or rupture of membranes. During the first stage of labor, which starts with contractions and ends with complete dilation of the cervix, the provider evaluates the patient usually every thirty minutes. During the second stage of labor, which lasts from complete dilation of the cervix through the birth of the baby, the provider usually evaluates the patient at 5 to 15 minute intervals. During labor, the provider may administer regional or local anesthesia to ease labor pains. He then continually monitors uterine contractions and the fetal heart rate using external monitors he places on the mother’s abdomen. The provider may instruct the patient on breathing technique, check the uterine contractions for regularity, and perform a vaginal examination to determine position of the fetal head. When he sees the dilation of the cervix is fully or nearly fully complete, he moves the patient to the delivery room, and the patient is prepped and draped. The provider instructs the patient to begin pushing the baby at this stage, and when the baby’s head begins to show through the vaginal opening, called crowning, the provider may perform a few maneuvers with the baby's emerging body to facilitate a smooth and better delivery. He may use low forceps to assist in the delivery of the head and shoulders or apply a vacuum extractor in some cases. He may also perform an episiotomy when the perineum does not stretch adequately, and it obstructs delivery. Once the head comes out, the provider gently supports the whole body with his hand so the body can rotate and come out through the birth canal. After the delivery is complete, the provider removes the placenta and incises the umbilical cord. The provider inspects the cervix and vagina for lacerations, repairs the episiotomy incision, and repairs any minor vaginal or cervical lacerations as well. Inpatient Postpartum Care: The provider transfers the patient to recovery. He writes orders for aftercare including monitoring vital signs, pain management if necessary, patient diet, and ambulation. The provider visits the patient several hours after delivery to check on her progress and follows up with additional visits until the day of discharge, which is normally 48 hours for a vaginal delivery. At discharge, the provider discusses with the patient, care of the breasts and vulva, diet, exercise, when the patient should present for her first visit, and when to come in if there are problems such as excess bleeding or cramping. Outpatient Postpartum Care: Typical outpatient postpartum care a provider performs includes ongoing evaluation of the mother’s physical and mental status following birth, a physical examination to ensure that the mother is recovering normally, discussion of lactation, nutrition, and exercise after delivery, review or initiation of birth control options, evaluation of immunizations, and collection of a screening Pap smear specimen if necessary. The provider schedules the first visit four to six weeks following delivery but may only order one visit at six weeks instead of two. The provider performs a physical examination, which includes measuring the patient’s weight and blood pressure, and an examination of the breasts, abdomen, and a pelvic exam. The provider will also incorporate preconception counseling into postpartum care, when appropriate, to prepare the patient for a future pregnancy. Terminology Antenatal testing: Tests a provider offers a mother to check on the health of the baby and mother. Antepartum period: Period from confirmation of pregnancy to delivery of the baby. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Episiotomy: An incision made in the perineum to allow passage of the baby’s head and to prevent ragged tearing of the perineal tissues. Forceps: A two bladed instrument used to compress or grasp. Forceps delivery: One of three types of delivery with forceps may occur, but they are still part of intrapartum care; a provider uses outlet forceps when the baby’s scalp is visible at the vaginal opening; low forceps when the baby's head is at +2 station or lower; and midforceps when the baby’s head is above +2 station, but the head is engaged. Intrapartum period: Period from the onset of labor to the complete expulsion of the placenta. Perineum: The short stretch of skin that starts at the bottom of the vulva, the external female genital organs, and continues to the anal opening. Placenta: A special layer developed during pregnancy to protect and nourish the fetus. Postpartum period: Period from the termination of labor to complete reduction of the uterus to its normal nonpregnant size and state, usually about forty two days. Uterine fundus: The top rounded portion of the uterus, above the openings of the fallopian tubes and is where an egg usually implants; a provider measures the fundus to determine the growth of the fetus. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vacuum extraction: Placement of a bell shaped cup on the baby’s head and application of vacuum pressure to create suction on the baby’s head; the provider then pulls on the device he attaches to the cup at the same time as the mother indicates a contraction is beginning, and he continues throughout the full contraction; at the end of the contraction the provider stops pulling and waits for the next contraction, continuing until the baby’s head begins to exit the vaginal opening. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Tips If the provider performs less than the requirements for global care, append a modifier 52, Reduced services to 59400. This may include providing fewer than normal antepartum visits or not being present for labor management, or the delivery of the baby. Add a modifier 22, Increased procedural services, to 59400 when the provider performs work greater than normal. This may occur because the patient was seen many more times than typical in the antepartum period due to complications, or the labor management, or delivery was significantly more work than for routine care. The provider must provide detailed documentation to get additional reimbursement. Read Less

In this procedure, a provider who did not perform the delivery manually removes the afterbirth. Explanation The patient is in lithotomy position after delivery. The physician examines her for a retained placenta. He is given IV sedation for this procedure if she has not already been given an anesthetic for the birth. The physician inserts his or her hand into the uterus to try to evacuate the placenta and uses the other hand to exert pressure on the top of the uterus from outside. This may take several attempts, but the physician ensures that the patient’s uterus is contracting during this procedure to ease the placenta out. Once the placenta is released, the physician examines it for completeness of all tissue. Terminology Forceps: A two bladed instrument used to compress or grasp. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups Placenta: An organ that forms during pregnancy to provide oxygen and nutrients to the fetus and which removes waste products from the fetal blood supply; it attaches to the wall of the uterus, and the umbilical cord arises from it; the placenta usually attaches at the top of side of the uterus. Umbilical cord: The connecting stalk between the fetus and the placenta, normally containing two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein; the umbilical vein supplies the fetus with oxygenated, nutrient rich blood from the placenta and the umbilical arteries transport deoxygenated, nutrient depleted blood from the fetal heart back to the placenta. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips The delivering provider may not report this code. All deliveries require removal of the placenta whether it occurs immediately after birth or much later, even if the provider uses forceps or does a manual extraction of the placenta. Read Less

The provider removes a growth in the uterus that results from an overproduction of tissue that was supposed to form the placenta. He removes this tissue through the vaginal canal. Explanation The provider places a patient in a dorsal lithotomy position and administers a general or regional anesthetic. The provider inserts a weighted speculum, cleanses the cervix, and performs gradual dilation of the cervix using mechanical dilators. The provider then uses a tenaculum to grasp and pull the cervix down. The provider then removes the hydatidiform mole and, using a sharp curette or a suction aspirator, removes the endometrial tissue lining the uterine cavity. Once all tissue is removed, the provider withdraws the instruments and controls bleeding. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, such as a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Curettage: The use of a curette to remove tissue by scraping or scooping. Curette: A spoon shaped instrument used to scrape tissue. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Hydatidiform mole: A benign tumor, eighty percent of the time, that develops in the uterus; a molar pregnancy occurs when there is an extra set of paternal chromosomes in a fertilized egg; this error at the time of conception transforms what would normally become the placenta into a growing mass of cysts; a partial molar pregnancy means there is an abnormal placenta and some fetal development; a complete molar pregnancy means there is an abnormal placenta but no fetus. The provider incises and drains an infected cyst of the thyroid. A thyroglossal duct cyst is a cyst in the midline of the neck caused by a segment of the thyroglossal duct that did not close or disappear during embryonic development. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision to puncture the skin of the cyst using a sterile instrument, such as a sharp needle, a pointed scalpel, or a lancet. He then allows the pus to escape by draining it out through the incision or through a tube. The provider then covers the site with a sterile dressing. Terminology Lancet: Surgical tool with a short, wide, pointed double–edged blade.

The provider removes a cyst or a blood–filled growth from the thyroid gland, or incises the tissue that connects the right and left side of the thyroid gland in the front of the throat. The procedure is indicated for nodules that affect breathing or swallowing and for suspected or confirmed cancer. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin crease at the base of the neck and creates skin flaps. She divides the platysmas, and separates the strap muscles. She dissects the lesion or cyst. She continues coring out the tissue. She controls the blood supply to and from the growth, and she removes the mass, sending it to the lab for further evaluation. She places a drain if necessary but generally closes the site in layers and then closes the flap with absorbable sutures. Terminology Adenoma: Blood–filled growth. Isthmus: Center band of tissue that joins the left and right lobes of the thyroid gland. Platysmas: Muscle fibers extending from the collarbone to the jaw. Strap muscles: Four pairs of muscles in the front of the neck, also called the infrahyoid muscles. Read Less

The provider removes the thyroid gland including the extension of the gland below the breastbone. The procedure is required for more complex benign conditions, such as a very large goiter, cyst, or benign or malignant conditions that extend into the upper chest. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the region of the enlarged cyst, goiter, or cancer. She divides the platysmas, and separates the strap muscles. She creates short flaps from this tissue, and she exposes the thyroid gland. Before dissecting the substernal thyroid, she ties off the vessels of the thyroid gland to free the gland and increase mobility. She then dissects the cyst or lesion releases the thyroid gland from the trachea, and removes the thyroid. Terminology Goiter: Swelling of the thyroid gland. Platysmas: Muscle fibers extending from the collarbone to the jaw. Strap muscles: Four pairs of muscles in the front of the neck, also called the infrahyoid muscles. Substernal: Under the breastbone. Thyroidectomy: Surgical removal of the thyroid gland. Tips Refer to code 60271 if the provider performs the procedure via a cervical incision. Read Less

The provider drains a thyroid cyst using a needle or catheter. The provider may use radiologic imaging to guide the needle/catheter into the target area to drain the cyst. Explanation The provider examines the thyroid cyst, and may perform other tests prior to injection or aspiration to confirm his manual findings. The provider positions the patient on his back with the neck extended and places a pillow under the patient’s shoulder. Next, he prepares the biopsy site by administering a local anesthetic to numb the area. The provider cleans the biopsy site and incises the skin. He inserts a needle or catheter through the incision and into the cyst to collect a sample of fluid for testing. Then he applies a sterile dressing. In some cases, the provider uses imaging to help locate the area to treat. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, such as a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Tips Separately report radiologic guidance for this procedure with codes 76942 or 77012. Read Less

The provider removes one or more of the parathyroid glands, which are small endocrine glands that are behind the thyroid gland. Providers perform the procedure to treat recurrent or persistent thyroid overactivity or cancer. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the base of the neck through an incision site previously explored. He exposes the thyroid and re–examines the parathyroid glands. He identifies all the parathyroid glands, and he isolates the diseased gland or glands. He biopsies a piece of the diseased glands and confirms the diagnosis by sending them to pathology for immediate microscopic examination. He then removes the diseased parathyroid glands, places a drain, and closes the wound. Terminology Parathyroidectomy: Surgical procedure to remove the parathyroid glands.

The provider removes a part of the thymus gland or the entire gland. The procedure is often done as a result of a benign or malignant tumor on the thymus gland, called a thymoma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises across the lower neck, called transcervical, and creates skin flaps. She explores the neck area and removes part of or the entire thymus gland located in the neck. If she decides it is necessary to remove some of the fatty tissues adjacent to the thymus, she will alter the patient’s position or make an additional incision into the chest for more complete exposure to the chest and removal of the thymus. She inspects the area for evidence of any residual thymic tissue, closes the site in layers, and applies a sterile dressing. Terminology Thymectomy: Surgical removal of the thymus gland. Thymus gland: Gland found in the base of the neck that is responsible for white blood cell developments that are important for immune system response. Read Less

This procedure involves removal of the entire thymus gland or a part thereof. The provider performs it using an incision on the sternum or an incision on one or both sides of the chest. The provider removes a part of or the entire thymus gland along with adjacent mediastinal structures. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a length–wise incision through the breast bone, or sternum, and splits the sternum vertically. In a transthoracic approach, the provider incises through one or both sides of the chest. She explores the chest and removes part of or the entire thymus gland along with adjacent affected mediastinal structures as indicated. She inspects the surgical field to ensure no residual thymic tissue remains and inserts chest tubes. She then closes the site in layers and applies a sterile dressing. The provider primarily performs this procedure as a treatment for a benign or malignant tumor on the thymus gland, called a thymoma. She may also perform this for treating the neuromuscular disease myasthenia gravis. Terminology Mediastinum: The tissues and organs situated in the chest in between the two lungs on the sides, and in between the breastbone in front and vertebral column behind. Radical mediastinal dissection: Surgical removal of all lymphatics in the neck along with nonlymphatic structures including: sternocleidomastoid muscle, one of the muscles that functions to flex the head; internal jugular, a neck vein; submandibular gland, one of the salivary glands; and the spinal accessory nerve, a nerve that helps control speech, swallowing, and certain movements of the head and neck. Thymectomy: Surgical removal of the thymus gland. Thymus gland: Gland found in the base of the neck that is responsible for white blood cell development that is important for immune system response. Tips Use 32673 if the provider performs thoracoscopy with unilateral or bilateral resection of the thymus. Use 60522 if the provider has performed resection of a malignant mediastinal thymoma with associated mediastinal tissue. If the provider also removes a portion of lung, you may be able to report a separate code from the respiratory section or append modifier 22 to 60522 to reflect the additional work. Read Less

The provider removes a tumor from the receptors located in the carotid artery near the fork, or bifurcation, in the upper neck but does not excise the carotid artery itself. The procedure is used to remove different types of carotid body tumors, often referred to as CBTs. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the neck at the tumor site. The provider isolates and preserves the blood vessels and cranial nerve by applying vessel loops on each. She then ties off smaller vessels along with some branches of the carotid artery. She begins slow and careful dissection of the tumor off the carotid artery and surrounding structures. After the procedure, the provider inserts drains, closes the site, and applies a sterile dressing. Terminology Vessel loop: A surgical device used to hold or position an organ to facilitate or improve the visualization of a surgical site.

The provider performs subsequent punctures of the dura, through the soft spot of the skull, known as the fontanelle, or the joint of the cranial bones in the skull, known as the coronal suture. The procedure is typically performed on infants to remove built up blood or cerebrospinal fluid and to relieve pressure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider performs a repeat insertion of a subdural needle or intravenous catheter into the skin where the fontanelle and coronal meet. He advances the needle slowly through the skin to the subdural level. He then removes the needle, and the fluid drains through the attached catheter. The provider collects the fluid and a sample is sent for testing. He then repeats the procedure on the other side as needed. The procedure is complete when the area becomes soft or concave, and the provider applies a gentle pressure dressing to the site. Terminology Dura: Outermost membrane that covers the brain. Subdural: Beneath the outermost membrane covering the brain and spinal cord. Tips Report code 61000 for the initial subdural tap. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider inserts a needle into one of the brain’s ventricles to withdraw cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, for testing but does not inject any substance. The provider accesses the brain through the patient’s skull through a previously created burr hole, the fontanelle, or coronal suture, or through an internal ventricular drain. This service is done to measure pressure, remove excess fluid, and or collect fluid samples to analyze the CSF for neurological conditions. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the intracranial ventricular system by inserting a needle through an established burr hole in the skull, through the fontanelle or coronal suture that extends across the top of the skull. He may also obtain a sample of CSF through an already established ventricular drainage system. To acquire the sample, the provider inserts a hollow needle into the brain through one of the entry points and slowly and steadily advances it into the ventricles. Once in place, he aspirates a sample of CSF and sends it to the laboratory for analysis. The provider then carefully and slowly withdraws the needle, applies gentle pressure, and covers the site with a sterile dressing. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, such as a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill, also called trepanation or trephination. Coronal: Relating to the crown, or top of the head, corona. Fontanelle: The fibrous connective joint of the cranial bones in the skull, also known as the coronal suture. Ventricles: Chambers in the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF. Ventricular catheter and reservoir: System used to drain CSF through an insertion of a catheter, or tube, into the ventricles of the brain, which drains the CSF to a small reservoir placed on the surface of the scalp, where CSF can be withdrawn for testing; the system then drains the fluid to the heart in a procedure known as a ventriculoatrial shunt, or VA shunt, or more commonly into the peritoneal cavity, or abdomen, known as a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, or VP shunt. Ventricular puncture: The piercing of a cerebral ventricle with a needle to withdraw fluid, administer medication, or another substance. Tips For ventricular puncture with injection of medication or other substance, see 61026, Ventricular puncture through previous burr hole, fontanelle, suture, or implanted ventricular catheter/reservoir; with injection of medication or other substance for diagnosis or treatment. In this procedure, the provider inserts a needle into one of the brain’s ventricles to inject a diagnostic or therapeutic agent. The provider accesses the brain through the patient’s skull through a previously created burr hole, the fontanelle or a coronal suture, or through an internal ventricular drain. This service is done to measure pressure, remove excess fluid, and or collect fluid samples to diagnose or treat neurological conditions such as an infection, known as meningitis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the intracranial ventricular system by inserting a needle through an established burr hole in the skull, or through the fontanelle or coronal suture that extends across the top of the skull. He also accesses the site through a previously placed ventricular drainage system. To access the ventricles, the provider inserts the needle into the brain through one of the entry points and slowly and steadily advances it into the ventricles. Once the needle is in place within the CSF, he aspirates a sample of fluid and sends it to the laboratory for analysis, and or he injects a medication such as an antibiotic or a diagnostic agent such as contrast into the CSF. The provider then carefully and slowly withdraws the needle, applies gentle pressure, and covers the site with a sterile dressing. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, such as a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill, also called trepanation or trephination. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Coronal: Relating to the crown, or top of the head, corona. Fontanelle: The fibrous connective joint of the cranial bones in the skull, also known as the coronal suture. Meningitis: An inflammation of the meninges, the three thin membranes that cover the brain and the spinal cord. Ventricles: Chambers in the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF. Ventricular catheter and reservoir: System used to drain CSF through an insertion of a catheter, or tube, into the ventricles of the brain, which drains the CSF to a small reservoir placed on the surface of the scalp, where CSF can be withdrawn for testing; the system then drains the fluid to the heart in a procedure known as a ventriculoatrial shunt, or VA shunt, or more commonly into the peritoneal cavity, or abdomen, known as a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, or VP shunt. Ventricular puncture: The piercing of a cerebral ventricle with a needle to withdraw fluid, administer medication, or administer another substance. Tips For ventricular puncture without injection, see 61020, Ventricular puncture through previous burr hole, fontanelle suture, or implanted ventricular catheter/reservoir; without injection. In this procedure, the provider inserts a needle at the craniocervical junction to access cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, in a procedure known as a cisternal puncture. Or the provider performs the same in a high cervical approach in a procedure known as a lateral cervical puncture. The provider does not inject a diagnostic or therapeutic agent. This service is done to measure pressure, remove excess CSF fluid, and or collect fluid samples to analyze the CSF for neurological conditions. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, through a cisternal puncture by inserting a hollow needle through the skin at the base of the skull between the cervical vertebrae, or the craniocervical junction, then through the dura mater, and into the cisterna magna at the base of the brain. In a lateral cervical puncture, the provider withdraws the CSF through the spine at the level of C1 and C2 by puncturing the subarachnoid space in the posterior part of the spinal canal to the side of the midline. She then slowly and steadily advances the hollow needle between the cervical vertebrae and into the CSF. Once the needle is in place within the CSF, she aspirates a sample of fluid and sends it to the laboratory for analysis. The provider then carefully and slowly withdraws the needle, applies gentle pressure, and covers the site with a sterile dressing. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, such as a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Cervical vertebrae: Seven vertebrae located in the upper neck of the spinal column, the vertebral column, indicated by the symbols C1 through C7. Cisterna magna: The largest of three primary openings in the subarachnoid space where cerebrospinal fluid drains from the fourth ventricle; also known as the cerebellomedullary cistern. Craniocervical junction:Area where the cranium and cervical vertebrae meet. Dura: Outermost of the three protective layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Subarachnoid space: The space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater, the middle and innermost of the three membranes covering the brain. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine. There are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal. Read Less

The provider inserts a needle at the junction between the skull and the first cervical vertebra, directing the needle toward the sagittal suture, the joint line that divides the skull in half vertically. Or, he inserts the needle laterally between the first and second cervical vertebra, which he may refer to as the atlantooccipital, craniovertebral, or occipitovertebral joint. He then injects a medication to treat a neurological condition or contrast material for an imaging study. Explanation The provider may choose between two techniques for this procedure. For the cisternal puncture, after the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a hollow needle through the skin between the base of the skull and the first the cervical vertebrae, or the craniocervical junction, then through the dura mater, and into the cisterna magna at the base of the brain. In a lateral cervical puncture, the provider inserts the hollow needle laterally between the first and second cervical vertebrae, which he may refer to as the atlantooccipital, craniovertebral, or occipitovertebral joint. When he detects cerebrospinal fluid, he halts the advancement of the needle, and injects a medication such as an antibiotic or a diagnostic agent such as contrast into the cerebrospinal space. The provider then carefully and slowly withdraws the needle, applies gentle pressure, and covers the site with a sterile dressing. Cisterna magna: The largest of three primary openings in the subarachnoid space where cerebrospinal fluid drains from the fourth ventricle; also known as the cerebellomedullary cistern. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Craniocervical junction: Area where the skull and first cervical vertebra meet. Dura or dura mater: The outer fibrous membrane just underneath the skull, the toughest of three membranes or meninges that protect the brain and spinal cord. Subarachnoid space: The space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater, the middle and innermost of the three membranes covering the brain. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine. There are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal. In this procedure, the provider uses a hand operated twist drill to create a hole in the skull to withdraw fluid from the area below the dura or from the ventricles of the brain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small scalp incision and moves the scalp away. Then she uses a manual twist drill at the incision site, which she cranks or twists by hand to perforate the skull and expose the dura mater, the tough outermost layer of the three protective layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. She then uses the hole to remove cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, to reduce pressure on the brain or remove fluid within the subdural level of the brain, or from within the ventricles for testing. The provider can also use the hole to perform additional surgical interventions as necessary. Terminology Hematoma: A collection of blood on the surface of the brain. Subdural: Beneath the dura, the outermost membrane covering the brain and spinal cord. Twist drill: Handheld and manually operated drill with one or more deep spiral grooves that extend from the point to the smooth part of the shaft. Ventricles: Chambers in the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF. Ventricular puncture: The piercing of a cerebral ventricle with a needle to withdraw fluid or administer medication or other substance. Terminology Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill, also called trepanation or trephination. Tips Whenever you encounter the term burr hole while reading the operative report, distinguish between a burr hole used as the primary surgical approach versus those used in conjunction with a craniotomy. In a procedure commonly described as a bone flap craniotomy, several burr holes are used to help develop a bone flap. If this is the case, the surgical approach is not a burr hole, but rather a craniotomy/craniectomy, and you should use the correct craniotomy/craniectomy code. Many of these codes include the parenthetical (s) with the term describing a burr hole [i.e., burr hole(s)]. The presence of the (s) indicates that these codes may be used only once regardless of the number of burr holes necessary to perform the procedure at the specific location of the brain. The provider drills a hole or holes into the skull to aspirate a cyst or a hematoma, a collection of blood on the surface of the brain. After she treats the abnormality, she implants a device to further drain the location or monitor the patient after surgery. The provider removes a part of the skull to treat raised intracranial pressure, or ICP, by allowing the swelling brain room to expand. The procedure may also include duraplasty, or reconstruction or expansion of the dura using a synthetic graft, or part of the patient’s pericranium, a membrane that covers the surface of the skull. The procedure excludes the removal of a related hematoma due to conditions such as a closed head injury, and there is no dissection to the lobes of the brain in this service. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skull and creates a large U–shaped opening. She then folds back the tissue to expose the bone. She is careful to preserve the pericranium, which she can later use for a graft if needed. Next, she drills burr holes in the skull. She inserts a surgical saw, called a craniotome, through the burr holes, and cuts between adjacent burr holes to create a bone flap, which she removes to expose the dura. The provider may need to open the dura and expose a swollen brain to reduce the ICP. After adequate pressure reduction and thorough control of bleeding, she closes the dura, if opened, with sutures or a graft to allow for expansion. She then replaces the bone flap if ICP and brain swelling permit; otherwise, she preserves the bone flap or places the flap in a subcutaneous pocket in the abdominal area, which is a separately reportable procedure. She then closes the wound in layers. Terminology Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill, also called trepanation or trephination. Craniectomy: Surgical procedure in which a piece of the skull, or brain flap used to gain access to the inside of the cranium is permanently removed and not returned to the patient’s body. Craniotomy: Surgical procedure in which a piece of the skull, or brain flap used to gain access to the inside of the cranium is temporarily removed to access the brain and returned to the patient’s body in its normal position prior to closure. Intracranial hypertension: Elevated pressure inside the skull. Intraparenchymal hematoma: When blood pools within the brain tissue itself, also known as intracerebral hematoma. Lobectomy: Removal of all or part of a lobe of the brain. In this procedure, the provider removes a small portion of the occipital bone at the back of the skull including the back of the upper one or two cervical vertebrae to relieve pressure on the medulla, or brain stem, and spinal cord. The provider may have to open and expand the dura by suturing in place a dural graft. The goal of this procedure is to reduce or eliminate compression of the spinal cord. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the back of the head. He then widely retracts the tissue. He exposes and removes the occipital bone. The provider then performs a laminectomy where he removes a portion of the first cervical vertebra called the lamina, which is the posterior arch or the back part of the vertebra that covers the spinal canal. If, the compression extends below the C2 level, then he may also remove the upper part of the lamina of the second cervical vertebra. If he does not achieve enough decompression, the provider may incise the dura to relieve pressure. Then he may need to use a tissue graft of dura, muscle, fat, or fascia. He harvests the graft from the patient’s thigh or from a cadaver. He may also use a synthetic dural substitute. He applies the graft to cover the defect and widen the margins of the dural opening, to close the wound without compression, and create a watertight seal. He then folds the tissue flap back, closes the scalp, and places a sterile dressing over the area. Terminology Arnold–Chiari malformation: A malformation where brain tissue extends into the spinal canal. Craniectomy: Surgical procedure in which a piece of the skull, or brain flap used to gain access to the inside of the cranium is permanently removed and not returned to the patient’s body. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine. There are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal. Read Less

This procedure is not done for a meningioma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp above the area where the tumor is present. He removes a circular portion of bone by drilling a burr hole. He now has adequate exposure of the tumor in the area of the brain above the tentorium cerebelli region. He identifies and excises the tumor. The provider then drains out any excess fluid or blood using a drain, and he sutures the layers of tissue together. In this add–on code, the provider implants a chemotherapy drug at the same time as the procedure where he removes a portion of the skull bone and excises a tumor. The service may be done when resection is incomplete or for cancer cells that might remain after tumor removal. Explanation During a surgical procedure, most often a craniotomy or craniectomy, the provider places a chemotherapy agent into the cavity in the brain where the provider just removed a tumor. This add–on code defines the implantation of chemotherapy agents other than brachytherapy, a cancer treatment where the provider places radioactive seeds or sources internally. Once the provider completes resection of the brain tumor and before closing the site, she inserts the agent using a catheter or by placing dime sized wafers, or discs, containing the chemotherapeutic drug on the walls in or near the cavity bed left after tumor removal. During individual placement of the discs, she is careful to avoid major structures. She then closes the area, and the agent slowly breaks down over time to release the chemotherapy drugs into the local region. In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of skull bone and excises a tumor of the meninges, which are connective tissue layers covering the brain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp located above the area where the tumor is present and removes a circular portion of bone. He now has adequate exposure of the tumor in the area of brain below the tentorium cerebella region or in the posterior fossa. He excises the tumor. The provider then drains out any excess fluid or blood using a drain, and he sutures the layers of dural tissue together. Finally, he attaches the bone flap back to its original position using plates, wires, or sutures, and he covers the wound with a sterile dressing. In this procedure, the provider removes the temporal lobe of the brain through an elevated portion of skull bone. The provider also performs an intraoperative electrocorticography (ECoG), to record the electrical activity in the brain and pinpoint the site of seizures. This procedure helps define the area in the temporal lobe where epileptic seizures begin. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp and creates burr holes to use a craniotome to elevate a portion of skull bone to expose the dura. He then opens and retracts the brain membranes to access the temporal lobe of the brain. Then he places electrodes on the surface of the brain over the first layer of membrane protecting the brain. He may also place depth electrodes into deep areas of the brain using very thin wires. Next, he connects the electrodes to continuous electroencephalogram, or EEG, equipment. He records and maps the brain’s activity, moving the electrodes as necessary to gather data, while he irrigates the cortex. He uses the resulting information to define the extent of the brain causing the seizures, and he identifies critical areas to avoid. He then removes the temporal lobe and any surrounding areas identified to remove. Next, he carefully and delicately dissects and coagulates the surrounding arteries and structures, and obtains hemostasis. The provider then drains out any excess fluid or blood using a drain. After the removal of the lobe, he uses the electrocorticography (ECoG) again to determine if any residual epileptic activity remains. When he obtains the result he desires, he removes the electrodes and sutures the layers of membranes. Finally, he attaches the bone flap back to its original position using plates, wires, or sutures, sutures the layers of tissue together, and he covers the wound with a sterile dressing. Terminology Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill, also called trepanation or trephination. Cerebral cortex: The superficial gray matter of the brain. Craniotome: A surgical saw. Craniotomy: Surgical procedure where the provider removes a piece of the skull or brain flap used to access the inside of the cranium and returns to the patient’s skull in its normal position prior to closure. Dura: The tough outermost layer of the three protective layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Electrocorticography: Recording the electrical activity of the brain by placing electrodes directly on the cerebral cortex. Electrodes: A conductor or small disc that attaches to the skin and detects tiny electrical charges; or brain activity. Electrocorticography, or ECoG: Recording of electrical activity from the cerebral cortex of the brain by placing electrodes on the surface of the brain; also called intracranial EEG, or iEEG. Epileptic seizures: A disorder of the central nervous system causing recurrent, unprovoked seizures. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Lobectomy: Removal of all or part of a lobe of the brain. Occipital lobe: Rearmost lobe in either of the two symmetrical halves of the brain. Reapproximates: To align or rejoin tissue. Temporal lobe: Lobe of each cerebral hemisphere located on the side and in front of the occipital lobe. Tips For temporal lobe lobectomy without electrocorticography, see 61537, Craniotomy with elevation of bone flap; for lobectomy, temporal lobe, without electrocorticography during surgery. Whenever you encounter the term burr hole while reading the operative report, distinguish between a burr hole the provider performs as a primary surgical approach versus those he makes in conjunction with a craniotomy. In a procedure commonly described as a bone flap craniotomy, a provider drills several burr holes to help develop a bone flap. If this is the case, the surgical approach is not a burr hole, but rather a craniotomy or craniectomy, and you should use the correct craniotomy or craniectomy code. Many of these codes include a parenthetical with the term describing a burr hole, having an "s" in parentheses, meaning burr hole or holes. The presence of the parentheses indicates that the provider should use these codes only once regardless of the number of burr holes necessary to perform the procedure at the specific location of the brain. Also, report these codes only once regardless of the side or number of burr holes involved at a specific location or for a specific lesion. When a burr hole or holes is medically necessary to perform procedures at a different anatomic location of the brain, a separate code identifying the burr hole and specific procedures the provider performs may be necessary. This often requires the use of a modifier in order to identify that a separate and distinct location was involved and documentation that supports the same. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider resects a portion of the pituitary gland or excises a pituitary tumor by accessing the gland either through the mouth or nose. This procedure does not use imaging guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider choses the best approach to access the pituitary gland either though an incision in the mouth or through the nose. In a transseptal approach, the provider makes an incision underneath the upper lip at the junction of the upper inner lip and gum and bluntly dissects along the nasal septum to the sphenoid sinus. In a transnasal approach, she uses an approach through the nostril and makes an incision in the nasal cavity. With either approach, she inserts a speculum and dissects the underlying structures to access the dura, the outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. She then opens the dura, identifies the sella turcica that holds the pituitary gland, and excises the pituitary tumor or a portion of the gland. After reconstructing and closing the tissue and bone, the provider may insert a graft made from fat or fascia tissue to stop or prevent cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, leakage. She harvests a fat graft from the lower abdomen or a fascia graft from the outside of the thigh. She then sutures the harvest site closed and covers the wound with a sterile dressing. In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of skull bone and resects an arteriovenous malformation, or AVM, from the supratentorial region of the brain. This region is located above the tentorium cerebella, a fold of dura mater separating the cerebellum from the occipital and temporal lobes. The AVM the provider treats is simple, meaning it is less than 3 cm and easily accessible with probably no deep venous drainage, meaning the AVM is not involved with the main conduits that drain blood from the brain, which would increase risk of bleeding, or the involvement of the cortex areas that relate to sense, speech, and language. Explanation The provider performs an angiogram prior to this procedure to identify the location of the arteriovenous malformation (AVM). When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the scalp above the simple arteriovenous malformation, or AVM, and removes a circular portion of bone by drilling burr holes and removing a section of the skull, called a bone flap. He incises the dura, the outermost layer of the brain, and retracts the membrane exposing the AVM. He then has adequate exposure of the AVM in the area of the brain above the tentorium cerebelli region. He then separates the AVM from surrounding brain tissue and resects the abnormal vessels, carefully controlling bleeding as he removes the tumor like mass. The provider then drains out any excess fluid or blood using a drain and he sutures the layers of dural tissue together. Finally, he may attach the bone flap back to its original position using plates, wires, or sutures, and he covers the wound with a sterile dressing. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique used to visualize the lumen, or inside, of blood vessels and organs of the body ; an angiogram is a record of the image. Tips Choose between codes 61680 and the other codes in the code set, 61682 through 61692, based upon the location of the AVM and the ease or difficulty to access the AVM. Read Less

The provider treats a simple intracranial aneurysm using intracranial surgical techniques to repair an abnormal dilation, or widening, of a blood vessel in the internal carotid circulation. This service helps treat an aneurysm that a subarachnoid hemorrhage causes. Explanation A simple intracranial aneurysm is usually small, 15 mm or less, in areas of the brain that are easy to access and does not require extra effort to control bleeding or prevent further damage to the blood vessels. The ultimate goal of the procedure is to exclude the aneurysm from the carotid circulation while trying to preserve the blood flow, with minimal brain dissection and retraction, if possible. The surgical technique he uses depends upon the location and complexity of the aneurysm in the brain. The provider performs an angiogram prior to this procedure to identify the location of the aneurysm. In an intracranial approach for a simple carotid vessel aneurysm, the provider incises in the scalp over the area of the aneurysm. He then retracts the scalp to expose the bone. Next, he uses a surgical drill to create a burr hole, or pattern of burr holes in the skull. He inserts a surgical saw, called a craniotome, through the burr holes and cuts between adjacent burr holes to create a bone flap, which he removes to expose the dura, the thick outer protective layer covering the brain. The provider incises the dura and exposes the underlying brain. He then carefully dissects down to expose the aneurysm, exposing the vessels and identifying the neck of the aneurysm. When he fully exposes the neck, he clips the neck of the aneurysm but is careful to exclude adjacent vessels. He obtains hemostasis at the end of the procedure and verifies the clip placement. When he is satisfied, he closes the dura and replaces and secures the bone flap. Before closing the scalp, he may place a drain and then reapproximates the tissue layers, closes the scalp, and applies sterile dressings. Terminology Aneurysm: An abnormal dilation, or widening, of a blood vessel due to weakness of the wall. Angiography: A medical imaging technique used to visualize the lumen, or inside, of blood vessels and organs of the body; an angiogram is a record of the image. Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill. Carotid circulation: The carotid circulation supplies oxygen and vital nutrients to the anterior part of the brain. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Intracranial: Within the skull on or in the brain. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Bleeding in the area between the brain and the thin tissues that cover the brain. Tips If the aneurysm is considered simple under CPT® guidelines, but it requires a complicated or difficult repair, append modifier 22, Unusual procedural services, to 61700 and 61702 for additional reimbursement. Make sure the documentation is clear in describing the additional work, including how much additional time was needed and what extra efforts were involved in the procedure. The additional work should represent at a minimum a 25 percent increase in physician work above that typically required. The charge for the procedure should reflect the additional work the provider performs. Also, prepare a clear and concise cover letter that describes why the procedure was unusual and make sure it includes a request for additional reimbursement. Check individual payer guidelines as well. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of skull bone to access an aneurysm and locates the blood vessel that feeds the aneurysm. He also accesses the internal carotid artery by making an incision in the neck and occludes the artery with a clamp. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the neck to access the internal carotid artery. He then makes an incision in the scalp to remove a portion of skull bone to access the aneurysm. He locates the blood vessel that feeds the aneurysm. He occludes the internal carotid artery with a clamp. He then places tiny metal clips around the base of the aneurysm to stop blood flow to it. He then releases the internal carotid artery from the clamp and ensures bleeding is controlled at the aneurysm site. The provider then drains out any excess fluid or blood using a drain, and he sutures the layers of dural tissue together. Finally, he attaches the bone flap back to its original position using plates, wires, or sutures, and he covers the wound with a sterile dressing. He also sutures the neck incision in layers. Terminology Aneurysm: Bulge in a blood vessel due to weakness in its wall. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider performs a craniotomy, removing a portion of skull bone. He then stops blood flow to an aneurysm, vascular malformation, or carotid cavernous fistula. During the procedure, the provider occludes, or blocks the blood flow, at the level of the cervical spine by placing surgical clips on the carotid artery, too. This service helps to treat aneurysms that a subarachnoid hemorrhage, congenital vascular malformation, and carotid cavernous fistula cause due to trauma, surgical damage, or rupture of an aneurysm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision high on the neck in the cervical spine and locates the carotid artery. Next, the provider incises the scalp over the area of the cerebrovascular anomaly. He then retracts the scalp to expose the bone. Next, he uses a surgical drill to create a burr hole, or pattern of burr holes in the skull. He inserts a surgical saw, called a craniotome, through the burr holes and cuts between adjacent burr holes to create a bone flap, which he removes to expose the dura, the thick outer protective layer covering the brain. The provider incises the dura and exposes the underlying brain. He then carefully spreads the brain tissue apart, exposes, and then identifies the neck of the defect. Before ligating, or tying, the defect, he clips the carotid artery at the level of the cervical spine. Then he places a small, hinged surgical clip across the neck of the vessel in the brain to stop blood flow into the defect, taking care to exclude adjacent vessels. He unclips the cervical carotid artery and checks the cerebral clip placement, monitoring bleeding and obtaining hemostasis. When he is satisfied, he closes the dura and replaces and secures the bone flap. Before closing the scalp, he may place a drain and then reapproximates the tissue layers, closes the scalp, and applies sterile dressings. Terminology Aneurysm: An abnormal dilation, or widening, of a blood vessel due to weakness of the wall. Anomaly: A deviation from normal; a defect. Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill. Carotid arteries: Two key arteries found in the front of the neck that transport blood from the heart to the brain. Carotid cavernous fistula: An abnormal connection between the carotid artery and the veins at the base of the skull; also known as CC fistula. Cerebrovascular: Pertains to the cerebrum and its associated blood vessels. Cervical vertebrae: Seven vertebrae located in the upper neck of the spinal column, the vertebral column, indicated by the symbols C1 through C7. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Intracranial: Within the skull on or in the brain. Occlusion: To obstruct or block. Reapproximates: To align or rejoin tissue. Vascular malformation: Refers to vascular anomalies that are present at birth in the veins, or only lymph vessels, or both veins and lymph vessels, or both arteries and veins. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine. There are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of skull bone to access an aneurysm, vascular malformation, or carotid–cavernous fistula. He then uses electric current to completely destroy the malformation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp to remove a portion of skull bone to access the aneurysm, vascular malformation, or carotid–cavernous fistula. He then uses electric current to completely destroy the abnormal malformation. The provider then drains out any excess fluid or blood using a drain, and he sutures the layers of dural tissue together. Finally, he attaches the bone flap back to its original position using plates, wires, or sutures, and he covers the wound with a sterile dressing. In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of skull bone and biopsies, aspirates, and or excises an intracranial lesion using mapped coordinates the provider obtains from computed tomography, or CT, and or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, scans to identify the lesion. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses coordinates he obtains from CT or MRI images of the brain to guide him in identifying the intracranial lesion. The imaging studies map the precise location of the lesion, and the provider uses the coordinates from the scans to locate the site. The provider incises the scalp over the mapped location and retracts the scalp to expose the bone. Next, he uses a surgical drill to create a burr hole and incises the dura. Using the coordinates from the scan, he inserts a biopsy probe to the targeted depth. He then obtains biopsy specimens through the probe using a biopsy needle. He immediately sends the specimens to the laboratory for testing. He may obtain additional samples based upon the laboratory results, or he may aspirate the lesion using the biopsy needle. He may decide to excise the lesion using electrocautery, a curette, or a surgical knife. When the procedure is complete, he removes the probe and closes the dura. He reapproximates the tissue layers, sutures the scalp, and applies sterile dressings. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, such as a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill. Computed tomography: Computed tomography, or CT, is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Curette: A surgical spoon or scoop shaped instrument designed to scrape tissue or debris from a body cavity or other surface. Dura: Outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Electrocautery: An instrument using heat produced by a high frequency electrical current for destruction of tissue. Intracranial: Within the skull on or in the brain. Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI: Radiographic imaging using magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Reapproximates: To align or rejoin tissue. Stereotactic: The creation of three dimensional coordinates to precisely locate a target site in the body and direct instrumentation or beam of radiation. Tips For intraoperative stereotactic procedure, see code 61751, Stereotactic biopsy, aspiration, or excision, including burr hole(s), for intracranial lesion; with computed tomography and or magnetic resonance guidance. Separately report the magnetic resonance imaging scan, or MRI, or computed tomography scan, or CT. Read Less
