In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of skull bone and inserts a catheter or probe using mapped coordinates from a computed tomography, or CT, and or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, scans to identify the site to place a radiation source in a brain lesion. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses coordinates he obtains from CT or MRI scans of the brain to guide him in locating the site of the intracranial tumor. The imaging studies map the precise location of the lesion, and the provider uses the scanned coordinates to locate the site and place a radiation source. Depending on the type of radiation source, the implants may be temporary or permanent. The provider incises the scalp over the mapped location and retracts the scalp to expose the bone. Next, he uses a surgical drill to create a burr hole and incises the dura. Using the coordinates from the scan, he inserts a catheter or hollow probe to the targeted depth. He then places the radiation source, usually seeds or pellets, through the catheter or probe and into the tumor bed. When the procedure is complete, he removes the catheter or probe and closes the dura. He reapproximates the tissue layers, sutures the scalp, and applies sterile dressings. In this procedure, the provider uses a nerve destroying agent that he administers percutaneously to make a lesion in the gasserian ganglion, a large group of nerves that lie at the root of the fifth cranial nerve. He uses a stereotactic method, which makes use of a three dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets inside the brain. This service is done to relieve pain that extends along a nerve or nerves. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the target area of the brain using the stereotactic method to view three–dimensional brain images. Previously taken computed tomography, or CT, or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, scans are imported into a computer system that provides three–dimensional images of the brain. The provider then makes a small incision through the skin and passes a hollow needle or other instrument to the target area. He checks the positioning of the needle using the stereotactic coordinates. Then he uses a neurolytic agent like alcohol, electric current, or radiofrequency to destroy the gasserian ganglion. He then withdraws the electrode or other instrument, and closes the skin incision. Terminology Fifth cranial nerve: The primary sensory nerve of the face and motor nerve for the muscles responsible for movement of the jaws; also known as the trigeminal nerve. Neurolytic: A neurodestructive agent. Percutaneous: Through the skin. Radiofrequency: Radio waves used to produce an electrical current to destroy tissue. Stereotactic: The creation of three dimensional coordinates to precisely locate a target site in the body and direct instrumentation or beam of radiation. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider uses a nerve destroying agent to make a lesion in the trigeminal medullary tract of the brainstem. He uses a percutaneous stereotactic method, which makes use of a three dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets inside the brain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the target area of the brain using the stereotactic method, in which previously taken CT or MRI images are imported into a computer system that provides three dimensional images of the brain. The provider then makes a small incision through the skin and passes a hollow needle electrode or other instrument to the target area. He uses a neurolytic agent like alcohol, electric current, or radiofrequency to create a lesion in the trigeminal medullary tract of the brainstem. He then withdraws the electrode or other instrument and closes the skin incision. Terminology Stereotactic surgery: Surgical intervention which makes use of a three–dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets inside the body. Trigeminal medullary tract: A tract of nerve fibers conveying temperature and pain sensation running posteriorly along the lateral side of the medulla of the brain stem. In this procedure, the provider creates one or more holes to remove a portion of skull bone. He then places electrodes on the brain cortex. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp and creates one or more twist drill or burr holes to remove a portion of skull bone. He now has adequate exposure of the cortex, the outermost layer of cerebrum. He then inserts a needle electrode and approaches the cortex area to be stimulated. He places the neurostimulator electrodes. He then ensures that the electrodes are correctly placed by stimulating the area. Finally, he sutures the layers of dural tissue together and covers the wound with a sterile dressing.

In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of skull bone and places neurostimulator electrodes on the cerebral cortex, the outermost portion of the cerebrum. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp and creates burr holes to remove a larger portion of skull bone. He now has adequate exposure of the cerebrum, the front part of the brain that is made up of two hemispheres. He then inserts a needle electrode and approaches the targeted area of cerebellum to be stimulated. He places the neurostimulator electrodes. He then ensures that the electrodes are correctly placed by stimulating the area. Finally, he may attach the bone flap back to its original position using plates, wires, or sutures, and he covers the wound with a sterile dressing. Terminology Cerebrum: Front part of the brain made up of two hemispheres.

In this add on procedure, the provider has removed a portion of the skull, or he may create additional twist drill or burr holes in a patient’s skull. He then uses the stereotactic method, which makes use of a three dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets inside the brain, and places an additional neurostimulator electrode array on the targeted location in a subcortical site after placing an initial array during the same session. In this procedure, the provider does not obtain an intraoperative microelectrode recording. The provider performs this service to treat chronic difficult to control tremors, or dystonia, involuntary movements and muscle contractions, or Parkinson’s disease. Explanation After the placement of an initial neurostimulator electrode array, the provider prepares the patient and places an additional electrode on the same site, or he may place the electrode array on a different site. The provider identifies the target area using the stereotactic method, in which previously taken computed tomography, or CT, or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, images are imported into a computer system that provides three dimensional images of the brain. Using these images, along with scalp markers, or imaging markers, and or an external stereotactic head frame, and the computer, the provider accurately pinpoints the additional targeted site. The provider locates the entry point in the same manner as the initial array. Next, he repreps and drapes the scalp for the second electrode implantation. He may use the same opening, or he may create another opening in the skull bone to access the identified target areas. After locating the additional target using the stereotactic coordinates, he administers a local anesthetic to the site and then inserts a guide cannula. Using the computer, he carefully places the electrode array at the target location. The provider then tests the array moving and repositioning the array as necessary until he discovers its optimal position. He ensures that the electrodes are correctly placed by stimulating the area looking to obtain tremor cessation, reduction in rigidity, and or mobility and coordination of a limb, with the least side effects from the electrode placement. He then removes the guide cannula and using imaging guidance anchors the array. He sutures the dura and obtains complete hemostasis before coiling the array lead in a pocket under the galea, the tough layer of dense fibrous tissue that covers the upper part of the skull. He then sutures the galea. He may replace the removed skull bone and then reapproximates the scalp and sutures or staples it closed. He then applies sterile dressings to the wound. Finally, he removes the stereotactic scalp markers or head frame and dresses the pin anchor wounds of the head frame if used. Terminology Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill. Cannula: A tube that a provider inserts into the body to draw off fluid or to introduce something such as medication. Cessation: To end or stop. Computed tomography: Computed tomography, or CT, is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Craniectomy: Surgical procedure where the provider permanently removes a piece of the skull or brain flap to access the inside of the cranium. Craniotomy: Surgical procedure where the provider removes a piece of the skull or brain flap used to access the inside of the cranium and returns to the patient’s skull in its normal position prior to closure. Dura: The outer protective covering of the brain. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Electrode array: Device that contains multiple plates or electrodes. Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI: Radiographic imaging using magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Microelectrode recording: The use of a high frequency electrical current to precisely identify a surgical site by passing an electrode through the brain along the planned surgical trajectory where it records electrical patterns from the brain structures to help guide the provider to the exact target. Neurostimulator: A nerve stimulator that transmits electrical impulses. Parkinson’s disease: A nervous system disorder that affects movement. Reapproximates: To align or rejoin tissue. Stereotactic: The creation of three dimensional coordinates to precisely locate a target site in the body and direct instrumentation or beam of radiation. Stereotactic head frame: A device attached to the head that is used as a measuring guide to determine the coordinates for targeting an abnormality and to position the head for brain surgery. Subcortical site: Nerve centers below the cerebral cortex, the superficial gray matter of the brain. Trajectory: The route or movement of an object along a three dimensional path. Twist drill: Handheld and manually operated drill with one or more deep spiral grooves that extend from the point to the smooth part of the shaft. Tips When the provider performs microelectrode recording intraoperatively, see codes 61867, Twist drill, burr hole, craniotomy, or craniectomy with stereotactic implantation of neurostimulator electrode array in subcortical site, e.g., thalamus, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, periventricular, periaqueductal gray, with use of intraoperative microelectrode recording; first array; and 61868, Twist drill, burr hole, craniotomy, or craniectomy with stereotactic implantation of neurostimulator electrode array in subcortical site, e.g., thalamus, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, periventricular, periaqueductal gray, with use of intraoperative microelectrode recording; each additional array. List 61868 separately in addition to primary procedure code 61867. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider may remove a portion of skull bone to remove or replace neurostimulator electrodes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp and removes a portion of the skull bone as necessary to access the area where electrodes are present. He then either removes or replaces the electrodes. He ensures that the replaced electrodes are correctly placed by stimulating the area. Finally, he sutures the layers of dural tissue together, closes the surgical wound, and covers the wound with a sterile dressing. The provider makes an incision and implants or replaces a direct or inductive cranial pulse generator or receiver in a subcutaneous pocket for connection to one electrode array. This service is generally done to treat Parkinson’s disease, tremors, or multiple sclerosis. The provider may replace the pulse generator or receiver due to a component malfunction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider selects a location for implantation of the device, usually in the upper left area of the chest or under the left arm, and makes an incision; or she incises the scar at the site of the original placement operation. For a new insertion, she bluntly dissects the tissue and creates a pocket for the neurostimulator device. She passes the lead subcutaneously from the array using a tunneling device to the generator pocket and connects the lead to the generator. For a neurostimulator replacement, she carefully excises the existing generator from the subcutaneous pocket and replaces the unit. The provider connects the generator to a previously placed single electrode array. She then tests the unit and when tests are successful, the provider places the generator into the pocket and secures it to the fibrous tissue under the skin with sutures. The provider then closes the wound and skin with sutures and or tissue adhesive. Terminology Direct or inductive coupling: Direct connection between implanted neurostimulator and external transmitter or a wireless connection from an external transmitter to the implantable device; inductive coupling occurs when an electrical current creates a magnetic field, which produces a specific electrical current; direct coupling refers to the transfer of electrical energy by physical contact. Electrode array: Device that contains multiple plates or electrodes. Lead: An insulated conductor or wire connected to or leading out from an electrode or other electrical device. Multiple sclerosis: Disease where the immune system eats away at the myelin, the protective sheath that covers the nerves. Neurostimulator pulse generator: A device that produces low voltage electrical pulses, with a regular or intermittent waveform that creates a mild tingling or massaging sensation that stimulates the nerve pathways; also known as an electronic pulse generator or nerve stimulator. Parkinson’s disease: A nervous system disorder that affects movement. Subcutaneous: Under the skin. Tips Do not report code 61885 for the replacement of only the cranial neurostimulator electrode array, when the existing pulse generator will remain in use. Report code 61885 with 61888, Revision or removal of cranial neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver, when the provider performs the services on two different generators. In this instance, apply modifier 59, Distinct procedural service, to one of the codes, as appropriate, to indicate the procedure is for performance on two different generators. For insertion or replacement of a neurostimulator generator or receiver for more than one electrode array, see code 61886, Insertion or replacement of cranial neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver, direct or inductive coupling; with connection to 2 or more electrode arrays. Use codes 61885, 61886 and 61888 when the pulse generator or receiver alone is placed, revised, or removed. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider makes a burr hole in the scalp and elevates the depressed skull fracture, meaning a portion of skull bone moved inward into the brain. It is a closed fracture that has not reached the dura, the outer membrane covering the brain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp to locate the depressed skull fracture. He then creates a burr hole in the skull to enter the cranium. He then elevates the depressed bone in the skull by pulling it outward to restore the anatomical position. Finally, he sutures the layers of scalp tissue together and covers the wound with a sterile dressing.

In this procedure, the provider reduces a craniomegalic, or enlarged, skull by maneuvering the bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp and gains access to the skull. He then manipulates and maneuvers the bones to remodel the cranium. He then ensures symmetry of the skull. He does not perform cranioplasty using bone grafts. Finally, he sutures the layers of scalp tissue together and covers the wound with a sterile dressing. Terminology Craniomegalic skull: Enlarged skull. Tips Report code 62115 when reduction of a craniomegalic skull is done without cranioplasty. This is a rare procedure that providers may perform on children who received late treatment of hydrocephalus.

In this procedure, the provider removes or reduces a portion of skull bone and reshapes the craniomegalic, or enlarged, skull. He may repair the defect with a bone graft. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp and gains access to the skull. He then creates a burr hole in the skull and uses a craniotome to remove a large portion of the skull bone. He then remodels the cranium defect using a graft, such as bone from another part of the body, like the ribs. He then ensures symmetry of the skull and reshapes the cranium to its proper anatomical position, including closing the craniotomy. Finally, he sutures the layers of scalp tissue together and covers the wound with a sterile dressing. Terminology Bone graft: A piece of bone used to replace a bone defect. Craniomegalic skull: Enlarged skull. Tips Read More

In this procedure, the provider removes a previously placed bone flap or prosthetic skull plate. The provider performs this service as a result of infection, swelling, overlying wound healing problems or regrowth of a tumor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp over the bone flap or prosthetic plate and lifts the skin and muscle and folds it back. He removes the screws or wires used to secure the bone flap or plate to the skull. After he lifts the flap or plate and removes it, he folds the tissue flap back over the dura, sutures the layers of scalp tissue together, and then covers the wound with a sterile dressing. Terminology Prosthetic plate: An artificial material or device used to replace a portion of the skull to repair a cranial defect or deformity.

The provider surgically corrects a skull defect. At the same session he repairs brain tissue. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the patient’s scalp above the target area. He raises a bone flap to examine the brain in that area as well as the tough membrane, called the dura, surrounding the brain. He repairs the tissue defects. He then corrects the bone defect. This may involve shaping and fixing the bone in proper position. He closes the wound. Terminology Cranioplasty: A surgery to repair defects of the cranium. Cranium: Bones of the head. Tips Code 62145 requires reparative brain surgery. Choose between 62140 and 62141 for cranioplasty without brain repair. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider uses a small neuroendoscope to access the pituitary gland to remove an abnormal growth of the gland. The provider approaches this procedure through the nasal cavity or through the sphenoidal sinuses. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places the patient’s head in a head holder, a fixation device to position and ensure the head remains still during the procedure. He then marks the location of the abdominal incision for harvesting of an abdominal fat graft, if necessary at the end of the procedure to help with reconstruction and stop or prevent cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage. The provider can use either a transnasal or transsphenoid approach using a neuroendoscope to access the pituitary gland. In a transnasal approach, the provider accesses the pituitary gland through an intranasal dissection separating the nasal tissue and removing a section of the central partition of the nose, allowing the provider to work through both nostrils to reach the sella turcica. In a transsphenoidal approach, the provider may approach the pituitary through the sphenoid bone either by way of the nose or through the mouth to reach the sella turcica. Providers tend use the nose and a neuroendoscope to perform the procedure. The provider inserts a retractor or nasal speculum to retract the nostril. Then he passes a small neuroendoscope down the nostril, and using the scope to provide illumination and magnification, he moves through the middle turbinate. Then he makes a small incision and dissects through the middle turbinate, widening the nasal passage further and advancing the endoscope until he sees the sphenoid ostium. A rongeurs is used to enlarge the sphenoid ostium, or opening, to the sphenoid sinus. He dissects the mucosal lining of the sinus and resects the anterior wall of the sphenoid and mucosal lining to reach the sella turcica. He then removes the bone of the floor of the sella turcica to expose the dura. He opens the dura and locates the tumor. He then excises several pieces of the tumor, which he sends to the laboratory for testing. Then he removes the entire tumor using a combination of curettage and suction. After he removes the tumor, he removes the neuroendoscope and passes an angled neuroendoscope through the hole in the dura into the sella turcica to identify any additional tumors or remnants of the tumor, by rotating the scope 360 degrees to the left and right, to suction any remaining tumor findings away. He then obtains hemostasis and irrigates the sella. He then withdraws the scope still further and uses it to aide in the reconstruction of the sella turcica floor. He may use a fat or muscle graft he harvests through the previously marked abdominal incision in the reconstruction of the floor of the sella to prevent CSF leakage. Finally, he closes the dural opening, withdraws the endoscope, removes all remaining instrumentation, and then he may pack the area with sterile gauze or simple place a gauze sponge at the base of the nose. In a patient with a buildup of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain ventricles, the provider places a shunt to move the fluid from a lateral ventricle to the cisterna magna, a space between the cerebellum at the brain’s base and the medulla part of the brainstem. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp and then creates a burr hole in the skull to allow access to the target brain ventricle. The provider places a shunt catheter in the lateral ventricle and tunnels the other end of the catheter under the scalp toward the neck. He exposes the first cervical vertebra and increases the hole at the base of the skull that the spinal cord passes through. This hole is called the foramen magnum. He removes part of the first cervical vertebra and splits the dura, the tough outer membrane covering the brain. He inserts the shunt catheter tip into the in the subarachnoid space, which is under the arachnoid mater, the second of the brain’s three protective membranes. He closes the dura, followed by the muscles, fascia, and scalp. He also closes the burr hole wound. He applies dressings. Terminology Shunt catheter: A system made of a small tube called a catheter and a valve that helps control the movement of fluid from one area to another. Read Less

In a patient with a buildup of fluid under the arachnoid or dural membrane covering the brain, the provider inserts a shunt to drain the fluid either to the heart’s atrial chamber, the jugular vein, or the heart’s auricle. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp. He then creates a burr hole in the skull to allow access to the fluid collection in the subarachnoid or subdural space. He inserts the shunt into the space and subcutaneously tunnels the far end of the shunt toward the drain site. He places a venous catheter and uses it to maneuver the shunt to the atrium, jugular vein, or cardiac auricle. The provider ensures the catheter functions to drain the fluid. He sutures the brain membranes and closes the surgical wounds. Terminology Auricle: An ear–shaped pouch that is an appendage to a heart’s atrial chamber; also called the left atrial appendage or right atrial appendage. Subarachnoid space: The space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater, the middle and innermost of the three membranes covering the brain. Subdural space: The space under the dura mater, the outermost of the three membranes covering the brain. Read Less

In a patient with a failed or malfunctioning cerebrospinal fluid shunt, the provider restores proper function by replacing or flushing a catheter that begins in the subarachnoid or subdural space under the brain’s protective membranes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp, pulling it back to allow access to the site. Through the skull, he accesses the dura, the tough outer membrane surrounding the brain. He makes an incision to reach the previously placed catheter. The provider either irrigates the catheter by instilling fluid or replaces the catheter to ensure proper function. He closes the surgical wounds. Terminology Subarachnoid space: The space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater, the middle and innermost of the three membranes covering the brain. Subdural space: The space under the dura mater, the outermost of the three membranes covering the brain. Read Less

The provider uses a small endoscope to access the brain, along with stereotactic imaging guidance, to perform a ventriculocisternostomy. In this procedure, the provider creates an artificial opening in the floor of the third ventricle of the brain to the cisterna magna, one of three principal openings in the subarachnoid space where cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, drains. The provider performs this procedure to treat hydrocephalus; most often a form known as noncommunicating hydrocephalus to allow CSF to drain inside the patient’s body. Explanation The provider uses a stereotactic computed tomography, or CT, or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, image to construct a three–dimensional image of the brain, which he uses to plan and direct the procedure. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the scalp. He then makes a burr hole in the skull with a surgical drill along the trajectory the images help to determine. He passes a neuroendoscope through the hole into the hollow fluid filled ventricular compartment. The neuroendoscope provides illumination and magnification to identify the anatomy of the ventricular system. Using direct visualization, he identifies and enters the foramen of Monro and then enters the third ventricle. Here, he carefully punctures the floor of the ventricle and opens it, being cautious not to injure the critical vascular structures nearby. He moves through the opening into the cisternal space to ensure the patency of the opening, meaning that it is open and unobstructed and that CSF is freely flowing. If he determines it necessary, he may insert and tunnel a ventricular catheter to an external collection system or insert a shunt through the opening to drain blood and debris from the procedure, along with the CSF and reduce the chance of occlusion. When the procedure is complete, he obtains hemostasis and removes all instrumentation. Finally, he closes the cerebral membranes and replaces and secures the bone flap. Then he closes the scalp in layers and covers the wounds with sterile dressings. Terminology Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill. Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove a fluid or to keep a passage open. Cisterna magna: The largest of three primary openings in the subarachnoid space where cerebrospinal fluid drains from the fourth ventricle; also known as the cerebellomedullary cistern. Computed tomography: Computed tomography, or CT, is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Cortex: The superficial gray matter of the brain. Dura: The outer protective covering of the brain. Foramen of Monro: The small openings on both sides of the brain that connects the third ventricle with the lateral ventricles. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Magnetic resonance imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, uses magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Neuroendoscope: A small, tubular type instrument with a fiberoptic light source used to view the brain and spinal cord. Noncommunicating hydrocephalus: An obstruction where the flow of CSF is blocked along one or more of the connecting passages between the ventricles, creating pressure on the brain; also referred to as water on the brain, or obstructive hydrocephalus. Shunt: A narrow tube that allows excess cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, that builds up inside the ventricles in the brain, to drain into another part of the body. Subarachnoid space: The space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater, the middle and innermost of the three membranes covering the brain. Ventricles: Chambers in the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF. Read Less

The provider creates a shunt, or tube, leading from the ventricles of the brain to the atria, jugular veins, or auricular processes to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF. Explanation The provider incises the scalp, pulls the scalp back, and drills a burr hole into the dura mater, or the covering of the brain. He then closes the scalp in layers. Terminology Atria: The upper chambers of the heart. Auricular processes: The ear shaped projection of the atria. Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill. Jugular veins: Veins that deliver oxygenated blood from the head to the heart. Ventricles: Chambers in the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF. Read Less

The provider blocks an arteriovenous malformation, or AVM, of the spinal cord with an injection of particles or glue to cut off its blood supply. Terminology Arteriovenous malformation: Also called an AVM; a condition where arteries connect directly to veins, without first carrying blood through capillaries, the smallest blood vessels. This procedure is laminectomy of more than two lumbar vertebral segments with exploration and/or decompression of the spinal cord and/or cauda equina. This procedure does not contain a facetectomy, foraminotomy, or discectomy. Explanation During a laminectomy, the surgeon removes the spinous process (the bony projection on the back of the vertebrae) and one or both laminae (the broad plates of bone on either side of the spinous process that complete the "arch" of the vertebrae and enclose the spinal cord), followed by decompression of the nerves. The focus of the work is the individual vertebra and the nerve roots emanating through the foramen (passageways) on either side of the vertebra. The surgeon may perform a laminectomy on several adjacent vertebral levels depending on the condition of the patient. Tips To report a laminectomy and hemilaminectomy (laminotomy) correctly, you must know whether the surgeon removed one or more complete laminae from a single vertebra or if they partially removed the laminae from two adjacent vertebrae. This procedure is laminotomy of one lumbar interspace with decompression of the nerve root(s), and includes a partial facetectomy, foraminotomy, and/or the excision of a herniated intervertebral disc. This procedure covers open and endoscopic approaches. Explanation Laminotomy, also known as hemilaminectomy or a partial laminectomy, involves removing the upper and lower portions of adjacent laminae (that is, the laminae on either side of a vertebral interspace), rather than removing the entire lamina(e) of a single vertebra. In this procedure, the surgeon removes upper and lower portions of the laminae surrounding two adjacent vertebral interspaces. If the surgeon performs two hemilaminectomies at adjacent levels, they may choose to remove the entire lamina. Although this may look like a complete laminectomy, the procedure qualifies as two hemilaminectomies as long as the surgeon excises the intervertebral discs as well. Tips Report an initial laminotomy using 63020 (cervical) or 63030 (lumbar), with +63035 for each additional cervical or lumbar level the provider treats beyond the first. You may append modifier 50 to laminotomy procedures if the provider performs the procedure bilaterally. CPT® states you should not append modifier 50 to add–on codes; instead, report the code twice. To relieve symptoms caused by spinal cord or nerve root pressure, the provider performs a decompression service on a single thoracic segment, such as removing a disc from the spine. He may use a drill or a biting instrument called a rongeur for access to the site. He removes the source of the compression, such as a herniated disc. The provider may insert a drain. He closes the wound in layers. Terminology Costovertebral: Relating to a rib and a vertebra. You should not report spine osteotomy codes 22206–22208 with 63064 for same–session, same–level services. The herniation of a cervical disc is one of the most common causes of cervical pain (cervicalgia or neck pain). Herniation occurs when an intervertebral disc moves out of its place, there is a tear in the annulus of the cervical disc caused by an accident or pathological causes, and the nucleus pulposus (the gelatinous substance inside the spinal disc) bulges out. A herniated disc puts pressure on the nerve roots or spinal cord and causes pain in the patient. When medication fails, herniation needs surgical intervention. The surgeon decompresses the nerve roots/spinal cord by removing the herniated portion of the disc. Grafts are used to fill the empty space created by the removal of the disc. Explanation A transverse incision is made in the skin over the herniated disc and the carotid artery along with the sternocleidomastoid muscle is retracted to access the disc. The surgeon cuts away the herniated disc material with the help of forceps to decompress the spinal cord/nerve roots. Graft bone harvested from the ilium or other body area of the patient is put into the disc space and the muscles and the blood vessels are released into place. The opening is closed with layered sutures. CPT® code 63075 is used to report a discectomy of a single interspace of the cervical spine. Terminology Intervertebral disc: These are soft pad like structures between two vertebrae. The spinal disc acts like a shock absorber and allows smooth movement of a vertebra over another. The disc is made of a hard outer structure called the annulus fibrosus and a soft jelly–like inner material called nucleus pulposus. Nucleus pulposus: The gelatinous substance inside the intervertebral disc. It is made of collagenous fibers and water (about 90%) that gives it a jelly like consistency and the capacity to bear and distribute load across the disc. Read Less

The provider excises (removes) part or all of a cervical vertebra via an frontal (anterior) approach and decompresses the spinal cord and/or nerve roots at a single level in the neck. Explanation The provider resects a single cervical vertebral segment using an anterior approach, which includes decompressing the spinal cord and or nerve root. Under anesthesia, the physician makes an incision and removes the diseased and damage part of the vertebral bone. This relieves pressure on the spinal cord. Then the physician removes the discs above and below the vertebrae and inserts bolts below and above the vertebrae. The physician opens the vertebral gap and inserts a bone graft. Once that is complete, the physician closes the vertebral gap and inserts a metal plate. Terminology Corpectomy: Surgical excision of the main body of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the back. Nerve root: The portion of a nerve where it connects to the central nervous system, i.e., the brain or spinal cord; the origin of a nerve. Spinal cord: Group of nerve fibers encased in the vertebral column that connects the brain to the rest of the body. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine and protect the spinal cord; there are 33 segments divided into five different levels — the neck (cervical spine, C1 through C7), upper and middle back (thoracic spine, T1 through T12), lower back (lumbar, L1 through L5), sacral (sacrum, S1 through S5), and tail bone (coccyx which consists of 4 fused bones). Tips There are many similarities among vertebral corpectomy, anterior discectomy, partial excision of vertebrae, and osteotomy of the spine which makes choosing among these codes a real challenge. If a difficult operative report overwhelms you, slow down and identify the component steps that distinguish the differences between each procedure. Your most effective tool to distinguish among spinal procedures is a firm grasp of what each code set includes: For example, an anterior vertebral corpectomy, also sometimes called a vertebral body resection, involves a total or near–total removal of the vertebral body. All vertebral corpectomy procedures include discectomy and can occur either with spinal canal decompression (CPT® codes 63081–63091) or with the excision of an intraspinal lesion (CPT® codes 63300–63308), the latter of which involves decompression of the spinal cord and/or nerve root(s). When reporting a vertebral corpectomy with decompression (CPT® codes 63081–63091), you should not report fracture care separately, even though it is common with procedures of this type. You may, however, separately bill for arthrodesis (CPT® codes 22548–22812, to stabilize the spine) and spinal reconstruction procedures, including bone grafts (CPT® codes 20930–20938) and spinal instrumentation (CPT® codes 22840–22855). Additional Info Example: To treat a compressed nerve caused by fracture, the surgeon performs discectomies followed by a corpectomy of segments C4 and C5. The physician frees compressed nerve roots and reconstructs the spine using a tricortical allograft and titanium plates. Although the surgeon removes only two vertebral bodies, the arthrodesis occurs across three interspaces. The instrumentation involves four segments because the fixation will extend above and below the two reconstructed segments. In this case, you would report CPT® codes: 63081, +63082, 22554, +22585 x 2, +20931, +22846 Read Less

A laminectomy with myelotomy, also known as DREZ lesioning, is a surgical procedure that destroys the posterolateral portion of the spinal cord; the procedure is performed to treat chronic severe neuropathic pain unmanageable with other therapies. Explanation Under anesthesia, the physician makes an incision and performs a laminectomy to expose the dorsal nerve roots. The laminectomy is extended to the level of the medial facets. A DREZ lesion is identified by direct visualization of the dorsal roots. DREZ stands for dorsal nerve root entry zone, the place where the nerve enters the spinal cord. Once the lesion is identified, the provider may choose one of the following techniques to destroy the nerve root so that pain signals can no longer pass through the spinal cord to the brain. The four most common procedures to lesion DREZ are as follow; 1. Cutting the nerve roots with a surgical blade and then coagulating the area with bipolar forceps under direct visual guidance. 2. Using a specially designed radiofrequency electrode to destroy the nerve roots. 3. Using CO2 or argon laser devices to destroy the nerve roots. 4. Using focused ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves) to destroy the nerve roots. Terminology Laminectomy: Surgical excision of the lamina, a thin plate of bone at the back of a vertebra, to decompress the spinal cord or nerve roots. Neuropathy: Nerve damage resulting in symptoms such as numbness, pain, or weakness. Read Less

The provider removes the lamina (thin bone that forms the back of a vertebra) as part of a procedure to drain a spinal cyst into the subarachnoid space. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized and face down, the provider makes an incision through the skin and fascia near the spinal cyst or syrinx. He retracts the muscles near the spine and performs a laminectomy, removing the lamina, which is the posterior arch of a vertebra. Then the provider removes the discs above and below the vertebrae and inserts bolts below and above the vertebrae. The provider opens the vertebral gap and inserts a bone graft. Extradural: Present inside the skull but outside the dura mater, which is the thick, outermost membrane covering the brain or within the spine but outside the dural sac enclosing the spinal cord, nerve roots and spinal fluid. Intervertebral disc: A round, flat, fibrous tissue layer between two adjacent vertebrae, the interlocking bones of the spine, consisting of a tough outer layer (anulus fibrosus) and a jellylike central part (nucleus pulposus) that acts as a flexible cushion between the vertebrae to aid in load bearing and shock absorption. Intradural: Within the dura, the tough outer membrane surrounding the central nervous system. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue, particularly an area that is well–defined. As with CPT® codes 63081–63091, report the appropriate code for the first vertebra removed, using add–on CPT® code 63308 for each additional segment. As with CPT® codes 63081–63091, you may claim arthrodesis and spinal reconstruction separately. For example, if the surgeon uses an anterior approach to access segments C4 and C5, opening the dura and exposing the tumor for excision, report the primary procedure using CPT® codes 63304 and 63308. You may report any grafts and/or instrumentation for spinal reconstruction separately. There are many similarities among vertebral corpectomy, anterior discectomy, partial excision of vertebrae, and osteotomy of the spine which makes choosing among these codes a real challenge. If a difficult operative report overwhelms you, slow down and identify the component steps that distinguish the differences between each procedure. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider uses the stereotactic method, which makes use of a three dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets inside the spinal cord, and inserts a needle electrode through the skin to stimulate targeted areas of the spinal cord. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the target area of the spinal cord using the stereotactic method, in which previously taken CT or MRI images are imported into a computer system that provides three dimensional images of the spinal cord. The goal of this procedure is to stimulate the spinal cord to treat chronic pain. The provider then makes a small incision through the skin and passes a hollow needle electrode to the target area. He then stimulates targeted areas of the spinal cord. He then withdraws the electrode and closes the skin incision. This procedure is not followed by any other surgery. Terminology Stereotactic surgery: Surgical intervention which makes use of a three–dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets inside the body. Read Less

In this add–on procedure, the provider uses externally generated ionized radiation to destroy an additional spinal lesion following destruction of an initial lesion at the same session. Explanation In this add–on procedure after the destruction of a first spinal lesion, the patient is appropriately prepped for destruction of an additional spinal lesion; the provider identifies the target area of the spinal cord using the stereotactic method in which previously taken CT or MRI images are imported into a computer system that provides three dimensional images of the spine. He then uses a robotic arm controlled by computer to focus radiation on the target area and destroy the spinal lesion. This is a noninvasive procedure that does not require creating a spine incision. Terminology Stereotactic radiosurgery: A noninvasive neurosurgical discipline that uses ionized radiation to destroy target areas. Read More

In this procedure, the provider places electrodes in the epidural space to relieve pain and reduce or eliminate spasms. Explanation When the patient is prepped and anesthetized, the provider advances a needle into the epidural space, under fluoroscopic guidance, and guides a percutaneous electrode through the needle up to the mid thoracic spine and attaches an external stimulator to the other free end of the electrode. The provider checks for the different combinations between the electrodes and the leads until the stimulator generates paresthesias that the patient feels. The provider then detaches the external unit, checks the impedance in the leads, and attaches the leads to the skin. Terminology Electrode: A device used to transmit electrical impulses. Electrode array: Composition of electrodes that measures the electric current. Epidural space: Space around the dura, the outermost covering of the spinal canal, that encloses the spinal nerve roots, blood vessels and lymphatics. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Impedance: Total opposition to alternating electrical current. Lamina: Thin layer on the surface of a bone; one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Neurostimulator: A device that uses electrical impulses to activate muscle contraction. Paresthesias: Abnormal sensations, like pricking or tingling, caused by any impairment to the peripheral nerves. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Peripheral nerve: One of many nerves that connect the brain and spinal cord to the body. Spasm: An abrupt, involuntary muscle contraction. Thoracic spine: Upper and middle back, containing vertebrae enumerated T1 through T12. Tips If the provider removes a portion of the lamina of the vertebra for the implantation of the neurostimulator electrodes in the epidural space, use 63655, Laminectomy for implantation of neurostimulator electrodes, plate or paddle, epidural. If the provider revises or removes the spinal neurostimulator electrode array, see 63661 to 63664. Read Less

The provider removes one or more spinal neurostimulator electrode percutaneous arrays. The provider may use fluoroscopy to guide the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the site of the original incision used for percutaneous electrode array placement. The provider may have placed the spinal cord stimulation device to treat chronic pain. For removal, the provider makes a small incision along the back to access the spinal area where the percutaneous array or arrays sit. An array is the collection of contacts on a single catheter–like lead. The provider may need to locate and extract any anchors, such as in the epidural space, used to hold the device in place. The provider may use fluoroscopy to guide this procedure. The provider may need to disconnect the array(s) from the system's pulse generator. After removing the array(s), the provider closes the access site. Terminology Epidural space: The space that surrounds the dura, which is the outermost layer that surrounds the spinal canal; the epidural space houses the spinal nerve roots, blood and lymphatic vessels, and fatty tissues. Fluoroscopy: A live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider replaces or irrigates a shunt previously placed in the lumbosubarachnoid region. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the site of the original incision from the shunt creation and makes a new incision in the same area. He then incises any adhesions and retracts the paravertebral muscles, fascia, and ligaments to gain access to the shunt. He may then irrigate the shunt with saline if it is not working properly, or he may replace it with a new shunt. He then closes the wound by suturing layers of tissue together. Terminology Lumbosubarachnoid shunt: An arrangement made up of tubing and a catheter in the lumbar subarachnoid area to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid to other areas of the body. Subarachnoid: Under the arachnoid mater, the second of the brain’s three protective membranes. Tips Report code 63746 when the provider removes the lumbosubarachnoid shunt without replacement. Read Less

The provider removes a previously implanted shunt, a small tube placed in the lumbar region near the base of the lumbar spine, to drain cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, from the cavity surrounding the spinal cord, known as the subarachnoid space. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reopens the incision made during the prior procedure and exposes the shunt system. She gently dissects adhesions and removes scar tissue to release the shunt, and she removes it. Next, she irrigates the location with an antibiotic solution and checks to be sure all bleeding stops before she closes the incision in layers and covers it with sterile dressings. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands that form between tissues and organs, often as a result of injury during surgery. They may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Epidural: Outer part of the spinal canal. Laminectomy: Removal of a portion of the cervical vertebra called the lamina, which is the posterior arch or the back part of the vertebra that covers the spinal canal, in order to decompress the spinal cord and/or spinal nerve root. Lumbar vertebrae: Vertebrae situated between the thoracic, or chest level, vertebrae and the sacral, or bottom vertebrae, in the spinal column, indicated by the symbols L1 through L5. Lumbosubarachnoid: Beneath the arachnoid, the middle of three membranes that cover the lumbar spine in the central nervous system. Read Less

A neurostimulator includes electrodes which are inserted under the skin and induced by a small pulse generator to stimulate the nerve tissue. Use of this stimulator involves implantation of electrodes around a selected peripheral or cranial nerve. Explanation The stimulating electrode is connected by an insulated lead to a receiver unit which is implanted under the skin at a depth not greater than 1/2 inch. Stimulation is induced by a generator connected to an antenna unit which is attached to the skin surface over the receiver unit. Implantation of electrodes requires surgery and usually necessitates an operating room. Report 64553 if the targeted area is a cranial nerve. Terminology The term percutaneous pertains to any medical procedure where access to inner organs or other tissue is done via needle–puncture of the skin, rather than by using an "open" approach where inner organs or tissue are exposed. A neurostimulator includes electrodes which are inserted under the skin and induced by a generator to stimulate the nerve tissue. Use of this stimulator involves implantation of electrodes around a selected peripheral nerve. Explanation The stimulating electrode is connected by an insulated lead to a receiver unit which is implanted under the skin at a depth not greater than 1/2 inch. Stimulation is induced by a generator connected to an antenna unit which is attached to the skin surface over the receiver unit. Implantation of electrodes requires surgery and usually necessitates an operating room. Report 64555 if the targeted area is peripheral nerve. Terminology The term percutaneous pertains to any medical procedure where access to inner organs or other tissue is done via needle–puncture of the skin, rather than by using an "open" approach where inner organs or tissue are exposed. The provider, under imaging guidance, implants electrodes around nerves in the sacral region to reduce the pain along the path of the nerve. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider fixes electrodes around the sacral nerves. The provider implants neurostimulator electrodes near the sacral nerves which do not penetrate the skin more than one–half inch. Using imaging guidance, he locates the sacral nerves and places the electrodes transforaminally, or into the opening on the side of the spine, called the foramen, where the nerve root exits. He stimulates the motor nerves to reduce pain sensation along the course of the nerve. Terminology Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Neurostimulator: A device that uses electrical impulses to stimulate nerves, often to activate muscle contraction. Tips If the provider places electrodes in the cervical region, rather than in the sacral region, see 61885 or 61886. If the provider repairs or removes the peripheral neurostimulator, use 64585. The provider revises or removes an integrated neurostimulation system that stimulates a peripheral nerve. This code includes imaging guidance and applies to the first or only electrode array. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision to begin the procedure for the previously implanted peripheral nerve electrode array with integrated neurostimulator. The provider may perform revision, such as by addressing an issue with the initial placement, or removal, taking the device out. For revision, the provider may move or adjust the device and confirm the system is in the proper position for electrical stimulation. The provider removes any surgical instruments and closes any incisions. Terminology Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Neurostimulator: A device that uses electrical impulses to stimulate nerves, often to activate muscle contraction. Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Peripheral motor nerve, peripheral nerve: One of many nerves that connect the brain and spinal cord to the body. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider uses an open approach to incise scar tissue or other sources of pressure to relieve tension on a nerve in a hand or foot. The nerves of the hand or foot include both sensory and motor nerves that innervate the back and the palm of the hand. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the target site in the patient’s hand or foot where the compressed nerve is present. He then locates the compressed nerve and performs external neurolysis, releasing the nerve by cutting down the surrounding scar and soft tissues without entering into the nerve. He may also remove any bone spur or damaged muscle putting pressure on the nerve. He closes the incision in layers once he has repaired and freed the nerve. Terminology Bone spur: Bony projection that occurs along a joint; also called an osteophyte. External neurolysis: Removing the surrounding scarring from a nerve without entering into the nerve. Neuroplasty: Surgery to repair a nerve. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider uses an open approach to incise scar tissue or other sources of pressure to relieve tension on the lumbar plexus, a network of nerves that innervate the upper leg and other areas. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the target site where the nerve is present. The lumbar plexus is a network of nerves supplying the lower abdomen, pelvis, and the upper leg. The provider locates the compressed nerve and performs external neurolysis, releasing the nerve by cutting down the surrounding scar and soft tissues without entering into the nerve. The provider also may remove any bone spur or damaged muscle putting pressure on the nerve. The provider closes the incision in layers after freeing the nerve. Terminology External neurolysis: Removing the surrounding scarring from a nerve without entering into the nerve. Neuroplasty: Surgery to repair a nerve. Tips Neuroplasty includes external neurolysis. Use 64712 when open neuroplasty is performed on the sciatic nerve. Use 64713 when open neuroplasty is performed on the brachial plexus. Use +64727 for internal neurolysis done with an operating microscope. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider relieves the pressure on a cranial nerve by incising the scar tissue or other source of pressure. He may also transpose the nerve to a nearby area so it’s in a more suitable area, free of pressure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the skin near where the target cranial nerve is present, or he may create an opening in bone if the nerve is present within bone. He then locates the compressed nerve and releases it by cutting down the surrounding scar and soft tissues. He may also remove any bone spur or damaged muscle putting pressure on the nerve. He may also shift the nerve to an adjacent site to relieve it from compressing structures. He closes the skin in layers once he has repaired and freed the nerve. Terminology Neuroplasty: Surgery to repair a nerve. Tips Code 64716’s descriptor instructs you to specify the nerve involved. Be sure to include the specific nerve on your claim. Read Less

Neuroplasty or transposition of the median nerve at the carpal tunnel is done to treat a condition called carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). The carpal tunnel is a narrow tunnel in the wrist through which the median nerve and nine flexor tendons of the hand pass. The tendons include the four flexor digitorum superficialis tendons, four flexor digitorum profundus tendons, and one flexor pollicis longus tendon. The top of the tunnel over the median nerve is covered by the transverse carpal ligament. Inflammation of any of these tendons results in the compression of the median nerve or CTS in which the patient feels numbness and weakness of the muscles in the hand. CTS may be caused due to disease conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, hypothyroidism, and amyloidosis; or due to work–related conditions that require repetitive movement of fingers such as working long hours on computer keyboards or playing keyboard instruments like the piano. Explanation A small incision over the carpal tunnel is made over the palm and wrist cutting through the palmar fascia and exposing the carpal ligament. The ligament is surgically divided to release pressure on the median nerve. Care is taken to ensure safety of the median nerve and the tendons surrounding it. A layered closure of the incisional wound is then made. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider performs a decompression of the plantar digital nerve, which passes in between two toes. He frees it from surrounding ligaments, which are exerting pressure on the nerve. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision dorsally, or on the sole of the foot, near the web space between two toes. He further deepens the incision below the subcutaneous tissues. He exposes the ligament where the nerve is compressed due to overgrowth or shrinking of surrounding ligament tissue, enclosing the nerve. With a sharp instrument he dissects the ligament tissue and creates space for the nerve. After confirming decompression of the nerve, he closes the skin and subcutaneous layer with sutures. Terminology Nerve decompression: A procedure of freeing a nerve from the surrounding tissues by cutting those tissues with a sharp object. Plantar digital nerve: The plantar digital nerves are derived from the medial and the lateral plantar nerve, which arise from the tibial nerve and carry sensations to or from the foot. Tips Code +64727 additionally if the provider documents performing internal neurolysis with the help of an operating microscope. Read Less

The provider excises scar tissue from within and between the nerve fibers in the protective nerve sheath using an operating microscope and microsurgical techniques. This procedure may be done during repair of a nerve compression injury to optimize nerve regeneration. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the affected nerve and locates and inspects the neurovascular bundle. Using an operating microscope and microsurgical techniques, he carefully opens the nerve’s outer sheath and gently excises scar tissue from within and between the nerve bundles of the nerve. Once the service is complete, he closes the skin and subcutaneous layer with sutures. Terminology Neurolysis: Application of heat, cold, or chemicals to a nerve to temporarily destroy the nerve. Neuroplasty: Surgery to repair or restore a nerve. Neurovascular bundle: Group of nerves and veins. Tips Report add–on code 64727 once, regardless of the number of branches the provider treats. Also, add–on code 64727 represents a microsurgical technique, so it is not appropriate to also report the add–on code 69990, Microsurgical techniques, requiring use of operating microscope. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider transects or forcibly tears the infraorbital nerve to give relief from facial pain by diminishing the sensation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision just above the eyebrow, retracts the skin edge and locates the supraorbital nerve. After locating the nerve he cuts the nerve with a sharp object or forcibly separates the nerve from its point of emergence. After the procedure, the provider closes the incision with sutures or tape. Terminology Avulsion: Tearing away of a structure or part. Supraorbital: Area just above the eye socket. Supraorbital nerve: A branch of the frontal nerve, that itself branches to the forehead, scalp, upper eyelid, and frontal sinus.

In this procedure, the provider transects or forcibly tears the infraorbital nerve to give relief from facial pain by diminishing the sensation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision just below the eyeball below the lower eyelid, retracts the skin edge, and locates the infraorbital nerve. The provider can also take an intraoral approach to reach the nerve by cutting mucosa above the upper gums. After locating the nerve he cuts the nerve with a sharp object or forcibly separates it from its point of emergence. After the procedure, the provider closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Avulsion: Tearing away of a structure or part. Infraorbital: Area just below the eye socket. Infraorbital nerve: The infraorbital nerve, ION, is the terminal branch of the maxillary nerve; it supplies the skin and mucous membranes of the middle portion of the face. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider transects or forcibly tears the mental nerve to give relief from a facial pain by diminishing the sensation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision inside the oral cavity at the base of the gums of the premolar teeth, technically known as a maxillary vestibular incision. Next the provider locates the mental nerve and either he cuts the nerve with a sharp object or forcibly separates it from its point of emergence. After the procedure, the provider closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Avulsion: Tearing away of a structure or part. Mental nerve: A general somatic afferent, also called sensory nerve, which provides sensation to the anterior aspects of the chin and lower lip as well as the buccal gingivae of the mandibular anterior teeth and the premolars.

In this procedure, the provider transects or forcibly tears the inferior alveolar nerve by cutting or drilling a hole in the mandible bone to give relief from facial pain by diminishing the sensation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the side of the lower jaw bone, known as the mandible. After incising, he retracts the skin and masseter muscle to expose the mandible. The provider cuts or drills a hole to create a window and access the inferior alveolar nerve. After locating the nerve, he cuts the nerve with a sharp object or forcibly separates the nerve from its point of emergence. After the procedure, the provider closes the incision with sutures or tape. Terminology Avulsion: Tearing away of a structure or part. Inferior alveolar nerve: A branch of the mandibular nerve; innervates teeth of lower jaw. Masseter muscle: A muscle that is situated over the cheek bone and jaw bone; assists in chewing motion while eating food. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider transects or forcibly tears the lingual nerve to give relief from facial pain by diminishing the sensation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision below the tongue in the anterior border of the ramus of the mandible. He retracts the skin edge and locates the lingual nerve. After locating the nerve he cuts the nerve with a sharp object or forcibly separates it from its point of emergence. After the procedure, the provider closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Avulsion: Tearing away of a structure or part. Lingual nerve: A branch of the mandibular nerve that supplies sensory innervation to the tongue. Mandible: Jaw bone. Ramus: The angled portion of the mandible that joins the body of the mandible in the posterior portion of the oral cavity.

In this procedure, the provider transects or forcibly tears the facial nerve or any branch of the facial nerve to give relief from facial pain by diminishing the sensation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision just behind the ear, also called a post–auricular incision. Next the provider locates the facial nerve and either he cuts the nerve with a sharp object or forcibly separates it from its point of emergence. The provider can perform the procedure on the main facial nerve, or he can extend the incision downward to cut or avulse a branch of the facial nerve causing the problem. After the procedure, the provider closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Avulsion: Tearing away of a structure or part. Facial nerve: The seventh cranial nerve; it emerges from the brainstem between the pons and the medulla, and controls the muscles of facial expression, taste, and part of the tongue. Read Less

The provider severs or removes a portion of the phrenic nerve, paralyzing the diaphragm on one side. The procedure may be done to collapse a diseased lung during an extended thoracic surgery or to replace or repair a damaged or diseased nerve. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the side of the neck just above the collarbone to expose the nerve. He identifies the phrenic nerve and divides or avulses the nerve. He visualizes the resulting affect, then closes the wound and applies appropriate dressings. Terminology Avulsion: Forcibly pulling or tearing away. Phrenic nerve: One of a pair of nerves that extend from the left and right side of the neck down to the lungs to control the function of the diaphragm muscle important for breathing. Transection: Divide by cutting across.

The provider severs or removes one or more branches of the vagus nerve nearest to the stomach to reduce the rate of gastric secretion when it cannot be reduced by other means to treat ulcers. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises down the middle of the abdomen. She locates then frees the anterior left vagus from the esophagus, divides and removes it, being careful to preserve selective branches. Next, she identifies the posterior right vagus nerve and mobilizes and excises it preserving selective branches. She continues to preserve or ligate and divide nerves, keeping her dissection close to the stomach. She dissects smaller nerve trunks from the esophagus and completes the procedure. She then closes the incised tissue and the abdomen and inserts a drain if indicated. Terminology Avulsion: Forcibly pulling or tearing away. Parietal cell: A cell of the stomach that secrete gastric acid, also called oxyntic cells. Transection: Divide by cutting across. Vagotomy: Surgical incision of the vagus nerve to reduce acid secretion in the stomach. Vagus nerve: The tenth cranial nerve that supplies nerves to the throat, voice box, windpipe, lungs, heart, esophagus and part of the intestinal tract; it also brings sensory messages back to the brain from the ear, tongue, pharynx, and larynx. Read Less

The provider severs or removes one or more branches of the vagus nerve through the abdomen to reduce the rate of gastric secretion when it cannot be reduced by other means to treat ulcers. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises down the middle of the abdomen. She then packs the spleen to protect it, and she mobilizes and retracts the liver. The provider then incises the tissue overlying the esophagus and mobilizes and loops the esophagus. She then frees the anterior left vagus from the esophagus, divides and removes it. Next, she identifies the posterior right vagus nerve and mobilizes and excises it. She then dissects smaller nerve trunks from the esophagus. To complete the procedure, she closes the incised tissue and the abdomen, inserting a drain. Terminology Avulsion: Forcibly pulling or tearing away. Transection: Divide by cutting across.

The provider severs or removes part of the obturator nerve through an incision in the buttocks and thigh to treat groin pain caused by damage or entrapment of the nerve. The procedure may also include a release of the tendon of the adductor muscle. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the buttocks in a question mark path to the midline of the back of the thigh. He then divides the fascia and dissects between the muscles locating the obturator nerve beneath a thick fascia. He then divides the thick fascia along the line of the nerve and divides or removes the nerve. He may also release the adductor muscle. He then closes the tissue and the skin. Terminology Adductor muscle: Any muscle that draws a body part away from the body or an extremity. Adductor tenotomy: Procedure where the tendon of the adductor muscle is snipped to release the muscle. Avulsion: Forcibly pulling or tearing away. Obturator nerve: Nerve that originates from the lumbar nerves entering the thigh through the obturator canal to supply the hip and knee joints and the adductor muscles of the thigh and the skin. Transection: Divide by cutting across. Read Less

The provider severs or removes part of the obturator nerve through an incision in the pelvis to treat groin pain caused by damage or entrapment of the nerve. The procedure may include a release of the tendon of the adductor muscle. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the pelvis. He then divides the fascia and dissects between the muscles locating the obturator nerve beneath a thick fascia. He then divides the thick fascia along the line of the nerve and divides or removes the nerve. He may also release the adductor muscle. He then closes the tissue and the skin. Terminology Adductor muscle: Any muscle that draws a body part away from the body or an extremity. Adductor tenotomy: Procedure where the tendon of the adductor muscle is snipped to release the muscle. Avulsion: Forcibly pulling or tearing away. Obturator nerve: Nerve that originates from the lumbar nerves entering the thigh through the obturator canal to supply the hip and knee joints and the adductor muscles of the thigh and the skin. Transection: Divide by cutting across. Read Less

The provider severs or removes other cranial nerves that are not listed elsewhere within CPT®. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the face or neck in the location of the other cranial nerve. She then dissects the tissue, locates and identifies the other cranial nerve and divides or removes the nerve. She then closes the tissue and the skin. Terminology Avulsion: Forcibly pulling or tearing away. Transection: Divide by cutting across.

The provider severs or removes other spinal nerves that are not identified in other codes within CPT®. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the location of the other spinal nerve anywhere from C1 to S4. She then dissects the tissue, locates and identifies the other spinal nerve, and divides or removes the nerve, destroying it. She then closes the incision in layers. Terminology Avulsion: Forcibly pulling or tearing away. Extradural: Outside the dura, the tough outer membrane surrounding the brain and central nervous system. Transection: Divide by cutting across. The provider repairs another nerve in a finger or toe after repair of an initial nerve repair at the same session. The procedure restores sensory and/or motor functions when the nerves become damaged or severed as a result of injury or trauma. Explanation Following repair of an initial nerve in a finger or toe at the same session, the provider accesses another digital nerve through the open wound or incision. He identifies the injured structure and debrides the wound as needed. He then trims the damaged ends of the nerve as needed to expose the healthy tissue. He carries out the dissection using high–power magnification and takes care not to injure the surrounding structures. He then sutures the healthy nerve ends together without creating tension. If the damaged nerve has motor as well as sensory functions, he gathers a group of nerve fibers and sutures them together. He then closes the wound or incision. TerminologyRead More

The provider repairs a sensory nerve in the hand or foot to restore sensory functions. The procedure restores sensory functions when the nerves become damaged or severed as a result of injury or trauma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the injured nerve through the open wound or by incising the hand or foot. She identifies the injured nerve, mobilizes it, and debrides the wound as needed. She then trims the damaged ends of the nerve to expose the healthy tissue. She carries out the dissection using high–power magnification and caution not to injure the surrounding structures. She sutures the healthy nerve ends together without creating tension. She then closes the wound or incision. Terminology Sensory nerve: A nerve that passes messages between different parts of the body and the brain or spinal cord to signal pain, pressure, and other sensations.

The provider uses suturing to repair the ulnar motor nerve, which innervates many muscles of the hand as well as certain forearm muscles. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider may make an incision or work in an open wound to locate the ulnar motor nerve. He cleans the edges of the damaged nerve ends to prepare them for repair. He aligns the nerve endings. He typically begins by placing two sutures through the epineurium, the outer connective tissue around a nerve, to connect the nerve endings. He may place additional sutures depending on the size of the nerve. He closes the wound. Terminology Neurorrhaphy: Joining together two parts of a divided nerve, typically by suturing.

The provider uses suturing to repair the posterior tibial nerve, which originates from the sciatic nerve and innervates the rear portion of the lower extremities. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider may make an incision or work in an open wound to locate the posterior tibial nerve on the back of a lower extremity. He cleans the edges of the damaged nerve ends to prepare them for repair. He aligns the nerve endings. He typically begins by placing two sutures through the epineurium, the outer connective tissue around a nerve, to connect the nerve endings. He may place additional sutures depending on the size of the nerve. He closes the wound. Terminology Neurorrhaphy: Joining together two parts of a divided nerve, typically by suturing.

The provider repairs damage to the lumbar plexus, which trauma, lesions, infection, or other conditions can cause. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision or works through an open wound and locates the lumbar plexus and the area of damage. He cleans the edges of the damaged nerve ends to prepare them for repair. He aligns the nerve endings. He typically begins by placing two sutures through the epineurium, the outer connective tissue around a nerve, to connect the nerve endings. He may place additional sutures depending on the size of the nerve. He joins the nerve back together to ensure that the nerve will function properly. The provider may also reconstruct the nerve, then suture the area closed. Terminology Lumbar plexus: A group of spinal nerves that extend into the lower body. Tips Separately report reconstruction or closure. Read Less

The provider repairs a portion of a nerve that is too short and can’t reconnect without tension by freeing the nerve from the nerve bed or repositioning the nerve in the bed. This restores sensory and/or motor functions when the nerves become damaged or severed as a result of injury or trauma. Explanation During repair of a nerve at the same session, the provider overcomes a small nerve gap, also referred to as a segmental defect, by freeing the nerve ends from surrounding structures to release the nerve and allow for a tension–free repair. If this nerve mobilization is not enough to relieve tension in the nerve when the ends connect, he may remove the nerve from adjacent tissues and reposition it to shorten the distance between severed ends. The provider removes a diseased or damaged eyeball with its contents intact. He inserts an ocular implant to fill the empty eye socket but does not attach it to the muscles.
