The provider removes a foreign object from the surface of the conjunctiva, the membrane covering the eye. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the provider irrigates the eye with sterile solution to dislodge and remove a foreign body. Terminology Conjunctiva: The transparent membrane covering the front of the eye and lining the eyelids. Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body, such as shards of metal or a bone fragment. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Tips When the provider removes multiple foreign bodies from the same part of the same eye, you should only code once for it. For example, if the provider’s notes indicate that he removed three superficial foreign bodies from the patient's right conjunctiva, you should report 65205 just once. However, if he removes foreign bodies from different parts of the same eye, you may report the codes separately. If a patient has foreign bodies in both the cornea and conjunctiva, you should be able to bill both removals separately. Select the appropriate codes from the section enumerated 65205 to 65265, Removal of foreign body procedures on the eyeball. You may be able to include an evaluation and management, or EM service, in some cases. For example, the provider examines a patient experiencing eye irritation after exposure to shattered glass. He looks for foreign bodies and then may perform an irrigation of the eye even though definitive glass particles are not identified. This constitutes a superficial conjunctival foreign body removal but also an evaluation and management, or EM service. Report 65205 for the foreign body removal and select the appropriate EM code and use modifier 25, Significant, separately identifiable evaluation and management service by the same provider on the same day of the procedure or other service, appended to the EM. Terminology Anterior chamber: The space in the anterior or front segment of the eye, between the cornea, that focuses incoming light, and the iris, the colored ring membrane around the pupil; contains a clear liquid called aqueous humor. Tips Coding guidelines recognize treatment of traumatic eye injuries in the office, often performed by a specialist provider, by including 99058, Services provided on an emergency basis in the office, which disrupts other scheduled office services, in addition to basic service. This reflects the additional time and skill needed. The trouble is that Medicare and many other carriers don't pay on 99058. Medicare doesn't even assign relative value units, RVUs, to this code. The bright side is that some third–party insurers may reimburse for the emergency and after hours codes. You will never know unless you submit the claim. Further, omitting the code means you are not accurately reporting the patient's visit. Ultrasound: The use of high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Vitreous cavity: Space between the lens and the retina that contains vitreous humor, a thick gelatinous substance that fills and gives shape to the posterior, or back, segment of the eye, and protects it. Tips If the provider uses ultrasound to localize, or identify, the foreign body, report this separately as 76529, Ophthalmic ultrasonic foreign body localization. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider repairs a laceration, or tear, in the conjunctiva, the transparent membrane that covers the eye. He brings the wound edges together and sews them in a direct closure. He closes a nonperforating laceration of the sclera, or white of the eye, if present. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses forceps or a wetted cotton–tipped applicator to restore any ragged ends of the conjunctiva back into position. He then closes the laceration with absorbable suture and applies antibiotic and a pressure patch. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Conjunctiva: The transparent membrane covering the front of the eye and lining the eyelids. Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Sclera: Thick fibrous outer covering of the eyeball. Additional Info Conjunctival lacerations smaller than 1 cm in size typically do not require sutures. The provider applies antibiotic ointment and they heal on their own. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider repairs a laceration, or tear, in the conjunctiva, the transparent membrane that covers the eye. The edges of the jagged wound do not come together directly and require rearranging and moving around of the tissues in order to close them. The procedure does not require hospitalization. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inspects the area of injury. He then carefully cleanses the tissue margins. He rearranges the tissue, making small incisions as necessary, to cover the wound and sutures all the wound edges. Terminology Conjunctiva: Transparent membrane covering the eyeball. Sclera: Thick fibrous outer covering of the eyeball. Tips If it is necessary to hospitalize the patient for this procedure, report 65273, Repair of laceration, conjunctiva, by mobilization and rearrangement, with hospitalization. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider repairs a laceration, or tear, in the conjunctiva, the transparent membrane that covers the eye. The edges of the jagged wound do not come together directly and require rearranging and moving around of the tissues in order to close them. The procedure requires hospitalization. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inspects the area of injury. He then carefully cleanses the tissue margins. He rearranges the tissue, making small incisions as necessary, to cover the wound and sutures all the wound edges. Terminology Conjunctiva: Transparent membrane covering the eyeball. Sclera: Thick fibrous outer covering of the eyeball. Tips If it is not necessary to hospitalize the patient for this procedure, report 65272, Repair of laceration, conjunctiva, by mobilization and rearrangement, without hospitalization. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider repairs a laceration, or tear, in the cornea, the front portion of the eye that focuses light on the lens. He removes a foreign object from the wound if present. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inspects the laceration site on the cornea. He replaces any extruded tissue and trims any unhealthy tissue from the edges of the wound. He uses fine sutures to bring the margins of the wound together. He then irrigates the eye with a sterile solution and looks for any foreign bodies on the cornea, which he then removes using a needle and gauze. He applies an eye patch. Terminology Cornea: Front portion of the eye that refracts, or focuses, incoming light. Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body, such as shards of metal or a bone fragment. Tips If during a foreign body removal, the provider discovers a laceration and repairs it, do not report these procedures separately as 65275 includes a laceration repair and a foreign body removal, if necessary. The provider removes any foreign body present in the eye, and repairs any injury in the cornea or sclera in the eye. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider examines the cornea and sclera for any laceration or injury. She removes any foreign body present, and repairs the laceration using sutures bringing the ends of the tear together. For this service, the uveal tissue or the vascular layer underneath the sclera remains intact and requires no repair. Finally, she flushes the site with sterile saline, assures hemostasis, and applies an antibiotic with a patch or gauze on the eye to prevent infection. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Cornea: Front portion of the eye that refracts, or focuses, incoming light. Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body, such as shards of metal or a bone fragment; foreign bodies in the upper gastrointestinal, or GI, tract are typically swallowed; a swallowed object may travel to the lower GI tract or be inserted through the anus and rectum; traumatic injury can also introduce foreign bodies into the GI tract. Hemostasis: Control of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Infection: A disease condition that bacterium, viruses, or other microorganisms cause. Laceration: A cut or tears in the skin. Perforation: A through and through tear or wound in a structure. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Sclera: Thick, fibrous, white, outer covering of the eyeball. Uvea: Dusky middle layer of the three layers in the eye, and consists of the iris, ciliary body and choroid; has melanocytes which imparts color to the eye. Tips Use 65285, Repair of laceration; cornea and or sclera, perforating, with reposition or resection of uveal tissue, if the procedure includes resection of uveal tissue along with repair of the laceration in the sclera and, or cornea. Read Less

In this procedure, the provider uses a special glue to repair lacerations, or tears in the cornea, the front portion of the eye that focuses light on the lens, and or the sclera, the white of the eye. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider dries the corneal surface with a sponge and debrides the epithelium surrounding the wound. He then applies tissue glue to the edge of the perforation. Terminology Anterior chamber: The space in the anterior or front segment of the eye, between the cornea, that focuses incoming light, and the iris, the colored ring membrane around the pupil; contains a clear liquid called aqueous humor. Cornea: Front portion of the eye that refracts, or focuses, incoming light. Debride: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Epithelium: Outermost tissue layer on all structures of the body. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Sclera: Thick fibrous outer covering of the eyeball. Tissue glue: Substance that glues tissue together, permitting healing to take place and providing a moisture barrier. Tips The injection of saline or air to restore fluid or pressure to the anterior chamber is included in this procedure and not reported separately. Read Less

The provider sutures a wound of the muscle, tendon, and/or Tenon’s capsule of the eye. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider carefully incises the conjunctiva of the eye. He then locates the extraocular muscles that control eye movement, the Tenon’s capsule, and/or the tendon that requires repair and sutures the wound. Finally, he ensures hemostasis, which is control of bleeding, at the site, and closes the excised area in layers. Terminology Conjunctiva: The thin, moist membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelids (palpebral conjunctiva) and the white part (sclera) of the eyeball (bulbar conjunctiva). Extraocular muscles: Muscles that control movement of the eye: the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, lateral rectus, superior oblique, and inferior oblique. Tendon: Fibrous connective tissue connecting muscle to bone. Tenon's capsule: A thin membrane that covers the eyeball from the limbus or the border between the cornea and the sclera up to the point where the optic nerve exits the eye and separates the globe from the orbital fat. Tips For repair of other injuries (lacerations) of the eyeball, see 65270–65286. Read Less

The provider inserts an intraocular lens into the eye of a patient who had previously had cataract removal. Explanation After the administration of local anesthesia, the provider makes a scleral incision. He inserts an intraocular lens of a specific power using a lens inserter. The lens is then sutured to the sclera or iris. The secondary implant of a lens for aphakia (the absence of a lens in the eye) is generally performed in cases of a complicated surgery or cases where the ophthalmologist is inserting an IOL implant in a patient who had cataract surgery previously but did not have a lens implanted at the time of that surgery. Terminology Cataract: A clouding or opacity of the lens in an eye that leads to a gradual loss of vision over time. Intraocular lens (IOL): A surgically implanted artificial lens that replaces a cloudy or opacified lens, or cataract; IOLs come in specific diopter strengths, or powers, allowing near or far vision; a multifocal lens allows both near and far vision. Tips See extensive notes included with this descriptor regarding codes you can or should not report with this code. Read Less

The provider removes a previously placed intraocular lens and places a new one. Explanation After the administration of local anesthesia, the physician makes an incision in the limbus or temporal area. Scissors are used to cut off the loupe. The presence of any fibrosis is removed from the loupe. Then the physician removes the lens. If necessary, an anterior vitrectomy can be performed, and an intraocular lens of the correct power is inserted. A balanced salt solution is injected into the eye to check for any leakage. Finally, the incision is closed. Terminology Cornea: The clear transparent outer layer in the front of the iris, pupil, and anterior chamber that refracts light entering the eye and provides almost two–thirds to three–quarters of the focusing power. Fibrosis: Thickened and scarred tissue. Intraocular lens (IOL): A surgically implanted artificial lens that replaces a cloudy or opacified lens, or cataract; IOLs come in specific diopter strengths, or powers, allowing near or far vision; a multifocal lens allows both near and far vision. Limbus: The junction of the cornea of the eye where it is continuous with the sclera. Sclera: The white outer part of the eye that covers all of the eyeball except for the cornea. Vitrectomy: Surgical method to remove some or all of the vitreous humor, a semifluid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. Tips The exchange of an intraocular lens is generally performed in the case of incorrect positioning or the placement of a lens of the wrong power. Read Less

In this add on procedure, the provider examines the internal structures of the eye using an ophthalmic endoscope. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized and at the same session as a primary eye procedure, the provider makes an incision in the sclera, the white, outer part of the eye. He then inserts the endoscopy probe through the scleral incision and places the scope in an appropriate position that allows the best view of all internal structures of the eye. He then removes the scope once the procedure is completed. He finally closes the incision with 2–3 sutures and injects the anterior chamber with saline solution to restore the intraocular pressure. He then places medications such as steroids and antibiotics in the operated eye and covers the eye with a bandage. Terminology Sclera: The white outer part of the eye that covers the eye ball except the cornea. Tips Because +66990 is an add–on code, payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code: 65820, 65875, 65920, 66985, 66986, 67036, 67039, 67040–67043, or 67113. Read Less

The provider removes a portion of vitreous humor, the gelatinous material that gives shape to the eye, to provide access to the retina or to remove material within the vitreous that obstructs vision. He accesses the vitreous anteriorly, or from the front of the eye, through the limbus or cornea. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the cornea. He then inserts a needle either through the juncture of the cornea and sclera or uses the open sky technique which involves the passage of needle through the cornea into the vitreous cavity. The needle then aspirates a portion of vitreous humor from the eye. Finally, he sutures the incision and restores the aspirated vitreous with a substitute. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Aspiration: Removal of fluid, gas, or other material through a tube attached to a suction device, often combined with irrigation, the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen or stomach. Cornea: Front portion of the eye that refracts, or focuses, incoming light. Limbus: Boundary between the cornea, the structure that focuses light, and the sclera, the fibrous outer covering of the eyeball. Open sky technique: Passage of a needle through the cornea to the vitreous cavity in the back of the eye. Prolapse: Collapse or slipping of a structure downward out of its normal location. Retina: Sensory membrane in the back of the eye, which contains cells called rods and cones that receive light impulses from the lens of the eye; it sends the impulse signals to the brain, which allow the person to see. Sclera: Thick, fibrous, white, outer covering of the eyeball. Vitrectomy: Surgical excision of the vitreous, the gelatinous substance in the eye. Vitreous cavity: Space between the lens and the retina that contains vitreous humor, a clear gel fluid that helps to maintain the shape of the eye. Vitreous, or vitreous humor: The gelatinous, transparent substance that fills the center of the eye between the lens and the retina. Vitreous substitute: Replacement material to retain the shape and volume of the vitreous cavity when vitreous has been removed, such as air, gas, saline solution, silicone oil, perfluorocarbon liquid, or semifluorinated alkanes. Tips Vitreous collapse can occur during the course of a cataract removal, and the provider finds it necessary to perform a vitrectomy. Medicare considers the vitrectomy a component of the cataract surgery and thus not separately payable. The exception is when a prolapsed vitreous exists and is known in advance and documented in the patient medical record. Then it is not considered a complication of a cataract surgery. Therefore, the provider who plans to perform a vitrectomy during the same operative session as a cataract surgery could code separately for the vitrectomy using modifier 59, Distinct procedural service. In this procedure, the provider cuts the vitreous strands of the eye through a pars plana incision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the pars plana, a thickened portion of the vascular layer of the eye located between the choroid and the iris. He then introduces microsurgical instruments and cuts the vitreous strands which are impairing the vision. He finally closes the pars plana incision with 2–3 sutures and injects the anterior chamber with saline solution to restore the intraocular pressure. He then places medications such as steroids and antibiotics in the operated eye and covers the eye with a bandage. Terminology Pars plana: A thickened portion of the vascular layer of the eye located between the vascular choroid and the iris. Vitreous strands: A vitreous abnormality causing retinal detachment and myopia.

In this procedure, the provider removes scar tissue from the retinal membrane that obscures vision. He removes vitreous humor, the gelatinous material that gives shape to the eye, using a mechanical cutting tool, to gain access to the scar tissue. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the pars plana. He then inserts a mechanical cutting tool through the incision and removes vitreous humor from the eye. The provider uses intraocular micro forceps, a grasping instrument to lift the edges of the cellular membrane. He gently peels it away and removes the scar to decrease the distortion in the retinal membrane. Finally, he closes the incision with sutures, restores the intraocular pressure, administers a topical antibiotic to the eye, and applies an eye pressure patch. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Macular pucker: A thin layer of scar tissue on the eye's macula that distorts the retina and impairs vision; also known as epiretinal membrane, cellophane retinopathy, and internal limiting membrane disease. Pars plana: A structure in the middle of the eye, between the retina and the iris, a common access point for excision of the vitreous, which is the gelatinous substance in the eye. Preretinal cellular membrane: A thin layer of scar tissue on the eye's macula that distorts the retina and impairs vision; also known as epiretinal membrane, cellophane retinopathy, internal limiting membrane disease, or macular pucker. Retina: Sensory membrane in the back of the eye, which contains cells called rods and cones that receive light impulses from the lens of the eye; it sends the impulse signals to the brain, which allow the person to see. Vitrectomy: Surgical excision of the vitreous, the gelatinous substance in the eye. Vitreous, or vitreous humor: The gelatinous, transparent substance that fills the center of the eye between the lens and the retina. Vitreous substitute: Replacement material to retain the shape and volume of the vitreous cavity when vitreous has been removed, such as air, gas, salt solution, silicone oil, or other chemicals with properties that mimic the vitreous. Tips If the provider injects a vitreous substitute, check with your payer before reporting it separately. Read Less

During this procedure, the provider performs an incision of the conjunctiva and drains a cyst to relieve pressure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the conjunctiva and drains the cyst. The provider incises the affected lining of the eyelid, then gains access to the cyst. The provider pokes a small needle into the cyst and drains the contents. Terminology Conjunctiva: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid. Cyst: Sac usually containing fluid; the term cyst can refer to an abnormal growth or to any saclike structure, such as the urinary bladder or gallbladder. Tips If the patient returns after the procedure complaining of the same problem, and the provider must excise the cyst, report the excision at the subsequent visit, even though it is a related procedure within the postoperative period of the first procedure. The fact that the excision, reported using 68110, Excision of lesion, conjunctiva; up to 1 cm or 68115, over 1 cm, is a more extensive procedure than the incision the provider performed earlier allows you to report 68110 or 68115 with modifier 58 appended, Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician during the postoperative period. During this procedure, the provider removes conjunctival follicles to relieve pain and irritation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reverts the eyelid to access the conjunctiva. With imaging help from a biomicroscope and slit lamp, he removes the follicles with a curette or cotton swab. Terminology Biomicroscope: Scope used to examine the structures of the eye. Conjunctiva: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid. Curette: Spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping. Follicle: A small cavity, sac, or gland that secretes fluid. Meibomian gland: A sebaceous gland at the edge of the eyelid that secretes an oily substance called meibum that prevents evaporation of tears. Revert: Turn inside out. Slit lamp: Lamp emitting an intense beam of light used for examining the interior of the eye. Trachoma: An infection caused by bacteria affecting the conjunctiva and cornea. Tips Use 0207T, Evacuation of meibomian glands, automated, using heat and intermittent pressure, unilateral, if the provider instead performs an automated evacuation of the Meibomian glands. Read Less

During this procedure, the provider performs a biopsy of the conjunctiva for diagnostic purposes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider removes a piece of the suspect tissue from the patient's conjunctiva using a curette and sends it to pathology for analysis. He may use sutures to repair the wound. Terminology Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, and open. Conjunctiva: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid. Curette: Spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping. Tips During biopsy, the provider removes a small piece of tissue for microscopic pathological examination. This seems straightforward, but confusion can occur if the provider uses the term excisional biopsy. CPT® does not use this term so you must determine whether the provider performed an actual full excision of the lesion and sent it for biopsy, or if the provider only biopsied a small portion of the lesion. If the provider actually performed an excision and not a biopsy, you should instead consider codes 68110 to 68130, Excision of lesion, conjunctiva. Read Less

During this procedure, the provider excises a lesion on the conjunctiva up to 1 cm in size to alleviate pain and pressure and often to improve vision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a lid speculum and examines the eye. He places a traction suture to the nasal limbus and uses a corneal light shield to prevent phototoxicity. He marks the conjunctival lesion using a fine tip marker, leaving a margin, or surrounding area, of approximately 3 to 4 mm. He excises the lesion, measuring up to 1 cm, and sutures the incision if necessary. Terminology Conjunctiva: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Limbus: Junction between the cornea and sclera in the eye. Phototoxicity: Skin irritation caused by a chemical or exposure to light. Speculum: A medical instrument used for investigating body orifices. Traction: Pulling force. Tips Report 68115 (Excision of lesion, conjunctiva; over 1 cm) if the provider excises a conjunctival lesion over 1 cm. This procedure describes an excision and not a biopsy. This seems straightforward, but confusion can occur if the provider uses the term excisional biopsy. CPT® does not use this term so you must determine whether the provider performed an actual full excision of the lesion and sent it for biopsy, or if the provider only biopsied a small portion of the lesion. If the provider actually performed a biopsy and not an excision, you should instead consider code 68100, Biopsy of conjunctiva. Read Less

During this procedure, the provider excises a lesion on the conjunctiva larger than 1 cm in size to alleviate pain and pressure and often to improve vision. Explanation The provider excises a lesion on the conjunctiva larger than 1 cm. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a lid speculum and examines the eye. He places a traction suture to the nasal limbus and uses a corneal light shield to prevent phototoxicity. He marks the conjunctival lesion using a fine tip marker, leaving a margin, or surrounding area, of approximately 3 to 4 mm. He excises the lesion, measuring over 1 cm, and sutures the incision if necessary. Terminology Conjunctiva: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Limbus: Junction between the cornea and sclera in the eye. Phototoxicity: Skin irritation caused by a chemical or exposure to light. Speculum: A medical instrument used for investigating body orifices. Traction: Pulling force. Tips This code refers to the excision of a lesion. This seems straightforward, but confusion can occur if the provider uses the term excisional biopsy. CPT® does not use this term so you must examine the operative note to determine if the provider performed an actual full excision of the lesion and sent it for biopsy or if the provider only biopsied a small portion of the lesion. If the provider actually performed a biopsy and not an excision, you should instead consider code 68100, Biopsy of conjunctiva. Read Less

During this procedure, the provider excises a lesion on the conjunctiva and the accompanying scleral tissue to alleviate pain and pressure and often to improve vision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a lid speculum and examines the eye. He places a traction suture to the nasal limbus and uses a corneal light shield to prevent phototoxicity. He marks the lesion on the conjunctiva and sclera using a fine tip marker, leaving a margin, or surrounding area, of approximately 3 to 4 mm. He excises the lesion and sutures the incision if necessary. Terminology Conjunctiva: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Limbus: A differentiating border or edge. Phototoxicity: Skin irritation caused by a chemical. Sclera: Outer layer of the eyeball. Speculum: A medical instrument for investigating body orifices. Traction: Pulling force. Tips This code refers to the excision of a lesion. This seems straightforward, but confusion can occur if the provider uses the term excisional biopsy. CPT® does not use this term so you must examine the operative note to determine if the provider performed an actual full excision of the lesion and sent it for biopsy or if the provider only biopsied a small portion of the lesion. If the provider actually performed a biopsy and not an excision, you should instead consider code 68100, Biopsy of conjunctiva. Read Less

During this procedure, the provider eradicates a conjunctival lesion to alleviate pain and pressure and often to improve vision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a lid speculum and examines the eye. He places a traction suture and uses a corneal light shield to prevent phototoxicity. He marks the lesion on the conjunctiva using a fine tip marker, and destroys the lesion using electrocautery, cryotherapy, chemicals, laser, or other methods. Terminology Conjunctiva: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid. Cryotherapy: Ice therapy. Electrocautery: Cautery using an electrically heated instrument. Laser: Adjustable focused light energy source used to destroy lesions or abnormal tissue and to control bleeding. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Phototoxicity: Skin irritation caused by a chemical. Speculum: A medical instrument for investigating body orifices. Traction: Pulling force. Tips When choosing between 68135 and the conjunctival lesion excision codes 68110 to 68130, keep in mind the distinction between excision and destruction. When a provider excises a lesion, he cuts it away from the surrounding tissue and sometimes sends it for biopsy. Destruction involves breaking down the lesion by any number of methods, including chemical and laser treatment, and cryosurgery, during which the lesion is frozen off using liquid nitrogen or carbon dioxide. In cryosurgery, the tissue of the lesion is destroyed, and no biopsy is conducted. Read Less

The provider injects medication into the subconjunctival space for a variety of reasons, such as to deliver antibiotics or to treat swelling. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider chooses the target site and raises or lowers the eyelid as appropriate. As the patient looks away from the needle, the provider inserts the needle into the space between the conjunctiva and the sclera, injecting the medication. After withdrawing the needle, he applies an eye pad. Terminology Conjunctiva: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid. Sclera: Layer of the eyeball. Subconjunctival: Beneath the conjunctiva. Tips If the injections occur postoperatively, for example, to control inflammation, append modifier 58, Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician during the postoperative period, to show that these injections were a staged procedure. Remember to use the appropriate HCPCS supply code, such as J9190, Fluorouracil, 500 mg, to report the supply of the medication. Read Less

The provider removes diseased tissue from the conjunctiva and uses tissue adhesive to graft a new membrane to the eye to treat conditions such as conjunctival chalasis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider surgically separates buccal mucous tissue, and prepares the graft site to receive the graft tissue. The provider then sutures the graft material into a cul de sac, or pouch. He then sutures the graft into place and irrigates the eye. Terminology Buccal mucous membrane: Lining of the mucous membrane inside of the mouth. Chalasis: Relaxation of a bodily opening. Conjunctiva: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid. Conjunctivoplasty: The provider removes excess conjunctival tissue and repairs the conjunctiva. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Tips This code refers to a conjunctivoplasty when the provider also obtains a buccal mucous membrane graft. If the provider does not obtain a buccal mucous membrane graft, you should instead report 68320, Conjunctivoplasty; with conjunctival graft or extensive rearrangement. Read Less

The provider repairs a symblepharon and performs conjunctivoplasty without using a graft. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider frees or excises the scar tissue or adhesions between the palpebral and bulbar conjunctivae and dissects the fibrotic tissue away from the healthy conjunctiva, which he then advances and secures with sutures. He does not use a graft during this procedure. Terminology Adhesions: Process of adhering to a surface or object. Conjunctivoplasty: The provider removes excess conjunctival tissue and repairs the conjunctiva. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. During this procedure, the provider repairs a symblepharon using a free graft of the conjunctiva or buccal mucous membrane. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider frees or excises the scar tissue or adhesions between the palpebral and bulbar conjunctivae, and dissects the fibrotic tissue away from the healthy conjunctiva. He then advances and secures it with sutures. The provider uses a free conjunctival graft or buccal mucosa to repair the defect. Terminology Adhesions: Process of adhering to a surface or object. Buccal mucous membrane: Lining of the mucous membrane the inside of the mouth. Bulbar conjunctiva: Part of the conjunctiva that covers the outer surface of the eye. Conjunctiva: The transparent membrane covering the front of the eye and lining the eyelids. Fibrotic tissue: Fibrous connective tissue. Free graft: A graft freed from its position by cutting, to repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure. Membrane: Layer of lipids and proteins which forms the boundary of cells. Palpebral conjunctiva: Part of the conjunctiva which lines the inside of the eyelids. Tarsal conjunctiva: Also known as palpebral conjunctiva. Symblepharon: Fusing of the conjunctiva of the eyelid to an opposing surface, such as the tarsal and bulbar conjunctivae. Tips Because the descriptor for this service also includes obtaining the graft, you should not separately report the graft harvest. Read Less

During this procedure, the provider repairs a symblepharon using a conformer or contact lens to improve the patient's vision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider frees or excises the scar tissue or adhesions between the palpebral and bulbar conjunctivae and dissects fibrotic tissue away from healthy conjunctiva. He then advances and secures it with sutures. He divides the symblepharon, removing adhesions and scarring, and he may leave the defect open or insert an appropriately sized conformer or contact lens between the lid conjunctiva and the globe of the eye. The provider removes the conformer or contact lens at a later date. Terminology Adhesions: Process of adhering to a surface or object. Bulbar conjunctiva: Part of the conjunctiva that covers the outer surface of the eye. Conformer: A clear plastic shell that holds the eye shape in a stable position. Conjunctiva: The transparent membrane covering the front of the eye and lining the eyelids. Fibrotic tissue: Fibrous connective tissue. Globe of the eye: Ball of the eye. Palpebral conjunctiva: Part of the conjunctiva which lines the inside of the eyelids. Symblepharon: Fusing of the conjunctiva of the eyelid to an opposing surface, such as the tarsal and bulbar conjunctiva. Tips Because this service refers to a repair with or without the conformer insertion, you should not separately report the conformer insertion in situations when the provider performs it. Read Less

During this procedure, the provider harvests a conjunctival allograft to use on another patient. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts an eyelid speculum for clear access to the surgical site. He brings an operating microscope into position and marks the donor site, then injects a solution to raise the conjunctiva at the donor site. The provider incises the tissue, performs blunt dissection to the appropriate depth, and then uses a sharp blade or scissors to remove the graft tissue. He places the graft in an appropriate container with solution for preservation. The provider advances and anchors the conjunctiva using sutures. He removes the eyelid speculum, and applies antibiotics and steroids. Terminology Allograft: A transplant from one individual to another of same species. Tips This service describes the harvesting of an allograft, but not the placement of the graft. The provider performs a simple incision and drainage an abscess, i.e., a collection of pus, or a hematoma, i.e., a mass of blood, in the external ear. He performs this procedure to relieve pain and prevent further infection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the lesion and drains purulent material from an abscess or blood from a hematoma of the external ear. He releases the patient after a brief period of observation. Terminology Incision and drainage, or I and D: A surgical procedure in which cysts, abscesses, or other lesions containing infective material are incised, or cut into, and the infective material drained; the procedure typically includes irrigation, or washing out, of the affected part. Infection: A disease condition caused by bacteria, viruses, or other microorganisms. Purulent material: Pus. The provider may pack the wound with gauze for better healing and applies a dressing over the ear. The provider pierces a patient’s ear as an elective procedure, i.e., performed for purposes other than treatment. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and given local anesthetic if the patient wishes it, the provider pierces a patient’s ear, typically the lobe, with a disposable piercing device that pushes the earring stud through the ear. Terminology Lobe, earlobe: The fleshy part at the bottom of the outer ear; it consists of fatty and fibrous tissue but no cartilage; also referred to the lobule.

The provider excises a portion of the external part of the ear, such as the earlobe or helix, that contains a lesion. He sends the specimen to the lab for diagnosis to determine whether the lesion is malignant or benign. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, typically with local anesthetic, the provider chooses among several techniques and removes a portion of the external ear that contains a lesion. He incises around the lesion and cuts below it with a scalpel. He then closes the surgical wound in a single layer that incorporates the skin and underlying tissues. He applies an antibiotic to the surgical site and dresses it. The provider then releases the patient after a short period of observation. He sends the specimen to the laboratory for analysis. Terminology Anesthetic: Substance that reduces sensitivity to pain. Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Benign: Not malignant, generally treatable or not needing treatment. Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Excision: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. Helix: The cartilaginous portion of the external ear above the lobe. Incise: Cut into a structure, typically with a surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Lobe, earlobe: The fleshy part at the bottom of the outer ear; it consists of fatty and fibrous tissue but no cartilage; also referred to the lobule. Malignant: Cancerous, capable of spreading and causing death if untreated. Scalpel: Surgical knife. Tips For complete removal of the external ear, report 69120, Excision external ear; complete amputation. Read Less

The provider removes the diseased external ear in its entirety. He performs this procedure when an extensive carcinoma involves the whole external ear. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises around the external ear. He carries the incision down through subcutaneous tissues and cartilage. He removes the external ear in its entirely, including the earlobe, helix, and external ear canal. He controls any bleeding and closes the surgical wound in layers. He applies an antibiotic to the surgical site and dresses it. He sends the specimen to the laboratory for analysis. Terminology Anesthetic: Substance that reduces sensitivity to pain. Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Benign: Not malignant, generally treatable or not needing treatment. Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Carcinoma: A malignant tumor likely to spread to other tissues. Excision: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. Helix: The cartilaginous portion of the external ear above the lobe. Incise: Cut into a structure, typically with a surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Lobe, earlobe: The fleshy part at the bottom of the outer ear; it consists of fatty and fibrous tissue but no cartilage; also referred to the lobule. The provider removes one or more bony osteophytes from the external ears canal. He performs the procedure to treat hearing impairment or headache. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the external ear canal over the bony growth. Using a chisel or a drill, he removes the bony projection. He smooths the remaining bone with a burr. He replaces the skin over the site and packs the ear with gauze soaked in antibiotic solution. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Canalplasty: Reconstruction, using plastic repair techniques, of a passage such as the external auditory canal. Exostosis: Bony projection off the external surface of a bone. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. Meatoplasty: Plastic reconstruction of the meatus, the opening of the ear canal; the external meatus consists primarily of cartilage while the internal meatus consists partly of bone. Osteoma: A benign, or noncancerous, growth of new bone on another piece of bone, typically in the skull. Osteophyte: Small bony growth that occurs at the edge of a bone where it meets another bone, often the result of arthritis; also called bone spur Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure; a stenosed valve becomes stiff affecting its ability to open and close properly. Tips Report this code only once regardless of the number of bony osteophytes or osteomas the provider removes. If the provider says he excised an osteoma, you should report 69140; to remove an exostosis, the provider normally makes an incision into the external ear canal, removes the osteoma, and replaces the skin. However, if the procedure involved drilling the bony canal or attaching skin grafts and documentation supports a canalplasty, you should assign code 69310, Reconstruction of external auditory canal, meatoplasty, e.g., for stenosis due to injury, infection, separate procedure. This code involves reconstructing the external auditory canal. Read Less

The provider resects an area of damaged or diseased tissue, such as a sebaceous cyst, lipoma, or cholesteatoma, from the external ear canal. He performs the procedure to establish a diagnosis and to relieve pain and difficulty hearing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the external ear canal over the lesion. He carries the incision down through the soft tissues and removes the suspicious tissue. He replaces the skin over the site and packs the ear with gauze soaked in antibiotic solution. He sends the tissue to the lab for analysis. Terminology Cholesteatoma: A benign tumor of the ear that often contains cholesterol, an important lipid, or steroid, component of all cells. Epithelial: Pertaining to the epithelium, the outermost tissue layer on all structures of the body. Excision: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. The provider removes a foreign body from the external auditory canal without the use of general anesthesia. Explanation The provider examines the ear for the presence of a foreign body, such as a pea, bead, swab, or insect. The provider removes the foreign body using an appropriate process depending on size, shape, and location, such as grasping the foreign body with forceps, using irrigation with a curette (small scraping tool), or suction. Tips Code 69200 is unilateral. Follow payer preference for reporting bilateral procedures, such as by appending modifier 50.

The provider removes a foreign body from the external auditory canal with the use of general anesthesia. Explanation Generally, foreign bodies (e.g., peas, beads, swabs, insects) in the ear are found in the external auditory canal. After administration of general anesthesia, the physician examines the ear for the presence of a foreign body. If necessary, a microscope can be used for such visualization. The foreign body is then grasped and removed with forceps (e.g., alligator forceps). The ear is then irrigated thoroughly with normal saline and antibiotic drops are instilled in the auditory canal to prevent any type of post procedural infection.

The provider uses an instrument such as a curette, vacuum evacuation, or forceps to remove entrapped wax from a patient's external auditory canal. Explanation When a patient has a complaint of fullness in the ears, ear pain, itching, or diminished hearing or blockage, the provider attempts to visualize the external auditory canal. If visualization using microscopy is not possible due to wax blockage, the provider uses an instrument to remove the impaction from the patient's external auditory canal. Terminology Impacted cerumen: Accumulation of ear wax in the ear canal; the blockage can cause difficulty in hearing and/or ear pain. Unilateral: One side. Tips Code 69210 is a unilateral procedure. If the provider removes impacted cerumen from both ears, follow payer guidelines for reporting a bilateral procedure, such as appending modifier 50 to the code. Also check the payer's bilateral indicator for the code. Some payers will not increase reimbursement for a bilateral 69210 service. If the cerumen is not impacted, you should count the documentation as part of the evaluation and management (E/M) code, such as 99202–99215. See 69209 for impacted cerumen removal using irrigation or lavage. For Medicare claims, report G0268 when the physician removes impacted ear wax on the same day as an audiologist conducts audiologic function testing. Read Less

The provider cleans out the cavity left by a mastoidectomy. Patients sometimes require one or more debridement procedures after mastoidectomy before the cavity settles down, i.e., dries out. Explanation The provider performs postoperative removal of granulation tissue from the mastoid cavity. He then irrigates the cavity and the external auditory canal with normal saline, instills antibiotic drops in the bony cavity, and applies a dressing. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. Granulation: Vascular tissue that forms to fill a defect as a wound heals. Granuloma: A nodule consisting of a collection of immune cells, called macrophages, and inflammation. Mastoid cavity: An air space, similar to a sinus cavity, except that it has septations, or walls, somewhat like a honey comb; it is located in the temporal bone above the area of the tympanic membrane. Mastoidectomy: A mastoidectomy can include a simple opening up of the cortex or outer covering of the mastoid cavity or excision of all the mastoid air cells and surrounding structures. Temporal bone: A bone at the base and side of the skull that houses the tympanic membrane and part of the incus and malleus; the three parts of the bone are referred to as the petrous bone, the squamous bone, and the tympanic bone; it also includes the styloid process, a projection off the inferior surface where several muscles and ligaments attach. Tips For more extensive or complex debridement of a mastoidectomy cavity, use 69222, Debridement, mastoidectomy cavity, complex, e.g., with anesthesia or more than routine cleaning. Read Less

The provider surgically creates an external auditory canal to correct congenital absence of the ear canal, which causes hearing impairment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision behind the ear in the natural crease where the ear meets the head. He carries the incision down through bone and tissue until he reaches the ear ossicles. He excises more tissue to create an external auditory canal. He places a tissue graft to create the eardrum and more grafts to create and support the ear canal. He controls any bleeding and closes the incisions. He packs the ear with gauze soaked in antibiotic solution and covers the ear with a bandage. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Congenital: Present at birth. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Ossicles: The three ear bones that vibrate and transmit sound to the eardrum or tympanic membrane; named for shapes they resemble, the bones consist of the malleus or hammer, the incus or anvil, and the stapes or stirrup. Meatus: The opening of the ear canal; the external meatus consists primarily of cartilage while the internal meatus consists partly of bone. Read Less

The provider removes a ventilating tube from the ear with the patient under general anesthesia. Explanation The patient is prepped and draped in a usual sterile fashion. General anesthesia is induced by an appropriate anesthetic agent. The provider then pulls out and retracts a previously secured middle ear tube with a grasping device. The procedure is usually done as an aftercare service following a previously performed related surgery. Tips Removal of a ventilating tube without general anesthesia is considered part of the E/M service. There is no separate code for reporting its removal.

The provider makes a small opening in the eardrum and inserts a ventilating tube under local or topical anesthesia. Explanation The patient is prepped and draped in a usual sterile fashion. Local anesthesia is induced by appropriate topical anesthetic agent. The provider makes a small opening in the eardrum (myringotomy) and secures a delicate tympanostomy tube into the ear drum to provide continuous drainage for the infectious fluid in middle ear and to keep the middle ear aerated while preventing the accumulation of fluid. Tips This code is for when a provider performs an office–based tympanostomy using local or topical anesthesia. When the provider performs a tympanostomy in an operating room using general anesthesia, report 69436. You should not report 99070 for the tympanostomy tube itself as the supply of the tube is included with the procedure. Read Less

General anesthesia is induced by appropriate anesthetic agent. Myringotomy is performed and a delicate tympanostomy tube is secured into the ear drum to provide continuous drainage route for the infectious fluid in middle ear and to keep the middle ear aerated, while preventing the accumulation of mucus. When the provider performs an office–based tympanostomy using local or topical anesthesia, the appropriate code is 69433. However, code 69436 does not include anesthesia services. The anesthesiologist should bill his own code for that according to the time the patient was anesthetized. The inclusion of "general anesthesia" in the descriptor for 69436 is meant to differentiate it from tympanostomy not requiring general anesthesia. This procedure is the exploration of the middle ear via a postauricular or ear canal incision. Explanation The physician performs a diagnostic evaluation (of the middle ear) while adopting an external ear approach to the middle ear and vestibular window. The technique is employed to rule out certain middle ear abnormalities (e.g., cholesteatoma, conductive hearing loss, and tympanic membrane perforation). Tips Clinical scenario Question: What is the appropriate CPT® for Silverstein permanent aeration tube? The surgery took 1.5 hours. My physician would like to report 69440 but I'm not so sure. Answer: You have two choices: (1) use the unlisted codes, or (2) use modifier 22 (Increased procedural service) with 69436 (Tympanostomy [requiring insertion of ventilating tube], general anesthesia) to describe the increased service. Make sure you create a standard letter describing the procedure, what differentiates it from standard tube placement, and the medical benefits for the patient over standard tubes (i.e., why should payer pay for the Silverstein tubes) to use to appeal and get paid appropriately. Important: If the op note does not show middle ear exploration, you cannot bill 69440 (Middle ear exploration through postauricular or ear canal incision). Even if the op note shows middle ear exploration but does not show medical necessity for doing the exploration, you still cannot code 69440. You must prove the medical necessity of the procedure. Don't report the middle ear exploration if it's not necessary only because it's a higher paying code. It could get you in trouble with your payer. Read Less

The provider destroys adhesions, or scar tissue, on the tympanic membrane, or ear drum, that interfere with hearing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses an operating microscope to visualize the tympanic membrane. He uses a scalpel to dissect and remove scar tissue from the surface of the tympanic membrane. He then checks for bleeding and uses cautery, if necessary, instills antibiotic drops, and applies a dressing. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery, that form between tissues and organs; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Operating microscope: A binocular microscope, meaning two eyepieces, for simultaneous viewing with both eyes, used to view fine structures during operations. Scalpel: Surgical knife. Tympanic membrane: Thin membrane that separates the middle ear from the external ear; also known as the eardrum. Read Less

This procedure is a transmastoid antrotomy (also referred to as a simple mastoidectomy). Explanation The physician extends an incision behind the ear. The mastoid bone is then exposed and opened up with a surgical drill. The infection or abnormal mucosal growth is then evacuated. A tube may be placed in the eardrum to drain any pus or secretions present in the middle ear. Antibiotics are then administered either orally or via intravenous route. This procedure is usually performed to treat cholesteatoma and subperiosteal abscess of mastoid. Terminology A simple mastoidectomy is generally performed to aid in the drainage of an infection. It is the removal of viable mucosa and disease from the mastoid cells along with the creation of a tympanic antrum opening, resulting in the improvement of ventilation. Tips Clinical scenario Question: Would you please explain when we should use modifier 55? I am not clear on what "management" means. If another otolaryngologist, not the physician who performed the surgery, sees a post–op patient and admits him to the hospital during the 42–day global period, is modifier 55 appropriate? Answer: You should use modifier 55 (Postoperative management only) when your otolaryngologist assumes all of a patient's postoperative care. For instance, if a patient moves after surgery or returns to his local otolaryngologist for postoperative care after a distant otolaryngologist performs the surgery (such as a neck surgery performed at a distant university medical center), you should claim the postoperative component with modifier 55. Nitty–gritty: Modifier 55 actually goes on the surgery code. Suppose a Chicago otolaryngologist performs a mastoidectomy (69501, Transmastoid antrotomy [simple mastoidectomy]) on a patient. The patient, who lives two hours away, chooses to see his local otolaryngologist for all postoperative care. The physician who performed the surgery should claim the surgical care only with 69501–54 (Surgical care only). To bill for the mastoidectomy's postoperative component, the local otolaryngologist should report 69501–55. There has to be a formal transfer of care from the surgeon to the otolaryngologist for the post op care and the date of that transfer goes in box 19 on the CMS1500 form. Without showing the formal transfer of care, there will be reimbursement problems when you use modifiers 54 and 55. The situation you describe does not require a modifier. First, modifier 55 does not apply because the otolaryngologist is performing an episode of care; he is not providing all of the patient's postoperative care. Second, you do not need a postoperative–period modifier since your physician did not perform the surgery and is not in a global period. Modifiers 24 (Unrelated evaluation and management service by the same physician during a postoperative period), 78 (Return to the operating room for a related procedure during the postoperative period) and 79 (Unrelated procedure or service by the same physician during the postoperative period) apply only to the otolaryngologist who performed the global–period procedure. Explanation The physician performs an extensive surgery to exenterate the air cell system from the mastoid process of the temporal bone for drainage of the suppuration in acute/chronic mastoiditis. This procedure is a modified radical mastoidectomy. Explanation The physician performs surgical resection of mastoid part of the posterior temporal bone in such a manner that few middle ear bones are left intact and the tympanic membrane is then reconstructed. This technique is utilized to treat mastoid disorders (e.g., cholesteatosis and cholesteatoma of mastoid). Terminology A mastoidectomy is generally performed to aid in the drainage of an infection. It is the removal of viable mucosa and disease from the mastoid cells along with the creation of a tympanic antrum opening, resulting in the improvement of ventilation.

This procedure is a radical mastoidectomy. Explanation The physician performs resection of the entire mastoid part of the posterior temporal bone (in case of extensive cholesteatoma of mastoid). The tympanum and middle ear components are removed in entirety. Stapes may be left out to retain minimum audibility. Terminology A mastoidectomy is generally performed to aid in the drainage of an infection. It is the removal of viable mucosa and disease from the mastoid cells along with the creation of a tympanic antrum opening, resulting in the improvement of ventilation.

The provider excises a polyp from inside the ear. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider removes a polyp from the ear using forceps. He then ensures hemostasis, applies antibiotics, and packs the site with cotton balls. Terminology Polyp: An abnormal tissue growth that extends from the mucous membrane. Tips If the procedure is performed bilaterally, you may append modifier 50 to the code for the second ear or LT and RT for left and right side, depending on payer preferences. If multiple polyps are removed from a single ear, you may append modifier 51 for multiple procedures, again depending on payer preferences. If the provider has to remove a ventilation tube in order to access the aural polyp, removal of the ventilation tube is included in this procedure; do not bill for its removal separately.

The provider removes an aural glomus tumor through an incision in the external auditory canal. He performs the procedure to relieve pain caused by the tumor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider enters the external auditory canal and makes an incision in the posterior canal skin. He reflects a skin flap and pushes the eardrum forward. The provider uses an operating microscope or loupes, i.e., magnifying lenses, attached to glasses or a headband to facilitate microdissection. The provider identifies the glomus tumor and grasps it with cup forceps to remove it. He uses packing to control the bleeding at the site, and once controlled, he packs the middle ear with absorbable material soaked in antibiotic. The provider repositions the eardrum and posterior canal skin, and then packs the ear canal. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Glomus tumor: A usually benign, painful, vascular tumor that occurs primarily in the fingers but may also appear in the nose or in the tympanic body of the jugular vein where it causes pain in the ear. Jugular vein: A vein in the neck that returns blood from the scalp, neck, and face to the heart. Transcanal approach: Surgical incision through the skin and tissues of the external auditory canal. Tips If the provider performs excision of an aural glomus tumor using a transmastoid approach, use 69552, Excision aural glomus tumor; transmastoid. For more extensive excision of an aural glomus tumor using an extratemporal approach, use 69554, Excision aural glomus tumor; extended, extratemporal. Read Less

The provider repairs a perforated eardrum, which may include site preparation, or roughening of the site before closure. The procedure may also include applying a paper patch to the closure. The provider applies pressure to the stapes bone of the middle ear to increase mobility and improve hearing.
Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates an incision in the posterior ear canal via the ear canal opening and uses microscopic visualization to move the skin flap and posterior eardrum forward. If needed, he removes a portion of the bony canal using a curette or drill. The provider identifies and moves the incus and stapes bones, applying pressure to the stapes using delicate instruments if it is fixated. He repositions the canal skin flap and eardrum and packs the ear canal.

The provider completes a mastoid obliteration by placing a lining in the mastoid cavity after he removes any remaining diseased tissue. This is a separately performed procedure and should not be considered part of the initial mastoidectomy. He performs the procedure to prevent or stop a cerebrospinal fluid leak.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates a postauricular incision to access the site of the previous mastoidectomy. He opens the mastoid cavity and removes any diseased mastoid tissue that remains. He then places a rotation flap of fascia or muscle and or a fat and skin graft to reduce the size of a large mastoid cavity or to prevent or stop a cerebrospinal leak. He sutures the graft or flap into place and closes the incision with sutures.

Parotid duct: The passage between the parotid gland in the mouth and the ear; also called salivary duct. Tympanic neurectomy: Excision of part or all of the tympanic nerve.

Surgical nasal endoscopy consists of the use of a medical device that has a thin rigid or a flexible tube to view the sinuses and nasal passages. In this procedure, the endoscopy provides an approach for the provider to insert a catheter with a balloon tip into the eustachian tube and expand it. Report this code when used for a single side. Explanation After appropriate preparation and anesthetization of the nasal passages, the provider inserts an endoscope through the nose. Through this, he inserts a specially designed, balloon??ipped catheter into the eustachian tube. He inflates the balloon to dilate the eustachian tube, after which he deflates the balloon and withdraws it through the endoscope. He then withdraws the endoscope. The eustachian tube is a narrow channel that links the tympanic cavity (the area behind the eardrum) and the nasopharynx (the portion of the throat open to the nasal cavity). The tube is lined with mucous membrane and ventilates the middle ear (adjusts the inner ear pressure to the external pressure). It also helps protect the middle ear from the intrusion of pathogens and helps drain secretions. Normally closed, it opens during swallowing, yawning, or chewing. Eustachian tube dysfunction (ETD) refers to failure of the eustachian tube valve to open and/or close properly or to loss of the ability to perform these functions. This procedure is indicated for moderately severe, chronic eustachian tube dysfunction or hearing loss due to fluid in the middle ear. Chronic: A condition that is long lasting, typically slow to develop, and with symptoms of less severity than an acute condition, or one of sudden onset. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Eustachian tube: The narrow passageway that leads from the middle ear to the nasopharynx, also known as the auditory tube or pharyngotympanic tube. Mucous membrane: A membrane that lines many body cavities and tubular organs and secretes a slimy substance called mucus. Pathogen: An organism, such as bacteria, virus, or fungi, that causes an infection. Sinuses: The air spaces within the skull bones that connect to the nasal passages. The provider removes or repairs a previously placed electromagnetic bone conduction hearing device in the temporal bone. These devices operate by passing an electric current into a coil that drives an adjacent magnet attached to one of the vibratory structures of the middle ear, e.g., tympanic membrane, ossicles, round window. The device requires removal if it cannot be repaired or if there is associated infection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates a postauricular incision overlying the location of the previously placed electromagnetic bone conduction hearing device. He either removes or repairs the device. The provider irrigates the area, sutures the incision closed, and applies a dressing. Terminology Cortex: The outer covering of an organ or bone, like the bark on a tree. Ossicles, or ossicular chain: Three tiny bones in the inner ear; when the eardrum or tympanic membrane vibrates, the vibrations transfer to the malleus or hammer, the incus or anvil, and the stapes or stirrup in that order, and then to the oval window; the bones are named for the shapes they resemble. Round window: A membrane between the middle and inner ear; situated below the oval window, it vibrates in opposition to the oval window; also called fenestra rotunda, fenestra cochleae, or cochlear window. Temporal bone: A bone at the base and side of the skull that houses the tympanic membrane and part of the incus and malleus; the three parts of the bone are referred to as the petrous bone, the squamous bone, and the tympanic bone; it also includes the styloid process, a projection off the inferior surface where several muscles and ligaments attach. Tympanic membrane: Eardrum. Tips For implantation or replacement of the device, report 69710, Implantation or replacement of electromagnetic bone conduction hearing device in temporal bone. Code 69745 is in the Surgery/Operating Microscope section. It is the code for suture of a facial nerve, with or without a nerve graft or nerve decompression. It is performed in the middle of the geniculate ganglion, in the middle ear. Explanation The patient is placed supine on the operating table with the head turned so that the involved temporal bone is upward. The hair is shaved anterior and posterior to the ear. Endotracheal anesthesia is administered. The physician makes an incision into the head of the patient (depending on the approach used it can be behind the ear or above the ear). He elevates the skin flap to expose the temporal muscle. The physician drills over the mastoid until the yellow bone of the otic capsule is identified. The nerve is confined in the labyrinthine segment. The physician then repairs the seventh cranial nerve through interrupted sutures. Additionally, he may perform nerve grafting or release of pressure from the midline of the nerve, where fibers turn sharply at the lateral end of the internal acoustic meatus. Read Less

Dialysis removes fluid, electrolytes, and other low??olecula??eight toxic substances from the blood by filtration through hollow artificial membranes and may be routinely performed in 3 weekly sessions. Peritoneal dialysis is carried out at home by the patient. Although support is helpful, it is not essential. The concept behind continuous renal replacement techniques is to dialyze patients in a more physiologic way, slowly, over 24 hours, just like the kidney does. Report 90947 if the procedure requires repeated physician evaluations, with or without substantial revision of a dialysis prescription. Explanation Other than hemodialysis, dialysis can also be performed by peritoneal, hemofiltration, or by other methods. In the case of peritoneal dialysis, the inner lining of the abdominal cavity is used as a filter (semipermeable membrane) to clean the blood. The physician makes a surgical opening over the abdominal area, and a large volume of fluid (dialysate) containing glucose is introduced to the abdomen (this is also referred to as "dwell"). This dwell remains in the abdomen; the lining of the abdominal cavity allows fluid, wastes, and electrolytes to pass from the blood to the fluid in the cavity, via osmosis. This is left inside for a certain period (generally 2?? hrs) The fluid is then drained out and it is replaced by fresh fluids. Report 90945 if this is performed and evaluated by a single physician. In the case of hemofiltration, the blood is pumped through a dialyzer or "hemofilter" as in dialysis, but no dialysate is used. A pressure gradient is applied; as a result, water moves across the very permeable membrane rapidly, "dragging" along with it many dissolved substances, importantly ones with large molecular weights, which are cleared less well by hemodialysis. Salts and water lost from the blood during this process are replaced with a "substitution fluid" that is infused into the extracorporeal circuit during the treatment. The various techniques used under other "continuous renal replacement therapies" include continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH), continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD), continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF), etc. Most of these modes can remove up to one liter of fluid per hour. Terminology Continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH): A form of convective dialysis; ultrafiltration rate is high, and replacement electrolyte solution is required to maintain hemodynamic stability. Very effective for clearing mid??ized molecules. Continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD): Continuous diffusive dialysis, in which the dialysate is driven in a direction countercurrent to the blood; mostly small molecules are removed. Continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF): The most popular method of dialysis in ICU; CVVHDF combines convective and diffusive dialysis; both small and middle molecules are cleared, and both dialysate and replacement fluids are required. Peritoneal dialysis: Filtration procedure using the inside lining of the abdominal cavity as a natural filter; during typical peritoneal dialysis wastes are removed using a cleansing fluid (dialysate) administered through a catheter using a cycler machine or through a machine??ree method, to wash the dialyzing fluid in and out of the abdomen. Heartburn: Burning pain in lower part of chest s. Hydrochloric acid: A clear, poisonous and highly acidic solution of gas hydrogen chloride in water, mainly used for food processing, pickling and metal cleaning and is found in the stomach in adulterated form. A new patient has not received any professional services from the provider or another provider of the same specialty in the same group practice within the past three years. Either comprehensive or intermediate can apply for both new and established patients.

To report the evaluation of new or existing conditions complicated by a new diagnostic or management problem for a new patient, use 92002; for an established patient, use 92012, Ophthalmological services: medical examination and evaluation, with initiation or continuation of diagnostic and treatment program; intermediate, established patient.

Both the E/M codes, 99202 to 99215, Office or other outpatient visit, etc., and the general ophthalmological services codes, 92002 to 92014, Ophthalmological services: medical examination and evaluation, etc., describe office visits. If the provider strictly evaluates the function of the eye, report an eye code. If, however, the provider evaluates the eye as it relates to a systemic disease process, report the appropriate E/M code.

For example, a new patient presents complaining of blurred vision. The provider performs a comprehensive examination including checking her visual acuity, gross visual fields, ocular mobility, retinas and intraocular pressure. Suppose, however, a patient with chronic blepharitis comes in due to a recent foreign body sensation, and the patient complains of a recurring headache. A slit lamp exam reveals a lash rubbing the cornea on the painful eye. Refraction indicates a significant increase in hyperopia, which may explain the patient?? headache.
