The provider performs a test similar to electromyography of extremity muscles, except that it is performed on the extraocular muscles of the eye; interpretation and report are included so do not report those components separately. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepared and anesthetized, the provider inserts a needle (needle electrode) connected by wires to a sophisticated machine (electromyograph). With the use of this machine and its graphic output on monitor, the provider is able to determine various electrophysiologic attributes of these muscles, such as the presence or absence of denervation, muscle fiber degeneration, and other aspects of the motor unit of the eye muscles. Because ocular muscle abnormalities are often a presenting feature of myasthenia gravis and often the only feature of myasthenia gravis (ocular myasthenia), this test has been found to be of value in diagnosing myasthenia gravis at an early stage when only the eye muscles are affected. It also has value in some forms of muscular dystrophy, isolated peripheral neuropathies involving the eye, and in inflammatory myopathies. Documentation of medical necessity and a formal report with interpretation of results and how the study will affect the patient's treatment and prognosis are required. Terminology Degeneration: Progressive decline or loss of function in the body or tissues that cause the body or part of the body to become weaker. Denervation: Loss or interruption of nerve supply; denervation can be caused by injury, disease, toxins, or surgical division of a nerve. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Electromyography (EMG): A diagnostic test that evaluates the health of muscles and the nerves that control them by measuring their electrical activity. Extraocular muscles: Muscles that control movement of the eye, the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, lateral rectus, superior oblique, and inferior oblique. Electrophysiologic: Relating to the electrical impulse generation phenomena of cells and tissues. Inflammatory myopathy: Disorders involving the muscles anywhere in the body due to injury or infection characterized by pain, heat, redness, and swelling. Muscular dystrophy: A group of genetic diseases in which progressive weakness and degeneration of the skeletal muscles that control movement occurs. Myasthenia gravis: A neuromuscular disease characterized by varying degrees of muscle weakness and fatigue. Peripheral neuropathy: Weakness, numbness, and/or pain in the hands and feet due to nerve damage or disease. Read Less

The provider performs all components of contact lens prescription and fitting for both eyes except when there is absence of the lens of the eye (aphakia) as a result of prior cataract surgery.



Explanation
The provider prescribes contact lenses for both eyes after determining the optical and physical characteristics of the cornea. The fitting includes training of the wearer and incidental revision of the lenses during training. Prescription and fitting of contact lenses is not part of the general ophthalmic services. This service does not apply to patients who are aphakic as a result of cataract surgery. This service must be performed by the medical provider and not by a technician.


Terminology
Aphakia: Absence of the crystalline lens of the eye after cataract surgery.

Astigmatism: Distorted vision in which part of an image is blurred due to uneven corneal curvature.

Cataract: A clouding or opacity of the lens in an eye that leads to a gradual loss of vision over time.

Farsightedness: A condition in which the eyes cannot focus on near objects; also known as hyperopia or presbyopia (the latter if the farsightedness is due to aging).

Keratoconus: A degenerative eye disease, which causes a change in the normal gradual curve of the cornea to a more conical shape and results in the distortion of vision and multiple images.

Nearsightedness: A condition in which the eyes cannot focus on far objects; also known as myopia.

Presbyopia: Farsightedness, generally associated with aging, in which a person cannot focus on near objects.


Tips
Medical plans vary in their coverage of contact lenses. Most will cover the cost in those cases where they are required for functional vision as after cataract surgery or for keratoconus. They will not cover such prescriptions to correct normal vision abnormalities such as farsightedness, nearsightedness, astigmatism, or presbyopia (loss of accommodation due to age).

Some insurance companies have a policy that vision with glasses must be 20/70 or worse before they will cover contact lenses.

If the corneal contact lens prescription is for a patient who is aphakic, see 92311 for one eye and 92312 for both eyes.

If the corneal contact lens fitting (both eyes, except for aphakia) is performed by an independent technician, see 92314, 92315 if the corneal lens is for a patient with aphakia (one eye) and the fitting is performed by an independent technician and 92316 for both eyes.

If the prescription is for a corneoscleral lens, see 92313 and if the fitting is by an independent technician, see 92317.

This code does not include the supply of the lens; however, you should not bill Medicare for the supplies.

Some insurance companies have a policy that vision with glasses must be 20/70 or worse before they will cover contact lenses. If the entire service is provided by a specialist for a patient who is aphakic, see 92311 for one eye and 92312 for both eyes. If the corneal contact lens fitting (both eyes, except for aphakia) is performed by an independent technician, see 92314, and if the corneal lens is for a patient with aphakia in both eyes, see 92316. If the prescription is for a corneoscleral lens, see 92313 and if the fitting is by an independent technician, see 92317. This code does not include the supply of the lens; check with the payer to determine whether the supply is covered if medical necessity is documented. Read Less

The provider prescribes and supervises the fitting by an independent technician of a corneoscleral contact lens. Corneoscleral lenses are generally hard, not soft and are seldom used except in cases of conjunctival burns or to prevent symblepharon (adhesions between the conjunctiva and eyelid). Explanation The provider determines medical necessity and prescribes a corneoscleral contact lens to include components of both a physical and optical nature, including size, power, curvature, flexibility, and gas permeability. An independent technician provides fitting and training. A corneoscleral contact lens covers both the cornea and the sclera of the eye. It is large and rests on the conjunctiva of the sclera with a large convexity over the cornea leaving a fluid??illed space between the cornea and the overlying lens. Terminology Cornea: The clear transparent outer layer in the front of the iris, pupil, and anterior chamber that refracts light entering the eye and provides almost two??hirds to three??uarters of the focusing power. Sclera: The white outer part of the eye that covers all of the eyeball except for the cornea. Tips If the ophthalmologist or another qualified physician performs the fitting, choose from 92310 to 92313, depending on the situation. Suppose an ophthalmologist fits both of a patient's eyes with corneal lenses. On the claim, you'd report 92310, Prescription of optical and physical characteristics of and fitting of contact lens, with medical supervision of adaptation; corneal lens, both eyes, except for aphakia, for the service. If an independent technician performs the fitting in the ophthalmologist's office, choose from 92314 to 92317, depending on the situation. Suppose a technician fits both of a patient's eyes with corneal lenses. On the claim, you'd report 92314, Prescription of optical and physical characteristics of contact lens, with medical supervision of adaptation and direction of fitting by independent technician; corneal lens, both eyes, except for aphakia, for the service. Report 92310 to 92313 only if the ophthalmologist or another physician in your office ??not an independent technician ??is doing the contact lens fitting as well as supervising the adaptation. If the ophthalmologist or optometrist is writing the prescription for the lenses but an independent contractor technician in your office does the actual fitting, report 92315, Prescription of optical and physical characteristics of contact lens, with medical supervision of adaptation and direction of fitting by independent technician; corneal lens for aphakia, one eye, 92316 for aphakia, both eyes, or 92317 for a corneoscleral lens. The provider makes changes to a contact lens. He provides instruction to the patient on adapting to the changes. Explanation The provider makes alterations to the contact lenses, such as reducing overall diameter, reducing optical zone diameter, flattening of peripheral curve, polishing edges, and changing strength or power of the lens. He also explains to the patient the necessity of these modifications made to the contact lens. Terminology Optical zone diameter: The portion of the lens that corrects the vision. Peripheral curve: The curved or rounded portion of a lens at its outward edge. Tips Code 92325 describes modification made while fitting contact lenses. The provider supervises the instruction to the patient of the importance of these modifications.

The provider prescribes the replacement of contact lenses due to wear and tear of existing lenses, patient discomfort, loss of lens, or some other reason. Explanation The provider examines the eyes with a flashlight, ophthalmoscope, or slit lamp. He hydrates, or wets, soft contact lenses using saline. He then removes each lens and replaces it. Terminology Ophthalmoscope: Instrument that examines the interior of the eye. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Slit lamp: Instrument that focuses a thin, high intensity light beam into the eye to see different parts of the eye. Tips Report RT, Right side, or LT, Left side, if applicable. The bilateral, or both sides, concept does not apply to contact lens codes.

Code 92340 describes the fitting of eyeglasses, except for aphakia (absence of the crystalline lens as after cataract surgery); monofocal Explanation It describes the fitting of monofocal eyeglasses, except for aphakia (absence of the crystalline lens as after cataract surgery). Fitting includes measurement of anatomical facial characteristics, the writing of laboratory specifications, and the final adjustment of the spectacles to the visual axes and anatomical topography. Supply of materials is a separate service component; it is not part of the service of fitting spectacles.

Code 92341 describes the fitting of eyeglasses of bifocal type, i.e., the lens has two separate areas of focus such as an area which gives best near vision and another area giving best far vision. Explanation It describes the fitting of bifocal eyeglasses, except for aphakia (absence of the crystalline lens as after cataract surgery). Fitting includes measurement of anatomical facial characteristics, the writing of laboratory specifications, and the final adjustment of the spectacles to the visual axes and anatomical topography. Supply of materials is a separate service component; it is not part of the service of fitting spectacles.

The provider fits eyeglasses that are multifocal other than bifocal, for example trifocal glasses. These are lenses that have more than two separate areas providing best vision are varying focal lengths, for example far vision, near or reading vision and an intermediate distance. Explanation The provider fits eyeglasses, or spectacles, with multifocal but not bifocal lenses, in a patient who does not have aphakia. Multifocal lenses have separate areas of varying focal lengths to address different vision needs, for example far vision, near or reading vision and an intermediate distance.

Code 92353 describes the fitting of eyeglasses following cataract surgery with intraocular implant, multifocal, i.e., bifocal or trifocal.
Explanation
It describes the fitting of bifocal or trifocal eyeglasses following cataract surgery with intraocular implant. Fitting includes measurement of anatomical facial characteristics, the writing of laboratory specifications, and the final adjustment of the spectacles to the visual axes and anatomical topography. Supply of materials is a separate service component; it is not part of the service of fitting spectacles.

The provider fits a magnifying lens on the eyeglasses to improve a patient?? near vision for tasks like reading. Explanation The provider fits a high??owered lens on the eyeglasses as a low vision aid. He analyzes the anatomical facial characteristics and provides the laboratory specifications. He makes the final adjustments of the spectacles to the visual axes and anatomical topography, to give the best fit and visual outcome. Terminology Anatomic topography: Study of regions or divisions of the body and determining the relationship between various structures in that region. Convex lens: Lens that converges light rays, used to correct short sightedness, in which a patient is unable to see distant objects. Low vision aid: A high powered lens or telescope with high magnification to help the patient perform tasks requiring better near vision, like reading. Tips Use code 92355, Fitting of spectacle mounted low vision aid, telescopic or other compound lens system, if the provider fits telescopic lens on the eyeglasses. A low vision aid is a high??owered lens or telescope with high magnification to help the patient perform tasks requiring better near vision, e.g., reading. Patients are candidates for low vision aids when their eyes cannot be corrected to a fully functional level by use of glasses or contact lenses. Codes are not provided for the low vision examination. Medicare considers 92354 and 92355 bundled into the payment for spectacles. Read Less

He analyzes the anatomical facial characteristics and provides the laboratory specifications. He makes the final adjustments of the spectacles to the visual axes and anatomical topography, to give the best fit and visual outcome. Terminology Anatomic topography: Study of regions or divisions of body and determining the relation between various structures in that region. Telescopic lens: Long focus multiple lens system that gives clear vision of distant objects. Tips Use code 92354, Fitting of spectacle mounted low vision aid, single element system, if the provider fits convex lens on the eyeglasses. The two codes for low vision exams are 92354, Fitting of spectacle mounted low vision aid, single element system, and 92355, Fitting of spectacle mounted low vision aid, telescopic or other compound lens system. A low vision aid is a high??owered lens or telescope with high magnification to help the patient perform tasks requiring better near vision, e.g., reading. Patients are candidates for low vision aids when their eyes cannot be corrected to a fully functional level by use of glasses or contact lenses. Codes are not provided for the low vision examination. Medicare considers 92354 and 92355 bundled into the payment for spectacles. Read Less

The provider implants a temporary lens into the eye to restore vision in a patient with aphakia, the absence of a lens. Explanation The provider inserts a temporary lens into the patient?? eye. Terminology Aphakia: Absence of the lens of an eye, either by surgical removal, or due to wound or congenital absence. Congenital: Present at birth. Prosthesis: An artificial or manmade replacement for a body part. Tips Report RT, Right side, or LT, Left side, if applicable. The bilateral, or both sides, concept does not apply to contact lens codes.

The provider makes adjustments and or repairs to eyeglasses in a patient who does not have aphakia, the absence of a lens in the eye. Explanation The provider repairs and refits the spectacles in a patient who is not aphakic, to include measurement of anatomical facial characteristics, the writing of laboratory specifications, and the final adjustment of the spectacles to the visual axes and anatomical topography. In this diagnostic procedure, the provider uses a microscope to examine the ears of a patient. He may also sometimes examine the patient?? nose for direct visualization to help with diagnosis determination. Explanation The provider uses a binocular microscope to examine the ears of a patient. He reports this code when the provider cannot examine the ears with an otoscope. He reports the code separately in the case of procedures that employ the use of microscope for completion. Terminology Anterior rhinoscopy: Examination of front part of the nose. Binocular microscope: An instrument with lens to enlarge the small parts, and consist of two eye pieces to use both the eyes for visualization. Cerumen: Ear wax. Impaction: Condition characterized by a deposit of ear wax in such a way that it tightly packs in the outer ear and blocks it. Otoscope: A medical instrument with a light source and lenses for magnification that helps the provider to visualize both the internal and external ear. Otoscopy: Examination of the ear using an instrument specially designed for the procedure. Tuning fork test: Medical test to determine the type of hearing loss in patients with the help of an instrument with a handle and two prongs that vibrate at a set frequency, and assess the ability of a person to hear. Tips Do not report the diagnostic or treatment procedures like otoscopy, anterior rhinoscopy, removal of nonimpacted cerumen, or tuning fork test, separately if the provider reports them as evaluation and management services; 92504 is a special diagnostic test that is not included in an evaluation and management service. Report 92504 when the provider performs no other related ear procedure during the same visit. For example, if an otolaryngologist suspects a foreign body in a patient's ear, looks in the ear, and doesn't find it. Because no object was found for removal, report the examination only using 92504. If the provider removes a foreign body from the external auditory canal, you would instead code the foreign body removal 69200, Removal foreign body from the external auditory canal; without general anesthesia. Similarly, you should report 92504 for placing an earwick because no code exists for this procedure. Also, report the code 92504 when the provider uses the binocular microscope and performs an unrelated procedure. For example, if an otolaryngologist looks in a patient's ear and also performs a nasal endoscopy. Because the ear examination and nasal endoscopy occur on separate body areas, report both procedures. Append modifier 59, Distinct procedural service, to 92504 to indicate the microscopy as a distinct procedural service from 31231, Nasal endoscopy, diagnostic, unilateral or bilateral, separate procedure. Do not append modifier 59 when a more specific modifier, such as XE (same date, separate encounter), XP (different practitioner), XS (separate organ or structure), or XU (service does not overlap with the usual components of the main service). Documentation must support the use of the modifier. Do not confuse modifier 59 with modifier 51 for multiple procedures (e.g., same procedure on different anatomic sites, related procedures on the same anatomic site, or the same procedure multiple times on the same anatomic site). The provider examines the nasal passages and throat with an endoscope, a tubular instrument with a light source and camera. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider passes an endoscope through the nose and examines the inside of the nose, mouth, and throat. He inspects for the presence of any fixed blockages in the airway such as deviation in the nasal septum, polyps, or enlargement in adenoids and tonsils, or lesions in the nasopharynx. Terminology Adenoids: Lymph tissue at the back of the throat near the base of the nose. Endoscope: A stiff or flexible tubular instrument with a light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon, bladder, or stomach; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Nasal septum: Thin wall that divides the inside of the nose into left and right nostrils; it is composed of cartilage and bone. Nasopharyngoscopy: Examination of the nose and throat using an instrument specially designed for the procedure. Nasopharynx: Nose and throat. Pharynx: Throat. Polyp: An abnormal growth originating from the mucous membrane lining of an organ or other structure, like the nose. Tonsils: Lymph tissue at the back of the throat. Tips If you're not sure how to classify a diagnostic scope in the office, the best thing to do is to look at the anatomy that the provider examines. If he examines the nasopharynx, you should report 92511. An example is when a provider looks at the nasopharynx to evaluate eustachian, or auditory, tube dysfunction or a mass in the nasopharynx. If an evaluation and management (E/M), service is involved and you'd like to report it as a standalone service, make sure you meet these qualifications: The office visit or consultation is for a different reason than the scope. The office visit or consultation is for the decision to perform the procedure. Generally, in a 92511 procedure, the provider is looking down the back of the throat, i.e., the nasopharynx area. This code should be used only for specific purposes, such as examining adenoidal size or identifying lesions in the nasopharynx. If the provider is doing something else, coders shouldn't bill this code. A good rule for coders to follow is to use whichever code best describes what the documentation supports. Read Less

The provider uses electroneuronography, a noninvasive test that uses electrical stimulation, to evaluate facial nerve function and integrity when the patient has facial nerve impairment. Explanation The provider uses electrical stimulation on the facial nerve, a procedure called electroneuronography (ENoG), and compares the nerve response of the normal side of the face to the abnormal side in order to help decide if surgery is necessary. In this service, the provider cleans the patient?? skin for application of a stimulus and recording electrodes. The provider places small cup stimulus electrodes at or near the base of the ear and measures and interprets the resulting response recorded by electrodes at or near the skin folds that run along each side of the nose to the corners of the mouth. The provider repeats the stimulation, moving the electrodes to different locations in the same area, and a computer records the greatest response possible. The study is done on the normal side first, and then the provider repeats the test on the impaired side. This study monitors the facial nerve and helps diagnose Bell's palsy and other facial nerve disorders. Terminology Bell's palsy: A form of facial paralysis affecting the facial nerve that causes an inability to control facial muscles on the affected side. Facial nerve: The nerve that allows movement of the facial expression muscles and sensory for taste. Tips Do not use this code for monitoring during radiologic guidance procedures. Read Less

In this procedure the provider uses aerodynamic testing and acoustic testing to assess proper functioning of the larynx and evaluate the presence of a voice disorder. Explanation The provider examines the laryngeal functions for swallowing disorders, hoarseness, or obstruction. He measures the vocal fold movements responsible for voice production by aerodynamic testing. In this test, the provider places a face mask or a mouthpiece around the patient?? mouth to measure the passage of air from the lungs between the vocal folds. He analyzes this through the sounds made by the patient in an air transducer, a device that registers air energy as electrical signals. The provider may also analyze acoustic properties of the voice using certain instruments. In this test, he has the patient speak into a microphone, which is connected to a display unit that translates and measures the acoustic properties of voice like pitch, loudness, and hoarseness. A spectrographic chart displays the voice properties of the patient on paper. Terminology Acoustic testing: Assessment of the perception or production of sound waves, in hearing and or speaking. Aerodynamic testing: Assessment of the pressure and flow of air into the larynx, or voice box. Hoarseness: Abnormal changes in the voice due to difficulty in making sounds while speaking. Laryngeal: Related to the larynx, the part of the respiratory system that produces voice and helps with swallowing action and breathing; also known as the voice box. Spectrograph: Instrument that records changes in wavelength of sound produced. Vocal folds: Membranous tissue forming slits in the throat; its edges vibrate when air passes through them to produce sound. Tips Knowing the difference between a screening versus a full evaluation could make a sizeable difference in your reimbursement check, as a screening is typically not a billable service. Report 92520 when actual instrumental and acoustic analysis takes place. Read Less

A speech??anguage pathologist (SLP) evaluates the patient's speech fluency for issues such as stuttering or cluttering. Explanation During a speech evaluation, a speech language pathologist (SLP) notes a person's number and types of speech disfluencies, assesses the ways the patient handles the disfluencies, and may gather information about modifying factors. The SLP then analyzes information about the person to determine whether a fluency disorder exists. If so, the SLP determines the extent to which the disorder affects the patient's activities of daily living. An evaluation consists of a series of tests, observations, and interviews designed to estimate a child's risk for continuing to stutter or for older children and adults to assess the disorder's severity of the disorder. The SLP uses information from the evaluation to develop a specific treatment program designed to help the individual speak more fluently, communicate more effectively, and participate more fully in activities of daily living. Terminology Cluttering (also called tachyphemia) : A speech and communication disorder characterized by a rapid rate making speech difficult to understand, erratic rhythm Disfluency: Breaks that occur in the flow of speech Stuttering: A disorder that causes more disfluencies in speech than other speakers Read Less

A speech??anguage pathologist (SLP) evaluates the patient's speech sound production for issues such as incorrect pronunciation and patterns. The jaw, lips, and tongue are examined for proper structure and function. Explanation An evaluation includes a speech??anguage pathologist (SLP) listening to and watching the patient. A formal articulation test records sound or phonological errors and gathers a speech sample to provide further clinical analysis. An oral mechanism examination is also done to determine whether the structure and function of the mouth are adequate for speaking. This involves looking in the patient's mouth and observing the accuracy and coordination of the movements of the articulators (jaw, lips, and tongue). A treatment plan that may range from therapy to surgery is created. Terminology Articulators: Jaw, lips and tongue. Dysarthria: A motor speech disorder. in which the muscles of the mouth, face, and respiratory system may become weak, move slowly, or not move at all after a stroke or other brain injury. Oral apraxia: A motor speech disorder in which difficulty with movements of tongue, lips or jaw. Speech sound disorders: Problems with articulation (pronouncing sounds correctly) and phonological processes (errors with sound patterns). Verbal apraxia: A motor speech disorder in which the person has difficulty producing sounds such as sequencing sounds, syllables and words due to a problem in sending the command to activate sound to the brain resulting in improper sequencing of the movements required to produce the sound/word. A speech??anguage pathologist (SLP) evaluates the patient's speech sound production for issues such as incorrect pronunciation and patterns.



Explanation
The speech language pathologist, or SLP, evaluates the patient's sound production, for example, articulation, phonological process, apraxia, dysarthria. In addition, the SLP assesses the patient's comprehension, or receptive language, and expressive language skills using standardized testing. The results provide an overall view of the patient's communication abilities, emerging skills, mastered skills and any challenged areas. When the assessment reveals that the patient may need therapy to improve speech sound production, the SLP may recommend speech therapy.


Terminology
Expressive language: Ability to use language to convey wants, needs and ideas.

Receptive language: Ability to understand, follow directions, etc.

The provider, typically a speech language pathologist, evaluates a patient for the quality of voice, nasality, and vocal behavior of the patient. Explanation Providers, typically speech language therapists, use qualitative assessment methods, including standardized tests, to analyze and diagnose the nature and extent of the patient's difficulty/problem with production and communication. The focus is on the voice and the resonance of the voice produced. The areas evaluated can include oral movement for speech, voice and/or fluency, and communication using voice. Terminology Resonance: Nasality or nasal quality of voice. Tips This code addresses a specific evaluation using qualitative methods/protocols for assessing voice and resonance of a patient.

The provider treats a swallowing disorder through medications, rehabilitation, or a feeding tube, to identify the cause of improper functioning. Explanation The provider uses various methods to treat a swallowing disorder or improve function depending on the cause of the dysfunction. He may use medications in patients with severe stomach acidity or to improve esophageal motility. Alternatively, he may use rehabilitation specialists to work with patients who have had a stroke and cannot undergo surgery or take drugs. In severe cases, the provider may also introduce a feeding tube through the nose or into the stomach. He performs this in patients who are unable to eat or refuse to eat, or those who have difficulty in eating. Terminology Anterior rhinoscopy: Examination of front part of the nose. Cerumen: Ear wax. Esophagus: The muscular tube that carries substances from the throat down to the stomach. Impaction: Condition characterized by a deposit of ear wax in such a way that it tightly packs in the outer ear and blocks it. Otoscopy: Examination of the ear using an instrument specially designed for the procedure. Rehabilitation: The act of bringing back something to its original state. Stroke: Sudden death of brain cells due to reduced blood supply to a part of the brain. Swallowing dysfunction: A condition characterized by difficulty or abnormality to ingest food. Tuning fork test: Medical test to determine the type of hearing loss in patients with the help of an instrument with a handle and two prongs that vibrate at a set frequency, and assess the ability of a person to hear. Tips Do not report the diagnostic or treatment procedures like otoscopy, anterior rhinoscopy, removal of nonimpacted cerumen, or tuning fork test, separately if the provider reports them as evaluation and management services. However, 92526 is a special diagnostic test that is not included in an evaluation and management service. 92526 almost always fits most aspects of treatments associated with dysphagia related to any of the upper throat mechanics. This one code is all you need when the focus of the treatment is for swallowing. It is an untimed code, billed as one unit per day. Read Less

The provider allows the patient to look in different directions and then observes the rapid movements of the eyeball. He performs this to identify any disturbance in the vestibular system of the patient. Explanation The provider asks the patient to look straight, as well as in the right and left directions. He then observes the inability of the eye to remain static and he measures any disturbance in the vestibular functions. He can measure this by analyzing the difference in the right and left vestibular functions of the patient, or his ability to control balance. In this procedure, the provider does not use electrodes and no recording is done. Terminology Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV: A disease characterized by brief dizziness due to changing the position of a patient?? head. Canalith repositioning procedure: A medical therapy to treat benign paroxysmal positional vertigo and relieve dizziness while moving the head. Domiciliary: Concerned with someone?? home. Fixation nystagmus: Uncontrolled movement of the eyes when staring at a stationary object. Gaze nystagmus: Uncontrolled movement of the eyes that is evident when a patient looks in the left and right directions. Maneuver: Movement that requires skills and care. Nystagmus: A regular, repetitive, and involuntary rhythmic ocular movement of the eyes; may be horizontal, vertical, rotary, or combination of these movements. Positional nystagmus: Uncontrolled movement of the eyes that occurs only when the head of the patient acquires certain positions. Spontaneous nystagmus: Uncontrolled random movement of the eyes in any direction or in a rotating motion. Vestibular system: The sensory system of the body that contributes to movement and provides a sense of balance. Tips Do not report 95992, Canalith repositioning procedures, eg, Epley maneuver, Semont maneuver, per day, along with 92531. This is because Medicare will not reimburse the provider for this service. If the provider tests fixation nystagmus along with gaze nystagmus, and records it, use code 92541, Spontaneous nystagmus test, including gaze and fixation nystagmus, with recording. If the provider observes the movement of eyes when the head is in different positions, use code 92532, Positional nystagmus test. Do not report 92531 with evaluation and management services including office or other outpatient services, observation care, observation or inpatient care including admission and discharge, hospital care, office or other outpatient consultations, nursing facility services, and domiciliary, rest home, or custodial care services. The provider allows the patient to move his head in different positions and observe the rapid movements of the eyeball when the patient changes the position of his head. He does this to examine if a disease of the inner ear is causing the patient?? dizziness. Explanation The provider asks the patient to move his head in different positions, such as lying supine with the head extended back, moving the head to the right or left, and sitting up. He then observes the ability or inability of the eye to remain stationary and assesses the complaints of dizziness. He also determines the relation of the abnormality with the central or peripheral nervous system. Terminology Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV: A disease characterized by brief dizziness due to changing the position of a patient?? head. Canalith repositioning procedure: A medical therapy to treat benign paroxysmal positional vertigo and relieve dizziness while moving the head. Dizziness: Lightheadedness, feeling faint, weak, or unsteady. Domiciliary: Concerned with someone?? home. Gaze nystagmus: Uncontrolled movement of the eyes that is evident when a patient looks in the left and right directions. Maneuver: Movement that requires skills and care. Nystagmus: A regular, repetitive, and involuntary rhythmic ocular movement of the eyes; may be horizontal, vertical, rotary, or combination of these movements. Positional nystagmus: Uncontrolled movement of the eyes that occurs only when the head of the patient acquires certain positions. Spontaneous nystagmus: Uncontrolled random movement of the eyes in any direction or in a rotating motion. Supine: Lying in the face up position. This is because Medicare will not reimburse the provider for this service. If the provider records the inability of the eye to remain stationary, use code 92542, Positional nystagmus test, minimum of 4 positions, with recording. If the provider observes the movement of the eyes looking in different directions, use code 92531, Spontaneous nystagmus, including gaze. Do not report 92532 with evaluation and management services including office or other outpatient services, observation care, observation or inpatient care including admission and discharge, hospital care, office or other outpatient consultations, nursing facility services, and domiciliary, rest home, or custodial care services. The caloric vestibular test involves irrigating cold and or warm water, or air into the ear to create nystagmus. This is done to identify a disturbance in the patient?? vestibular system. Explanation The provider irrigates each of the ears of a patient with warm and cold water. This helps to generate nystagmus in the patient. The provider then observes the patient for any difference between the reaction of the left and right ear after each of the four total irrigation maneuvers. The provider sometimes refers to the test as a vestibular caloric stimulation. Terminology Binaural: Both ears. Bithermal: Dual temperature. Caloric vestibular test: A medical test to assess nystagmus in a patient by flushing warm and cold water into the ear; also called as vestibular caloric stimulation. Electroneurography: Measurement of electric charges and speed of conduction of peripheral nerves. Irrigation: A flushing or washout procedure. Nystagmus: A regular, repetitive, and involuntary rhythmic ocular movement of the eyes; may be horizontal, vertical, rotary, or combination of these movements. Peripheral nerve: One of many nerves that connect the brain and spinal cord to the body. Vestibular system: The sensory system of the body that contributes to movement and provides a sense of balance to the organism. Tips If the provider irrigates one ear only or uses one temperature, you should report the corresponding number of irrigations. For instance, if the audiologist irrigates the right ear with warm water without recording, report 92533. If she irrigates both ears with warm water, assign 92533 x 2. If three irrigations occur, bill 92533 x 3. And for a typical series of binaural, bithermal irrigations, record 92533 x 4. Read Less

The provider assesses the involuntary movement of the eyeball by allowing the patient to focus on a moving object while keeping the head still. He examines the hyperactive reflex of the patient to the movement of the object. Explanation The provider places the patient in front of a drum with light and dark vertical stripes. He then asks the patient to stare at the drum, keeping his head straight and fixed. The provider then rotates the drum slowly in one direction, and then in the opposite direction. He observes the movement of the eyeball for nystagmus with the rotation of the drum. In a normal eye, the eyeball moves in a particular direction with the drum stripes. When the drum rotates in opposite direction, the eyeball also follows that way. However, in case of nystagmus, the eyeball of the patient moves in irregular and involuntary manner and is not able to follow the drum stripes. Terminology Hyperactive reflex: An unconscious, overactive reaction of a person to a stimulus Nystagmus: A regular, repetitive, and involuntary rhythmic ocular movement of the eyes; may be horizontal, vertical, rotary, or combination of these movements. Optokinetic nystagmus: Hyperactive reflex and irregular eye movement due to motion of objects in the visual field. Vertical: Straight up and down the length of a structure; perpendicular to the base, forming a right angle. The provider performs four specific tests, with recording, to check balance disorders. This code represents both the technical and professional components of the service. Explanation This code represents the technical and professional components of a service in which the provider assesses the vestibular, or balance, portion of the inner ear using four tests with recording by an infrared system or electronystagmography. To test spontaneous nystagmus, the provider first preps the skin of the patient and applies electrodes that record the nystagmus by electronystagmography (ENG). After affixing the electrodes to the skin with conducting gel or paste, the provider monitors the system for a short time to allow the impedance to stabilize. After this, the provider measures the spontaneous nystagmus by measuring the eye movements as the patient looks at specific targets, such as while tracking a light stimulus. The provider may use an infrared system to record the patient?? rapid eye movements. For a positional nystagmus test, the provider again uses ENG to record eye movement. The provider moves the patient?? head into at least four different positions, typically including lying face upward with the head extended back, left, right, and sitting. The provider may use an infrared system to record the patient?? rapid eye movements. During optokinetic nystagmus testing, the provider presents a large visual field stimulus typically composed of stripes or random dots that are set into motion to generate optokinetic nystagmus. You may see the terms bidirectional foveal and peripheral stimulation, meaning that the provider stimulates the eye of the patient to check the movement of the eyes. The fovea is a small part of the eye that allows for acute vision. The provider then records this optokinetic nystagmus, again using ENG, and analyzes the speed of the eye referenced to the speed of the target. The provider may use an infrared system to record the patient?? rapid eye movements. During oscillating tracking, the provider records eye movements by ENG while the patient views a target that moves in the patient?? visual field. The provider may use an infrared system to record the patient?? rapid eye movements. After completing the testing, the provider performs the necessary calculations to determine the magnitude and direction of nystagmus under the test conditions. He then reviews the data to ensure there is nothing that could adversely influence the results and interpretation. The provider then prints the nystagmus recordings for documentation and prepares a report of the diagnostic results and interpretation. Terminology Electronystagmography (ENG): An electrodiagnostic procedure to evaluate the movement of the eyes to rule out disorders of the nervous system including the brain, the spinal cord, and the nerves. Impedance: Opposition that an electronic component or circuit offers to electric current. Nystagmus: Rapid involuntary movement of the eyeballs; different types include rotary, where the eye moves circularly; horizontal where the eyes move side to side; or vertical, where the eyes move up and down. Vestibular evaluation: A number of tests that help determine if there is something wrong with the vestibular, or balance, portion of the inner ear. Tips Code 92540 includes the tests described by 92541, 92542, 92544, and 92545, so you should not report those codes in addition to 92540. The provider administers a test to assess the bidirectional movement of the eyes with foveal or peripheral stimulation and records the results. Explanation A drum is used for the test. The drum is covered with light and dark vertical stripes and it is placed in front of the patient's eyes. The patient is made to stare at the drum, keeping his head straight and fixed. Slowly the drum is rotated in one direction, and then in the opposite direction. In a normal eye, the eyeball will be seen pursuing the drum stripes moving in a particular direction. When the drum is rotated in the opposite direction, the eyeball will also follow that way. This is a natural eye reflex. But in cases of nystagmus, there will be irregular and involuntary movements of the eyeball and it may not be able to follow the rotating drum stripes. A few electrodes attached from the patient's body to the device can estimate the extent of the patient's visual acuity. The rhythmic, rapid, and involuntary movement of the eyeball is actually not a disease but a symptom. Normal eyeball??otion is a reflex that develops as early as 6 months of age. This reflex allows us to follow a moving object in front of our eyes when the head is kept still. Optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) causes hyperactive reflex and irregular eye movement which can be tested using a simple OKN drum test. Terminology Nystagmus: A regular, repetitive, and involuntary rhythmic ocular movement of the eyes. It may be horizontal, vertical, rotary, or any combination of these movements superimposed upon each other. The direction and frequency of eye movement can vary. Tips Electronystagmography (ENG) refers to the recording of ocular nystagmus or eye movements by electrooculography in response to vestibular dysfunction. During ENG testing, the eye movements are recorded and analyzed by placing small electrodes on the skin around the eyes. There are seven codes most often associated with ENG machines. The codes include 92541??2546 and +92547. Read Less

The provider delivers a limited series of tones or sounds to a patient to determine if the patient?? hearing is in an acceptable range to detect hearing problems. 



Explanation
The provider has the patient listen to a series of tones and notates whether or not the patient responds to each one. The service begins with the patient seated and wearing headphones. The provider delivers different tones and instructs the patient to respond to the sounds or tones she hears by raising either hand when a tone is heard in the respective ear. If a patient?? responses are inadequate for the test, the provider recommends additional testing to further evaluate the patient?? hearing.

This is an air conduction test because the sound waves travel through the outer ear and middle ear to the inner ear. When headphones are used, each ear can be tested separately. Sometimes, especially with children, headphones cannot be used, and the patient is placed in a soundproof room, which does not allow for testing of each ear separately. Pure tone refers to a basic single??requency sound; a sine wave, a repeating pattern of oscillation at a constant amplitude.


Terminology
Bone conduction mode: Placing a vibrating device over the mastoid bone behind the ear to conduct sound through the bones of the skull to test the cochlea (inner ear); this test may be performed if a middle or outer ear problem is suspected.

Conductive hearing loss: Hearing loss due to a problem that prevents sound waves from reaching the inner ear; conductive hearing loss may be caused by infection, fluid in the middle ear, eustachian tube dysfunction, a tear in the tympanic membrane (eardrum), cerumen (earwax) impaction, deformity of the ear canal, or dysfunction or deformity of the ossicles (three tiny bones in the inner ear).

Mastoid bone: Bony projection of the temporal bone behind the external ear.

Pure tone air conduction testing: A hearing test using headphones to determine the faintest tones a person can hear at selected frequencies or pitches; air conduction means the sounds go through the outer and middle ear.

Sensorineural hearing loss: Hearing deficit related to problems with the vestibulocochlear (eighth cranial) nerve.

Speech reception threshold (SRT): The lowest volume at which a patient can understand fifty percent of spoken words.

Temporal bone: A thick, compound bone located at the sides and base of the skull that surrounds the inner ear.


Tips
This service includes testing of both ears. Use modifier 52, reduced services, if a test is applied to one ear instead of both.

There are many different hearing tests, and some of the codes bundle two tests together under one code. Study the descriptions of 92550 to 92597, Audiologic Function Tests, to determine which code to report when the provider assesses a patient's hearing.

The provider administers a hearing test delivering tones alternately between both ears of a patient, which can help determine the patient?? type of hearing loss. Explanation The provider alternates test tones between a patient?? ears, keeping the level of the tone in one ear set and varying the level up and down in the other ear. In this service, the patient sits while wearing earphones, and the provider instructs the patient to report when the sound is louder in the right ear and then in the left ear. When the patient responds that the sounds are equal in both ears, the provider documents the two decibel levels. He records these levels, as they represent the loudness balance. Cochlear deafness: Condition that happens when the cochlea, the part of the inner ear that contains the nerve endings that transmit sound vibrations, is not working correctly because the tiny hair cells that move sound vibrations for hearing are damaged or destroyed. The provider then passes loud sound through both of the ears and measures the variation in opposition due to contraction of the stapedius muscle in one ear. The provider interprets and reports on the results of a routine 12??ead (or more) electrocardiogram. Explanation An electrocardiogram (ECG) is the recording of the electrical activity of the heart and its interpretation by a physician. The sinoatrial node located in the right atrium sends electrical impulses to the heart muscles which contract, resulting in systole. Electrodes placed on the skin over different regions of the heart record the electrical impulses of heart muscles in those regions and these recordings are reproduced in a graphic format. Interpretation of these graphs helps in the correct diagnosis of heart disorders. The graphs produced in diseased conditions, such as acute myocardial infarction, sinus bradycardia, atrial fibrillation, or mitral stenosis, are significantly different from those of a normal healthy heart. An ECG can be conducted using an ECG machine at a physician's office, hospital, or even in a home setting (using a portable ECG monitor). The patient is required to wear a loose??itting dress during the test. The sticky (due to the presence of gel) disclike parts of 12 or more different electrodes are placed on different parts of the skin, such as the chest, wrist, and ankles. The other ends of the leads remain connected to the recorder. The physician or the technician under the direct supervision of the physician performs the ECG. The machine is started, and the monitor will show the electrical pulses through a continuous graphical representation. Any weakness on the heart muscle or any irregularity of the heartbeat is traced out during the recording of electrical impulse monitoring. The ECG is taken for a continuous stretch of time. A printout of the recording is made on a strip of paper. At the end of the procedure, the physician interprets the result and prepares the report based on the ECG results. Terminology Acute myocardial infarction (AMI): Tissue death caused by a lack of blood flow to the heart muscle, typically caused by blockage of a coronary artery. Atrial fibrillation (afib): A heart rhythm disorder where the atrial appendage, a small pouch in the heart, does not squeeze rhythmically with the left atrium, causing blood inside the pouch to become stagnant and prone to produce blood clots. Bradycardia: Slow, or lower than normal, heart rate. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Mitral valve: The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle, so named because its two cusps look like a bishop's hat or a mitered joint in carpentry; also called bicuspid or atrioventricular valve. Stenosis: Narrowing in a tubular or hollow structure or opening, such as an artery, valve, the colon, or ear canal. Do not use modifier 26 or TC with ECG code(s) since the professional part and technical part have separate codes. Read Less

In this procedure the provider evaluates and reprograms the various electrophysiologic and therapeutic parameters of a single or dual chamber pacing defibrillator system.



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider evaluates the various electrophysiologic signals from a pacing cardioverter defibrillator already in place. To check the optimal function of the device, the provider may artificially induce arrhythmia in the patient under control conditions; which the device should be able to recognize and correct immediately. By checking the threshold at which the arrhythmia begins, the provider may reset the therapeutic parameters of the device so as to optimize its function.


Terminology
Arrhythmia: An irregular heart beat rhythm.

Electrophysiologic: Relating to the electrical impulse generation phenomena of the heart that controls its contraction and resultant heart beat.

Implantable cardioverter defibrillator system: A device that continuously senses, monitors, and regulates the heart rate; it can deliver a mild electrical shock to regulate the abnormal or fast rhythm of the heart when needed.

Pacemaker: A device implanted in the patient?? body that senses and regulates the heart?? rhythm in two chambers of the heart only.

Therapeutic: Referring to treatment.

Ventricular: Referring to the ventricle of the heart that pumps blood to various parts of the body.

Ventricular fibrillation: The state of heart where the ventricles are unable to contract in the normal manner so as to pump blood, the provider uses a defibrillator and delivers a mild shock to the heart to make it start beating normally.


Tips
Because implantable cardioverter defibrillator, or ICD, systems are responsible for saving a patient's life when the heart goes into life threatening abnormal rhythm, providers need to confirm that they implant and program the system appropriately. Providers may therefore induce an arrhythmia in the patient under controlled conditions to confirm that the ICD system successfully detects and terminates the rhythm. When the provider tests the system after an implant has taken place, report 93642.

The provider measures variations in temperature in different locations in the walls of the heart via a temperature sensor mounted on a catheter inserted through a vessel in the groin. He maps the temperature variations to identify areas where the heart muscle is malfunctioning. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider threads a catheter with a temperature sensor into the coronary arteries through an incision in the groin. Tips Temperature gradient studies are distinct from surface thermography, in which a heat sensing camera detects variations in temperature through the skin. Thermography for any indication is typically excluded from Medicare coverage because, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, available evidence does not support this test as a useful aid in the diagnosis or treatment of illness or injury as it only detects the presence of differences without providing any useful diagnostic information. The provider performs an ultrasound of the arteries inside the head using Doppler technique to study the flow and speed of blood through the arteries. He performs the procedure to assess blood flow to the brain, most often after a procedure on the arteries of the head or neck or to assess the effect of various medical treatments for spasm. Explanation The provider applies a gel to the skin, typically over the base of the skull and the area over the ears. The provider holds a transducer in place on the skin's surface to record blood flow information. Doppler ultrasound: An imaging procedure that records sound waves reflecting off moving objects, such as blood, to measure their speed and other aspects of how they flow. Hemorrhage: Bleeding, typically used to refer to active or significant bleed. Intracranial: Inside of or including the skull. Noninvasive: Refers to a procedure that does not involve a surgical incision. Occlusion: A blockage or closure in a vessel or organ. Posterior: Closer to the back part of the body. Sickle cell anemia: A genetic disease in which an individual produces red blood cells shaped like a crescent or sickle; these blood don't last as long as normal, round red blood cells, which leads to anemia; when the sickle cells get stuck in blood vessels, blocking blood flow, it can cause pain and organ damage. Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure; a stenosed valve becomes stiff affecting its ability to open and close properly. Stroke: Lay term for a cerebrovascular accident, or CVA; an ischemic stroke happens when a blood clot blocks flow to the brain; a hemorrhagic stroke happens when a blood vessel breaks and bleeds into the brain; transient ischemic attack, or TIA, refers to mini strokes that occur when the blood supply to the brain is briefly interrupted. Transcranial: Through the skull. Ultrasound transducer: A small hand held device that resembles a microphone and attaches to an ultrasound scanner by a cord; the transducer sends out high frequency sound waves into the body and then detects the returning echoes from the tissues in the body. Vertebral arteries: Major arteries that supply blood to the brain. Tips Transcranial Doppler, or TCD, study is a noninvasive diagnostic ultrasound evaluation of the intracranial arteries. To report a complete transcranial study, report 93886. To qualify as complete, 93886 documentation must show ultrasound evaluation of the right and left anterior circulation territories and the posterior circulation territory to include vertebral arteries and basilar artery. The provider assesses the flow of blood through a hemodialysis graft using duplex ultrasound scanning. He performs this procedure to evaluate the condition of the graft.



Explanation
The provider performs the examination with ultrasound equipment that can perform duplex Doppler, often with color flow mapping. He evaluates the inflow artery for size and wall structure, Doppler flow characteristics, velocity through the artery, and evidence of stenosis. He then evaluates the connection between the artery and vein for intimal overgrowth, thrombosis, aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, hematoma, or seroma.

Using several studies, he evaluates the venous outflow of the graft. He evaluates the venous flow for increased velocity, diminished pulsatility, compressibility, and evidence of thrombus within the vessel. The study follows the outflow vein through the arm into the subclavian vein, particularly if the studies suggest a proximal abnormality. The provider may also examine the arterial runoff vessel in the hand.


Terminology
Aneurysm: Weakness in the wall of a blood vessel or wall of a ventricle of the heart, typically the left ventricle, causing the wall to balloon out; sometimes requiring surgical excision or repair to prevent rupture.

Compressibility: The response of a structure, such as the skin or a blood vessel, to pressure; a normal response consists of a return to normal size and shape.

Duplex ultrasound scan: A duplex ultrasound scan combines traditional ultrasound, the use of sound waves that bounce off blood vessels to create images, with Doppler ultrasound, which records sound waves reflecting off moving objects, such as blood, to measure their speed and other aspects of how they flow.

Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together.

Hematoma: A collection of blood or blood clot in the tissues, usually caused by damage to blood vessels.

Hemodialysis: A procedure that removes waste products from the blood and extra fluid from body tissues; it helps correct electrolyte imbalances for patients with impaired kidney function.

Hyperplasia: Excessive growth.

Intima: The wall of arteries, which consists of three layers; intima interna refers to the innermost layer, intima media refers to the thicker muscular middle layer, and intima externa to the outermost layer; the intima media plays an important role because it provides strength and structure to the wall of the artery and changes the diameter of the artery to increase or decrease blood pressure.

Occlusion: A blockage or closure in a vessel or organ.

Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure?? point of attachment.

Pseudoaneurysm: A widened area in a vessel that looks like an aneurysm but isn??.

The provider administers a stinging insect venom for a single type of insect in the office to treat or prevent a reaction in a patient allergic to the sting. 



Explanation
When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider injects the patient with an allergenic extract for desensitization to a single stinging insect venom. 


Terminology
Allergen: A substance, such as pollen, dust, dander, or venom, which triggers an allergic response.

Allergenic extract: Protein containing an extract purified from a substance that causes an allergic reaction in some individuals.

Allergic reaction: The result of the body's reaction to a specific substance that otherwise seems to be harmless but causes a severe reaction in a person allergic to the substance; also called anaphylaxis.

Allergen immunotherapy: A treatment that involves periodic, gradual administration of purified allergen extracts via injection, aimed at overcoming or minimizing allergic reactions so that a patient develops tolerance to the allergens with fewer or no symptoms when exposed; allergy shots decrease the sensitivity to allergens and often lead to lasting relief of allergy symptoms.

Desensitization: Using allergen immunotherapy to decrease or prevent allergic reactions. 


Tips
This provider administers this injection as part of a series of injections over time, gradually increasing quantities of a specific allergenic extract to achieve clinical tolerance of those allergens. Use this code when the provider administers a stinging insect venom for a single type of insect. The code includes the allergenic extract as well as administration. A prescribing provider or other qualified healthcare professional can report this code.

If the preparation of the allergen extract is performed by someone other than the provider who administers the injection, for the preparation of the antigen, each visit, use 95145, Professional services for the supervision of preparation and provision of antigens for allergen immunotherapy; specify number of doses; one single stinging insect venom; and 95115, Professional services for allergen immunotherapy not including provision of allergenic extracts; single injection separately.

For the same service involving two insect venoms, use 95131, Professional services for allergen immunotherapy in the office or institution of the prescribing physician or other qualified health care professional, including provision of allergenic extract; two stinging insect venoms.

For the same service involving three insect venoms, use 95132, Professional services for allergen immunotherapy in the office or institution of the prescribing physician or other qualified health care professional, including provision of allergenic extract; three stinging insect venoms.

For the same service involving four insect venoms, use 95133, Professional services for allergen immunotherapy in the office or institution of the prescribing physician or other qualified health care professional, including provision of allergenic extract, four stinging insect venoms.,

For the same service involving five insect venoms, use 95134, Professional services for allergen immunotherapy in the office or institution of the prescribing physician or other qualified health care professional, including provision of allergenic extract; five stinging insect venoms.

Codes 95115??5199, Allergen immunotherapy services and procedures, include the professional services necessary for allergen immunotherapy. Office visit codes may be used in addition to allergen immunotherapy if other identifiable services are provided at that time.


Additional Info
Physician or other qualified health care professional means an individual who by education, training, licensure or regulation, and facility privileging, when applicable, who performs a professional service within his or her scope of practice and independently reports a professional service. Clinical staff means a person who works under the supervision of a physician or other qualified health care professional and who, as allowed by law, regulation and facility policy, can perform or assist in the performance of a specified professional service. An electrocorticogram (ECoG), also called an intracranial electrocorticogram (iEEG), refers to a recording of the brain?? electrical activity from the cerebral cortex, which is obtained when the provider places electrodes on the surface of the patient?? brain. Explanation The provider performs this electrocorticogram (ECoG) during surgery to monitor the brain?? electrical activity, which transmits signals to a computer. During surgery on the brain, after the patient is appropriately prepped and draped and under anesthesia, the surgeon makes an incision into the skull (craniotomy) to remove a portion of it and expose the surface of the brain. The surgeon surgically implants the electrodes onto the cerebral cortex. He uses the results of an electroencephalogram performed before the procedure to determine the area to place the electrodes, which is either outside of or under the dura mater. He may also use radiography to guide the placement. Then, the provider, who may be the surgeon or a neurologist, analyzes the ECoG to assess the brain's function. He analyzes cortical potentials and assesses brain waves, which are classified according to their frequency, amplitude, shape, and sometimes location and similar to those that might be seen on an electroencephalogram (EEG). He prepares a report. Report this code for interpretation and report of the ECoG in addition to the code for the brain surgery. After completing the surgery, the surgeon removes the electrodes, replaces the bone flap, securing it with permanent plates, wires, and screws. He closes the wound with sutures or surgical staples. He then places a soft turban??ike dressing over the area. Terminology Cerebral cortex: Outer layer of the brain. Dura mater: Outer layer of three layers of membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord. The provider introduces a catheter intravenously for supplementation of fluid and electrolytes for 31 minutes to one hour to treat severe cases of dehydration.



Explanation

Terminology
Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder.

Electrolytes: Solution of sodium chloride, or NaCl, that may also contain potassium, calcium, magnesium, and other essential constituents; terms frequently associated with electrolyte infusions include normal saline, half normal saline, and Ringer's lactate or lactated Ringer solution.

Intravascular: Within a blood vessel.

Intravenous push: Large amount of drug rapidly administered through a vein.

Port: An opening, typically a surgically placed flexible or rigid tubelike device that permits the instillation or withdrawal of fluids or the insertion of instruments.

Hydration: Addition of body fluids by mouth or intravenously.

Intravenous, or IV, infusion: The administration of medication, fluid, electrolytes, and or nutrition to a patient via vein access when the patient cannot take these treatments orally or because of the need for an immediate response.

Therapeutic: For treatment purposes, as opposed to diagnostic, which refers to procedures performed for the purpose of determining the type of disease and its causes.


Tips

Append modifier 59, Distinct procedural service, when the initial and the second infusion do not last more than 31 minutes each. Do not report 96360 if the hydration infusion lasts on 30 minutes or less.

If the provider performs IV hydration infusion for more than one hour, use add on code 96361, Intravenous infusion, hydration; each additional hour, list separately in addition to code for primary procedure.

Although many medications can be taken orally, sometimes that route is not an option because of time concerns or the need to get medicines or other treatments directly into the veins. In these situations, the provider or other qualified professionals can establish an intravenous, or IV, line that goes directly into a vein to deliver medications or other substances.

Code 96360 represents initial IV hydration infusion. You should code one initial service code per patient per day unless protocol or circumstances require the provider to use two separate IV sites. If a second IV is started on the same day, verify that the record states why the first initial hydration failed and that you have notes describing the second initial hydration procedure in the other arm.

Coding and billing for IV hydration depends on accurate documentation. The provider or nurse should clearly note the start and stop times for each bag, the route of administration, and whether a flush or hydration is performed. If only a flush or clearing of lines occurs, you should not code the procedure unless the flush occurs with medication, known as an IV push.

An IV push can be coded using code 96374, Therapeutic, prophylactic, or diagnostic injection, specify substance or drug; intravenous push, single or initial substance or drug. For each additional sequential IV push of a new substance or drug, use +96375 separately in addition to code for primary procedure.

Do not report 96360 with initial IV push 96374 or the add on code 96375 unless protocol requires two separate IV sites and your provider has multiple encounters with the patient on the same date of service. You can charge for hydration before or after a therapeutic infusion, but don't count the time for the hydration running at the same time as the therapeutic infusion. Concurrent means at the same time through the same access site, but can be through a different lumen of the same catheter. Multiple substances mixed in one bag are considered to be one infusion, not a concurrent infusion.

When reporting IV infusion codes, select the initial code using a hierarchy whereby chemotherapy services are primary to therapeutic, prophylactic, and diagnostic services, which are primary to hydration services. Infusions are primary to pushes, which are primary to injections. This instruction was written so a facility coder would not have to prioritize these services by making an independent determination of the clinical priority of a service. The provider reporting the service in the office setting determines the primary reason for the hydration or other administration service and thus would be able to select the primary hydration or drug administration service code.

According to CPT? guidelines for both the hydration and therapeutic, prophylactic, and diagnostic injection and infusion codes, these codes are not intended to be reported by the provider in the facility setting.

The provider then exposes the area to light. The photosensitizing drug in the lesion absorbs the light and produces an active form of oxygen that destroys abnormal cells. The provider plucks hairs from the patient?? head and examines them with a microscope to calculate telogen and anagen counts or structural hair shaft abnormality. Explanation The provider plucks a hair sample from the patient?? head and examines the hairs with a microscope to determine the telogen and anagen counts, i.e., the rest and growth cycle of the hair. Terminology Anagen: The active phase of the hair growth cycle; in this phase, the hair grows about 1 cm every 28 days. Telogen: The resting phase of the hair growth cycle; it accounts for 10 to 15 percent of all hairs and lasts for about 100 days.

Dermatoscopy: Examination of skin lesions with a binocular microscope after applying oil and using a glass slide to reduce light reflection; also called epiluminescent microscopy. Dysplastic nevus syndrome: A condition characterized by lesions with irregular borders and color that resemble melanoma and which may be precursors of melanoma, a potentially fatal skin cancer. Mechanical traction is a highly successful alternative to surgery. Techniques applied in mechanical traction are dependent on the patient's condition, disorder, tolerance level, and the spinal level to be treated. Traction may be applied intermittently or as a continuous force. The gentle traction force or weight helps in pulling away the vertebrae, thereby relieving pain, widening intervertebral foramen to relieve nerve root impingement, and increasing circulation and fluid movement within spinal discs. This treatment is very effective for patients suffering from DJD, herniated disc, general neck, arm, leg and back pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, etc. Explanation Before starting the therapy, the physician evaluates the patient carefully to decide on the type of traction, the amount of weight to be applied, and the duration of the treatment. Mechanical traction begins with a series of 10??2 minute sessions, typically 10??2 minutes each, 2?? times a week. In case of cervical traction, a mechanical traction device is used to treat the cervical spine. The patient lies on his back, and a head halter is placed under the back of head and jaw and attached to a machine. A certain time period and specific weight for the pulling action are set. The traction can remain for the specified time (continuous traction) or intermittently (on/off cycle) during the treatment session. For lumbar traction, a motorized split??raction table is used. The patient is placed in a pelvic harness secured to one end of the table. Some motorized units are programmed by the therapist to maintain the traction session. Sometimes a pelvic belt with straps can also be used for distraction. Following each session, electrical muscle stimulation is applied to relax the muscle and ligaments. Expert supervision is an absolute must. Care is taken to keep the therapy session relaxing, so that no additional strain or pain is caused due to the force applied. Terminology Physical therapy modalities are a variety of treatment tools used by therapists to heal the muscle??elated problems of a patient. Physical therapists use different treatment modalities that can help strengthen, relax, and heal muscles and joints from their strained conditions. Traction is the act of pulling on a bone or limb (as in a fracture), manually or using an instrument, to relieve pressure or align body parts in a certain way during healing. Therapeutic spinal traction uses manually??or mechanically??reated forces to stretch and mobilize the spine. Tips This code is modifier 51??xempt. Read Less

The provider places electrodes on the patient's skin in one or more locations to deliver an electrical current to a muscle or group of muscles or nerves. The provider determines the amount of electrical current needed to contract the muscle.
